docs.title: About this book
docs.text: The course aims to impart comprehensive knowledge about operations research and optimization techniques. Its objectives are to help students understand the fundamental concepts of operations research, to discuss and analyze the need for various optimization techniques, to design and develop appropriate mathematical models, and to formulate and optimize real-world problems using these models.

docs.title: Lesson 29: Applications and the Economic Analysis of Queues
29.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Choose the optimal number of servers by total-cost minimisation and marginal analysis.
  2. Justify the choice between \(L_s\) and \(L_q\) in the cost objective, and show that it matters.
  3. Use the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula to price the cost of service variability.
  4. Cross-check an analytic result against a simulation, and know when simulation is mandatory.
  5. State the assumptions that queuing formulas rest on, and what to do when they fail.

docs.title: 29.2 The Optimal Number of Servers
docs.text:
The structure is that of Lesson 25, with the discrete decision variable \(c\):

\[\boxed{\ TC(c) = C_w\,L(c) + C_s\,c\ }\tag{1.1}\]

where \(L\) is \(L_s\) or \(L_q\) according to what is genuinely costly, \(C_w\) is the cost per customer per unit time and \(C_s\) the cost per server per unit time.

Because \(c\) is an integer, calculus is unavailable. Two equivalent procedures:

Enumeration. Compute \(TC(c)\) for \(c = c_{\min}, c_{\min}+1,\dots\) where \(c_{\min}=\lceil \lambda/\mu\rceil\) is the smallest number giving stability. Stop when \(TC\) starts rising: \(TC(c)\) is convex in \(c\), so the first rise is the optimum.

Marginal analysis. Add a server while

\[C_w\left[L(c)-L(c+1)\right] > C_s,\]

that is, while the waiting cost saved exceeds the cost of the extra server. This is the form to present to management, because it makes the trade-off explicit.

docs.title: 29.3 Variability Costs Money: the Pollaczek–Khinchine Formula
docs.text:
Everything so far assumed exponential service. Real service times are usually less variable (a standard procedure) or far more variable (a helpdesk where most calls are trivial and a few take hours). The \(M/G/1\) model handles any service distribution.

Pollaczek–Khinchine formula. For \(M/G/1\) with mean service time \(1/\mu\) and service-time coefficient of variation \(C_v=\sigma_S\mu\), $\(\boxed{\ L_q=\frac{\rho^{2}\left(1+C_v^{2}\right)}{2(1-\rho)}\ }\tag{2.1}\)$

Three special cases, all at the same \(\rho\):

Service distribution \(C_v\) \(L_q\) Relative to \(M/M/1\) Deterministic (\(M/D/1\)) 0 \(\dfrac{\rho^2}{2(1-\rho)}\) \(\times\,0.5\) Exponential (\(M/M/1\)) 1 \(\dfrac{\rho^2}{1-\rho}\) \(\times\,1\) Highly variable 2 \(\dfrac{5\rho^2}{2(1-\rho)}\) \(\times\,2.5\)

The variability lesson. Waiting time is driven by two things: how loaded the system is, and how variable it is. Halving the variability of service is worth as much as a substantial capacity increase — and standardising a process usually costs far less than buying a server.

docs.title: 29.4 When Formulas Fail: Simulation
docs.text:
Analytic queuing formulas assume steady state, Poisson arrivals, a stationary environment and simple routing. Reach for discrete-event simulation when any of these fails:

Situation Why formulas fail Arrival rate varies by hour of day No steady state exists; Lesson 25 Problem 4 showed averaging is invalid Customers balk, renege or jockey between queues State-dependent behaviour not captured by \(\lambda_n\) alone Networks of queues with feedback and blocking Departures are no longer Poisson Priority classes with pre-emption Different classes need different \(W\); means diverge Non-standard shift patterns and breaks Server availability is itself a stochastic process Only a short horizon matters (opening rush) Transient, not steady-state, behaviour

But always compute the analytic answer first. It costs minutes, provides a sanity check on the simulation, and identifies the regime you are in. A simulation that disagrees materially with \(M/M/c\) under \(M/M/c\) conditions has a bug.

docs.title: Problem 1 — How many servers to hire
docs.text:
A service facility faces \(\lambda=6\) customers per hour; each server works at \(\mu=4\) per hour. A customer's time in the system costs the firm \(₹300\) per hour; a server costs \(₹150\) per hour. Find the optimal \(c\).

Solution. Stability needs \(c\mu>\lambda\), i.e. \(c\ge2\). Offered load \(r=1.5\).

\(c\) \(\rho\) \(L_s\) Waiting cost \(300L_s\) Server cost \(150c\) Total 2 0.750 3.42857 ₹1028.57 ₹300 ₹1328.57 3 0.500 1.73684 ₹521.05 ₹450 ₹971.05 4 0.375 1.54475 ₹463.43 ₹600 ₹1063.43 5 0.300 1.50863 ₹452.59 ₹750 ₹1202.59 6 0.250 1.50157 ₹450.47 ₹900 ₹1350.47 \[\boxed{c^{*}=3\ \text{servers},\ TC=₹971.05\text{ per hour}}\]

Marginal analysis.

Step Waiting cost saved Server cost Decision 2 → 3 ₹507.52 ₹150 add 3 → 4 ₹57.62 ₹150 stop 4 → 5 ₹10.84 ₹150 no

The saving collapses by a factor of nine at the third step. Note also that \(L_s\) can never fall below \(r=1.5\) — the customers in service. Beyond the point where the queue is nearly empty, extra servers buy nothing at all, because the residual \(L_s\) is service time, not waiting.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Does L_s or L_q change the answer?
docs.text:
Repeat Problem 1 charging only for waiting time (\(L_q\)), as would be right if service time is value-adding and only queueing is waste.

Solution.

\(c\) \(L_q\) Waiting cost \(300L_q\) Server cost Total 2 1.92857 ₹578.57 ₹300 ₹878.57 3 0.23684 ₹71.05 ₹450 ₹521.05 4 0.04475 ₹13.43 ₹600 ₹613.43 5 0.00863 ₹2.59 ₹750 ₹752.59 \[\boxed{c^{*}=3\text{ again, at }₹521.05\text{ per hour}}\]

Interpretation. The decision is unchanged but the reported cost is not — ₹971 versus ₹521. The two differ by exactly \(300r=₹450\) per hour, the cost of unavoidable service time, which is a constant and therefore cannot affect the optimum.

Rule. When \(L_s\) and \(L_q\) differ by a constant (as in \(M/M/c\) with fixed \(\lambda,\mu\)), the choice does not change the optimal \(c\). It does change the headline number quoted to management, so state which convention you used. In models where \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) varies with the decision — a finite-capacity or finite-source system — the constant is no longer constant, and the choice can flip the decision.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Airport check-in counters
docs.text:
An airline expects \(100\) passengers per hour at check-in. Each counter processes \(15\) per hour. Passenger time is valued at \(₹500\) per hour; a staffed counter costs \(₹800\) per hour. How many counters should be opened?

Solution. Stability requires \(15c>100\), so \(c\ge7\). Here \(r=100/15=6.667\).

\(c\) \(\rho\) \(L_q\) \(W_q\) Waiting cost Counter cost Total 7 0.9524 17.2227 10.33 min ₹8611.4 ₹5600 ₹14211.4 8 0.8333 2.6634 1.60 min ₹1331.7 ₹6400 ₹7731.7 9 0.7407 0.8950 0.54 min ₹447.5 ₹7200 ₹7647.5 10 0.6667 0.3492 0.21 min ₹174.6 ₹8000 ₹8174.6 11 0.6061 0.1415 0.08 min ₹70.8 ₹8800 ₹8870.8 \[\boxed{c^{*}=9\text{ counters}}\]

Interpretation.

  • The minimum-stability choice \(c=7\) is catastrophic: it nearly doubles total cost because \(\rho=0.95\) sits on the vertical part of the congestion curve. Never staff to bare stability.
  • \(c=8\) and \(c=9\) are within \(1\,\%\) of each other — the optimum is flat, so either is defensible. The tie-breaker should be robustness: at \(c=8\) a \(10\,\%\) demand surge to \(110\)/h pushes \(\rho\) to \(0.917\) and \(L_q\) past \(12\); at \(c=9\) it only reaches \(\rho=0.815\). Choose \(c=9\) for the safety margin, not for the ₹84 per hour.
  • The famous square-root staffing rule predicts \(c \approx r + \beta\sqrt r = 6.67+\beta(2.58)\); with the usual \(\beta\approx1\) that gives \(c\approx9.25\), agreeing with the exact answer at almost no computational cost.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Cross-checking with a simulation
docs.text:
A simulation of an \(M/M/1\) queue with \(\lambda=8\)/h and \(\mu=10\)/h over \(200{,}000\) customers reports a mean time in system of \(0.4961\) hours. Is the simulation trustworthy?

Solution. The theoretical value is

\[W_s=\frac{1}{\mu-\lambda}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\text{ hours}\]

Discrepancy: \(|0.4961-0.5| = 0.0039\) h, a relative error of \(0.78\,\%\).

Is that within sampling error? For \(M/M/1\), \(W_s\) is exponential with mean \(0.5\), so \(\sigma_W = 0.5\) and the standard error of the mean over \(n=200{,}000\) observations is

\[\frac{\sigma_W}{\sqrt n}=\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{200000}}=0.00112\text{ h}.\]

The discrepancy is \(0.0039/0.00112 = 3.5\) standard errors — larger than one would like, but successive customers' waiting times are strongly positively correlated (a busy period makes everyone in it wait), so the true standard error is several times the i.i.d. figure. The result is consistent.

Also check Little's law inside the simulation:

\[L_s=\lambda W_s = 8(0.4961)=3.969\quad\text{versus theory } 4.000\ \checkmark\]

Verdict: the simulation is behaving correctly.

How to validate any queuing simulation. (1) Run it under conditions where a formula exists and compare. (2) Check Little's law internally — it must hold in any correct simulation. (3) Discard a warm-up period; a simulation started empty is biased low. (4) Report a confidence interval, never a single number. A simulation without a validation step is an expensive random-number generator.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Pricing the cost of variability
docs.text:
A single-server process has \(\lambda=8\)/h and mean service time \(6\) minutes (\(\mu=10\)/h), so \(\rho=0.8\). Compare the queue under (a) exponential service, (b) perfectly standardised service, and (c) a poorly controlled process with \(C_v=2\). Waiting is worth \(₹250\) per customer-hour.

Solution. Apply (2.1) with \(\rho=0.8\), \(\dfrac{\rho^2}{2(1-\rho)}=\dfrac{0.64}{0.4}=1.6\).

Case \(C_v\) \(L_q=1.6(1+C_v^2)\) \(W_q=L_q/8\) Waiting cost \(250L_q\) (b) Standardised (\(M/D/1\)) 0 1.60 12 min ₹400/h (a) Exponential (\(M/M/1\)) 1 3.20 24 min ₹800/h (c) Poorly controlled 2 8.00 60 min ₹2000/h

Interpretation.

  • Moving from (a) to (b) — eliminating variability without adding any capacity — halves the queue and saves \(₹400\) per hour.
  • Letting variability rise from (a) to (c) multiplies the queue by 2.5 at unchanged capacity and unchanged mean service time. Every number a manager watches (\(\rho\), throughput, mean service time) is identical in the three cases; only the queue differs.
  • To achieve the \(M/D/1\) queue length by adding capacity instead, one would need \(\rho\) such that \(\rho^2/(1-\rho)=1.6\), i.e. \(\rho=0.685\) — a \(17\,\%\) increase in service rate. Standardising the process is usually far cheaper than buying that capacity.

This is the quantitative justification for standard operating procedures, checklists and Six Sigma programmes. They do not make the average task faster; they make it more predictable, and by (2.1) predictability alone buys shorter queues.

docs.title: 29.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda=15\)/h, \(\mu=6\)/h per server, \(C_w=₹100\)/customer-hour (use \(L_q\)), \(C_s=₹80\)/server-hour. Find \(c^{*}\). (Answer: \(c^*=4\), \(TC=₹373.31\)/h; \(c=3\) costs ₹591.12 and \(c=5\) costs ₹413.04)
  2. In Problem 3, at what value of \(C_w\) would \(c=8\) become optimal? (Answer: below \(₹452\) per passenger-hour; equate \(C_w(2.6634-0.8950)=800\))
  3. Using (2.1), find \(L_q\) for \(\rho=0.9\) and \(C_v = 0, 1, 3\). Comment on the spread. (Answer: \(4.05\), \(8.10\), \(40.50\) — a tenfold range at identical utilisation)
  4. A simulation of \(M/M/2\) with \(\lambda=6\), \(\mu=4\) reports \(L_q=1.95\). Is it plausible? (Answer: theory gives \(1.92857\); a \(1.1\,\%\) discrepancy — plausible)
  5. List three real systems from your own experience where the steady-state assumption fails, and say what you would do instead.

docs.title: 29.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Choose \(c\) by minimising \(TC(c)=C_wL(c)+C_sc\). \(TC\) is convex in \(c\), so enumerate upwards and stop at the first rise.
  • Present the decision as marginal analysis: add a server while the waiting cost saved exceeds the server's cost.
  • Never staff to bare stability. In Problem 3 the minimum-stable choice cost nearly twice the optimum.
  • The optimum is usually flat; break ties on robustness to demand surges, not on rupees.
  • The square-root staffing rule \(c\approx r+\sqrt r\) gets very close to the exact answer instantly.
  • Pollaczek–Khinchine: \(L_q=\dfrac{\rho^2(1+C_v^2)}{2(1-\rho)}\). Deterministic service halves the \(M/M/1\) queue; \(C_v=2\) multiplies it by \(2.5\). Reducing variability is a genuine alternative to buying capacity, and usually a cheaper one.
  • Use simulation when arrivals are non-stationary, customers balk or renege, or only a short horizon matters — but always compute the analytic answer first as a check, and always validate against Little's law.

Next lesson: L30 — Inventory control: concepts, cost structure and classification.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Cost Optimiser and Variability Lab: sweep \(c\) to find the minimum-cost staffing, then vary \(C_v\) to see the P–K formula move the queue.

docs.title: Lesson 6: Big-M, Two-Phase Methods and Special Cases
6.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain why \(\ge\) and \(=\) constraints need artificial variables.
  2. Apply the Big-M method and interpret its tableaus.
  3. Apply the two-phase method and know when to prefer it.
  4. Detect infeasibility, unboundedness, alternate optima and degeneracy from a tableau.
  5. Diagnose and repair a failing model.

docs.title: 6.2 Why Artificial Variables Are Needed
docs.text:
Simplex requires a starting basic feasible solution. When every constraint is \(\le\) with \(b_i \ge 0\), the slacks provide one immediately: set all real variables to zero and read \(s_i = b_i \ge 0\). The origin is feasible.

With a \(\ge\) constraint this fails. Consider \(3x_1 + x_2 \ge 6\). In standard form,

\[ 3x_1 + x_2 - s_1 = 6 \]

Setting \(x_1 = x_2 = 0\) gives \(s_1 = -6 < 0\) — not feasible. The surplus variable enters with coefficient \(-1\), so it cannot be a starting basic variable.

Similarly for \(=\): \(3x_1+x_2 = 3\) has no slack at all, so no basic variable exists in that row.

The fix. Add an artificial variable \(A_i \ge 0\) with coefficient \(+1\):

\[ 3x_1 + x_2 - s_1 + A_1 = 6, \qquad 3x_1 + x_2 + A_2 = 3 \]

Now \(A_1 = 6\) and \(A_2 = 3\) give a starting basis. But this solves a different problem — the artificials must be driven to zero before the answer means anything.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Artificial variables buy a starting point at the price of having to expel them.}\ } \]

docs.title: 6.3 The Big-M Method
docs.text:
Idea. Attach a huge penalty \(M\) to each artificial variable so that the optimiser expels them automatically.

\[ \text{maximisation: } \ \max\ Z = \sum c_jx_j - M\sum A_i \] \[ \text{minimisation: } \ \min\ Z = \sum c_jx_j + M\sum A_i \]

with \(M\) larger than any number that could otherwise arise.

The three outcomes.

At optimality Conclusion All \(A_i = 0\) the solution is optimal for the original problem ✓ Some \(A_i > 0\) the original problem is INFEASIBLE \(Z\) unbounded with all \(A_i = 0\) the original problem is UNBOUNDED

docs.title: Handling M in the tableau
docs.text:
Entries in the \(z_j - c_j\) row become expressions like \(-6996\) or, symbolically, \(-7M + 4\). Two equivalent conventions:

  • Symbolic: keep \(M\) as a symbol and compare coefficients of \(M\) first, then the constants.
  • Numeric: set \(M\) to a large number (say 1000, safely above any coefficient in the problem).

This lesson uses \(M = 1000\) for readability; the symbolic form is given alongside.

docs.title: 6.4 Worked Big-M Example
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \min\ & Z = 4x_1 + x_2\\ \text{s.t. } & 3x_1 + x_2 = 3\\ & 4x_1 + 3x_2 \ge 6\\ & x_1 + 2x_2 \le 4\\ & x_1, x_2 \ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

Standard form. Convert to maximisation of \(Z' = -4x_1 - x_2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} 3x_1 + x_2 + A_1 &= 3\\ 4x_1 + 3x_2 - s_2 + A_2 &= 6\\ x_1 + 2x_2 + s_3 &= 4 \end{aligned} \] \[ \max\ Z' = -4x_1 - x_2 + 0s_2 + 0s_3 - MA_1 - MA_2 \]

docs.title: Iteration 3
docs.text:
Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_2\) \(A_1\) \(A_2\) \(s_3\) RHS \(x_1\) −4 1 0 0 \(2/5\) 0 \(-1/5\) 2/5 \(x_2\) −1 0 1 0 \(-1/5\) 0 \(3/5\) 9/5 \(s_2\) 0 0 0 1 1 −1 1 1 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 0 \(4993/5\) \(1000\) \(1/5\) \(-17/5\)

All \(z_j-c_j \ge 0\) ⟹ OPTIMAL.

\[ \boxed{\ x_1^{*} = \tfrac25 = 0.4,\quad x_2^{*} = \tfrac95 = 1.8,\quad Z_{\min} = -Z'_{\max} = \tfrac{17}{5} = 3.4\ } \]

Verification against the original problem.

\[ 3(0.4)+1.8 = 1.2+1.8 = 3 = 3 \ \checkmark \ \text{(equality holds)} \] \[ 4(0.4)+3(1.8) = 1.6+5.4 = 7.0 \ge 6 \ \checkmark \ \text{(surplus } s_2 = 1) \] \[ 0.4+2(1.8) = 0.4+3.6 = 4.0 \le 4 \ \checkmark \ \text{(binding, } s_3 = 0) \] \[ Z = 4(0.4)+1.8 = 1.6+1.8 = 3.4 \ \checkmark \]

Both artificials are zero, so the answer is valid for the original problem.

Note the near-miss at iteration 2. Both artificials had left, yet the solution \((0.6,\ 1.2)\) with \(Z = 3.6\) was not optimal. Expelling the artificials makes the solution feasible, not optimal — the algorithm must continue until the \(z_j-c_j\) test passes.

docs.title: 6.5 The Two-Phase Method
docs.text:
Idea. Split the work into two clean stages instead of juggling \(M\).

Phase I — find feasibility. Replace the objective by

\[ \min\ W = \sum_i A_i \qquad\left(\text{equivalently } \max\ -\sum_i A_i\right) \]

subject to the same constraints.

  • If \(W^{*} > 0\) ⟹ the original problem is INFEASIBLE. Stop.
  • If \(W^{*} = 0\) ⟹ a BFS of the original problem has been found. Proceed.

Phase II — find optimality. Drop the artificial columns, restore the original objective, recompute the \(z_j - c_j\) row, and continue simplex from the Phase I final tableau.

docs.title: Big-M versus two-phase
docs.text:
Big-M Two-phase Number of tableaus fewer more Arithmetic mixes \(M\) with ordinary numbers clean numbers throughout Numerical stability poor — huge \(M\) swamps small coefficients in floating point good Infeasibility detection at the end at the end of Phase I — earlier Hand calculation fine fine Computer implementation avoided used in practice \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Every real solver uses two-phase (or a dual/crash start). Big-M is a teaching device.}\ } \]

Why Big-M fails numerically. With \(M = 10^{6}\) and a genuine coefficient of \(10^{-3}\), double precision (≈16 significant digits) cannot represent their sum accurately. Round-off then corrupts the \(z_j-c_j\) signs and the algorithm terminates at a wrong basis.

docs.title: Phase I on the same example
docs.text:
\[ \min\ W = A_1 + A_2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max\ -A_1 - A_2 \]

Iteration 0. \(c_B = (-1,-1,0)\), \(W = 3+6 = 9\). The \(z_j-c_j\) row is obtained by summing the artificial rows and negating the real-variable entries:

\[ z_j - c_j \ =\ (-7,\ -4,\ +1,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0), \qquad W = 9 \]

Entering \(x_1\), leaving \(A_1\) — the same pivots as Big-M, because the \(M\)-terms dominated there and the \(M\)-terms are the Phase I objective.

Phase I terminates at iteration 2 with \(W^{*} = 0\) and the BFS \((x_1, x_2) = (0.6, 1.2)\).

Phase II restores \(\max\ Z' = -4x_1 - x_2\), recomputes \(z_j-c_j\), finds \(z_{s_2}-c_{s_2} = -\frac15\), performs the one remaining pivot, and reaches the same optimum.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Two-phase does the same work, but with numbers instead of } M.\ } \]

docs.title: 6.6 The Four Special Cases in the Tableau
docs.text: Case Tableau signature Action Infeasible some \(A_i > 0\) at optimality (or \(W^{*}>0\) in Phase I) relax a constraint Unbounded entering column has no positive entry add the missing constraint Alternate optima a non-basic variable has \(z_j - c_j = 0\) pivot to find the second optimum Degenerate a basic variable equals 0 continue; watch for stalling

docs.title: Problem 1 — Detecting infeasibility with Big-M
docs.text:
Solve \(\max\ Z = 3x_1+2x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2 \le 4\), \(x_1+x_2\ge 8\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\).

Solution.

Standard form.

\[ x_1+x_2+s_1 = 4, \qquad x_1+x_2-s_2+A_1 = 8 \] \[ \max\ Z = 3x_1+2x_2 - MA_1 \]

Iteration 0. Basis \(\{s_1, A_1\}\), \(Z = -8M\).

\[ z_j - c_j = (-M-3,\ -M-2,\ 0,\ M,\ 0) \]

Entering \(x_1\); ratios \(\frac41 = 4\) and \(\frac81 = 8\) ⟹ leaving \(s_1\), pivot 1.

Iteration 1.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) \(A_1\) RHS \(x_1\) 3 1 1 1 0 0 4 \(A_1\) \(-M\) 0 0 −1 −1 1 4 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 1 \(M+3\) \(M\) 0 \(12-4M\)

All \(z_j - c_j \ge 0\) (since \(M\) is large) ⟹ the algorithm STOPS.

But \(A_1 = 4 > 0\).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{INFEASIBLE.}\ } \]

Why, obviously. The constraints demand \(x_1+x_2 \le 4\) and \(x_1+x_2\ge8\) simultaneously — impossible since \(4 < 8\).

What the tableau tells us more precisely. The final \(Z = 12 - 4M\) contains the term \(-4M\): the "cost" of the infeasibility is 4 units of violation. Modern solvers report exactly this — the minimum total constraint violation — which points the modeller straight at the problem.

Practical response. Either the capacity 4 is wrong, or the requirement 8 is wrong. The infeasibility of 4 units tells management exactly how much extra capacity (or how much demand reduction) would be needed.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Two-phase method, complete
docs.text:
Solve by two-phase: \(\min\ Z = 2x_1+3x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2\ge5\), \(x_1+2x_2\ge6\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\).

Solution.

Standard form.

\[ x_1+x_2-s_1+A_1 = 5, \qquad x_1+2x_2-s_2+A_2 = 6 \]

docs.title: PHASE I: min W = A₁+A₂, i.e. max -A₁-A₂
PHASE II: min Z = 2x₁ + 3x₂
docs.text:
Drop the artificial columns and restore the true objective. With \(c_B = (2, 3)\):

\[ z_{s_1} = 2(-2) + 3(1) = -1, \qquad z_{s_1}-c_{s_1} = -1 - 0 = -1 \] \[ z_{s_2} = 2(1) + 3(-1) = -1, \qquad z_{s_2}-c_{s_2} = -1 \] Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_1\) 2 1 0 −2 1 4 \(x_2\) 3 0 1 1 −1 1 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 −1 −1 \(Z = 11\)

For a MINIMISATION in this form, optimality requires \(z_j - c_j \le 0\). Both are \(-1 \le 0\) ✓.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{OPTIMAL: } x_1^{*} = 4,\ x_2^{*} = 1,\ Z_{\min} = 2(4)+3(1) = 11\ } \]

Verification.

\[ 4+1 = 5 \ge 5 \ \checkmark \text{ (binding)}, \qquad 4+2(1) = 6 \ge 6 \ \checkmark \text{ (binding)} \]

Graphical cross-check. The corners of the feasible region are \((6,0)\) with \(Z = 12\), \((4,1)\) with \(Z = 11\), and \((0,5)\) with \(Z = 15\). Minimum is \((4,1)\), \(Z = 11\) ✓.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Detecting unboundedness
docs.text:
Solve \(\max\ Z = 2x_1 + x_2\) s.t. \(x_1 - x_2 \le 10\), \(2x_1 - x_2 \le 40\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\).

Solution.

Iteration 0. Basis \(\{s_1, s_2\}\).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS Ratio \(s_1\) 0 1 −1 1 0 10 10 ← \(s_2\) 0 2 −1 0 1 40 20 \(z_j-c_j\) −2 −1 0 0 0

Entering \(x_1\); ratios \(\{10, 20\}\); leaving \(s_1\); pivot 1.

Iteration 1. Row 2 ← row 2 − 2(row 1).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_1\) 2 1 −1 1 0 10 \(s_2\) 0 0 1 −2 1 20 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 −3 2 0 20

Entering \(x_2\) (\(-3\)). Column entries: \((-1,\ 1)^T\). Ratio for row 2: \(20/1 = 20\). Leaving \(s_2\).

Iteration 2.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_1\) 2 1 0 −1 1 30 \(x_2\) 1 0 1 −2 1 20 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 −4 3 80

Entering \(s_1\) (\(-4\)). Column entries \((-1, -2)^T\) — BOTH NEGATIVE.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{No positive entry in the pivot column} \ \Longrightarrow\ \textbf{UNBOUNDED.}\ } \]

The direction of unboundedness. Increasing \(s_1\) by \(t\) gives

\[ x_1 = 30 + t, \qquad x_2 = 20 + 2t, \qquad Z = 80 + 4t \ \longrightarrow\ \infty \]

Check feasibility along the ray. At \(x_1 = 30+t\), \(x_2 = 20+2t\):

\[ x_1 - x_2 = 10 - t \le 10 \ \checkmark \quad \text{for all } t \ge 0 \] \[ 2x_1 - x_2 = 60+2t - 20-2t = 40 \le 40 \ \checkmark \quad \text{always binding} \]

Both constraints remain satisfied for every \(t \ge 0\) ✓ — genuinely unbounded.

Why it happened. Both constraints have the form (something) \(-x_2 \le\) (constant). Increasing \(x_2\) loosens both. Nothing in the model limits \(x_2\), yet \(x_2\) contributes positively to profit.

The modelling lesson. Every LP claiming unbounded profit has a missing constraint — here, no limit on the resource consumed by \(x_2\). The unbounded ray names the culprit precisely.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Alternate optima found by pivoting
docs.text:
A final tableau for \(\max\ Z = 2x_1+4x_2\) is shown. Identify alternate optima and find the second optimal solution.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_2\) 4 \(1/2\) 1 \(1/2\) 0 4 \(s_2\) 0 \(3/2\) 0 \(-1/2\) 1 2 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 2 0 16

Solution.

Diagnosis. \(x_1\) is non-basic (it is not a basis label) yet \(z_1 - c_1 = 0\).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{ALTERNATE OPTIMA.}\ } \]

Current optimum. \(x_1 = 0\), \(x_2 = 4\), \(Z = 4(4) = 16\) ✓.

Find the second. Bring \(x_1\) into the basis. Column \(x_1 = (\frac12,\ \frac32)^T\); ratios

\[ \frac{4}{1/2} = 8, \qquad \frac{2}{3/2} = \frac43 \ \leftarrow \text{minimum} \]

Leaving \(s_2\); pivot \(\frac32\).

Row 2 ÷ \(\frac32\): \((1,\ 0,\ -\frac13,\ \frac23\ |\ \frac43)\). Row 1 ← row 1 − \(\frac12\)(new row 2): \((0,\ 1,\ \frac12+\frac16,\ -\frac13\ |\ 4-\frac23)\) \(= (0,\ 1,\ \frac23,\ -\frac13\ |\ \frac{10}{3})\).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_2\) 4 0 1 \(2/3\) \(-1/3\) \(10/3\) \(x_1\) 2 1 0 \(-1/3\) \(2/3\) \(4/3\) \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 2 0 16 \[ \boxed{\ \text{Second optimum: } x_1 = \tfrac43,\ x_2 = \tfrac{10}{3},\ Z = 16\ } \]

Check. \(Z = 2(\frac43)+4(\frac{10}{3}) = \frac83+\frac{40}{3} = \frac{48}{3} = 16\) ✓ — identical, as required.

The complete optimal set.

\[ \vec x(\lambda) = \lambda(0,\ 4) + (1-\lambda)\left(\tfrac43,\ \tfrac{10}{3}\right), \qquad \lambda\in[0,1] \]

At \(\lambda = \frac12\): \(\vec x = (\frac23,\ \frac{11}{3})\), giving \(Z = \frac43 + \frac{44}{3} = \frac{48}{3} = 16\) ✓.

Note that \(s_2\) also has \(z_j-c_j = 0\) but is BASIC in the first tableau — that is not a signal of alternate optima. Only non-basic zeros count.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Diagnosing and repairing a failing model
docs.text:
A production LP returns "infeasible". The model is: produce \(x_1, x_2\) with \(2x_1+3x_2 \le 100\) (machine hours), \(x_1 \ge 30\) (contract), \(x_2 \ge 25\) (contract). Diagnose and propose three repairs, quantifying each.

Solution.

Diagnosis. The two contracts consume, at minimum,

\[ 2(30) + 3(25) = 60 + 75 = \mathbf{135\ \text{machine hours}} \]

but only 100 are available.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Infeasible by 35 machine hours.}\ } \]

How the simplex method reports this. Phase I terminates with \(W^{*} = 35/1 = 35\) (in units of the violated constraint), or in Big-M form an artificial variable remains at a positive value. Commercial solvers additionally report the Irreducible Infeasible Subsystem — here, exactly these three constraints, since removing any one restores feasibility.

Repair 1 — buy capacity. Increase machine hours to at least 135.

\[ \text{extra needed} = 35 \text{ hours}. \]

If overtime costs ₹200/hour, the cost is ₹7 000. Feasible if the contract penalties exceed ₹7 000.

Repair 2 — renegotiate a contract. Suppose \(x_2 \ge 25\) is relaxed to \(x_2 \ge q\). Feasibility requires

\[ 2(30) + 3q \le 100 \ \Longrightarrow\ 3q \le 40 \ \Longrightarrow\ q \le 13.33 \]

So product 2's commitment must fall from 25 to at most 13 units — a 48 % reduction.

Alternatively relax \(x_1 \ge 30\) to \(x_1 \ge p\):

\[ 2p + 75 \le 100 \ \Longrightarrow\ p \le 12.5 \ \Longrightarrow\ p \le 12 \]

— a 60 % reduction. Relaxing product 2 is the cheaper repair in units of commitment.

Repair 3 — soften the constraints (goal programming). Convert the hard contracts to soft targets with penalties, using the technique of L02 Problem 3:

\[ x_1 + d_1^{-} - d_1^{+} = 30, \qquad x_2 + d_2^{-} - d_2^{+} = 25 \] \[ \min\ Z = p_1d_1^{-} + p_2d_2^{-} \qquad \text{s.t. } 2x_1+3x_2 \le 100 \]

where \(p_1, p_2\) are the per-unit penalties for missing each contract. This model is always feasible and tells you the least-cost way to break the promises — which is exactly the decision management actually faces.

Worked example of Repair 3. With penalties \(p_1 = ₹500\) and \(p_2 = ₹300\) per unit short:

Since product 1 costs 2 hours/unit and product 2 costs 3 hours/unit, the shortfall penalty per machine hour saved is

\[ \text{product 1: } \frac{500}{2} = ₹250/\text{hour}, \qquad \text{product 2: } \frac{300}{3} = ₹100/\text{hour} \]

Cut product 2 — it is cheaper per hour saved. Need to save 35 hours:

\[ \text{units of } x_2 \text{ to cut} = \frac{35}{3} = 11.67 \ \Longrightarrow\ x_2 = 25 - 11.67 = 13.33 \] \[ x_1 = 30, \quad x_2 = 13.33, \quad d_2^{-} = 11.67 \] \[ \text{Check: } 2(30)+3(13.33) = 60+40 = 100 \ \checkmark \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{Minimum penalty} = 11.67\times₹300 = ₹3{,}500\ } \]

Compare the three repairs.

Repair Cost Notes Buy 35 overtime hours ₹7 000 keeps both contracts intact Goal programming (cut product 2) ₹3 500 cheapest — breaks the cheaper promise Cut product 1 instead \(\frac{35}{2}\times500 = ₹8{,}750\) worst option \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Recommendation: buy overtime only if the ₹7 000 cost is below the true reputational cost of breaking the product-2 contract.}\ } \]

The general lesson. "Infeasible" is not a failure of the algorithm — it is information. It says the requirements as stated cannot all be met, and the Phase I objective quantifies by exactly how much. The right response is to model the trade-off explicitly, which is what goal programming does.

docs.title: 6.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Set up the Big-M tableau for \(\min\ 3x_1+5x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2\ge4\), \(2x_1+x_2 = 6\).
  2. Solve Problem 2 of §6 by Big-M and confirm the same answer.
  3. A Phase I ends with \(W^{*} = 3\). What do you conclude?
  4. Column entries in the pivot column are \((0, -2, -5)^T\). Diagnose. [Ans: unbounded]
  5. Why is Big-M numerically dangerous on a computer?
  6. In a minimisation tableau, state the optimality condition.
  7. A final tableau has a basic variable equal to 0 and all \(z_j-c_j > 0\). Is it optimal? [Ans: yes — optimal and degenerate]

docs.title: 6.9 Summary
docs.text:
• \(\ge\) and \(=\) constraints leave no starting basic feasible solution, so artificial variables are added — they buy a starting point and must then be expelled.
  • Big-M: penalise artificials with a huge \(M\). At optimality, all \(A_i = 0\) ⟹ valid; any \(A_i > 0\) ⟹ INFEASIBLE.
  • Expelling the artificials gives feasibility, not optimality — continue until the \(z_j-c_j\) test passes.
  • Two-phase: Phase I minimises \(\sum A_i\) (if \(W^{*}>0\), infeasible); Phase II restores the real objective. Numerically far safer, and what real solvers use.
  • Tableau signatures: infeasible (\(A_i > 0\) / \(W^{*}>0\)), unbounded (no positive entry in the pivot column), alternate optima (a non-basic variable with \(z_j-c_j = 0\)), degenerate (a basic variable equal to 0).
  • Infeasibility is information. The Phase I objective measures the total violation, and goal programming converts hard constraints into penalised targets — always feasible, and it prices the trade-off management actually faces.

Next lesson: L07 — Duality and sensitivity analysis.

Practise now: unit1-lp-lab.html → Simplex Stepper: switch on artificial variables and watch Big-M and two-phase run side by side on the same problem.

docs.title: Lesson 23: Birth–Death Processes and Steady-State Balance Equations
23.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define a birth–death process and draw its rate-transition diagram.
  2. Write the balance equations from a diagram, using both the node method and the cut method.
  3. Derive the general steady-state solution \(P_n = P_0\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\dfrac{\lambda_k}{\mu_{k+1}}\).
  4. State and apply the ergodicity condition that guarantees a steady state exists.
  5. Specialise the general result to \(M/M/1\), \(M/M/\infty\), discouraged arrivals and the machine-repair model.

docs.title: 23.2 Why One Framework Covers Every Queue
docs.text:
Lesson 21 described queues qualitatively and Lesson 22 established that Poisson arrivals and exponential service make the system Markovian. This hour builds the single mathematical engine that produces every formula in Lessons 24–29. Rather than deriving \(M/M/1\), then \(M/M/1/N\), then \(M/M/c\) from scratch, we derive one result and then substitute different rate functions.

That is the real payoff of the Markov assumption: a queue whose arrival and service rates may depend on the current number in the system is still completely described by a one-dimensional chain.

docs.title: The definition
docs.text:
Definition (Birth–death process). A continuous-time Markov chain on the states \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\) is a birth–death process if from state \(n\) the only permitted transitions are to \(n+1\) (a birth, at rate \(\lambda_n\)) and to \(n-1\) (a death, at rate \(\mu_n\), defined for \(n\ge 1\) with \(\mu_0 = 0\)).

The state \(n\) is the number of customers in the system — those waiting plus those in service. The defining restriction is that the state changes by one unit at a time. This is precisely the orderliness axiom of Lesson 22: two events cannot occur simultaneously.

docs.title: The rate-transition diagram
docs.text:
lam_0        lam_1        lam_2        lam_3
    (0) ------>  (1) ------>  (2) ------>  (3) ------>  ...
        <------      <------      <------      <------
        mu_1         mu_2         mu_3         mu_4

Each circle is a state; each arrow carries a rate, not a probability. Rates have units of "events per unit time" and may exceed 1.

Reading the diagram is the whole skill. Almost every queuing model in this course is obtained by choosing \(\lambda_n\) and \(\mu_n\) and turning the crank.

Model \(\lambda_n\) \(\mu_n\) \(M/M/1\) \(\lambda\) for all \(n\) \(\mu\) for all \(n\ge1\) \(M/M/1/N\) \(\lambda\) for \(n<N\), else \(0\) \(\mu\) for all \(n\ge1\) \(M/M/c\) \(\lambda\) for all \(n\) \(n\mu\) for \(n<c\), else \(c\mu\) \(M/M/\infty\) \(\lambda\) for all \(n\) \(n\mu\) Discouraged arrivals \(\lambda/(n+1)\) \(\mu\) Machine repair (\(M\) machines) \((M-n)\lambda\) for \(n<M\) \(\mu\)

docs.title: The steady state
docs.text:
Let \(P_n(t)\) be the probability of being in state \(n\) at time \(t\). In steady state (also called statistical equilibrium) these probabilities settle to constants \(P_n\) with \(\dfrac{dP_n}{dt}=0\).

Warning. Steady state does not mean the queue length stops changing. The queue keeps fluctuating; what stops changing is the probability distribution of its length. A steady-state analysis tells you nothing about the transient rush in the first few minutes after opening.

docs.title: The node (global balance) equations
docs.text:
Principle of balance. In steady state, the rate of flow into any state equals the rate of flow out of it.

Consider state \(n\ge1\). Flow enters from \(n-1\) (rate \(\lambda_{n-1}P_{n-1}\)) and from \(n+1\) (rate \(\mu_{n+1}P_{n+1}\)). Flow leaves at rate \((\lambda_n+\mu_n)P_n\). Hence

\[\lambda_{n-1}P_{n-1} + \mu_{n+1}P_{n+1} = (\lambda_n+\mu_n)P_n, \qquad n\ge 1 \tag{2.1}\]

and, for the boundary state \(0\) (which has no death transition),

\[\mu_1 P_1 = \lambda_0 P_0. \tag{2.2}\]

docs.title: The cut (detailed balance) equations — the shortcut
docs.text:
Equation (2.1) is a three-term recurrence and is awkward. There is a far better route.

Imagine cutting the diagram with a vertical line between state \(n\) and state \(n+1\). Because the process moves one step at a time, every crossing from left to right must eventually be matched by a crossing from right to left. In steady state the two flow rates must be equal:

\[\boxed{\ \lambda_n P_n = \mu_{n+1}P_{n+1}\ } \qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots \tag{2.3}\]

This is a two-term recurrence and solves immediately. Equation (2.3) is called the detailed balance or cut equation.

Why the cut method is legitimate. Adding (2.2) to (2.1) for \(n=1\) gives \(\lambda_1 P_1 = \mu_2 P_2\); induction then yields (2.3) for every \(n\). The three-term equations are implied by the two-term ones, so nothing is lost. Always use cuts.

docs.title: 23.4 The General Solution
docs.text:
Apply (2.3) repeatedly starting from \(P_0\):

\[P_1 = \frac{\lambda_0}{\mu_1}P_0,\qquad P_2 = \frac{\lambda_1}{\mu_2}P_1 = \frac{\lambda_1\lambda_0}{\mu_2\mu_1}P_0,\qquad \dots\]

Theorem (General birth–death solution). $\(P_n = P_0\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\lambda_k}{\mu_{k+1}}, \qquad n\ge 1 \tag{3.1}\)$ with \(P_0\) fixed by the normalisation \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_n = 1\), giving $\(P_0 = \left[1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\lambda_k}{\mu_{k+1}}\right]^{-1}. \tag{3.2}\)$

Write \(C_n = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\lambda_k/\mu_{k+1}\) (with \(C_0=1\)); then \(P_n = C_nP_0\) and \(P_0 = 1/\sum_n C_n\). Every queuing formula in this unit is (3.1) and (3.2) with a particular \(C_n\).

docs.title: Ergodicity — when does a steady state exist?
docs.text:
Ergodicity condition. A steady-state distribution exists iff the series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_n\) converges.

If the series diverges, (3.2) forces \(P_0=0\), which means the queue length drifts to infinity: the system is unstable. For \(M/M/1\), \(C_n=\rho^n\) and the geometric series converges iff \(\rho = \lambda/\mu < 1\) — the familiar stability condition, now seen as a special case.

Three consequences worth remembering:

  • A finite-capacity queue is always ergodic: the sum has finitely many terms, so it always converges. \(M/M/1/N\) is stable even when \(\lambda>\mu\) — arrivals are simply turned away.
  • \(M/M/\infty\) is always ergodic: \(C_n=(\lambda/\mu)^n/n!\) sums to \(e^{\lambda/\mu}\) for any load.
  • \(\rho = 1\) exactly is unstable for \(M/M/1\): the queue grows without bound, just more slowly than when \(\rho>1\). There is no such thing as running a single-server queue "at exactly 100 %".

docs.title: The performance measures
docs.text:
Once \(\{P_n\}\) is known, everything else follows:

\[L_s=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nP_n, \qquad L_q=\sum_{n=c}^{\infty}(n-c)P_n, \qquad \lambda_{\text{eff}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda_nP_n \tag{3.3}\]

and Little's law converts stock to time:

\[W_s = \frac{L_s}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}, \qquad W_q = \frac{L_q}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}. \tag{3.4}\]

Use \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\), not \(\lambda\). When arrivals can be blocked or discouraged, the rate that actually enters the system is \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\), and that is the rate Little's law requires. Using the nominal \(\lambda\) here is the single most common error in this topic.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Balance equations for a finite chain
docs.text:
A system has states \(0,1,2,3\) with birth rates \(\lambda_0=3\), \(\lambda_1=2\), \(\lambda_2=1\) per hour and death rates \(\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=4\) per hour. Find \(P_n\), \(L_s\), \(L_q\), \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\), \(W_s\) and \(W_q\).

Solution.

Step 1 — cut equations.

\[\lambda_0P_0=\mu_1P_1 \Rightarrow P_1=\tfrac34P_0, \quad \lambda_1P_1=\mu_2P_2 \Rightarrow P_2=\tfrac24P_1=\tfrac38P_0, \quad P_3=\tfrac14P_2=\tfrac3{32}P_0.\]

Step 2 — normalise.

\[P_0\left(1+\tfrac34+\tfrac38+\tfrac3{32}\right)=P_0\cdot\frac{32+24+12+3}{32}=\frac{71}{32}P_0=1\] \[\boxed{P_0=\tfrac{32}{71}=0.4507,\quad P_1=\tfrac{24}{71}=0.3380,\quad P_2=\tfrac{12}{71}=0.1690,\quad P_3=\tfrac{3}{71}=0.0423}\]

Step 3 — measures.

\[L_s=\frac{0(32)+1(24)+2(12)+3(3)}{71}=\frac{57}{71}=0.8028 \text{ customers}\] \[L_q=\sum_{n\ge1}(n-1)P_n=\frac{0(24)+1(12)+2(3)}{71}=\frac{18}{71}=0.2535\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=3P_0+2P_1+1P_2=\frac{96+48+12}{71}=\frac{156}{71}=2.1972\text{ per hour}\]

Step 4 — Little's law.

\[W_s=\frac{57/71}{156/71}=\frac{57}{156}=\frac{19}{52}=0.3654\text{ h}=21.9\text{ min},\qquad W_q=\frac{18}{156}=\frac{3}{26}=0.1154\text{ h}=6.9\text{ min}\]

Check. Throughput must also equal \(\mu(1-P_0)=4\left(1-\tfrac{32}{71}\right)=4\cdot\tfrac{39}{71}=\tfrac{156}{71}\) ✓. The server is busy a fraction \(1-P_0=0.5493\) of the time.

Note \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}=2.197 < \lambda_0=3\): because arrivals slow as the system fills, more than a quarter of the nominal demand never materialises.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Recovering M/M/1
docs.text:
Show that constant rates \(\lambda_n=\lambda\), \(\mu_n=\mu\) reproduce the geometric distribution, and state the stability condition.

Solution. Here \(C_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\lambda/\mu=(\lambda/\mu)^n=\rho^n\). So

\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_n=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\rho^n=\frac{1}{1-\rho}\quad\text{provided }\rho<1.\]

Therefore \(P_0=1-\rho\) and

\[\boxed{P_n=(1-\rho)\rho^{\,n}}\]

a geometric distribution with parameter \(\rho\). The mean is

\[L_s=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(1-\rho)\rho^n=(1-\rho)\rho\sum_{n\ge1}n\rho^{n-1} =(1-\rho)\rho\cdot\frac{1}{(1-\rho)^2}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.\]

The series diverges for \(\rho\ge1\), giving the stability condition \(\rho<1\), i.e. \(\lambda<\mu\). Lesson 24 develops this model fully.

docs.title: Problem 3 — M/M/∞: unlimited servers
docs.text:
Every arriving customer is served immediately, so with \(n\) customers present there are \(n\) busy servers: \(\lambda_n=\lambda\), \(\mu_n=n\mu\). Find the distribution and \(L_s\) when \(\lambda=6\)/h and \(\mu=3\)/h.

Solution.

\[C_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\lambda}{(k+1)\mu}=\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^n =\frac{a^n}{n!},\qquad a=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}=2.\] \[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a^n}{n!}=e^{a}\ \Rightarrow\ P_0=e^{-a},\qquad \boxed{P_n=\frac{a^ne^{-a}}{n!}}\]

The number in the system is Poisson with mean \(a=\lambda/\mu\). Hence

\[L_s=a=2\text{ customers},\qquad L_q=0 \text{ (nobody ever waits)},\qquad W_s=\frac1\mu=\frac13\text{ h}=20\text{ min}.\]

Numerically \(P_0=e^{-2}=0.1353\), \(P_1=2e^{-2}=0.2707\), \(P_2=2e^{-2}=0.2707\).

Observation. The series \(\sum a^n/n!\) converges for every \(a\), so \(M/M/\infty\) is stable at any load — there is no \(\rho<1\) condition. This is the natural model for self-service systems (a supermarket's aisles, a website's connections) where "service" needs no scarce server.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Discouraged arrivals
docs.text:
Customers who see a long queue balk, so \(\lambda_n = \dfrac{\lambda}{n+1}\) while \(\mu_n=\mu\). With \(\lambda=8\)/h and \(\mu=4\)/h, find \(P_0\), \(L_s\) and \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\).

Solution.

\[C_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\lambda/(k+1)}{\mu}=\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac\lambda\mu\right)^n=\frac{a^n}{n!}, \qquad a=\frac\lambda\mu=2.\]

Remarkably this is the same \(C_n\) as \(M/M/\infty\), so again the state distribution is Poisson with mean 2:

\[P_0=e^{-2}=0.1353,\qquad L_s=a=2 \text{ customers}.\]

But the two systems differ where it matters. Here there is only one server, so

\[L_q=L_s-(1-P_0)=2-0.8647=1.1353\text{ customers},\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{\lambda}{n+1}P_n = \mu(1-P_0)=4(0.8647)=3.4587\text{ per hour},\]

using the fact that in steady state throughput in = throughput out = \(\mu\Pr[\text{busy}]\).

\[W_s=\frac{L_s}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}=\frac{2}{3.4587}=0.5783\text{ h}=34.7\text{ min}.\]

Interpretation. Note \(\lambda=8 > \mu=4\): a plain \(M/M/1\) queue would be unstable. Discouragement stabilises it, because arrivals throttle themselves as congestion builds. Only \(3.46\) of the \(8\) customers per hour are actually served — the other \(4.54\) balk. Balking is a hidden loss that never appears in a queue-length statistic.

docs.title: Problem 5 — The machine-repair (finite-source) model
docs.text:
A workshop has \(M=4\) machines and one repairman. Each running machine breaks down at rate \(\lambda=0.1\) per hour; a repair takes an exponential time with mean \(2\) hours (\(\mu=0.5\)/h). Find the distribution of broken machines, the expected number running, the repairman's utilisation and the average downtime per machine.

Solution.

Step 1 — rates. With \(n\) machines broken, \(M-n\) are running and each can fail, so \(\lambda_n=(M-n)\lambda\) for \(n<M\) and \(\lambda_M=0\). There is one repairman, so \(\mu_n=\mu\).

Step 2 — coefficients. With \(\lambda/\mu = 0.1/0.5 = 1/5\):

\[C_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(M-k)\lambda}{\mu}=\frac{M!}{(M-n)!}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^n\] \(n\) \(C_n\) value 0 \(1\) \(1\) 1 \(4\cdot\frac15\) \(0.8\) 2 \(4\cdot3\cdot\frac1{25}\) \(0.48\) 3 \(4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot\frac1{125}\) \(0.192\) 4 \(4!\cdot\frac1{625}\) \(0.0384\) \[\sum C_n = 2.5104 \Rightarrow P_0 = \frac{1}{2.5104}=\frac{625}{1569}=0.3983\] \[\boxed{P_0=0.3983,\ P_1=0.3187,\ P_2=0.1912,\ P_3=0.0765,\ P_4=0.0153}\]

Step 3 — measures.

\[L_s=\sum nP_n = 0.3187+2(0.1912)+3(0.0765)+4(0.0153)=\frac{1556}{1569}=\mathbf{0.9917}\text{ machines broken}\] \[\text{Machines running}=M-L_s=4-0.9917=\mathbf{3.0083}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\sum_n (M-n)\lambda P_n=\lambda(M-L_s)=0.1(3.0083)=\frac{472}{1569}=0.3008\text{ breakdowns/h}\] \[W_s=\frac{L_s}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}=\frac{0.9917}{0.3008}=\frac{389}{118}=\mathbf{3.297\text{ hours}}\text{ average downtime}\] \[\text{Repairman utilisation}=1-P_0=\mathbf{0.6017}\]

Interpretation. Of the \(3.30\) hours a broken machine is down, only \(2\) hours are actual repair; the other \(1.30\) hours are spent waiting for the repairman. Downtime is \(65\,\%\) longer than repair time even though the repairman is idle \(40\,\%\) of the time — the standard, and deeply counter-intuitive, lesson of queuing theory.

Why the finite-source model is different. Here \(\lambda_n\) falls as the queue grows, because broken machines cannot break again. The population is its own regulator, so the system can never be unstable. Applying the ordinary \(M/M/1\) formula with \(\lambda=4(0.1)=0.4\) would give \(L_s=\rho/(1-\rho)=4\) broken machines — four times the truth. Never use an infinite-source formula on a small finite population.

docs.title: 23.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. A birth–death process has \(\lambda_0=2,\lambda_1=1\) and \(\mu_1=\mu_2=3\) (states \(0,1,2\)). Find \(P_0,P_1,P_2\) and \(L_s\). (Answer: \(P_0=\tfrac{9}{17}, P_1=\tfrac{6}{17}, P_2=\tfrac{2}{17}\); \(L_s=\tfrac{10}{17}=0.5882\))
  2. For \(M/M/1\) with \(\lambda=5\)/h, \(\mu=8\)/h, use (3.1) to find \(\Pr[n\ge2]\). (Answer: \(\rho^2=0.3906\))
  3. In a two-server system with \(\lambda_n=\lambda=4\) and \(\mu_n=\min(n,2)\mu\) with \(\mu=3\), compute \(C_0,C_1,C_2,C_3\) and \(P_0\). (Answer: \(1,\ \tfrac43,\ \tfrac89,\ \tfrac{16}{27}\); \(P_0=0.2\))
  4. Repeat Problem 5 with two repairmen (\(\mu_n=\min(n,2)\mu\)). Does the average downtime fall by half? (Answer: \(L_s=0.6896\), \(W_s=2.083\) h — a \(36.8\,\%\) cut, not \(50\,\%\))
  5. Show that for discouraged arrivals with \(\lambda_n=\lambda/(n+1)\), the system is stable for every \(\lambda\), and explain why in one sentence.

docs.title: 23.7 Summary
docs.text:
• A birth–death process changes state by one unit at a time; that single restriction is what makes queues solvable.
  • Read a queue from its rate diagram. Choosing \(\lambda_n\) and \(\mu_n\) selects the model.
  • Use the cut equations \(\lambda_nP_n=\mu_{n+1}P_{n+1}\), never the three-term node equations.
  • General solution: \(P_n=P_0\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\dfrac{\lambda_k}{\mu_{k+1}}\), with \(P_0\) from normalisation. Everything in Lessons 24–29 is a special case.
  • Ergodicity = convergence of \(\sum C_n\). Finite capacity and \(M/M/\infty\) are always stable; \(M/M/1\) needs \(\rho<1\) strictly.
  • Compute \(L_s\) and \(L_q\) by summation, then convert to times with Little's law using \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\), not the nominal \(\lambda\).
  • Finite-source systems (machine repair) have decreasing \(\lambda_n\) and must never be analysed with infinite-source formulas — the error is large and always optimistic in the wrong direction.

Next lesson: L24 — Model I, \((M/M/1):(\infty/\text{FCFS})\), derived in full.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Birth–Death Builder: enter any \(\lambda_n\) and \(\mu_n\), see the rate diagram, the balance equations and the resulting distribution.

docs.title: 21.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Identify the six components of a queuing system.
  2. Read and write Kendall–Lee notation.
  3. Define the standard performance measures \(L_s, L_q, W_s, W_q\).
  4. State and apply Little's Law.
  5. Explain why utilisation below 1 is essential and why congestion grows non-linearly.

docs.title: 21.2 What Is a Queuing System?
docs.text:
Definition. A queuing (waiting-line) system consists of customers arriving at a service facility, possibly waiting, receiving service, and departing.

Why we study it. Waiting is expensive — in customer goodwill, in idle machines, in lost sales — but so is capacity. Queuing theory quantifies the trade-off.

The universal structure.

   Arrivals            Queue                Service              Departures
  ----------->  [ o o o o o ]  ----->  [ Server 1 ]  ----------->
   (rate λ)      (waiting line)         [ Server 2 ]   (rate μ each)
                                        [   ...    ]
                                        [ Server c ]

Examples across domains.

Setting Customers Servers Bank people tellers Hospital A&E patients doctors Factory jobs machines Computer network data packets routers Call centre calls agents Airport aircraft runways Repair shop broken machines technicians

docs.title: The input (arrival) process
docs.text:
Aspect Options Size of source infinite (a bank's customers) or finite (10 machines needing repair) Pattern random (Poisson) or scheduled (appointments) Behaviour patient; or balking (refusing to join a long queue), reneging (leaving after waiting), jockeying (switching lines) Batch or single one at a time, or in groups (a bus arriving at a restaurant)

Definition (Arrival rate \(\lambda\)). The mean number of arrivals per unit time. Mean inter-arrival time \(= 1/\lambda\).

docs.title: The queue (waiting line)
docs.text:
Aspect Options Capacity infinite or finite (\(N\) — a car park, a phone system's hold slots) Number of lines single line, or one per server

A single line feeding all servers is provably better than separate lines: it eliminates the risk of being stuck behind one slow customer while another server idles. This is why banks and airports adopted the snake queue.

docs.title: The queue discipline
docs.text:
Discipline Meaning FCFS / FIFO first come, first served — the default and the fairest LCFS / LIFO last come, first served — a stack; e.g. items on a pallet SIRO service in random order Priority urgent cases first — pre-emptive (interrupt current service) or non-pre-emptive SPT shortest processing time first — minimises average waiting

Important fact. For the standard measures, the discipline does not affect \(L_s\) or \(W_s\) as long as it is non-pre-emptive and independent of service times. It changes who waits, not the average. Priority disciplines change the distribution of waiting, not its mean.

docs.title: The service mechanism
docs.text:
Aspect Options Number of servers \(c\) 1, several, or infinite (self-service) Arrangement parallel (independent servers) or series (stages in sequence) Service-time distribution exponential (M), deterministic (D), Erlang (\(E_k\)), general (G)

Definition (Service rate \(\mu\)). The mean number of customers one busy server can serve per unit time. Mean service time \(= 1/\mu\).

docs.title: System capacity and 2.6 population
docs.text: Covered above under queue capacity and source size.

docs.title: 21.4 Kendall–Lee Notation
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ (a\ /\ b\ /\ c)\ :\ (d\ /\ e\ /\ f)\ } \] Position Meaning Common symbols \(a\) arrival distribution M (Markovian/Poisson), D (deterministic), \(E_k\) (Erlang), G (general) \(b\) service distribution same symbols \(c\) number of servers \(1, 2, \ldots, \infty\) \(d\) system capacity \(\infty\) or \(N\) \(e\) population size \(\infty\) or \(M\) \(f\) queue discipline FCFS, LCFS, SIRO, PRI

"M" stands for Markovian or memoryless — Poisson arrivals and exponential service times.

Common shorthand. \(M/M/1\) alone means \((M/M/1):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})\).

docs.title: The five models on the DSC301 syllabus
docs.text: Model Kendall notation Name Lesson I \((M/M/1):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) single server, infinite queue L24–L25 II \((M/M/1):(N/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) single server, finite capacity L26 III \((M/M/c):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) multi-server, infinite queue L27 IV \((M/M/c):(N/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) multi-server, finite capacity L28 V \((M/M/1):(\infty/\infty/\text{SIRO})\) single server, random order L28

docs.title: 21.5 Performance Measures
docs.text: Symbol Meaning \(\lambda\) mean arrival rate \(\mu\) mean service rate per busy server \(c\) number of servers \(\rho\) utilisation (traffic intensity) \(= \lambda/(c\mu)\) \(P_n\) steady-state probability of exactly \(n\) customers in the system \(P_0\) probability the system is empty \(L_s\) expected number in the system (waiting + being served) \(L_q\) expected number in the queue (waiting only) \(W_s\) expected time in the system \(W_q\) expected waiting time in the queue

docs.title: The stability condition
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \rho = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu} \ <\ 1\ } \]

If \(\rho \ge 1\), arrivals outpace service and the queue grows without bound — no steady state exists. Every formula in Unit III assumes \(\rho < 1\).

docs.title: The relationships
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ L_s = L_q + \frac{\lambda}{\mu} \qquad\text{and}\qquad W_s = W_q + \frac{1}{\mu}\ } \]

In words: system = queue + service. The term \(\lambda/\mu\) is the expected number in service (which equals \(c\rho\)).

docs.title: 21.6 Little's Law
docs.text:
Theorem (Little, 1961). For any queuing system in steady state, whatever the distributions, discipline or number of servers:

\[ \boxed{\ L_s = \lambda\,W_s \qquad\text{and}\qquad L_q = \lambda\,W_q\ } \]

The intuition. A customer spends \(W_s\) in the system. During that time, \(\lambda W_s\) new customers arrive. By the time they leave, on average \(\lambda W_s\) are present. Hence \(L_s = \lambda W_s\).

Why it is remarkable. Little's Law requires no assumptions about arrival or service distributions, the number of servers, or the queue discipline. It holds for \(M/M/1\), \(G/G/c\), priority queues, networks of queues — everything in steady state.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Little's Law is the single most useful result in queuing theory.}\ } \]

Practical uses.

  1. Compute any one of \(L, W, \lambda\) from the other two.
  2. Validate a model — if simulated \(L \ne \lambda W\), there is a bug.
  3. Measure a real system without timing individual customers: count the average number present and divide by the arrival rate.

With finite capacity, use the effective arrival rate \(\lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda(1-P_N)\), since blocked customers never enter (L26).

docs.title: 21.7 Why Congestion Grows Non-Linearly
docs.text:
For \(M/M/1\) (derived in L24):

\[ L_q = \frac{\rho^{2}}{1-\rho} \] \(\rho\) \(L_q\) Interpretation 0.50 0.50 comfortable 0.70 1.63 busy 0.80 3.20 congested 0.90 8.10 severe 0.95 18.05 critical 0.99 98.01 collapse \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Going from 90 \% to 95 \% utilisation MORE THAN DOUBLES the queue.}\ } \]

The \(\frac{1}{1-\rho}\) term explodes as \(\rho\to1\). This single fact explains:

  • why hospitals cannot run at 100 % bed occupancy;
  • why motorways jam suddenly rather than gradually;
  • why "improving utilisation" from 85 % to 95 % is usually a false economy;
  • why manufacturing bottlenecks (L15) should be kept below ~85 %.

The design rule.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Target } \rho \le 0.80\text{--}0.85 \textbf{ for systems where waiting matters.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 1 — Reading and writing Kendall notation
docs.text:
Interpret each notation, and write the notation for the described systems.

(a) \((M/M/3):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) (b) \((M/D/1):(10/\infty/\text{FCFS})\) (c) \((M/M/2):(\infty/8/\text{FCFS})\) (d) A bank with 4 tellers, random arrivals, exponential service, unlimited waiting room, served in order. (e) An automated car wash: appointments every 5 minutes exactly, wash takes exactly 4 minutes, one bay, 3 waiting spaces.

Solution.

(a) \((M/M/3):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})\)

  • Poisson arrivals, exponential service, 3 parallel servers
  • Unlimited queue, unlimited population, first come first served.
  • Example: a bank with 3 tellers and a single snake queue.

(b) \((M/D/1):(10/\infty/\text{FCFS})\)

  • Poisson arrivals, deterministic (constant) service, 1 server
  • System capacity 10 — an 11th arrival is turned away.
  • Example: an automated machine with a fixed cycle time and a 10-place buffer.

(c) \((M/M/2):(\infty/8/\text{FCFS})\)

  • Poisson arrivals, exponential service, 2 servers, unlimited queue
  • Finite population of 8 — e.g. 8 machines that can break down, with 2 repair technicians.
  • Note: with a finite source, the arrival rate falls as more customers are already in the system (fewer machines left to break).

(d) The bank.

\[ \boxed{(M/M/4):(\infty/\infty/\text{FCFS})} \]

(e) The car wash.

  • Arrivals every 5 minutes exactly ⟹ D
  • Service exactly 4 minutes ⟹ D
  • 1 bay ⟹ \(c = 1\)
  • 3 waiting spaces + 1 in service ⟹ capacity 4
\[ \boxed{(D/D/1):(4/\infty/\text{FCFS})} \]

A note on (e). With both arrivals and service deterministic and \(\mu = 15/\text{hr} > \lambda = 12/\text{hr}\), no queue ever forms — each car finishes 1 minute before the next arrives.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Queues are caused by VARIABILITY, not merely by high utilisation.}\ } \]

If arrivals were Poisson at the same mean rate (\(M/D/1\) with \(\rho = 0.8\)), a substantial queue would form. Removing variability is often cheaper than adding capacity — the insight behind appointment systems, scheduled deliveries and level production.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Little's Law in practice
docs.text:
A hospital emergency department sees 60 patients per day. On average 9 patients are present at any time. (a) What is the average length of stay? (b) If a new triage process cuts the average stay to 2.5 hours, how many patients will be present? (c) A consultant claims the department can handle 90 patients/day with 12 present — is this consistent?

Solution.

Given. \(\lambda = 60\)/day \(= 2.5\)/hour, \(L_s = 9\) patients.

(a) Average length of stay. By Little's Law:

\[ W_s = \frac{L_s}{\lambda} = \frac{9}{2.5} = \mathbf{3.6\ \text{hours}} \]

(b) After the improvement. \(W_s = 2.5\) hours, \(\lambda\) unchanged:

\[ L_s = \lambda W_s = 2.5\times2.5 = \mathbf{6.25\ \text{patients}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Reducing stay from 3.6 to 2.5 hours cuts occupancy from 9 to 6.25 — freeing 2.75 bed-spaces.}\ } \]

(c) Checking the consultant's claim. \(\lambda = 90\)/day \(= 3.75\)/hour, \(L_s = 12\):

\[ W_s = \frac{12}{3.75} = \mathbf{3.2\ \text{hours}} \]

Is this consistent? Little's Law is satisfied arithmetically — but it says nothing about whether the system can achieve those numbers.

The real question is capacity. Raising throughput by 50 % (60 → 90) while reducing stay from 3.6 to 3.2 hours means the department must become substantially faster and more heavily loaded. From §6, if utilisation rises from, say, 0.80 to 0.95, waiting time would rise steeply, not fall.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The claim is arithmetically consistent but operationally implausible without added capacity.}\ } \]

What to ask the consultant. "What is the current utilisation, and what will it be at 90 patients/day? If it exceeds 0.9, the queuing formulas predict waiting times will rise sharply, not fall — what capacity is being added to prevent that?"

The general lesson. Little's Law is a constraint, not a prediction. It tells you that \(L\), \(\lambda\) and \(W\) must be mutually consistent; it does not tell you which combinations are achievable.

docs.title: Problem 3 — The non-linearity of congestion
docs.text:
A machine shop has \(\lambda = 8\) jobs/hour and \(\mu = 10\) jobs/hour. (a) Compute \(L_q\) and \(W_q\). (b) Demand rises 12.5 % to 9 jobs/hour — recompute. (c) Comment.

Solution.

(a) At \(\lambda = 8\).

\[ \rho = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8 \] \[ L_q = \frac{\rho^2}{1-\rho} = \frac{0.64}{0.2} = \mathbf{3.2\ \text{jobs}} \] \[ W_q = \frac{L_q}{\lambda} = \frac{3.2}{8} = \mathbf{0.4\ \text{hours} = 24\ \text{minutes}} \]

(b) At \(\lambda = 9\).

\[ \rho = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9 \] \[ L_q = \frac{0.81}{0.1} = \mathbf{8.1\ \text{jobs}} \] \[ W_q = \frac{8.1}{9} = \mathbf{0.9\ \text{hours} = 54\ \text{minutes}} \]

(c) The comparison.

Measure \(\lambda = 8\) \(\lambda = 9\) Change Arrival rate 8 9 +12.5 % Utilisation \(\rho\) 0.80 0.90 +12.5 % Queue length \(L_q\) 3.2 8.1 +153 % Waiting time \(W_q\) 24 min 54 min +125 % \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A 12.5 \% rise in demand caused a 153 \% rise in queue length.}\ } \]

Why. The factor \(\frac{1}{1-\rho}\) went from \(\frac{1}{0.2} = 5\) to \(\frac{1}{0.1} = 10\) — it doubled — while \(\rho^2\) rose only from 0.64 to 0.81.

Push further to \(\lambda = 9.5\):

\[ \rho = 0.95, \qquad L_q = \frac{0.9025}{0.05} = \mathbf{18.05}, \qquad W_q = 1.9\ \text{hours} \]

A further 5.6 % rise in demand more than doubles the queue again.

Management implications.

  1. Capacity planning must be non-linear. Sizing for average demand at high utilisation guarantees poor service.
  2. Small demand increases can be catastrophic near capacity. A shop comfortable at 8 jobs/hour is in crisis at 9.5.
  3. Conversely, small capacity increases pay enormous dividends. Raising \(\mu\) from 10 to 11 at \(\lambda = 9\) gives \(\rho = 0.818\), \(L_q = \frac{0.669}{0.182} = 3.68\) — a 55 % reduction in queue for a 10 % capacity increase.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Near saturation, capacity investment has enormously leveraged returns.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 4 — Choosing the queue discipline
docs.text:
A repair shop serves jobs with these processing times: 2, 8, 3, 12, 5 hours (all present at time 0). Compare FCFS (in the order given) and SPT (shortest processing time first) on total and average waiting time.

Solution.

FCFS — order \(2, 8, 3, 12, 5\).

Job Duration Start Finish Wait 1 2 0 2 0 2 8 2 10 2 3 3 10 13 10 4 12 13 25 13 5 5 25 30 25 Total 50 \[ \bar W_{\text{FCFS}} = \frac{50}{5} = \mathbf{10\ \text{hours}} \]

SPT — order \(2, 3, 5, 8, 12\).

Job Duration Start Finish Wait 1 2 0 2 0 3 3 2 5 2 5 5 5 10 5 2 8 10 18 10 4 12 18 30 18 Total 35 \[ \bar W_{\text{SPT}} = \frac{35}{5} = \mathbf{7\ \text{hours}} \]

Comparison.

Discipline Total wait Mean wait Makespan FCFS 50 h 10 h 30 h SPT 35 h 7 h 30 h \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{SPT cuts mean waiting by 30 \% — and the makespan is IDENTICAL at 30 hours.}\ } \]

Theorem (SPT optimality). On a single machine with all jobs available at time 0, SPT minimises the mean flow time (and hence mean waiting time). Proof by adjacent pairwise interchange, exactly as for Johnson's rule (L14).

Why the makespan is unchanged. The total work is \(2+8+3+12+5 = 30\) hours regardless of order, and the single machine never idles. Sequencing redistributes waiting; it does not create capacity.

The trade-off SPT hides.

Job FCFS wait SPT wait Change 2 (8 h) 2 10 +8 4 (12 h) 13 18 +5 3 (3 h) 10 2 −8 5 (5 h) 25 5 −20 \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{SPT improves the AVERAGE by making LONG jobs wait longer. Short jobs win; long jobs lose.}\ } \]

Practical consequences.

  1. SPT can starve long jobs if new short jobs keep arriving. The standard fix is ageing — increase a job's priority the longer it waits.
  2. Fairness versus efficiency. FCFS is perceived as fair; SPT is more efficient. Many systems use a hybrid (priority classes with FCFS inside each).
  3. This is why hospital triage is not FCFS, and why operating systems use multi-level feedback queues rather than pure SPT.

Connecting to §2.3's claim. The discipline does not change \(L_s\) or \(W_s\) when service times are independent of the discipline — SPT violates this by using the service times to order the queue, which is exactly why it can improve the average.

docs.title: Problem 5 — A complete system-design study
docs.text:
A bank branch is being designed. Customers arrive Poisson at 30/hour. A teller serves exponentially at 12/hour. Staff cost ₹200/hour; customer waiting is valued at ₹150/hour. How many tellers should be employed?

Solution.

Step 1 — the stability requirement.

\[ \rho = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu} = \frac{30}{12c} < 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c > 2.5 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{c \ge 3} \]

With 2 tellers the queue would grow without bound. Any analysis must start at \(c = 3\).

Step 2 — compute the measures for each \(c\) (using the \(M/M/c\) formulas of L27; \(r = \lambda/\mu = 2.5\)).

\(c\) \(\rho\) \(L_q\) \(W_q\) (min) \(L_s\) 3 0.833 3.511 7.02 6.011 4 0.625 0.533 1.07 3.033 5 0.500 0.130 0.26 2.630 6 0.417 0.030 0.06 2.530

Step 3 — the cost analysis.

\[ \text{Total cost per hour} = \underbrace{200c}_{\text{staff}} + \underbrace{150\,L_s}_{\text{waiting}} \]

(Using \(L_s\) — the number in the system — values the customer's whole time in the branch. Using \(L_q\) would value only queueing time; either is defensible, but state which you used.)

\(c\) Staff cost Waiting cost \(150L_s\) Total 3 600 \(150(6.011) = 902\) ₹1 502 4 800 \(150(3.033) = 455\) ₹1 255 ← 5 1000 \(150(2.630) = 395\) ₹1 395 6 1200 \(150(2.530) = 380\) ₹1 580 \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Employ 4 tellers. Total cost ₹1 255/hour.}\ } \]

Step 4 — sensitivity.

If waiting were valued at only ₹80/hour:

\(c\) Staff Waiting Total 3 600 \(80(6.011) = 481\) ₹1 081 ← 4 800 243 ₹1 043 5 1000 210 ₹1 210

At ₹80/hour, \(c = 4\) still wins (₹1 043 versus ₹1 081) — but only just.

If waiting were valued at ₹50/hour:

\[ c=3: 600+301 = ₹901; \qquad c=4: 800+152 = ₹952 \]

Now \(c=3\) wins. The switch point is around ₹65/hour.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The recommendation flips at a waiting valuation of about ₹65/hour. Verify that figure carefully.}\ } \]

Step 5 — service-level checks.

\(c\) \(W_q\) Meets "under 2 minutes"? 3 7.0 min ✗ 4 1.07 min ✓ 5 0.26 min ✓ (over-provisioned)

If the bank has a published service standard of "under 2 minutes' wait", \(c = 4\) is required regardless of the cost analysis — and conveniently it is also the cost optimum.

Step 6 — the recommendation.

"Employ 4 tellers. This minimises total cost at ₹1 255/hour and meets a 2-minute service standard with \(W_q = 1.07\) minutes. Three tellers would run at 83 % utilisation with a 7-minute average wait — technically stable but poor service and, at our assumed waiting valuation, more expensive overall. Note the recommendation is sensitive to the value placed on customer waiting time: below about ₹65/hour, three tellers becomes cheaper."

Caveats to state.

  1. Poisson arrivals assume a constant rate. Real banks have lunchtime peaks. Recommend analysing peak-hour \(\lambda\) separately — at \(\lambda = 45\)/hour, \(c=4\) gives \(\rho = 0.94\) and an unacceptable wait.
  2. Exponential service times assume high variability. If teller times are more regular (\(M/D/c\)), actual queues would be roughly half those predicted — so this analysis is conservative.
  3. Staffing is not continuous. Consider 3 tellers off-peak and 5 at peak, rather than a fixed 4.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Steady-state queuing formulas describe a constant-rate system. Peaked demand needs peak-hour analysis or simulation.}\ } \]

docs.title: 21.9 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Write the Kendall notation for: Poisson arrivals, exponential service, 5 servers, capacity 20, infinite population, FCFS. [Ans: \((M/M/5):(20/\infty/\text{FCFS})\)]
  2. \(\lambda = 15\)/hr, \(L_s = 6\). Find \(W_s\). [Ans: 0.4 h = 24 min]
  3. \(\lambda = 20\)/hr, \(\mu = 25\)/hr, \(c=1\). Find \(\rho\) and \(L_q\). [Ans: 0.8, 3.2]
  4. Why does the queue explode as \(\rho\to1\)?
  5. State Little's Law and one assumption it does NOT require.
  6. \(L_q = 4\), \(\lambda = 10\)/hr. Find \(W_q\) in minutes. [Ans: 24 min]
  7. For \(\lambda=12\), \(\mu=5\), what is the minimum number of servers? [Ans: 3]

docs.title: 21.10 Summary
docs.text:
• A queuing system has six components: input process, queue, discipline, service mechanism, system capacity, population.
  • Kendall–Lee notation \((a/b/c):(d/e/f)\) — arrival dist. / service dist. / servers : capacity / population / discipline. M = Markovian (Poisson arrivals, exponential service).
  • Measures: \(L_s, L_q\) (numbers) and \(W_s, W_q\) (times), with \(L_s = L_q + \lambda/\mu\) and \(W_s = W_q + 1/\mu\).
  • Stability requires \(\rho = \lambda/(c\mu) < 1\); otherwise no steady state exists.
  • Little's Law \(L = \lambda W\) holds for any steady-state system regardless of distributions, servers or discipline — the most useful result in the subject, and a powerful model-validation check.
  • Congestion grows non-linearly: \(L_q = \rho^2/(1-\rho)\) explodes as \(\rho\to1\). Going from 90 % to 95 % utilisation more than doubles the queue. Target \(\rho\le0.85\).
  • Queues are caused by VARIABILITY, not just high utilisation — a \(D/D/1\) system with \(\rho = 0.8\) has no queue at all. Reducing variability is often cheaper than adding capacity.
  • SPT minimises mean waiting but at the cost of starving long jobs; FCFS is fairer. The discipline redistributes waiting, it does not create capacity.

Next lesson: L22 — The Poisson process and the exponential distribution.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Queue Explorer: set \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) and \(c\), and watch \(L_q\), \(W_q\) and the utilisation curve update live, with the \(\rho\to1\) explosion plotted.

docs.title: 37.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State and apply the necessary and sufficient conditions for a single-variable optimum.
  2. Apply the higher-order derivative test when \(f''(x^{*})=0\).
  3. Find stationary points of a multivariable function by solving \(\nabla f=\mathbf{0}\).
  4. Classify them with the Hessian and the leading-principal-minor test.
  5. Solve applied unconstrained optimisation problems and interpret the answers.

docs.title: Necessary condition
docs.text:
Theorem (first-order necessary condition). If \(f\) is differentiable and \(x^{*}\) is a local minimum or maximum in the interior of the domain, then \(f'(x^{*})=0\).

A point with \(f'(x^{*})=0\) is a stationary (or critical) point. The condition is necessary, not sufficient — it is also satisfied at maxima and at inflection points.

Two ways this can mislead. (i) \(f(x)=x^3\) has \(f'(0)=0\) but \(0\) is neither a max nor a min. (ii) \(f(x)=|x|\) has a minimum at \(0\) where \(f'\) does not exist. Non-differentiable points must be checked separately, as must the endpoints of a closed interval.

docs.title: Sufficient condition
docs.text: Theorem (second-order sufficient condition). If \(f'(x^{*})=0\) and $\(f''(x^{*})>0 \Rightarrow x^{*}\text{ is a strict local MINIMUM},\)$ $\(f''(x^{*})<0 \Rightarrow x^{*}\text{ is a strict local MAXIMUM}.\)$ If \(f''(x^{*})=0\) the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: The higher-order test
docs.text:
When \(f''(x^{*})=0\), differentiate until a derivative is non-zero.

Theorem. Suppose \(f'(x^{*})=f''(x^{*})=\dots=f^{(n-1)}(x^{*})=0\) but \(f^{(n)}(x^{*})\ne0\). Then:

\(n\) \(f^{(n)}(x^{*})\) Conclusion even \(>0\) local minimum even \(<0\) local maximum odd any inflection — neither

Why. Taylor's theorem gives \(f(x^{*}+h)-f(x^{*})=\dfrac{f^{(n)}(x^{*})}{n!}h^{n}+o(h^{n})\). If \(n\) is even, \(h^{n}>0\) for both signs of \(h\), so the difference keeps one sign. If \(n\) is odd, \(h^{n}\) changes sign with \(h\), so \(f\) rises on one side and falls on the other.

docs.title: The gradient and the Hessian
docs.text:
\[ abla f= egin{pmatrix}\partial f/\partial x_1\ \vdots\ \partial f/\partial x_n\end{pmatrix}, \qquad abla^{2}f=H=\left[ rac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} ight]_{n imes n}\]

\(H\) is symmetric whenever the second partials are continuous (Young's theorem).

Necessary condition. \( abla f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=\mathbf{0}\).

Sufficient conditions. With \( abla f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=\mathbf{0}\),

\(H(\mathbf{x}^{*})\) Conclusion positive definite strict local minimum negative definite strict local maximum indefinite saddle point semi-definite (singular) inconclusive

docs.title: Testing definiteness
docs.text:
Leading principal minors (Sylvester's criterion). Let \(D_k\) be the determinant of the top-left \(k\times k\) block.

  • Positive definite \(\iff D_1>0,\ D_2>0,\ \dots,\ D_n>0\) — all positive.
  • Negative definite \(\iff D_1<0,\ D_2>0,\ D_3<0,\dots\) — signs alternate, starting negative.
  • Otherwise, if \(\det H\ne0\), the matrix is indefinite.

Eigenvalues give the same answer and are more informative: all \(\lambda_i>0\) (definite positive), all \(<0\) (definite negative), mixed signs (indefinite), some zero (semi-definite, inconclusive).

docs.title: The convexity shortcut
docs.text:
If \(f\) is convex on the whole domain (Lesson 36), then \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=\mathbf{0}\) is both necessary and sufficient for a global minimum — no second-order test at the point is needed, and no other stationary point can be better.

\[\boxed{\text{convex} + \nabla f=\mathbf{0}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{global minimum}}\]

docs.title: Problem 1 — The complete single-variable procedure
docs.text:
Find and classify all stationary points of \(f(x)=x^{3}-3x+1\), and find the global optimum on \([-3,3]\).

Solution.

Step 1 — stationary points.

\[f'(x)=3x^{2}-3=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=\pm1\]

Step 2 — classify.

\[f''(x)=6x:\qquad f''(1)=6>0,\qquad f''(-1)=-6<0\] \[\boxed{x=1\text{ is a local MINIMUM},\ f(1)=1-3+1=-1}\] \[\boxed{x=-1\text{ is a local MAXIMUM},\ f(-1)=-1+3+1=3}\]

Step 3 — the global optimum on \([-3,3]\) requires the endpoints too.

\(x\) \(-3\) \(-1\) \(1\) \(3\) \(f(x)\) \(-17\) \(3\) \(-1\) \(19\) \[\text{Global minimum } f=-17\text{ at }x=-3;\qquad \text{global maximum } f=19\text{ at }x=3\]

Interpretation. Neither global optimum is at a stationary point. On a closed interval the optimum may sit at a boundary, where the derivative need not vanish. Forgetting the endpoints is the most common error in single-variable optimisation, and it is the reason Unit IV's constrained theory (Lessons 43–44) exists at all: a constraint is exactly a boundary that the derivative test cannot see.

docs.title: Problem 2 — When the second derivative vanishes
docs.text:
Classify the stationary point at \(x=0\) for (a) \(f(x)=x^{4}\), (b) \(g(x)=x^{5}\), (c) \(h(x)=-x^{6}\).

Solution.

(a) \(f(x)=x^{4}\).

\[f'=4x^{3},\ f''=12x^{2},\ f'''=24x,\ f^{(4)}=24\]

At \(x=0\): \(f'=f''=f'''=0\) and \(f^{(4)}=24\ne0\). Here \(n=4\), even, and \(f^{(4)}>0\).

\[\boxed{\text{local (indeed global) MINIMUM}}\]

(b) \(g(x)=x^{5}\).

\[g'=5x^{4},\ g''=20x^{3},\ g'''=60x^{2},\ g^{(4)}=120x,\ g^{(5)}=120\]

First non-zero derivative at \(0\) is the 5th, which is odd.

\[\boxed{\text{INFLECTION — neither maximum nor minimum}}\]

Indeed \(g(-0.1)=-10^{-5}<0<10^{-5}=g(0.1)\): the function passes straight through.

(c) \(h(x)=-x^{6}\). First non-zero derivative is the 6th, \(h^{(6)}=-720<0\); \(n=6\) is even.

\[\boxed{\text{local (and global) MAXIMUM}}\]

Interpretation. Note that in case (a) the minimum is perfectly genuine but completely invisible to the second-derivative test. Numerically this matters: near a "flat" minimum like \(x^4\), the gradient is tiny over a wide region, so gradient-based algorithms crawl. A vanishing second derivative signals a hard problem for an algorithm, not just for the classification.

docs.title: Problem 3 — A two-variable minimum
docs.text:
Find and classify the stationary points of

\[f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+x_1x_2-6x_1-9x_2+20.\]

Solution.

Step 1 — gradient.

\[\nabla f=\begin{pmatrix}2x_1+x_2-6\\ x_1+2x_2-9\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{0}\]

Step 2 — solve. From the first, \(x_2=6-2x_1\). Substituting:

\[x_1+2(6-2x_1)=9\ \Rightarrow\ x_1+12-4x_1=9\ \Rightarrow\ -3x_1=-3\ \Rightarrow\ x_1=1\] \[x_2=6-2(1)=4\] \[\mathbf{x}^{*}=(1,4)\]

Step 3 — Hessian.

\[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_1=2>0,\qquad D_2=\det H=4-1=3>0\]

Positive definite (eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\)).

\[\boxed{(1,4)\text{ is a strict local minimum}}\]

Step 4 — is it global? \(H\) is constant and positive definite everywhere, so \(f\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\). By Lesson 36's theorem the local minimum is the unique global minimum.

\[f(1,4)=1+16+4-6-36+20=\mathbf{-1}\]

Check by an independent route — completing the square.

\[f=\left(x_1+\tfrac{x_2}{2}-3\right)^{2}+\tfrac34\left(x_2-4\right)^{2}-1\]

a sum of two non-negative terms minus \(1\), minimised at \(x_2=4\) and \(x_1+2-3=0\), i.e. \(x_1=1\), with value \(-1\) ✓. Completing the square is a reliable check on any two-variable quadratic.

docs.title: Problem 4 — A saddle and a genuine maximum
docs.text:
Find and classify all stationary points of

\[f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^{3}+x_2^{3}-3x_1x_2.\]

Solution.

Step 1 — gradient.

\[\nabla f=\begin{pmatrix}3x_1^{2}-3x_2\\ 3x_2^{2}-3x_1\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{0} \ \Rightarrow\ x_2=x_1^{2}\ \text{ and }\ x_1=x_2^{2}\]

Substituting: \(x_1=(x_1^{2})^{2}=x_1^{4}\), so \(x_1(x_1^{3}-1)=0\), giving \(x_1=0\) or \(x_1=1\).

\[\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=(0,0),\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(2)}=(1,1)\]

Step 2 — Hessian.

\[H(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}6x_1&-3\\-3&6x_2\end{pmatrix}\]

At \((0,0)\):

\[H=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3\\-3&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det H=0-9=-9<0\]

Indefinite (eigenvalues \(\pm3\)).

\[\boxed{(0,0)\text{ is a SADDLE POINT}}\]

At \((1,1)\):

\[H=\begin{pmatrix}6&-3\\-3&6\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_1=6>0,\qquad D_2=36-9=27>0\]

Positive definite (eigenvalues \(3\) and \(9\)).

\[\boxed{(1,1)\text{ is a strict local MINIMUM},\qquad f(1,1)=1+1-3=-1}\]

Step 3 — global? No. \(H\) depends on \(\mathbf{x}\) and is indefinite at the origin, so \(f\) is not convex and Lesson 36's theorem does not apply. Indeed along \(x_2=0\), \(f=x_1^{3}\to-\infty\) as \(x_1\to-\infty\): the function is unbounded below and has no global minimum at all.

Interpretation. This example carries the central warning of unconstrained optimisation. An algorithm started near \((1,1)\) converges there and reports \(\nabla f=\mathbf{0}\) with a positive-definite Hessian — a certificate of a local minimum. That certificate says nothing whatever about the rest of \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\), where the function falls without bound. Local optimality is all that gradient-based methods can ever deliver on a non-convex problem.

docs.title: Problem 5 — An applied problem: profit maximisation
docs.text:
A firm makes two products. Selling \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) units per week yields a weekly profit

\[P(x_1,x_2)=100x_1+120x_2-2x_1^{2}-3x_2^{2}-2x_1x_2\quad(₹\text{ hundreds}).\]

Find the profit-maximising output and prove it is the global maximum. Interpret the cross-term.

Solution.

Step 1 — gradient.

\[\frac{\partial P}{\partial x_1}=100-4x_1-2x_2=0,\qquad \frac{\partial P}{\partial x_2}=120-6x_2-2x_1=0\]

Step 2 — solve.

\[2x_1+x_2=50 \tag{i}\] \[x_1+3x_2=60 \tag{ii}\]

From (i), \(x_2=50-2x_1\). Substituting into (ii):

\[x_1+150-6x_1=60\ \Rightarrow\ -5x_1=-90\ \Rightarrow\ x_1=18,\qquad x_2=50-36=14\] \[\boxed{x_1^{*}=18,\quad x_2^{*}=14}\]

Step 3 — Hessian.

\[H=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-6\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_1=-4<0,\qquad D_2=24-4=20>0\]

Signs alternate starting negative \(\Rightarrow\) negative definite \(\Rightarrow\) \(P\) is strictly concave, and since \(H\) is constant this holds everywhere.

\[\boxed{(18,14)\text{ is the UNIQUE GLOBAL maximum}}\]

Step 4 — the profit.

\[P=100(18)+120(14)-2(324)-3(196)-2(18)(14)\] \[=1800+1680-648-588-504=\mathbf{₹1740\text{ hundred}}=₹1{,}74{,}000\text{ per week}\]

Interpretation of the cross-term.
