The \(-2x_1x_2\) term means the products compete: raising \(x_2\) lowers the marginal profit of \(x_1\) by \(2\) per unit, as they draw on the same market or the same capacity. Because of it the products cannot be planned separately. Ignoring the interaction — solving \(\partial P/\partial x_1=0\) with \(x_2\) treated as fixed at \(0\) — would give \(x_1=25\), \(x_2=20\) and a computed profit of

\[P(25,20)=2500+2400-1250-1200-1000=₹1450\text{ hundred},\]

which is \(₹29{,}000\) a week worse than the true optimum. Interaction terms are precisely what single-variable reasoning cannot see, and they are why multivariable optimality conditions are needed rather than a sequence of one-variable ones.

docs.title: 37.5 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Classify the stationary points of \(f(x)=2x^{3}-9x^{2}+12x-3\). (Answer: \(f'=6(x-1)(x-2)\); \(x=1\) local max \(f=2\); \(x=2\) local min \(f=1\))
  2. Classify \(x=0\) for \(f(x)=x^{6}-x^{4}\) — take care. (Answer: \(f'=6x^5-4x^3=2x^3(3x^2-2)\); at \(0\) the first non-zero derivative is \(f^{(4)}(0)=-24<0\), \(n=4\) even, so \(x=0\) is a local maximum; global minima at \(x=\pm\sqrt{2/3}\) with \(f=-4/27\))
  3. Find and classify the stationary point of \(f=3x_1^{2}+2x_2^{2}-4x_1x_2+6x_1-8x_2\). (Answer: \(\nabla f=0\) at \((1,3)\); \(H=\begin{pmatrix}6&-4\\-4&4\end{pmatrix}\), \(D_1=6>0\), \(D_2=8>0\) — strict global minimum, \(f=-9\))
  4. Show that \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^{2}-4x_1x_2+x_2^{2}\) has a saddle at the origin, and find two directions along which \(f\) increases and decreases. (Answer: \(D_2=1-4=-3<0\); \(f\) rises along \(x_2=0\) and falls along \(x_1=x_2\), where \(f=-2x_1^2\))
  5. An open-topped box is made from a \(12\times12\) cm sheet by cutting squares of side \(x\) from the corners. Maximise the volume. (Answer: \(V=x(12-2x)^2\), \(V'=(12-2x)(12-6x)\), so \(x=2\); \(V''(2)=-48<0\); \(V_{\max}=2(8)^2=128\) cm³)

docs.title: 37.6 Summary
docs.text:
• Necessary: \(f'(x^{*})=0\) in one variable, \( abla f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=\mathbf{0}\) in several. This is satisfied at maxima, minima, saddles and inflections alike.
  • Sufficient (1-D): \(f''>0\) minimum, \(f''<0\) maximum. If \(f''=0\), use the higher-order test: first non-zero \(f^{(n)}\) with \(n\) even gives an extremum (sign of \(f^{(n)}\) decides which), \(n\) odd gives an inflection.
  • Sufficient (\(n\)-D): \(H\) positive definite \(\Rightarrow\) minimum; negative definite \(\Rightarrow\) maximum; indefinite \(\Rightarrow\) saddle; singular \(\Rightarrow\) inconclusive.
  • Sylvester's test: all leading minors positive \(\Rightarrow\) positive definite; alternating from negative \(\Rightarrow\) negative definite.
  • If \(f\) is convex everywhere, \( abla f=\mathbf{0}\) alone certifies a global minimum. Check convexity first — it is the cheapest possible strengthening of a result.
  • On a closed interval or bounded region, check the boundary: the global optimum is often there, where no derivative vanishes. This is the gap that Lessons 43–44 close.
  • Cross-terms couple the variables. Optimising one variable at a time gives the wrong answer whenever \(\partial^{2}f/\partial x_1\partial x_2 e0\).

Next lesson: L38 — One-dimensional minimisation: bracketing and elimination methods.

Practise now: unit4-nlp-search-lab.html → Stationary Point Finder: enter a function of one or two variables, get its gradient, Hessian, eigenvalues and a classification of every stationary point, plotted on a contour map.

docs.title: Lesson 43: Constrained Optimisation: Graphical Solution and Lagrange Multipliers
43.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Solve a two-variable constrained problem graphically using the tangency condition.
  2. Form the Lagrangian and derive the first-order conditions for equality constraints.
  3. Interpret \(\lambda\) as the shadow price — the rate of change of \(f^{*}\) with the RHS.
  4. Apply the bordered Hessian test to classify a constrained stationary point.
  5. Extend the method to several equality constraints.

docs.title: 43.2 The Problem and the Geometry
docs.text:
\[\begin{aligned} \text{minimise (or maximise)}\quad & f(\mathbf{x})\\ \text{subject to}\quad & h_j(\mathbf{x})=0,\quad j=1,\dots,p\quad (p<n) \end{aligned}\]

Lesson 37's condition \(\nabla f=\mathbf{0}\) no longer applies: the constrained optimum is generally at a point where the gradient is not zero, because moving downhill would leave the feasible set.

docs.title: The tangency condition
docs.text:
x2
      |        contours of f
      |     _________
      |    /  ______ \        h(x)=0
      |   /  /  __  \ \      /
      |  |  |  ( * ) |  |---/------
      |  |  |   \__/ |  |  /  <- tangency: the constraint curve
      |   \  \______/  / /       just touches a contour
      |____\__________/_/________ x1

At a constrained optimum the constraint curve is tangent to a contour of \(f\). If it crossed a contour, one could slide along the constraint to a lower contour, so the point would not be optimal.

Tangency means the two curves have parallel normals:

\[\boxed{\ \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=-\lambda\,\nabla h(\mathbf{x}^{*})\ }\tag{1.1}\]

for some scalar \(\lambda\). The sign and the symbol are conventions; the content is parallelism.

docs.title: 43.3 The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
docs.text:
Definition (Lagrangian). For one constraint, $\(L(\mathbf{x},\lambda)=f(\mathbf{x})+\lambda\,h(\mathbf{x})\)$ and in general $\(L(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\lambda)=f(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lambda_j h_j(\mathbf{x}).\)$

First-order necessary conditions. At a constrained optimum, $\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i}=0\ (i=1,\dots,n),\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \lambda_j}=h_j(\mathbf{x})=0\ (j=1,\dots,p).\)$

The second group simply restates the constraints, so the Lagrangian converts a constrained problem in \(n\) variables into an unconstrained one in \(n+p\) variables. That single idea is the whole method.

A caution — the constraint qualification. The conditions require the constraint gradients \(\nabla h_j(\mathbf{x}^{*})\) to be linearly independent. Where they are not (a cusp, or duplicated constraints), (1.1) can fail even at a genuine optimum. This regularity assumption reappears, more prominently, in Lesson 44.

docs.title: The meaning of λ
docs.text:
Theorem (sensitivity). If the constraint is \(h(\mathbf{x})=b\) and \(f^{*}(b)\) is the optimal value, then $\(\boxed{\ \frac{df^{*}}{db}=-\lambda\ }\tag{2.1}\)$ (with the sign convention \(L=f+\lambda(h-b)\)).

\(|\lambda|\) is therefore the shadow price of the constraint — the improvement in the objective per unit of relaxation. This is precisely the dual variable of Lesson 7, now in a non-linear setting, and it is usually the number a decision-maker actually wants.

docs.title: 43.4 Second-Order Conditions: the Bordered Hessian
docs.text:
The first-order conditions locate candidates; they do not say whether a candidate is a minimum, a maximum or neither. The test uses the bordered Hessian:

\[\bar H=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_2}\\[6pt] \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x_1^{2}} & \dfrac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}\\[6pt] \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x_2\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x_2^{2}} \end{pmatrix}\]

Test for \(n=2\), \(p=1\). $\(\det\bar H<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{constrained local MINIMUM},\)$ $\(\det\bar H>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{constrained local MAXIMUM}.\)$

Note the reversed signs compared with the ordinary Hessian test of Lesson 37 — a standard source of error. The reason is that the test is really about the sign of \(\mathbf{d}^{T}\nabla^{2}L\,\mathbf{d}\) restricted to directions \(\mathbf{d}\) tangent to the constraint, and the border encodes that restriction with a sign flip.

Shortcut. If \(f\) is convex and the constraints are linear, the feasible set is convex and any stationary point of \(L\) is a global minimum. No bordered Hessian is needed. This covers most problems met in practice, including all of §4 below except Problem 2.

docs.title: Problem 1 — The basic method
docs.text:
Minimise \(f=x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}\) subject to \(x_1+x_2=10\).

Solution.

Step 1 — the Lagrangian.

\[L=x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+\lambda(x_1+x_2-10)\]

Step 2 — first-order conditions.

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_1}=2x_1+\lambda=0,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_2}=2x_2+\lambda=0,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \lambda}=x_1+x_2-10=0\]

Step 3 — solve. The first two give \(x_1=x_2=-\lambda/2\). Substituting into the third: \(-\lambda=10\), so \(\lambda=-10\) and

\[\boxed{x_1^{*}=x_2^{*}=5,\qquad f^{*}=25+25=50,\qquad \lambda=-10}\]

Step 4 — verify with the bordered Hessian. \(\nabla h=(1,1)\) and \(\nabla^{2}L=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\):

\[\det\bar H=\det\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\1&2&0\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix} =0(4)-1(2-0)+1(0-2)=-4<0\ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{minimum}\ \checkmark\]

Step 5 — interpret \(\lambda\). By (2.1), \(\dfrac{df^{*}}{db}=-\lambda=10\). Check directly: with \(x_1+x_2=b\) the optimum is \(x_1=x_2=b/2\) and \(f^{*}=b^{2}/2\), so \(df^{*}/db=b=10\) at \(b=10\) ✓.

Geometric reading. The contours of \(f\) are circles centred at the origin; the constraint is a straight line. The smallest circle touching the line does so at the foot of the perpendicular from the origin, which is \((5,5)\). The Lagrange conditions are the algebra of that tangency.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Maximisation with three variables
docs.text:
Maximise \(f=x_1x_2x_3\) subject to \(x_1+x_2+x_3=12\), with \(x_i>0\).

Solution.

\[L=x_1x_2x_3+\lambda(x_1+x_2+x_3-12)\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_1}=x_2x_3+\lambda=0,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_2}=x_1x_3+\lambda=0,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_3}=x_1x_2+\lambda=0\]

Subtracting the first two: \(x_3(x_2-x_1)=0\), and since \(x_3>0\), \(x_1=x_2\). Similarly \(x_2=x_3\). The constraint then gives \(3x_1=12\):

\[\boxed{x_1^{*}=x_2^{*}=x_3^{*}=4,\qquad f^{*}=64,\qquad \lambda=-16}\]

Interpretation. This is the classical result that a product is maximised when the factors are equal — the AM–GM inequality, recovered by calculus. It answers the practical question "what rectangular box of given total edge length has the largest volume?": a cube.

The multiplier \(\lambda=-16\) says that one extra unit of total length would raise the maximum volume by \(16\). Check: with total \(13\) the optimum is \((13/3)^{3}=81.37\), an increase of \(17.37\) — close to \(16\), the difference being second-order curvature. \(\lambda\) is a derivative, so it is exact only for infinitesimal changes.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Sensitivity in action
docs.text:
Minimise \(f=4x_1^{2}+5x_2^{2}\) subject to \(2x_1+3x_2=6\). Then predict the optimum for a right-hand side of \(7\) and check.

Solution.

\[L=4x_1^{2}+5x_2^{2}+\lambda(2x_1+3x_2-6)\] \[8x_1+2\lambda=0\ \Rightarrow\ x_1=-\frac{\lambda}{4};\qquad 10x_2+3\lambda=0\ \Rightarrow\ x_2=-\frac{3\lambda}{10}\]

Substituting into the constraint:

\[2\left(-\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)+3\left(-\frac{3\lambda}{10}\right) =-\frac{\lambda}{2}-\frac{9\lambda}{10}=-\frac{14\lambda}{10}=6 \ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=-\frac{30}{7}=-4.28571\] \[\boxed{x_1^{*}=\frac{15}{14}=1.07143,\quad x_2^{*}=\frac{9}{7}=1.28571,\quad f^{*}=\frac{90}{7}=12.85714}\]

Check the objective. \(4(1.07143)^{2}+5(1.28571)^{2}=4.59184+8.26531=12.85714\) ✓

Prediction for \(b=7\). \(\dfrac{df^{*}}{db}=-\lambda=\dfrac{30}{7}=4.28571\), so

\[f^{*}(7)\approx12.85714+4.28571=17.14286\]

Exact answer. Solving again with \(b=7\) (or noting \(f^{*}(b)=\tfrac{5}{14}b^{2}\)):

\[f^{*}(7)=\frac{5}{14}(49)=17.50000\]

Interpretation. The linear prediction is \(17.143\) against the true \(17.500\) — an error of \(2\,\%\) for a \(17\,\%\) change in the right-hand side. \(\lambda\) gives the tangent, and the tangent under-predicts for a convex \(f^{*}\). Exactly as with the 100 % rule of Lesson 7, a shadow price is reliable for small changes and must be recomputed for large ones. Here \(f^{*}\) is quadratic in \(b\), so the curvature shows up immediately.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Two constraints
docs.text:
Minimise \(f=x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+x_3^{2}\) subject to \(x_1+x_2+x_3=9\) and \(x_1-x_2=1\).

Solution. Two constraints require two multipliers:

\[L=x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}+x_3^{2}+\lambda_1(x_1+x_2+x_3-9)+\lambda_2(x_1-x_2-1)\] \[2x_1+\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0,\qquad 2x_2+\lambda_1-\lambda_2=0,\qquad 2x_3+\lambda_1=0\]

From these, \(x_3=-\lambda_1/2\) and \(x_1+x_2=-\lambda_1\) (adding the first two), so \(x_1+x_2=2x_3\). With \(x_1+x_2+x_3=9\): \(3x_3=9\), giving \(x_3=3\), \(x_1+x_2=6\). Combined with \(x_1-x_2=1\):

\[\boxed{x_1^{*}=3.5,\quad x_2^{*}=2.5,\quad x_3^{*}=3,\qquad f^{*}=12.25+6.25+9=27.5}\]

Back-substituting: \(\lambda_1=-2x_3=-6\); then \(2(3.5)-6+\lambda_2=0\) gives \(\lambda_2=-1\).

Interpretation of the two multipliers.

  • \(-\lambda_1=6\): relaxing the total from \(9\) to \(10\) would raise \(f^{*}\) by about \(6\) — costly, since \(f\) is being minimised and a larger total forces larger squares.
  • \(-\lambda_2=1\): relaxing \(x_1-x_2=1\) to \(=2\) would raise \(f^{*}\) by about \(1\).

The second constraint is six times less binding than the first. With several constraints, the multipliers immediately rank them by importance, which is usually the most valuable output of the calculation — the same insight as the shadow-price analysis of Lesson 7.

Check the constraint qualification. \(\nabla h_1=(1,1,1)\) and \(\nabla h_2=(1,-1,0)\) are linearly independent ✓, so the conditions are valid.

docs.title: Problem 5 — An applied problem: least-cost design
docs.text:
A closed cylindrical can must hold \(V=1000\) cm³. Material costs \(₹2\) per cm² for the curved surface and \(₹3\) per cm² for each circular end. Minimise the cost.

Solution.

Step 1 — formulate. With radius \(r\) and height \(h\):

\[\text{minimise } C=2(2\pi rh)+3(2\pi r^{2})=4\pi rh+6\pi r^{2}\] \[\text{subject to } \pi r^{2}h=1000\]

Step 2 — Lagrangian.

\[L=4\pi rh+6\pi r^{2}+\lambda(\pi r^{2}h-1000)\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=4\pi h+12\pi r+2\lambda\pi rh=0 \tag{i}\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}=4\pi r+\lambda\pi r^{2}=0 \tag{ii}\]

Step 3 — solve. From (ii), dividing by \(\pi r\ne0\): \(4+\lambda r=0\), so \(\lambda=-\dfrac{4}{r}\).

Substituting into (i) and dividing by \(\pi\): \(4h+12r+2\left(-\dfrac4r\right)rh=0\), i.e.

\[4h+12r-8h=0\ \Rightarrow\ 12r=4h\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{h=3r}\]

Step 4 — apply the volume constraint. \(\pi r^{2}(3r)=1000\), so

\[r^{3}=\frac{1000}{3\pi}=106.1033\ \Rightarrow\ r^{*}=4.7342\text{ cm},\qquad h^{*}=14.2025\text{ cm}\] \[C^{*}=4\pi(4.7342)(14.2025)+6\pi(4.7342)^{2}=844.92+422.46=\mathbf{₹1267.38}\] \[\lambda=-\frac{4}{4.7342}=-0.84492\]

Step 5 — interpret.

  • The shape rule \(h=3r\) is independent of the volume. Whatever the required capacity, the optimal can has height three times its radius. Notice too that \(h/r=3=2\times(3/2)\): the ratio is exactly twice the ratio of end cost to side cost. With equal costs the rule becomes \(h=2r\) — the familiar result that the cheapest can is as tall as it is wide.
  • \(-\lambda=0.8449\) says that requiring one extra cm³ of capacity costs about \(₹0.84\). For a \(10\,\%\) larger can (\(100\) cm³ more) the linear estimate is \(₹84.49\); the exact recomputation gives \(r=4.8870\), \(h=14.6609\), \(C=₹1350.53\), an increase of \(₹83.14\). The tangent over-predicts by \(1.6\,\%\) because \(C^{*}\propto V^{2/3}\) is concave in \(V\).
  • The cost splits \(₹844.92\) on the side and \(₹422.46\) on the ends: exactly \(2:1\). That is not a coincidence — it follows from \(h=3r\) and is the constrained analogue of the "equal costs at the optimum" property of the EOQ in Lesson 31.

docs.title: 43.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Minimise \(f=x_1^{2}+2x_2^{2}\) subject to \(x_1+x_2=6\). (Answer: \(\lambda=-8\), \(x^{*}=(4,2)\), \(f^{*}=24\))
  2. Maximise \(f=x_1x_2\) subject to \(2x_1+3x_2=12\). (Answer: \(x^{*}=(3,2)\), \(f^{*}=6\), \(\lambda=-1\))
  3. Find the point on the plane \(x_1+2x_2+3x_3=14\) closest to the origin. (Answer: minimise \(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\); \(x^{*}=(1,2,3)\), distance \(\sqrt{14}=3.742\))
  4. In Problem 3 of §4, use \(\lambda\) to predict \(f^{*}\) when \(b=6.5\), and compare with the exact value. (Answer: predicted \(12.857+0.5(4.286)=15.000\); exact \(\tfrac{5}{14}(42.25)=15.089\) — a \(0.6\,\%\) error)
  5. A rectangular box without a lid has volume \(32\) m³. Minimise its surface area. (Answer: \(L=W=4\), \(H=2\); area \(=48\) m²)

docs.title: 43.7 Summary
docs.text:
• At a constrained optimum the constraint curve is tangent to a contour of \(f\), i.e. \(\nabla f=-\lambda\nabla h\).
  • The Lagrangian \(L=f+\sum_j\lambda_jh_j\) converts a constrained problem in \(n\) variables into an unconstrained one in \(n+p\); setting \(\partial L/\partial\lambda_j=0\) just restates the constraints.
  • \(\boxed{df^{*}/db=-\lambda}\): \(|\lambda|\) is the shadow price, the non-linear counterpart of the LP dual variable. It is a tangent, so it is reliable only for small changes.
  • With several constraints, the multipliers rank the constraints by how binding they are — usually the most useful output.
  • The bordered Hessian classifies the candidate, with signs reversed relative to Lesson 37: \(\det\bar H<0\) is a minimum for \(n=2\), \(p=1\).
  • Shortcut: convex \(f\) with linear constraints \(\Rightarrow\) any stationary point of \(L\) is a global minimum, and no second-order test is needed.
  • The constraint qualification — linearly independent constraint gradients — is required for the conditions to be valid.
  • Equality constraints only. Inequalities need Lesson 44.

Next lesson: L44 — the Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions for inequality constraints.

Practise now: unit4-nlp-search-lab.html → Lagrange Lab: drag a constraint line across a contour map and watch the tangency point and the value of \(\lambda\) update live.

docs.title: 7.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Construct the dual of any LP.
  2. State and apply weak duality, strong duality and complementary slackness.
  3. Interpret dual variables as shadow prices and use them for economic decisions.
  4. Compute ranging on objective coefficients and right-hand sides.
  5. Apply the 100 % rule for simultaneous changes.

docs.title: 7.2 The Dual Problem
docs.text: Every LP (the primal) has a companion LP (the dual). They describe the same situation from opposite viewpoints: the primal allocates resources to activities; the dual prices those resources.

docs.title: The construction
docs.text:
Primal (canonical maximisation):

\[ \max\ Z = \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_jx_j \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j \le b_i\ (i=1..m), \quad x_j\ge0 \]

Dual:

\[ \min\ W = \sum_{i=1}^{m} b_iy_i \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{ij}y_i \ge c_j\ (j=1..n), \quad y_i\ge0 \]

In words. Transpose everything.

Primal Dual \(\max\) \(\min\) \(m\) constraints \(m\) variables \(n\) variables \(n\) constraints objective coefficients \(\vec c\) right-hand sides \(\vec c\) right-hand sides \(\vec b\) objective coefficients \(\vec b\) constraint matrix \(A\) \(A^{T}\) \(\le\) constraints \(\ge\) constraints

docs.title: The full correspondence rules
docs.text:
Primal (max) Dual (min) constraint \(\le\) variable \(\ge 0\) constraint \(\ge\) variable \(\le 0\) constraint \(=\) variable unrestricted variable \(\ge 0\) constraint \(\ge\) variable \(\le 0\) constraint \(\le\) variable unrestricted constraint \(=\)

Theorem. The dual of the dual is the primal.

docs.title: Weak duality
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(\vec x\) is feasible for the primal (max) and \(\vec y\) is feasible for the dual (min), then

\[ \boxed{\ \vec c^{T}\vec x \ \le\ \vec b^{T}\vec y\ } \]

Proof.

\[ \vec c^{T}\vec x \ \le\ (A^{T}\vec y)^{T}\vec x = \vec y^{T}A\vec x \ \le\ \vec y^{T}\vec b \]

The first inequality uses the dual constraints \(A^{T}\vec y \ge \vec c\) with \(\vec x\ge0\); the second uses the primal constraints \(A\vec x\le\vec b\) with \(\vec y\ge0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollaries.

  • Any dual-feasible \(\vec y\) gives an upper bound on the primal optimum — useful for certifying near-optimality.
  • If the primal is unbounded, the dual is infeasible (and vice versa).

docs.title: Strong duality
docs.text:
Theorem. If either problem has a finite optimum, so does the other, and

\[ \boxed{\ Z^{*}_{\text{primal}} \ =\ W^{*}_{\text{dual}}\ } \]

The four possible outcome pairs.

Primal Dual Possible? finite optimum finite optimum ✓ (the usual case) unbounded infeasible ✓ infeasible unbounded ✓ infeasible infeasible ✓ (rare but possible) finite infeasible/unbounded ✗ impossible

docs.title: Complementary slackness
docs.text:
Theorem. \(\vec x^{*}\) and \(\vec y^{*}\) are optimal for their respective problems iff

\[ \boxed{\ y_i^{*}\left(b_i - \sum_j a_{ij}x_j^{*}\right) = 0 \quad\text{for all } i\ } \] \[ \boxed{\ x_j^{*}\left(\sum_i a_{ij}y_i^{*} - c_j\right) = 0 \quad\text{for all } j\ } \]

In words — the two rules that matter.

\[ \textbf{Rule 1: } \ \text{slack}_i > 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ y_i^{*} = 0 \] \[ \textbf{Rule 2: } \ y_i^{*} > 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{constraint } i \text{ is binding} \]

The economic reading. A resource that is not fully used has zero marginal value. If you have idle machine hours, an extra machine hour is worth nothing.

Symmetrically: an activity that is used (\(x_j > 0\)) must exactly break even at the shadow prices — its dual constraint holds with equality.

docs.title: 7.4 Shadow Prices
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ y_i^{*} = \frac{\partial Z^{*}}{\partial b_i}\ } \]

The marginal value of one extra unit of resource \(i\).

Where to read them. In the final simplex tableau, \(y_i = (z_j - c_j)\) in the column of slack \(s_i\).

Four practical uses.

  1. Purchasing. Buy an extra unit if its price is below \(y_i\).
  2. Pricing. \(y_i\) is the internal transfer price of the resource.
  3. Priorities. The largest \(y_i\) identifies the tightest bottleneck.
  4. Product costing. A new product is worth introducing only if its revenue exceeds \(\sum_i a_{i,\text{new}}y_i\) — its imputed resource cost.

docs.title: Ranging an objective coefficient c_j
docs.text:
For a NON-BASIC variable \(x_j\). It stays non-basic (so the plan is unchanged) while

\[ c_j \ \le\ z_j \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad c_j \le c_j^{\text{current}} + (z_j - c_j) \]

For a BASIC variable \(x_j\). Changing \(c_j\) alters the whole \(z_k - c_k\) row. The basis stays optimal while, for every non-basic \(k\),

\[ z_k - c_k + \Delta c_j\,\alpha_{jk} \ \ge\ 0 \]

where \(\alpha_{jk}\) is the entry in row \(x_j\), column \(k\) of the final tableau. Solving gives

\[ \max_{k:\ \alpha_{jk}<0}\left\{\frac{-(z_k-c_k)}{\alpha_{jk}}\right\} \ \le\ \Delta c_j \ \le\ \min_{k:\ \alpha_{jk}>0}\left\{\frac{-(z_k-c_k)}{\alpha_{jk}}\right\} \]

docs.title: Ranging a right-hand side b_i
docs.text:
Changing \(b_i\) by \(\Delta\) changes the basic variables to

\[ \vec x_B^{\text{new}} = \vec x_B + \Delta\,\big(B^{-1}\big)_{\cdot i} \]

where \((B^{-1})_{\cdot i}\) is the \(s_i\) column of the final tableau. Feasibility requires \(\vec x_B^{\text{new}} \ge 0\):

\[ \boxed{\ \max_{k:\ \beta_{ki}>0}\left\{\frac{-x_{B_k}}{\beta_{ki}}\right\} \ \le\ \Delta \ \le\ \min_{k:\ \beta_{ki}<0}\left\{\frac{-x_{B_k}}{\beta_{ki}}\right\}\ } \]

Within this range the shadow price \(y_i\) is constant; outside it, the basis changes and a new shadow price applies.

docs.title: The 100 % rule
docs.text:
For simultaneous changes, compute each change as a fraction of its allowable range in the direction of change. If

\[ \sum_i \frac{|\Delta_i|}{\text{allowable range}_i} \ \le\ 1 \]

then the basis (and therefore all shadow prices) remain valid. If the sum exceeds 1, re-solve — the rule gives no conclusion either way.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Constructing and verifying a dual
docs.text:
Form the dual of the following, solve both, and verify strong duality.

\[ \max\ Z = 3x_1+5x_2 \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x_1\le4,\ \ 2x_2\le12,\ \ 3x_1+2x_2\le18,\ \ x_1,x_2\ge0 \]

Solution.

The dual. Three constraints ⟹ three dual variables \(y_1,y_2,y_3 \ge 0\); two primal variables ⟹ two dual constraints.

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\ & W = 4y_1 + 12y_2 + 18y_3\\ \text{s.t. } & y_1 + 3y_3 \ge 3 && \text{(from the } x_1 \text{ column)}\\ & 2y_2 + 2y_3 \ge 5 && \text{(from the } x_2 \text{ column)}\\ & y_1,y_2,y_3 \ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

Solving the primal by simplex. The final tableau is

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) \(s_3\) RHS \(s_1\) 0 0 0 1 \(1/3\) \(-1/3\) 2 \(x_2\) 5 0 1 0 \(1/2\) 0 6 \(x_1\) 3 1 0 0 \(-1/3\) \(1/3\) 2 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 0 3/2 1 36 \[ \boxed{\ x_1^{*} = 2,\ x_2^{*} = 6,\ Z^{*} = 3(2)+5(6) = 36\ } \]

Reading the dual solution off the slack columns.

\[ y_1^{*} = 0, \qquad y_2^{*} = \tfrac32 = 1.5, \qquad y_3^{*} = 1 \]

Verifying dual feasibility.

\[ y_1 + 3y_3 = 0 + 3 = 3 \ge 3 \ \checkmark \ \text{(equality)} \] \[ 2y_2 + 2y_3 = 3 + 2 = 5 \ge 5 \ \checkmark \ \text{(equality)} \]

Verifying strong duality.

\[ W = 4(0) + 12(1.5) + 18(1) = 0 + 18 + 18 = \mathbf{36} = Z^{*} \ \checkmark \] \[ \boxed{\ Z^{*} = W^{*} = 36\ } \]

Verifying complementary slackness.

\(i\) Constraint LHS at optimum Slack \(y_i\) \(y_i\times\text{slack}\) 1 \(x_1\le4\) \(2\) \(\mathbf{2}\) \(\mathbf{0}\) 0 ✓ 2 \(2x_2\le12\) \(12\) 0 \(3/2\) 0 ✓ 3 \(3x_1+2x_2\le18\) \(18\) 0 \(1\) 0 ✓

Constraint 1 has slack 2, and its shadow price is exactly 0 — Rule 1 confirmed. Resource 1 is not scarce, so an extra unit of it is worthless.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Economic decisions from shadow prices
docs.text:
Using Problem 1's shadow prices \((0,\ 1.5,\ 1)\): (a) Should the firm buy 3 more units of resource 2 at ₹1.20 each? (b) At ₹2.00 each? (c) A new product needs 1 unit of resource 1, 2 of resource 2 and 2 of resource 3, and sells for ₹6. Should it be introduced?

Solution.

(a) 3 units of resource 2 at ₹1.20.

\[ \text{marginal value} = ₹1.50 > ₹1.20 = \text{price} \] \[ \text{net gain} = 3\times(1.50-1.20) = \mathbf{₹0.90} \] \[ \boxed{\textbf{BUY}} \]

Range check. The \(s_2\) column of the final tableau is \(\left(\frac13,\ \frac12,\ -\frac13\right)^T\) against basic values \((2,\ 6,\ 2)\). Increasing \(b_2\) by \(\Delta\):

\[ s_1 = 2 + \tfrac{\Delta}{3} \ge 0 \ \ \text{always}; \quad x_2 = 6+\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\ge0 \ \ \text{always}; \quad x_1 = 2 - \tfrac{\Delta}{3}\ge0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \le 6 \]

\(\Delta = 3 \le 6\) ✓ — the ₹1.50 rate applies fully.

(b) At ₹2.00.

\[ ₹2.00 > ₹1.50 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{net loss of } 3\times0.50 = ₹1.50 \] \[ \boxed{\textbf{DO NOT BUY}} \]

The general rule: buy resource \(i\) if and only if its market price is below \(y_i\).

(c) The new product.

Its imputed resource cost at the shadow prices is

\[ \sum_i a_{i,\text{new}}\,y_i = 1(0) + 2(1.5) + 2(1) = 0 + 3 + 2 = ₹5 \]

Its revenue is ₹6.

\[ \text{reduced cost} = c_{\text{new}} - z_{\text{new}} = 6 - 5 = \mathbf{+₹1} > 0 \] \[ \boxed{\textbf{INTRODUCE IT — it earns ₹1 more than the resources it consumes are worth.}} \]

This is exactly the simplex entering-variable test, applied to a column that was not in the original problem. It is called column generation and is the engine behind large-scale LP (airline crew scheduling, cutting-stock problems), where columns are generated on demand rather than enumerated in advance.

(If instead the product sold for ₹4, the reduced cost would be \(4-5 = -1 < 0\) and it should not be produced — it would destroy ₹1 of value per unit by consuming resources worth more than it earns.)

docs.title: Problem 3 — Ranging a right-hand side
docs.text:
For Problem 1, find the range over which \(b_3 = 18\) may vary with the shadow price \(y_3 = 1\) still valid, and compute \(Z^{*}\) at the endpoints.

Solution.

The \(s_3\) column of the final tableau is \(\left(-\frac13,\ 0,\ \frac13\right)^{T}\) against basic values \((s_1, x_2, x_1) = (2,\ 6,\ 2)\).

Changing \(b_3\) by \(\Delta\):

\[ s_1 = 2 - \tfrac{\Delta}{3}, \qquad x_2 = 6 + 0 = 6, \qquad x_1 = 2 + \tfrac{\Delta}{3} \]

Feasibility conditions.

\[ s_1 \ge 0: \quad 2 - \tfrac{\Delta}{3} \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \le 6 \] \[ x_1 \ge 0: \quad 2 + \tfrac{\Delta}{3} \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \ge -6 \] \[ \boxed{\ -6 \le \Delta \le 6 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 12 \le b_3 \le 24\ } \]

Objective at the endpoints.

At \(b_3 = 24\) (\(\Delta = +6\)): \(x_1 = 4\), \(x_2 = 6\), \(s_1 = 0\).

\[ Z = 3(4)+5(6) = 12+30 = 42 = 36 + 6(1) \ \checkmark \]

At \(b_3 = 12\) (\(\Delta = -6\)): \(x_1 = 0\), \(x_2 = 6\), \(s_1 = 4\).

\[ Z = 0 + 30 = 30 = 36 - 6(1) \ \checkmark \]

Both confirm \(y_3 = 1\) exactly.

What happens beyond the range? At \(b_3 = 24\), \(s_1\) hits zero — constraint 1 (\(x_1\le4\)) becomes binding. Push further and the basis must change: \(x_1\) can no longer grow, so the extra resource 3 becomes useless.

\[ \text{At } b_3 = 30: \ x_1 = 4, x_2 = 6 \ \text{still, so } Z = 42 \ \text{— unchanged.} \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{For } b_3 > 24 \text{ the shadow price DROPS TO ZERO.}\ } \]

The management lesson. "Resource 3 is worth ₹1 per unit" is true only up to 24 units. Beyond that, buying more is pointless. Never quote a shadow price without its range — this is the single most common error in applying LP results.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Ranging an objective coefficient
docs.text:
For Problem 1, find the range of \(c_2 = 5\) (the profit on \(x_2\)) keeping the current basis optimal.

Solution.

\(x_2\) is basic, in row 2 of the final tableau. Its row is

\[ (x_1,\ x_2,\ s_1,\ s_2,\ s_3) = \left(0,\ 1,\ 0,\ \tfrac12,\ 0\right) \]

The non-basic variables are \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) with \(z_j-c_j = (0,\ \frac32,\ 1)\).

Changing \(c_2\) by \(\Delta\) changes each \(z_k - c_k\) by \(\Delta\alpha_{2k}\), where \(\alpha_{2k}\) is the entry in \(x_2\)'s row:

Non-basic \(k\) \(z_k-c_k\) \(\alpha_{2k}\) New value \(s_1\) 0 0 \(0\) (unaffected) \(s_2\) \(3/2\) \(1/2\) \(\tfrac32 + \tfrac{\Delta}{2}\) \(s_3\) 1 0 \(1\) (unaffected)

Optimality requires all \(\ge 0\):

\[ \tfrac32 + \tfrac{\Delta}{2} \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \ge -3 \]

No upper restriction (no non-basic column has a negative entry in \(x_2\)'s row).

\[ \boxed{\ \Delta \ge -3 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad c_2 \ge 2, \ \text{ with no upper limit}\ } \]

Interpretation. The plan \((2, 6)\) stays optimal as long as product 2's profit is at least ₹2 — and however high it goes. Only \(Z\) changes.

Verification at \(c_2 = 2\).

\[ Z(2,6) = 3(2)+2(6) = 6+12 = 18 \]

Compare the neighbouring corner \((4, 3)\): \(Z = 3(4)+2(3) = 12+6 = 18\) — a tie, confirming that \(c_2 = 2\) is exactly the boundary where alternate optima appear ✓.

Verification at \(c_2 = 1.9\) (just below).

\[ Z(2,6) = 6 + 11.4 = 17.4, \qquad Z(4,3) = 12 + 5.7 = 17.7 \]

\((4,3)\) now wins — the basis has changed, as predicted ✓.

docs.title: Problem 5 — The 100 % rule for simultaneous changes
docs.text:
For Problem 1, suppose \(b_2\) increases by 2 and \(b_3\) increases by 3 simultaneously. Are the shadow prices still valid? Compute the new \(Z^{*}\).

Solution.

Step 1 — the individual allowable ranges.

For \(b_2\) (column \(\left(\frac13,\ \frac12,\ -\frac13\right)^T\), basics \((2,6,2)\)):

\[ x_1 = 2 - \tfrac{\Delta_2}{3} \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta_2 \le 6 \]

Allowable increase in \(b_2\): 6.

For \(b_3\) (from Problem 3): allowable increase: 6.

Step 2 — the fractions.

\[ \frac{\Delta_2}{6} + \frac{\Delta_3}{6} = \frac{2}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = 0.333 + 0.500 = \mathbf{0.833} \] \[ 0.833 \ \le\ 1 \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The 100 \% rule holds — the basis and both shadow prices remain valid.}\ } \]

Step 3 — the new objective value.

\[ Z^{*}_{\text{new}} = 36 + 2(1.5) + 3(1) = 36 + 3 + 3 = \mathbf{42} \]

Step 4 — direct verification. With \(b_2 = 14\) and \(b_3 = 21\), the new basic values are

\[ s_1 = 2 + \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{3}{3} = 2 + 0.667 - 1 = 1.667 \] \[ x_2 = 6 + \tfrac{2}{2} + 0 = 7 \] \[ x_1 = 2 - \tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{3}{3} = 2 - 0.667 + 1 = 2.333 \]

All non-negative ✓ — the basis is indeed still feasible.

\[ Z = 3(2.333) + 5(7) = 7.00 + 35 = \mathbf{42} \ \checkmark \]

Check the original constraints.

\[ x_1 = 2.333 \le 4 \ \checkmark \ (s_1 = 1.667) \] \[ 2x_2 = 14 \le 14 \ \checkmark \ \text{(binding)} \] \[ 3(2.333)+2(7) = 7+14 = 21 \le 21 \ \checkmark \ \text{(binding)} \]

A cautionary counter-example. Had the changes been \(\Delta_2 = 5\) and \(\Delta_3 = 5\):

\[ \frac{5}{6}+\frac{5}{6} = 1.667 > 1 \]

The rule gives no guarantee — you must re-solve. (Note the rule is only sufficient: exceeding 100 % does not prove the basis changed, it merely means you cannot conclude it did not.)

Checking directly: \(x_1 = 2 - \frac53 + \frac53 = 2 \ge 0\) ✓ and \(s_1 = 2+\frac53-\frac53 = 2 \ge 0\) ✓ — the basis actually does survive here. The 100 % rule is conservative, which is exactly what you want from a safety check.

docs.title: 7.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Write the dual of \(\min\ 4y_1+6y_2\) s.t. \(y_1+2y_2\ge3\), \(3y_1+y_2\ge5\), \(y\ge0\).
  2. If a primal is unbounded, what can you say about its dual? [Ans: infeasible]
  3. Given slack \(= 5\) on constraint 2, what is \(y_2\)? [Ans: 0, by complementary slackness]
  4. A resource costs ₹8/unit in the market and has shadow price ₹6. Buy or not? [Ans: do not buy]
  5. Verify \(\vec b^{T}\vec y^{*} = Z^{*}\) for the furniture problem of L05.
  6. Changes use 40 %, 30 % and 20 % of their ranges. Is the basis still optimal? [Ans: 90 % ≤ 100 %, yes]
  7. A new product's imputed cost is ₹12 and it sells for ₹10. Introduce it? [Ans: no — reduced cost \(-2\)]

docs.title: 7.8 Summary
docs.text:
• The dual transposes the primal: \(m\) constraints ↔ \(m\) variables, \(\vec b\) ↔ \(\vec c\), \(A\) ↔ \(A^{T}\), \(\le\) ↔ \(\ge\). The dual of the dual is the primal.
  • Weak duality: any dual-feasible solution bounds the primal optimum. Strong duality: \(Z^{*} = W^{*}\). Complementary slackness: slack > 0 ⟹ shadow price 0, and shadow price > 0 ⟹ constraint binding.
  • Shadow prices \(y_i = \partial Z^{*}/\partial b_i\) are read from the slack columns' \(z_j-c_j\) entries. Use them for buying decisions, bottleneck priorities and product costing (reduced cost \(= c_{\text{new}} - \sum_i a_iy_i\) — the basis of column generation).
  • Ranging: an RHS range comes from keeping \(\vec x_B + \Delta(B^{-1})_{\cdot i} \ge 0\); an objective-coefficient range comes from keeping all \(z_k-c_k \ge 0\).
  • Never quote a shadow price without its range — beyond the range the price changes, often to zero.
  • The 100 % rule validates simultaneous changes: if the fractions of the allowable ranges sum to at most 1, the basis survives. It is sufficient but not necessary — conservative by design.

Next lesson: L08 — The transportation problem: formulation and initial basic feasible solutions.

Practise now: unit1-lp-lab.html → Duality & Sensitivity: solve any LP and see the dual, shadow prices, ranging tables and a live 100 %-rule calculator.

docs.title: Lesson 32: EOQ with Shortages Permitted (the Backorder Model)
32.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Draw the inventory profile when planned backorders are allowed and identify \(S\), \(B\) and \(Q\).
  2. Derive the average holding and shortage levels from the geometry of that profile.
  3. Derive \(Q^{*}\) and \(S^{*}\) for the backorder model and interpret the backorder factor.
  4. Show that the model reduces to classical EOQ as \(C_s\to\infty\).
  5. Decide whether a planned-shortage policy is appropriate for a given business.

docs.title: 32.2 Why Plan to Run Out?
docs.text:
Deliberately allowing stock-outs sounds like bad management. It is not, provided customers are willing to wait — that is, the demand is backordered rather than lost.

The logic: if a customer is content to wait a few days, the firm can carry less stock and save holding cost, paying instead a smaller shortage cost. Whenever \(C_s\) is genuinely finite and comparable to \(C_h\), the optimal policy is to run out for part of each cycle.

The essential distinction.

  • Backorders — unfilled demand waits and is satisfied from the next delivery. The sale is kept; only a penalty is paid. This lesson's model.
  • Lost sales — the customer goes elsewhere. The sale, and possibly the customer, is gone. Shortage cost is then per unit short, not per unit per unit time, and the model differs.

Backordering is realistic for made-to-order machinery, spare parts, books and furniture. It is unrealistic for groceries, petrol and medicines.

docs.title: 32.3 The Inventory Profile
docs.text:
stock
   S |\             |\             |\
     | \            | \            | \
     |  \           |  \           |  \
   0 |---\----------|---\----------|---\-------  time
     |    \        /|    \        /|
  -B |     \______/ |     \______/ |
     |<-t1->|<-t2->|
     |<------ t ---->|

Notation:

Symbol Meaning \(Q\) order quantity (the whole delivery) \(S\) maximum inventory level — what remains after clearing backorders \(B=Q-S\) maximum shortage (backorder) level \(t_1=S/D\) time with stock on hand \(t_2=B/D\) time in shortage \(t=Q/D\) full cycle

When a delivery of \(Q\) arrives, \(B\) units go immediately to waiting customers and \(S=Q-B\) enter stock.

docs.title: Average inventory and average shortage
docs.text:
Both come from triangle areas divided by the full cycle \(t\) — this is the step students most often get wrong, because each average is taken over the whole cycle, not over the sub-interval in which it is non-zero.

\[\text{average stock}=\frac{\tfrac12 S\,t_1}{t}=\frac{\tfrac12 S(S/D)}{Q/D}=\boxed{\frac{S^2}{2Q}}\] \[\text{average shortage}=\frac{\tfrac12 B\,t_2}{t}=\boxed{\frac{B^2}{2Q}=\frac{(Q-S)^2}{2Q}}\]

Setting \(B=0\) recovers \(S=Q\) and average stock \(=Q/2\), the classical result — a useful check.

docs.title: The cost function
docs.text:
\[TRC(Q,S)=\underbrace{\frac{C_oD}{Q}}_{\text{ordering}} +\underbrace{\frac{C_hS^{2}}{2Q}}_{\text{holding}} +\underbrace{\frac{C_s(Q-S)^{2}}{2Q}}_{\text{shortage}} \tag{3.1}\]

This is a function of two variables, so we need both partial derivatives.

docs.title: Optimising over S
docs.text:
\[\frac{\partial TRC}{\partial S}=\frac{C_hS}{Q}-\frac{C_s(Q-S)}{Q}=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ C_hS=C_s(Q-S)\]

Result 1. $\(\boxed{\ S^{*}=\frac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\,Q\ },\qquad B^{*}=Q-S^{*}=\frac{C_h}{C_h+C_s}\,Q \tag{3.2}\)$

The fraction \(\dfrac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\) is the critical ratio or service level: the proportion of the cycle spent in stock. It has an immediate reading — if shortage is ten times as expensive as holding, \(S^*=\tfrac{10}{11}Q\) and the system is in stock \(91\,\%\) of the time.

docs.title: Optimising over Q
docs.text:
Substituting (3.2) into (3.1) and simplifying, the cost becomes

\[TRC(Q)=\frac{C_oD}{Q}+\frac{Q}{2}\cdot\frac{C_hC_s}{C_h+C_s}\]

which is an ordinary EOQ with \(C_h\) replaced by the harmonic-type combination \(\dfrac{C_hC_s}{C_h+C_s}\). Hence

Result 2 (EOQ with backorders). $\(\boxed{\ Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\ \sqrt{\frac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}}\ =\ Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\cdot k, \qquad k=\sqrt{\frac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}}\ }\tag{3.3}\)$ $\(\boxed{\ S^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\ \sqrt{\frac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}}=\frac{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}{k}\ }\tag{3.4}\)$ $\(\boxed{\ TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2C_oDC_h}\ \sqrt{\frac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}}=\frac{TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}{k}\ }\tag{3.5}\)$

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The single factor \(k=\sqrt{\dfrac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}}>1\) governs everything:

Quantity Effect of allowing backorders Order quantity \(Q^*\) multiplied by \(k\) — order more, less often Maximum stock \(S^*\) divided by \(k\) — hold less Total cost \(TRC^*\) divided by \(k\) — always cheaper

Backordering is never worse than the classical policy, because the classical policy (\(B=0\)) is available and was not chosen. The saving is the factor \(1/k\).

Two limits worth checking:

  • \(C_s\to\infty\) (shortages intolerable): \(k\to1\), so \(Q^*\to Q^*_{\text{EOQ}}\), \(S^*\to Q^*\), \(B^*\to0\). The model collapses to Lesson 31, exactly as it must.
  • \(C_s\to0\) (shortages free): \(k\to\infty\), \(Q^*\to\infty\), \(S^*\to0\). Order enormous quantities and hold nothing — degenerate, and a warning that a low \(C_s\) estimate produces absurd advice.

docs.title: Problem 1 — The standard backorder calculation
docs.text:
A firm uses \(10{,}000\) units a year. Ordering costs \(₹150\); holding costs \(₹8\) per unit per year; backordering costs \(₹25\) per unit per year. Find \(Q^*\), \(S^*\), \(B^*\), the cost breakdown and the saving over the no-shortage policy.

Solution.

Step 1 — the backorder factor.

\[k=\sqrt{\frac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}}=\sqrt{\frac{8+25}{25}}=\sqrt{1.32}=1.14891\]

Step 2 — the classical EOQ as a base. From Lesson 31, \(Q^*_{\text{EOQ}}=612.37\), \(TRC^*_{\text{EOQ}}=₹4898.98\).

Step 3 — the backorder optimum.

\[Q^{*}=612.37\times1.14891=\mathbf{703.56\text{ units}}\] \[S^{*}=\frac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}Q^{*}=\frac{25}{33}(703.56)=\mathbf{533.00\text{ units}}\] \[B^{*}=Q^{*}-S^{*}=703.56-533.00=\mathbf{170.56\text{ units}}\] \[TRC^{*}=\frac{4898.98}{1.14891}=\mathbf{₹4264.01\text{ per year}}\]

Step 4 — cost breakdown (an essential check).

\[\text{ordering}=\frac{150(10000)}{703.56}=₹2132.01\] \[\text{holding}=\frac{8(533.00)^2}{2(703.56)}=\frac{8(284{,}089)}{1407.12}=₹1615.16\] \[\text{shortage}=\frac{25(170.56)^2}{2(703.56)}=\frac{25(29{,}090.7)}{1407.12}=₹516.85\] \[\text{TOTAL}=2132.01+1615.16+516.85=₹4264.02\ \checkmark\]

Note that here ordering cost equals holding + shortage cost (\(2132.01 = 1615.16+516.85\)) — the generalisation of the equal-costs check from Lesson 31.

Step 5 — the saving.

\[4898.98-4264.01=\mathbf{₹634.97\text{ per year}}\ (13.0\,\%)\]

Interpretation. The optimal policy runs out of stock for \(t_2/t=B^*/Q^*=170.56/703.56=24.2\,\%\) of every cycle. That is a deliberate, costed decision, not a failure. The saving of \(₹635\) a year is genuine — provided customers really do wait. If even a quarter of the backordered demand were actually lost at a \(₹40\) margin, the lost contribution would be \(0.25\times170.56\times14.21\text{ cycles}\times ₹40 \approx ₹24{,}000\) a year, dwarfing the saving. Verify the backorder assumption before trusting this model.

docs.title: Problem 2 — A second calculation with different economics
docs.text:
\(D=1200\) units/yr, \(C_o=₹100\), \(C_h=₹5\)/unit/yr, \(C_s=₹15\)/unit/yr. Find the full policy.

Solution.

\[k=\sqrt{\frac{5+15}{15}}=\sqrt{1.3333}=1.15470\] \[Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(100)(1200)}{5}}=\sqrt{48000}=219.09\] \[Q^{*}=219.09(1.15470)=\mathbf{252.98\text{ units}}\] \[S^{*}=\frac{15}{20}(252.98)=\mathbf{189.74\text{ units}}\] \[B^{*}=\mathbf{63.25\text{ units}}\] \[TRC^{*}=\frac{\sqrt{2(100)(1200)(5)}}{1.15470}=\frac{1095.45}{1.15470}=\mathbf{₹948.68\text{ per year}}\]

Breakdown: ordering \(₹474.34\), holding \(₹355.76\), shortage \(₹118.59\); total \(₹948.69\) ✓.

Cycle structure. \(t=Q/D=252.98/1200=0.2108\) yr \(=77\) days, of which \(t_1=189.74/1200=57.7\) days in stock and \(t_2=63.25/1200=19.2\) days short. The firm is out of stock for 19 days in every 77 — one quarter of the time — by design.

docs.title: Problem 3 — How the policy responds to C_s
docs.text:
For Problem 2's data, tabulate the policy as \(C_s\) varies, and comment.

Solution. \(Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=219.09\), \(TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=₹1095.45\) throughout.

\(C_s\) \(k\) \(Q^{*}\) \(S^{*}\) \(B^{*}\) Fraction of cycle short \(TRC^{*}\) Saving 1 2.4495 536.66 89.44 447.21 83.3 % ₹447.21 59.2 % 5 1.4142 309.84 154.92 154.92 50.0 % ₹774.60 29.3 % 15 1.1547 252.98 189.74 63.25 25.0 % ₹948.68 13.4 % 45 1.0541 230.94 207.85 23.09 10.0 % ₹1039.23 5.1 % 495 1.0050 220.19 217.99 2.20 1.0 % ₹1089.95 0.5 % \(\infty\) 1.0000 219.09 219.09 0 0 % ₹1095.45 0

Interpretation.

  • The fraction of the cycle spent short is exactly \(\dfrac{C_h}{C_h+C_s}\) — read straight from (3.2). At \(C_s=C_h=5\) the system is short half the time.
  • The saving is substantial only when \(C_s\) is comparable to or smaller than \(C_h\). Once \(C_s>10C_h\) the model is barely distinguishable from classical EOQ.
  • This is a strong practical guide. If a stock-out costs more than about ten times the holding cost — which it usually does in retail — do not bother with the backorder model. Its complexity buys under \(5\,\%\).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Inferring C_s from a chosen service level
docs.text:
A firm cannot estimate \(C_s\) but insists on being in stock \(95\,\%\) of the time. With \(C_h=₹8\), \(C_o=₹150\) and \(D=10{,}000\), what \(C_s\) does that imply, and what policy follows?

Solution. From (3.2), the in-stock fraction is \(\dfrac{S^*}{Q^*}=\dfrac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\). Setting this to \(0.95\):

\[\frac{C_s}{8+C_s}=0.95 \Rightarrow C_s=0.95(8)+0.95C_s \Rightarrow 0.05C_s=7.6 \Rightarrow \mathbf{C_s=₹152\text{ per unit per year}}\] \[k=\sqrt{\frac{8+152}{152}}=\sqrt{1.05263}=1.02598\] \[Q^{*}=612.37(1.02598)=\mathbf{628.28},\quad S^{*}=0.95(628.28)=\mathbf{596.87},\quad B^{*}=\mathbf{31.41}\] \[TRC^{*}=\frac{4898.98}{1.02598}=\mathbf{₹4774.93}\]

Interpretation — why this inversion is the professional approach. The firm never had to name a shortage cost. Instead it named a service level, which managers can discuss meaningfully, and the model reports the implied \(C_s=₹152\) per unit-year. The conversation then becomes: "Your 95 % target is equivalent to valuing a stock-out at ₹152 per unit per year — about 19 times the holding cost. Is that right?" That question can be answered; "what is your shortage cost?" usually cannot.

The policy saves only \(₹124\) a year over pure EOQ — consistent with Problem 3's finding that a high implied \(C_s\) leaves little on the table.

docs.title: Problem 5 — When the model must not be used
docs.text:
A pharmacy considers a planned-shortage policy for a life-saving drug, arguing that \(C_h\) is high (refrigeration) and patients will wait for the next delivery. Critique this.

Solution.

The model is inapplicable, for four separate reasons.

  1. Demand is not backordered. A patient needing the drug today cannot wait a week. The demand is lost (or worse), so the shortage cost is not "per unit per unit time" but a step function of catastrophic size.
  2. \(C_s\) is not commensurable with money. Any finite \(C_s\) produces a \(B^*>0\); the model structurally cannot recommend zero shortage unless \(C_s=\infty\). A model whose form forbids the right answer must not be used to justify the wrong one.
  3. Demand is probabilistic, violating Lesson 31's assumption 1. Even a policy of never planning shortages would need safety stock.
  4. Regulatory and ethical constraints are hard constraints, not costs to be traded off.

What to do instead. Formulate as a service-level problem: choose the stock policy that meets demand with probability \(\ge99.9\,\%\), then minimise cost subject to that constraint. The constraint expresses the ethical requirement; optimisation happens inside it.

The general principle. An optimisation model trades off whatever you put in its objective. If something must not be traded off, it belongs in the constraints, not the objective. Recognising that distinction is the mark of a competent modeller — and misplacing it is how quantitative methods acquire a bad name.

docs.title: 32.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(D=2000\)/yr, \(C_o=₹250\), \(C_h=₹10\), \(C_s=₹40\). Find \(Q^*\), \(S^*\), \(B^*\), \(TRC^*\). (Answer: \(353.55\), \(282.84\), \(70.71\), \(₹2828.43\))
  2. Show that \(S^{*}/Q^{*}\) is independent of \(D\) and \(C_o\), and explain why that makes sense.
  3. For Problem 1 of §4, how long is the firm out of stock in each cycle, in days on a 250-day year? (Answer: \(t=17.59\) days, \(t_2=4.26\) days)
  4. A firm's data give \(Q^{*}=500\) and \(S^{*}=400\). What is \(C_s/C_h\)? (Answer: \(S/Q=0.8=C_s/(C_h+C_s)\), so \(C_s=4C_h\))
  5. Prove that \(TRC^{*}_{\text{backorder}} \le TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\) for all \(C_s>0\), with equality only in the limit \(C_s\to\infty\).

docs.title: 32.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Planned shortages are rational only when demand is genuinely backordered, not lost.
  • Averages are taken over the whole cycle: average stock \(=S^2/2Q\), average shortage \(=(Q-S)^2/2Q\).
  • \(TRC(Q,S)=\dfrac{C_oD}{Q}+\dfrac{C_hS^2}{2Q}+\dfrac{C_s(Q-S)^2}{2Q}\), optimised in two variables.
  • Critical ratio: \(\dfrac{S^*}{Q^*}=\dfrac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\) — the fraction of the cycle in stock, and a directly interpretable service level.
  • With \(k=\sqrt{\dfrac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}}\): \(\ Q^*=kQ^*_{\text{EOQ}}\), \(\ S^*=Q^*_{\text{EOQ}}/k\), \(\ TRC^*=TRC^*_{\text{EOQ}}/k\). Order more, hold less, pay less.
  • As \(C_s\to\infty\) the model reduces exactly to classical EOQ — the required consistency check.
  • The saving matters only when \(C_s\) is within about an order of magnitude of \(C_h\). Beyond that, use plain EOQ.
  • When shortage cost cannot be priced, invert the model: choose a service level and report the implied \(C_s\).
  • Requirements that must never be traded off belong in the constraints, never in the objective.

Next lesson: L33 — The production (finite replenishment) model without shortages.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Backorder Lab: drag \(C_s\) and watch \(S^*\), \(B^*\) and the shaded shortage region of the sawtooth respond.

docs.title: Lesson 11: Game Theory: Two-Person Zero-Sum Games and Pure Strategies
11.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define a two-person zero-sum game and construct its payoff matrix.
  2. Apply the maximin and minimax criteria.
  3. Identify a saddle point and the value of the game.
  4. Apply the dominance principle to reduce a game.
  5. Recognise when no pure-strategy solution exists.

docs.title: 11.2 What Is a Game?
docs.text:
Definition. A game is a decision situation in which two or more rational participants (players) choose among strategies, and each player's payoff depends on the choices of all players.

Key elements.

Element Meaning Players the decision-makers Strategies the complete plans of action available to each Payoff the outcome to each player for each strategy combination Payoff matrix the tabulation of all payoffs

Definition (Two-person zero-sum game). Exactly two players, and

\[ \text{(payoff to A)} + \text{(payoff to B)} = 0 \qquad\text{for every outcome.} \]

One player's gain is exactly the other's loss. Examples: dividing a fixed market share, competitive bidding for a single contract, most parlour games.

Convention used throughout. The matrix records player A's (the row player's) payoff. A positive entry means A gains and B loses that amount.

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1n}\\ \vdots & & \vdots\\ a_{m1} & \cdots & a_{mn}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a_{ij} = \text{A's gain when A plays } i \text{ and B plays } j \]

Player A maximises; player B minimises.

What zero-sum excludes. Cooperation, side payments and mutual gain are impossible by construction. Real business rivalry is usually non-zero-sum (both firms can profit from market growth), so zero-sum models are best read as worst-case analyses of purely competitive situations.

docs.title: 11.3 The Maximin and Minimax Criteria
docs.text: Both players are assumed rational and conservative: each protects against the opponent's best reply.

docs.title: Player A's reasoning — maximin
docs.text:
If A plays row \(i\), the worst that can happen is \(\min_j a_{ij}\). A therefore chooses the row whose worst case is best:

\[ \boxed{\ \underline{v} \ =\ \max_i\ \min_j\ a_{ij} \qquad \text{(the \textbf{maximin} or \emph{lower value})}\ } \]

\(\underline{v}\) is A's guaranteed minimum gain, whatever B does.

docs.title: Player B's reasoning — minimax
docs.text:
If B plays column \(j\), the worst for B is \(\max_i a_{ij}\) (A's largest gain). B chooses the column minimising this:

\[ \boxed{\ \overline{v} \ =\ \min_j\ \max_i\ a_{ij} \qquad \text{(the \textbf{minimax} or \emph{upper value})}\ } \]

\(\overline{v}\) is B's guaranteed maximum loss.

docs.title: The fundamental inequality
docs.text:
Theorem. \(\underline{v} \le \overline{v}\) always.

Proof. For any \(i_0, j_0\): \(\min_j a_{i_0 j} \le a_{i_0j_0} \le \max_i a_{ij_0}\). Taking the maximum over \(i_0\) on the left and the minimum over \(j_0\) on the right preserves the inequality. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 11.4 Saddle Points and the Value of the Game
docs.text:
Definition (Saddle point). A cell \((r,s)\) is a saddle point if

\[ a_{rs} = \min_j a_{rj} = \max_i a_{is} \]

— it is simultaneously the smallest in its row and the largest in its column.

Theorem. A saddle point exists iff \(\underline{v} = \overline{v}\), and then

\[ \boxed{\ v \ =\ \underline{v} \ =\ \overline{v} \ =\ a_{rs} \qquad \text{— the \textbf{value of the game}}\ } \]

The pair (row \(r\), column \(s\)) is the optimal pure strategy for A and B respectively, and it is an equilibrium: neither player can gain by unilaterally deviating.

Terminology.

Condition Name \(v > 0\) the game favours A \(v < 0\) the game favours B \(v = 0\) the game is fair saddle point exists strictly determined game; pure strategies suffice no saddle point mixed strategies are required (L12)

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Compute the ROW MINIMA;  maximin = the largest of them
2. Compute the COLUMN MAXIMA;  minimax = the smallest of them
3. If maximin = minimax  ->  SADDLE POINT at that cell; v = that value
4. Otherwise  ->  no pure-strategy solution; use mixed strategies (L12)

docs.title: 11.5 The Dominance Principle
docs.text:
Definition (Row dominance). Row \(i\) dominates row \(k\) if

\[ a_{ij} \ \ge\ a_{kj} \qquad \text{for every } j \]

Row \(i\) is at least as good as row \(k\) against every opponent choice, so row \(k\) may be deleted — a rational A would never play it.

Definition (Column dominance). Column \(j\) dominates column \(l\) if

\[ a_{ij} \ \le\ a_{il} \qquad \text{for every } i \]

(Note the reversal: B minimises, so a smaller entry is better for B.) Column \(l\) may be deleted.

The direction of the inequality is the single most common error. Remember: A wants big, B wants small. A keeps the row with larger entries; B keeps the column with smaller entries.

Generalised (convex) dominance. A row may also be deleted if it is dominated by a convex combination (an average) of other rows:

\[ a_{kj} \ \le\ \sum_{i\ne k}\lambda_i a_{ij} \ \ \forall j, \qquad \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum\lambda_i = 1 \]

Why dominance matters. It reduces the matrix, often to \(2\times2\), where a closed-form solution exists (L12).

docs.title: Problem 1 — Finding a saddle point
docs.text:
Solve the game with payoff matrix (A's gains):

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_2\) \(B_3\) \(B_4\) \(A_1\) 9 3 1 8 \(A_2\) 6 5 4 6 \(A_3\) 2 4 3 3 \(A_4\) 5 6 2 2

Solution.

Step 1 — row minima.

Row Entries Minimum \(A_1\) 9, 3, 1, 8 1 \(A_2\) 6, 5, 4, 6 4 ← maximum \(A_3\) 2, 4, 3, 3 2 \(A_4\) 5, 6, 2, 2 2 \[ \underline{v} = \text{maximin} = \max\{1, 4, 2, 2\} = \mathbf{4} \ \text{ in row } A_2 \]

Step 2 — column maxima.

Column Entries Maximum \(B_1\) 9, 6, 2, 5 9 \(B_2\) 3, 5, 4, 6 6 \(B_3\) 1, 4, 3, 2 4 ← minimum \(B_4\) 8, 6, 3, 2 8 \[ \overline{v} = \text{minimax} = \min\{9, 6, 4, 8\} = \mathbf{4} \ \text{ in column } B_3 \]

Step 3 — test.

\[ \underline{v} = \overline{v} = 4 \ \Longrightarrow\ \textbf{SADDLE POINT at } (A_2, B_3) \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{A plays } A_2,\quad \text{B plays } B_3,\quad v = 4\ } \]

Verify the saddle-point property. The entry \(a_{23} = 4\) is:

  • the smallest in row \(A_2\): \(\min(6,5,4,6) = 4\) ✓
  • the largest in column \(B_3\): \(\max(1,4,3,2) = 4\) ✓

Verify the equilibrium. Neither player benefits from deviating alone.

If A deviates (B still plays \(B_3\)): \(A_1\) gives 1, \(A_3\) gives 3, \(A_4\) gives 2 — all less than 4. A loses by deviating ✓.

If B deviates (A still plays \(A_2\)): \(B_1\) gives 6, \(B_2\) gives 5, \(B_4\) gives 6 — all more than 4, and B is paying these. B loses by deviating ✓.

Interpretation. The game favours A (\(v = 4 > 0\)): A can guarantee a gain of 4 units per play regardless of B's actions, and B can hold the loss to exactly 4.

docs.title: Problem 2 — No saddle point
docs.text:
Determine whether the following game has a pure-strategy solution.

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_2\) \(A_1\) 5 1 \(A_2\) 3 4

Solution.

Row minima. \(A_1: \min(5,1) = 1\); \(A_2: \min(3,4) = 3\).

\[ \underline{v} = \max(1, 3) = \mathbf{3} \]

Column maxima. \(B_1: \max(5,3) = 5\); \(B_2: \max(1,4) = 4\).

\[ \overline{v} = \min(5, 4) = \mathbf{4} \]

Test.

\[ \underline{v} = 3 \ne 4 = \overline{v} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{NO SADDLE POINT — no pure-strategy solution exists.}\ } \]

Why the instability arises — trace the reasoning.

  • A reasons: "\(A_2\) guarantees me at least 3."
  • B reasons: "Against \(A_2\), I should play \(B_1\) (paying 3, not 4)."
  • A reasons: "If B plays \(B_1\), I should switch to \(A_1\) and get 5!"
  • B reasons: "If A plays \(A_1\), I should switch to \(B_2\) and pay only 1."
  • A reasons: "If B plays \(B_2\), I should switch back to \(A_2\) and get 4."
  • …and the cycle repeats forever.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{No stable pure-strategy pair exists. The players must RANDOMISE.}\ } \]

The value lies strictly between the bounds: \(3 \le v \le 4\). L12 shows the exact solution is \(v = 3.4\), with A playing \(A_1\) with probability 0.2 and \(A_2\) with probability 0.8.

The economic meaning of randomising. If A always played \(A_2\), B would learn and exploit it. Unpredictability is itself valuable — the same reason a bowler varies deliveries or a firm varies its promotional timing.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Reduction by dominance to a saddle point
docs.text:
Reduce and solve.

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_2\) \(B_3\) \(B_4\) \(B_5\) \(A_1\) 6 3 1 0 3 \(A_2\) 3 2 4 2 4 \(A_3\) 1 2 3 2 2 \(A_4\) 3 3 1 2 3

Solution.

Step 1 — column dominance (B minimises, so B keeps SMALL entries).

Compare \(B_4\) and \(B_2\): entries \((0,2,2,2)\) versus \((3,2,2,3)\). Since \(0\le3\), \(2\le2\), \(2\le2\), \(2\le3\) — \(B_4\) dominates \(B_2\) (every entry is \(\le\)).

\[ \textbf{Delete } B_2 . \]

Compare \(B_4\) and \(B_5\): \((0,2,2,2)\) versus \((3,4,2,3)\). Every entry of \(B_4\) is \(\le\) ⟹ delete \(B_5\).

Compare \(B_4\) and \(B_1\): \((0,2,2,2)\) versus \((6,3,1,3)\). Here \(2 > 1\) in row 3, so no dominance — keep \(B_1\).

After column reduction:

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_3\) \(B_4\) \(A_1\) 6 1 0 \(A_2\) 3 4 2 \(A_3\) 1 3 2 \(A_4\) 3 1 2

Step 2 — row dominance (A maximises, so A keeps LARGE entries).

Compare \(A_2 = (3,4,2)\) with \(A_3 = (1,3,2)\): \(3\ge1\), \(4\ge3\), \(2\ge2\) ⟹ \(A_2\) dominates \(A_3\).

\[ \textbf{Delete } A_3 . \]

Compare \(A_2 = (3,4,2)\) with \(A_4 = (3,1,2)\): \(3\ge3\), \(4\ge1\), \(2\ge2\) ⟹ \(A_2\) dominates \(A_4\).

\[ \textbf{Delete } A_4 . \]

After row reduction:

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_3\) \(B_4\) \(A_1\) 6 1 0 \(A_2\) 3 4 2

Step 3 — column dominance again. Compare \(B_4 = (0,2)\) with \(B_3 = (1,4)\): both entries smaller ⟹ delete \(B_3\). Compare \(B_4 = (0,2)\) with \(B_1 = (6,3)\): both smaller ⟹ delete \(B_1\).

A \ B \(B_4\) \(A_1\) 0 \(A_2\) 2

Step 4 — solve. A picks the larger: \(A_2\) with payoff 2.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{A plays } A_2,\quad \text{B plays } B_4,\quad v = 2\ } \]

Verify against the ORIGINAL matrix.

Row minima: \(A_1: 0\), \(A_2: \mathbf{2}\), \(A_3: 1\), \(A_4: 1\) ⟹ maximin \(= 2\). Column maxima: \(B_1: 6\), \(B_2: 3\), \(B_3: 4\), \(B_4: \mathbf{2}\), \(B_5: 4\) ⟹ minimax \(= 2\).

\[ \underline{v} = \overline{v} = 2 \ \checkmark \ \textbf{ — saddle point at } (A_2, B_4). \]

Dominance gave the right answer while reducing a \(4\times5\) matrix to \(2\times1\). On larger games this reduction is what makes hand solution feasible at all.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Convex (generalised) dominance
docs.text:
Show that row \(A_3\) can be deleted from the following, even though no single row dominates it.

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_2\) \(B_3\) \(A_1\) 8 2 4 \(A_2\) 2 8 4 \(A_3\) 4 4 3

Solution.

No simple dominance.

  • \(A_1\) vs \(A_3\): \(8\ge4\) ✓ but \(2 < 4\) ✗ — no dominance.
  • \(A_2\) vs \(A_3\): \(2 < 4\) ✗ — no dominance.

Try the average of \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) (i.e. \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \tfrac12\)):

\[ \tfrac12 A_1 + \tfrac12 A_2 = \left(\tfrac{8+2}{2},\ \tfrac{2+8}{2},\ \tfrac{4+4}{2}\right) = (5,\ 5,\ 4) \]

Compare with \(A_3 = (4, 4, 3)\):

\[ 5 \ge 4 \ \checkmark, \qquad 5\ge4 \ \checkmark, \qquad 4\ge3 \ \checkmark \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The mixture } \tfrac12A_1+\tfrac12A_2 \textbf{ dominates } A_3 \ \Longrightarrow\ \textbf{delete } A_3.\ } \]

Why this is legitimate. A can achieve the payoff vector \((5,5,4)\) by randomising 50–50 between \(A_1\) and \(A_2\). Since that mixture beats \(A_3\) against every column, a rational A would never place positive probability on \(A_3\).

Reduced game.

A \ B \(B_1\) \(B_2\) \(B_3\) \(A_1\) 8 2 4 \(A_2\) 2 8 4

Continue with column dominance. \(B_3 = (4,4)\) against \(B_1 = (8,2)\): \(4 \le 8\) ✓ but \(4 > 2\) ✗ — no dominance. Against \(B_2 = (2,8)\): \(4 > 2\) ✗ — no dominance.

So the game reduces to \(2\times3\) and requires the graphical method of L13.

Checking for a saddle point. Row minima: \(A_1: 2\), \(A_2: 2\) ⟹ maximin \(= 2\). Column maxima: \(8, 8, 4\) ⟹ minimax \(= 4\). Since \(2 \ne 4\), mixed strategies are needed.

(By symmetry, A will play \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) with probability \(\frac12\) each, guaranteeing \(\min(5,5,4) = 4\) — and B will play \(B_3\), giving \(v = 4\).)

docs.title: Problem 5 — A business application of the maximin criterion
docs.text:
Two firms compete for a market. Firm A chooses an advertising level (Low, Medium, High); firm B does the same. The matrix gives A's market-share gain (percentage points).

A \ B Low Medium High Low 0 −3 −6 Medium 4 1 −2 High 7 3 −1

Analyse and advise firm A.

Solution.

Step 1 — saddle-point test.

Row minima: Low \(= -6\); Medium \(= -2\); High \(= -1\) ← maximum.

\[ \underline{v} = \mathbf{-1} \]

Column maxima: Low \(= 7\); Medium \(= 3\); High \(= -1\) ← minimum.

\[ \overline{v} = \mathbf{-1} \] \[ \underline{v} = \overline{v} = -1 \ \Longrightarrow\ \textbf{SADDLE POINT at (High, High)} \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{Both firms advertise HIGH; } v = -1 \text{ — firm A LOSES 1 percentage point.}\ } \]

Step 2 — check the dominance structure. Notice that for firm A:

  • High dominates Medium: \(7\ge4\), \(3\ge1\), \(-1\ge-2\) ✓
  • High dominates Low: \(7\ge0\), \(3\ge-3\), \(-1\ge-6\) ✓

High is a strictly dominant strategy for A — best regardless of what B does.

By the symmetry of the situation, High is dominant for B as well (B's column maxima are minimised by High).

Step 3 — the strategic interpretation.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{This is a PRISONER'S DILEMMA structure.}\ } \]
  • Both firms are compelled to advertise High, because it is individually dominant.
  • But compare the outcomes: at (Low, Low) the payoff is 0 — no share change, and both firms save the cost of heavy advertising. At (High, High) the payoff is \(-1\) plus both firms have incurred the full advertising expense.
  • The equilibrium is worse for both than the cooperative outcome — yet neither can move to it unilaterally, because deviating to Low against a High opponent costs \(-6\).

Advice to firm A.

  1. In the zero-sum framing, play High. It is dominant, and it limits the loss to 1 point.

  2. But question the framing. The zero-sum model captures only share, not profit. If both firms spend heavily on advertising, total industry profit falls — this is genuinely a non-zero-sum situation, and the model is understating the cost of the arms race.

  3. The real strategic options lie outside the matrix. Change the game rather than play it better:

    • Product differentiation, so the firms are no longer competing for the same share;
    • Industry advertising standards or a joint category-building campaign (subject to competition law);
    • Signalling restraint — repeated interaction can sustain cooperation, which a one-shot model cannot capture.

  4. The \(-1\) deserves scrutiny. A loses 1 point at equilibrium, meaning B has a structural advantage — perhaps better brand recognition. A should investigate why the payoffs are asymmetric, since fixing that changes every entry in the table.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The most valuable use of a game model is often to reveal that you are playing the wrong game.}\ } \]

docs.title: 11.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Find the saddle point: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&7&3\\5&6&4\\7&2&0\end{pmatrix}\). [Ans: \((2,3)\), \(v = 4\)]
  2. Does \(\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\6&3\end{pmatrix}\) have a saddle point? [Ans: no — maximin 3, minimax 4]
  3. Reduce by dominance: \(\begin{pmatrix}4&2&3\\5&6&7\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}\). [Ans: row 2 dominates rows 1 and 3; \(v = 5\)]
  4. State the direction of column dominance and explain why.
  5. Prove \(\underline{v}\le\overline{v}\).
  6. A game has \(v = 0\). What is it called, and what does it mean? [Ans: fair]
  7. Show that a \(2\times2\) game with entries \(a > b\), \(c < d\), \(a > c\), \(b < d\) has no saddle point.

docs.title: 11.8 Summary
docs.text:
• A two-person zero-sum game has one player's gain exactly equal to the other's loss; the matrix records the row player's payoff. A maximises, B minimises.
  • Maximin \(\underline{v} = \max_i\min_j a_{ij}\) is A's guarantee; minimax \(\overline{v} = \min_j\max_i a_{ij}\) is B's. Always \(\underline{v}\le\overline{v}\).
  • A saddle point exists iff \(\underline{v} = \overline{v}\), and then \(v\) is the value of the game and the pure strategies form an equilibrium — neither player gains by deviating alone.
  • \(v>0\) favours A, \(v<0\) favours B, \(v=0\) is fair.
  • Dominance: A deletes rows with uniformly smaller entries; B deletes columns with uniformly larger entries. Convex dominance allows a mixture of rows to dominate another.
  • No saddle point ⟹ mixed strategies are required (L12); the players must randomise, because any predictable pure strategy is exploitable.
  • The most valuable use of a game model is often diagnostic — recognising a prisoner's-dilemma structure, or that the zero-sum framing itself is wrong.

Next lesson: L12 — Mixed strategies and the odds method.

Practise now: unit2-games-networks-lab.html → Game Solver: enter any payoff matrix and see row minima, column maxima, saddle-point detection and step-by-step dominance reduction.

docs.title: 40.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive the golden ratio from the requirement that one probe be reusable at every stage.
  2. State the reduction law \(L_n=(0.618)^{\,n-1}L_0\) and use it to size a search.
  3. Execute golden section search by hand and verify the reduction at each stage.
  4. Compare golden section with Fibonacci search on cost, accuracy and convenience.
  5. Choose sensibly between the elimination methods of Lessons 38–40.

docs.title: 40.2 Deriving the Golden Ratio
docs.text:
Fibonacci search is optimal but requires \(n\) to be fixed in advance, because the first placement depends on \(F_{n-2}/F_n\). Golden section removes that restriction by asking a different question:

Is there a single, constant fraction \(\tau\) such that placing the probes at \(\tau\) of the way in from each end lets one probe be reused for ever?

docs.title: The derivation
docs.text:
Let the interval be \([0,1]\) and place probes at \(x_1=1-\tau\) and \(x_2=\tau\) (with \(\tau>\tfrac12\)). Suppose the right portion is discarded, leaving \([0,\tau]\) of length \(\tau\).

The surviving probe \(x_1=1-\tau\) must land exactly where the new stage wants its right-hand probe, which by the same rule is at \(\tau\) of the way along the new interval, i.e. at \(\tau\cdot\tau=\tau^{2}\) from the left end. Therefore

\[1-\tau=\tau^{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \tau^{2}+\tau-1=0\] \[\tau=\frac{-1+\sqrt5}{2}=0.6180339887\dots\]

The golden ratio. $\(\boxed{\ \tau=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}=0.618034,\qquad 1-\tau=0.381966,\qquad \tau^{2}=1-\tau\ }\)$ The reciprocal \(1/\tau=1.618034=\tau+1\) is denoted \(\phi\).

The self-reproducing property \(\tau^2=1-\tau\) is exactly what makes the inheritance work at every stage, with no reference to how many stages remain.

docs.title: Connection to Fibonacci
docs.text:
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_{n-1}}{F_n}=\tau\]

so golden section is the limiting form of Fibonacci search as \(n\to\infty\). Fibonacci uses the exact ratios for a known finite \(n\); golden section uses the limiting ratio for all stages, giving up a little efficiency for complete flexibility.

docs.title: 40.3 The Algorithm
docs.text:
Step 1. On \([a,b]\) with \(L=b-a\), set $\(x_1=a+0.382L,\qquad x_2=a+0.618L\)$ and evaluate \(f(x_1)\), \(f(x_2)\). (2 evaluations)

Step 2. Compare: - If \(f(x_1)<f(x_2)\): set \(b\leftarrow x_2\), then \(x_2\leftarrow x_1\) and \(f_2\leftarrow f_1\) (inherited), and compute the new \(x_1=a+0.382(b-a)\). (1 evaluation) - Else: set \(a\leftarrow x_1\), then \(x_1\leftarrow x_2\) and \(f_1\leftarrow f_2\) (inherited), and compute the new \(x_2=a+0.618(b-a)\). (1 evaluation)

Step 3. Repeat until \(b-a<\epsilon\). Report \(x^{*}\approx(a+b)/2\).

docs.title: The reduction law
docs.text:
Each stage multiplies the interval by \(\tau=0.618\), and the first stage costs two evaluations while each later one costs one. Hence after \(n\) evaluations there have been \(n-1\) reductions:

\[\boxed{\ L_n=(0.618)^{\,n-1}L_0\ }\tag{2.1}\]

To reach an accuracy \(\epsilon\):

\[n\ \ge\ 1+\frac{\ln(\epsilon/L_0)}{\ln 0.618}\tag{2.2}\]

docs.title: Comparison with Fibonacci
docs.text:
Fibonacci Golden section Final interval after \(n\) evaluations \(L_0/F_n\) \(L_0(0.618)^{n-1}\) \(n=5\) \(L_0/8=0.1250L_0\) \(0.1459L_0\) \(n=10\) \(L_0/89=0.01124L_0\) \(0.01316L_0\) \(n=20\) \(L_0/10946=9.14\times10^{-5}L_0\) \(1.07\times10^{-4}L_0\) Must fix \(n\) in advance? yes no Ratios needed a Fibonacci table one constant, \(0.618\) Degenerate final step? yes (\(\varepsilon\)-perturbation) no

Golden section is about \(17\,\%\) worse per interval, which costs roughly ONE extra evaluation — and that gap does not grow with \(n\). In exchange it can be stopped at any moment, needs no table, and has no awkward final step. In practice golden section is almost always the right choice; Fibonacci is studied because it establishes the theoretical bound.

docs.title: Problem 1 — A complete golden section search
Problem 2 — Golden section against Fibonacci on the same problem
docs.text:
Compare the result of Problem 1 with Fibonacci search (Lesson 39, Problem 1) on the same function and interval.

Solution.

Fibonacci, \(n=6\) Golden section, \(n=7\) Final interval \([2.84615,\ 3.15485]\) \([2.88854,\ 3.11146]\) Width 0.30869 0.22291 Midpoint estimate 3.00050 3.00000 Evaluations 6 7 Interval per evaluation \(L_0/F_6=0.30769\) \(L_0(0.618)^6=0.22291\)

Like-for-like at \(n=6\). Golden section with \(6\) evaluations would give \(4(0.618)^{5}=0.36068\) against Fibonacci's \(0.30769\) — Fibonacci is \(14.7\,\%\) better.

Like-for-like at a target of \(0.30\). Fibonacci needs \(F_n\ge4/0.3=13.33\), so \(F_7=21\) and \(n=7\). Golden section needs \((0.618)^{n-1}\le0.075\), i.e. \(n-1\ge5.38\), so \(n=7\). A dead heat.

Interpretation. The gap is one evaluation at most, and often zero because both must round up to a whole number. Set against that, golden section:

  • needs no decision about \(n\) before starting, so the search can simply run until the answer is good enough;
  • has no degenerate last step and no \(\varepsilon\) to choose;
  • can be stopped early if the outer algorithm no longer needs precision — which, as Lesson 39 Problem 5 argued, is the normal situation inside a multivariable method.

Golden section wins on every practical criterion and loses only on the theoretical one.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Sizing a search
docs.text:
How many evaluations does golden section need to locate the minimum of a function on \([0,\,50]\) to within \(\pm0.01\) (an interval of \(0.02\))?

Solution. Require \(L_n=(0.618)^{n-1}(50)\le0.02\), i.e. \((0.618)^{n-1}\le4\times10^{-4}\).

\[n-1\ \ge\ \frac{\ln(4\times10^{-4})}{\ln 0.618}=\frac{-7.8240}{-0.4812}=16.26\ \Rightarrow\ n=\mathbf{18}\]

Verify: \((0.618)^{17}=2.798\times10^{-4}\) and \(50(2.798\times10^{-4})=0.0140\le0.02\) ✓, while \(n=17\) gives \(50(0.618)^{16}=0.0226>0.02\) ✗.

Comparison.

Method Evaluations for \(L=0.02\) on \([0,50]\) Exhaustive \(2(50)/0.02-1=4999\) Interval halving \((0.5)^{(n-1)/2}\le4\times10^{-4}\Rightarrow (n-1)/2\ge11.29\), so 25 (n odd) Golden section 18 Fibonacci \(F_n\ge2500\Rightarrow F_{17}=2584\), so 17

Interpretation. Golden section needs 18 evaluations where exhaustive search needs 4999 — a factor of \(278\). The reason is structural: exhaustive search discards nothing, so its interval falls like \(1/n\), while every sequential method discards a fixed fraction each stage and so falls like \(c^{n}\). Linear versus exponential is the whole story of Lessons 38–40.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Golden section inside steepest descent
docs.text:
Minimise \(f(x_1,x_2)=(x_1-2)^{2}+(x_2-3)^{2}\) from \(\mathbf{x}_0=(0,0)\): find the descent direction, set up the line search, run three stages of golden section on \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), and compare with the exact step.

Solution.

Step 1 — direction.

\[\nabla f=\begin{pmatrix}2(x_1-2)\\2(x_2-3)\end{pmatrix},\qquad \nabla f(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-6\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{d}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\6\end{pmatrix}\]

Step 2 — the line-search function. With \(\mathbf{x}(\alpha)=(4\alpha,\ 6\alpha)\):

\[\phi(\alpha)=(4\alpha-2)^{2}+(6\alpha-3)^{2}=16\alpha^{2}-16\alpha+4+36\alpha^{2}-36\alpha+9\] \[\phi(\alpha)=52\alpha^{2}-52\alpha+13\]

Step 3 — three stages of golden section on \([0,1]\).

Stage \([a,b]\) \(L\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(\phi_1\) \(\phi_2\) Discard 1 \([0.00000,\ 1.00000]\) 1.00000 0.38197 0.61803 0.72447 0.72447 tie — break either way (here, left) 2 \([0.38197,\ 1.00000]\) 0.61803 0.61803 0.76393 0.72447 3.62233 right 3 \([0.38197,\ 0.76393]\) 0.38197 0.52786 0.61803 0.04037 0.72447 right — \([0.38197,\ 0.61803]\) 0.23607

Step 4 — the exact answer. \(\phi'(\alpha)=104\alpha-52=0\Rightarrow \alpha^{*}=0.5\), \(\phi(0.5)=13-26+13=0\).

The interval \([0.38197,\ 0.61803]\) contains \(0.5\) and its midpoint is exactly \(0.5\) ✓.

\[\mathbf{x}_1=(0,0)+0.5(4,6)=(2,3)\]

which is the exact minimum of \(f\), reached in one steepest-descent step.

Interpretation — two points.

  1. The tie at stage 1 is not an accident. \(\phi\) is symmetric about \(\alpha=0.5\), and the golden probes \(0.382\) and \(0.618\) are symmetric about \(0.5\) too, so the two values are equal. A tie is resolved either way without harm, since the minimum lies in the overlap; a good implementation should test for it explicitly rather than let floating-point noise decide.
  2. One step sufficed because the contours of \(f\) are perfect circles, so the negative gradient points straight at the minimum. Lesson 42 shows that as soon as the contours become elongated ellipses, steepest descent starts to zig-zag and needs many steps — the failing that conjugate gradient methods were invented to cure.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Choosing among the elimination methods
docs.text:
A colleague must minimise each of the following. Recommend a method for each, with a reason.

Case Recommendation Reason (a) Smooth cheap analytic function, high accuracy wanted Interpolation (L41), safeguarded by golden section Quadratic/Newton methods converge superlinearly on smooth functions; the safeguard covers the cases where they diverge (b) Each evaluation is a 6-hour simulation; budget 12 runs Fibonacci with \(n=12\) With a hard, known budget, the optimal method is worth the inconvenience: \(L_0/F_{12}=L_0/233\) against golden section's \(L_0/198\) (c) Function known only from a table of measurements Exhaustive over the tabulated points No derivatives exist and the points are fixed; nothing else applies (d) Function possibly multi-modal Coarse exhaustive first, then golden section on each promising bracket Only exhaustive search does not assume unimodality; refine locally afterwards (e) Line search inside a steepest-descent code Inexact search (a few golden-section stages, or an Armijo backtrack) The direction changes next iteration, so precision here is wasted (f) Noisy function (measurement error \(\pm0.01\)) Golden section, stopped when the interval reaches the noise scale Never resolve below the noise: comparisons become meaningless. Dichotomous search is especially dangerous here

The general rule. Match the method to the cost structure and the smoothness, not to a preference. The three questions to ask are: How expensive is one evaluation? Is the function smooth? Is it unimodal? The table above is simply those three questions applied six times.

docs.title: 40.5 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Perform three stages of golden section on \(f(x)=(x-4)^{2}\) over \([0,10]\). (Answer: stage 1 \(x_1=3.81966\), \(x_2=6.18034\), \(f_1=0.03252<f_2=4.75388\), keep \([0,\ 6.18034]\); stage 2 \(f(2.36068)=2.68737>f(3.81966)=0.03252\), keep \([2.36068,\ 6.18034]\); stage 3 \(f(3.81966)=0.03252<f(4.72136)=0.52036\), keep \([2.36068,\ 4.72136]\))
  2. How many evaluations does golden section need to reduce \([10,\,60]\) to \(0.5\)? (Answer: \((0.618)^{n-1}\le0.01\), \(n-1\ge9.57\), so \(n=11\))
  3. Verify algebraically that \(\tau^{2}=1-\tau\) for \(\tau=(\sqrt5-1)/2\), and deduce \(1/\tau=\tau+1\).
  4. Show that golden section needs at most one more evaluation than Fibonacci for any accuracy target, using \(F_n\approx\phi^{n}/\sqrt5\).
  5. A golden-section search returns the interval \([2.88854,\ 3.11146]\). What is the best point estimate, and what is the maximum possible error? (Answer: midpoint \(3.00000\); maximum error \(L/2=0.11146\) — though the actual error here is zero)

docs.title: 40.6 Summary
docs.text:
• The golden ratio \(\tau=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}=0.618034\) is forced by the requirement \(\boxed{\tau^{2}=1-\tau}\) — that one probe be reusable at every stage, for ever.
  • Probes go at \(0.382L\) and \(0.618L\) from the left end. After the first stage each iteration costs one evaluation.
  • \(\boxed{L_n=(0.618)^{\,n-1}L_0}\), so \(n\ge1+\dfrac{\ln(\epsilon/L_0)}{\ln 0.618}\).
  • Golden section is the limiting case of Fibonacci as \(n\to\infty\): about \(17\,\%\) worse per interval, which is at most one extra evaluation regardless of the target.
  • In exchange it needs no advance choice of \(n\), no Fibonacci table, and has no degenerate final step — so it is the practical default.
  • Both are exponential (\(c^{n}\)) where exhaustive search is linear (\(1/n\)): \(18\) evaluations against \(4999\) in Problem 3.
  • The midpoint of the final interval is usually far more accurate than the interval width guarantees, but only the width is a guarantee.
  • Never search below the noise level of the function, and inside a multivariable algorithm do not over-solve the line search.

Next lesson: L41 — Interpolation and gradient-based one-dimensional methods: quadratic fitting, Newton–Raphson and the secant method.

Practise now: unit4-nlp-search-lab.html → Golden Section Trace: watch the interval shrink by \(0.618\) each stage, with the inherited probe highlighted and the running comparison against Fibonacci.

docs.title: Lesson 17: Gomory's Method for Mixed Integer Programmes
17.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Distinguish a mixed integer programme from a pure one.
  2. Explain why the pure Gomory cut is invalid when continuous variables are present.
  3. Derive the Gomory mixed-integer (GMI) cut.
