Interpretation. Note that (c) beats (b) even though the expert costs \(₹50\) per hour more than two ordinary mechanics combined — the consolidation effect of Problem 2 again. Note too that the present system spends eight times more on downtime than on labour: whenever the waiting cost dwarfs the service cost, the system is almost certainly under-resourced, and that ratio is the quickest diagnostic a manager can apply.

docs.title: 25.5 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda = 12\)/h, \(C_w = ₹80\) per customer-hour, \(C_s = ₹20\) per unit \(\mu\) per hour. Find \(\mu^{*}\) and the minimum total cost. (Answer: \(\mu^*=12+\sqrt{48}=18.93\)/h; \(TC=₹517.13\)/h)
  2. Recompute Problem 1 using \(L_q\) instead of \(L_s\) in the objective. Does the recommendation change? (Answer: \(\mu=15\) still wins; the totals fall but their ordering does not)
  3. Two clerks each handle their own queue at \(\mu=5\)/h with \(\lambda=4\)/h each. Compute \(W_q\); then compute \(W_q\) for an \(M/M/2\) system with \(\lambda=8\)/h, \(\mu=5\)/h. (Answer: \(48\) min vs \(21.33\) min — pooling cuts waiting by \(55.6\,\%\))
  4. In Problem 3, at what lease cost per hour does the faster machine become worthwhile? (Answer: below \(₹180\) per hour)
  5. A firm reports "our servers run at 92 % utilisation, which is excellent efficiency." Write a three-sentence reply using the results of Lesson 24 and this lesson.

docs.title: 25.6 Summary
docs.text:
• Total cost = waiting cost + service cost: \(TC = C_wL_s + C_s\mu\). Use \(L_s\) when the whole sojourn is costly, \(L_q\) when only waiting is wasted.
  • The optimum is \(\mu^{*}=\lambda+\sqrt{C_w\lambda/C_s}\); the required excess capacity grows as \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), and the cost curve is flat near the optimum, so approximate choices are cheap.
  • Pooling is the best free improvement in operations. One shared queue beat two separate queues by \(43\,\%\) in Problem 2 with no new equipment.
  • One fast server beats several slow ones of equal total capacity — when that choice is physically available.
  • Investment decisions should be reported as break-even values of \(C_w\), since \(C_w\) is the least reliable input.
  • Never average the arrival rate. \(L_s(\lambda)\) is convex, so Jensen's inequality guarantees the averaged figure understates congestion — by a factor of \(2.6\) in Problem 4.
  • If waiting cost hugely exceeds service cost, the system is under-resourced. That ratio is the fastest diagnostic available.

Next lesson: L26 — Model II, \((M/M/1):(N/\text{FCFS})\), the finite-capacity queue.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Cost Optimiser: enter \(C_w\) and \(C_s\), sweep \(\mu\), and see the waiting-cost and service-cost curves cross at \(\mu^{*}\).

docs.title: Lesson 24: Model I: (M/M/1):(∞/FCFS) Derived in Full
24.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive \(P_n=(1-\rho)\rho^n\) for the \(M/M/1\) queue from the birth–death equations.
  2. Derive \(L_s\), \(L_q\), \(W_s\) and \(W_q\) and connect them by Little's law.
  3. Derive the waiting-time distributions and compute percentiles.
  4. Explain why congestion grows non-linearly as \(\rho\to1\), and quantify it.
  5. Apply the complete formula set to a design problem and interpret each number.

docs.title: 24.2 The Model
docs.text:
Kendall notation. \((M/M/1):(\infty/\text{FCFS})\) means: Markovian (Poisson) arrivals, Markovian (exponential) service, 1 server, infinite system capacity, infinite calling population, served first come first served.

Assumptions, stated explicitly so you know what you are trusting:

  1. Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\).
  2. Service times are exponential with mean \(1/\mu\); the service rate is \(\mu\).
  3. One server; the queue may grow without limit; nobody balks or reneges.
  4. Arrivals and service times are independent of each other and of the state.

The traffic intensity (or utilisation factor) is

\[\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} = \frac{\text{mean service time}}{\text{mean inter-arrival time}}.\]

It is dimensionless: it is the fraction of time the server is busy, and for a single server it is also the expected number of customers in service.

docs.title: 24.3 Deriving the State Distribution
docs.text:
Apply Lesson 23 with \(\lambda_n=\lambda\) and \(\mu_n=\mu\) for all \(n\). The cut equations give

\[\lambda P_n = \mu P_{n+1} \ \Longrightarrow\ P_{n+1} = \rho P_n \ \Longrightarrow\ P_n = \rho^{\,n}P_0.\]

Normalising, and using the geometric series (which converges only if \(\rho<1\)):

\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\rho^nP_0 = \frac{P_0}{1-\rho}=1 \ \Longrightarrow\ P_0 = 1-\rho.\]

Result 1 (state distribution). $\(\boxed{\ P_n = (1-\rho)\rho^{\,n},\qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots\ }\tag{2.1}\)$ valid if and only if \(\rho<1\).

Two immediate consequences:

\[P_0 = 1-\rho = \Pr[\text{system empty}] = \Pr[\text{server idle}],\] \[\Pr[n\ge k]=\sum_{n\ge k}(1-\rho)\rho^n = \rho^{\,k}. \tag{2.2}\]

Equation (2.2) is worth memorising: the probability of finding at least \(k\) customers is simply \(\rho^k\).

docs.title: Expected number in the system
docs.text:
\[L_s=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nP_n=(1-\rho)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\rho^n =(1-\rho)\rho\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\rho^{\,n-1}.\]

Using \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge1}n x^{n-1}=\frac{d}{dx}\frac{1}{1-x}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}\),

\[L_s=(1-\rho)\rho\cdot\frac{1}{(1-\rho)^2}\]

Result 2. \(\qquad\boxed{\ L_s = \dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}=\dfrac{\lambda}{\mu-\lambda}\ }\tag{3.1}\)

docs.title: Expected queue length
docs.text:
\(L_q\) counts only those waiting, i.e. \(n-1\) when \(n\ge1\):

\[L_q=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(n-1)P_n=L_s-\sum_{n\ge1}P_n=L_s-(1-P_0)=L_s-\rho.\]

Result 3. \(\qquad\boxed{\ L_q = \dfrac{\rho^2}{1-\rho}=\dfrac{\lambda^2}{\mu(\mu-\lambda)}=\rho L_s\ }\tag{3.2}\)

The identity \(L_s-L_q=\rho\) has a clean reading: the average number in service equals the utilisation. It is the fastest check available on any \(M/M/1\) answer.

docs.title: The waiting times, via Little's law
docs.text:
Little's law (\(L=\lambda W\)) applies to any stable system, whatever the distributions:

Result 4. \(\qquad\boxed{\ W_s=\dfrac{L_s}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1}{\mu-\lambda},\qquad W_q=\dfrac{L_q}{\lambda}=\dfrac{\rho}{\mu-\lambda}=\dfrac{\lambda}{\mu(\mu-\lambda)}\ }\tag{3.3}\)

Also \(W_s = W_q + \dfrac1\mu\): total time = waiting + service. Since nothing here is blocked or discouraged, \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda\).

docs.title: The complete formula set
docs.text: Quantity Formula In terms of \(\rho\) \(P_0\) \(1-\lambda/\mu\) \(1-\rho\) \(P_n\) \((1-\rho)\rho^n\) \((1-\rho)\rho^n\) \(\Pr[n\ge k]\) \(\rho^k\) \(\rho^k\) \(L_s\) \(\lambda/(\mu-\lambda)\) \(\rho/(1-\rho)\) \(L_q\) \(\lambda^2/[\mu(\mu-\lambda)]\) \(\rho^2/(1-\rho)\) \(W_s\) \(1/(\mu-\lambda)\) \(\dfrac{1}{\mu}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1-\rho}\) \(W_q\) \(\lambda/[\mu(\mu-\lambda)]\) \(\dfrac{1}{\mu}\cdot\dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\) \(L_q\) of a busy period \(1/(1-\rho)\) \(1/(1-\rho)\)

docs.title: 24.5 The Waiting-Time Distributions
docs.text:
The averages above hide the variability. Fortunately the full distributions are simple.

Theorem. For \(M/M/1\) under FCFS, the total time in the system is exponential with rate \(\mu-\lambda\): $\(\Pr[W_s > t] = e^{-(\mu-\lambda)t}. \tag{4.1}\)$ The waiting time in the queue has an atom at zero: $\(\Pr[W_q = 0]=1-\rho,\qquad \Pr[W_q>t]=\rho\,e^{-(\mu-\lambda)t}. \tag{4.2}\)$

Sketch of proof. An arrival who finds \(n\) ahead must wait for \(n+1\) services (its own included), a sum of \(n+1\) i.i.d. exponentials — an Erlang. Averaging that Erlang over the geometric distribution of \(n\) from (2.1) collapses the mixture back to a single exponential of rate \(\mu-\lambda\). ∎

Two practical uses:

  • Percentiles. The \(100p\)-th percentile of \(W_s\) is \(t_p = \dfrac{-\ln(1-p)}{\mu-\lambda}\). Service-level agreements are written in percentiles, not means.
  • The atom at 0. A fraction \(1-\rho\) of customers wait not at all. Quoting only the mean \(W_q\) misrepresents everyone's experience: most customers either sail through or wait a long time.

docs.title: Problem 1 — The complete standard calculation
docs.text:
At a single-window bank counter customers arrive in a Poisson stream at \(8\) per hour and service is exponential at a mean rate of \(10\) per hour. Compute every standard measure.

Solution.

\[\rho=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}=\frac{8}{10}=0.8 <1 \ \checkmark\ \text{(stable)}\] Quantity Working Value \(P_0\) \(1-0.8\) \(0.20\) — idle \(20\,\%\) of the time \(\Pr[n\ge2]\) \(\rho^2=0.8^2\) \(0.64\) \(\Pr[n\ge4]\) \(0.8^4\) \(0.4096\) \(L_s\) \(\dfrac{8}{10-8}\) \(\mathbf{4}\) customers \(L_q\) \(\dfrac{8^2}{10(2)}=\dfrac{64}{20}\) \(\mathbf{3.2}\) customers \(W_s\) \(\dfrac{1}{10-8}=0.5\) h \(\mathbf{30}\) minutes \(W_q\) \(\dfrac{8}{10(2)}=0.4\) h \(\mathbf{24}\) minutes

Checks. \(L_s-L_q=4-3.2=0.8=\rho\) ✓. \(W_s-W_q=0.1\text{ h}=6\text{ min}=1/\mu\) ✓. \(L_s=\lambda W_s = 8(0.5)=4\) ✓.

Interpretation. The server is idle one hour in five, yet the average customer spends half an hour for six minutes of service — 80 % of the customer's time is pure waiting. Idle servers and long queues coexist; that is not a contradiction but the essence of the phenomenon.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Waiting-time distribution and percentiles
docs.text:
For the counter in Problem 1, find (a) \(\Pr[W_s>20\text{ min}]\), (b) \(\Pr[W_q>20\text{ min}]\), (c) the probability a customer does not wait at all, (d) the time within which \(90\,\%\) of customers are finished.

Solution. Here \(\mu-\lambda=2\) per hour.

(a) With \(t=\tfrac13\) h:

\[\Pr[W_s>t]=e^{-2(1/3)}=e^{-0.6667}=\mathbf{0.5134}\]

Over half of all customers spend more than \(20\) minutes in the bank.

(b) \(\Pr[W_q>t]=\rho e^{-2/3}=0.8(0.5134)=\mathbf{0.4107}\)

(c) \(\Pr[W_q=0]=1-\rho=\mathbf{0.20}\) — one customer in five walks straight to the window.

(d) Solve \(e^{-2t}=0.10\):

\[t=\frac{\ln 10}{2}=\frac{2.3026}{2}=1.1513\text{ h}=\mathbf{69.1\text{ minutes}}\]

Interpretation. The mean is \(30\) minutes but the 90th percentile is 69 minutes — more than twice the mean. Publishing the average would understate the worst experience badly. Always quote a percentile alongside a mean.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Verifying Little's law
docs.text:
Cars arrive at a service bay at \(15\) per hour; servicing is exponential at \(20\) per hour. Compute all measures and verify \(L=\lambda W\) in both forms.

Solution. \(\rho = 15/20 = 0.75\).

\[L_s=\frac{0.75}{0.25}=3\text{ cars},\qquad L_q=\frac{0.75^2}{0.25}=2.25\text{ cars}\] \[W_s=\frac{1}{20-15}=0.2\text{ h}=12\text{ min},\qquad W_q=\frac{15}{20(5)}=0.15\text{ h}=9\text{ min}\]

Verification.

\[\lambda W_s=15(0.2)=3=L_s\ \checkmark \qquad \lambda W_q=15(0.15)=2.25=L_q\ \checkmark\] \[L_s-L_q=0.75=\rho\ \checkmark\qquad W_s-W_q=0.05\text{ h}=3\text{ min}=1/\mu\ \checkmark\]

Remark. Little's law needed no distributional assumption — only that the system is stable and that we are averaging over the long run. That is why it holds for \(M/G/1\), \(G/G/c\) and every model in this unit, and why it is the right tool for cross-checking any answer.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Why the last 10 % of capacity is unaffordable
docs.text:
Tabulate \(L_s\), \(L_q\) and \(W_s\) (as a multiple of the service time \(1/\mu\)) for \(\rho=0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99\), and interpret.

Solution.

\(\rho\) \(L_s=\dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\) \(L_q=\dfrac{\rho^2}{1-\rho}\) \(W_s\div(1/\mu)=\dfrac{1}{1-\rho}\) 0.50 1.00 0.50 2 0.80 4.00 3.20 5 0.90 9.00 8.10 10 0.95 19.00 18.05 20 0.99 99.00 98.01 100

Interpretation. Everything is governed by the factor \(\dfrac{1}{1-\rho}\), which blows up as \(\rho\to1\):

  • From \(\rho=0.5\) to \(\rho=0.9\), utilisation rises \(1.8\times\) but the queue grows \(16\times\).
  • From \(\rho=0.9\) to \(\rho=0.95\) — a mere five extra percentage points of utilisation — waiting time doubles.
  • At \(\rho=0.99\) a customer spends 100 service times in the system.

The central management lesson of queuing theory. Utilisation and responsiveness are in direct conflict, and the trade-off is not linear. Systems that must stay responsive (hospitals, emergency services, data-centre links) are deliberately run at \(60\)–\(80\,\%\) utilisation. A manager who demands \(95\,\%\) utilisation of a single server has, unknowingly, demanded a twenty-fold queue.

docs.title: Problem 5 — A design problem
docs.text:
A one-chair barber shop has Poisson arrivals at \(4\) customers per hour; a haircut takes an average of \(12\) minutes, exponentially distributed. The shop is open \(10\) hours a day. Find: (a) the fraction of the day the barber is idle, (b) the average time a customer spends in the shop, (c) the average number waiting, (d) the probability that a customer must wait, (e) the probability of finding more than \(3\) people in the shop. (f) The barber can train to cut the mean time to \(10\) minutes. What happens?

Solution. Mean service \(12\) min \(\Rightarrow \mu = 60/12 = 5\) per hour; \(\lambda = 4\); \(\rho = 4/5 = 0.8\).

(a) \(P_0=1-\rho=0.2\), so the barber is idle \(0.2\times10 = \mathbf{2\text{ hours per day}}\).

(b) \(W_s = \dfrac{1}{5-4}=1\) hour \(=\mathbf{60\text{ minutes}}\) for a \(12\)-minute haircut.

(c) \(L_q = \dfrac{0.8^2}{0.2}=\mathbf{3.2\text{ customers waiting}}\) on average.

(d) \(\Pr[\text{must wait}]=\Pr[n\ge1]=\rho=\mathbf{0.8}\) — four customers in five must wait.

(e) \(\Pr[n>3]=\Pr[n\ge4]=\rho^4=0.8^4=\mathbf{0.4096}\). The shop needs seating for four or more about \(41\,\%\) of the time.

(f) With \(\mu = 6\) per hour, \(\rho = 4/6 = 0.6667\):

\[L_s=\frac{0.6667}{0.3333}=2,\qquad L_q=1.333,\qquad W_s=\frac{1}{6-4}=0.5\text{ h}=30\text{ min}\] before after change Mean service time 12 min 10 min \(-17\,\%\) \(\rho\) 0.800 0.667 \(-17\,\%\) \(L_q\) 3.20 1.33 \(\mathbf{-58\,\%}\) \(W_s\) 60 min 30 min \(\mathbf{-50\,\%}\)

Interpretation. A 17 % cut in service time halves the customer's time in the shop and reduces the queue by 58 %. This leverage — small improvements in the service rate producing large improvements in congestion — is the strongest practical argument in this unit, and it works in reverse too: a small slippage in service speed can produce a spectacular collapse in service level.

docs.title: 24.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda=10\)/h, \(\mu=15\)/h. Find \(\rho\), \(P_0\), \(L_s\), \(L_q\), \(W_s\), \(W_q\). (Answer: \(0.6667\), \(0.3333\), \(2\), \(1.333\), \(12\) min, \(8\) min)
  2. For Problem 1's counter, find the probability that the queue (excluding the customer in service) has at least \(2\) people. (Answer: \(\Pr[n\ge3]=\rho^3=0.512\))
  3. A repair shop has \(\lambda=3\)/day and \(\mu=4\)/day. What fraction of arriving jobs find the shop empty, and what is the mean time a job spends there? (Answer: \(0.25\); \(1\) day)
  4. If \(W_q\) must not exceed \(5\) minutes when \(\lambda=20\)/h, what is the minimum \(\mu\)? (Answer: solve \(\mu^2-20\mu-240=0\), giving \(\mu\ge 28.44\)/h)
  5. Show that \(\mathrm{Var}[n]=\dfrac{\rho}{(1-\rho)^2}\) for the geometric distribution (2.1), and evaluate it at \(\rho=0.8\). (Answer: \(20\), so \(\sigma=4.47\) — as large as the mean \(L_s=4\))

docs.title: 24.8 Summary
docs.text:
• \(M/M/1\) has \(P_n=(1-\rho)\rho^n\): a geometric distribution, valid only when \(\rho<1\).
  • \(\Pr[n\ge k]=\rho^k\) — the single most useful one-line result in the model.
  • \(L_s=\dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\), \(L_q=\rho L_s\), \(W_s=\dfrac{1}{\mu-\lambda}\), \(W_q=\rho W_s\).
  • Two universal checks: \(L_s-L_q=\rho\) and \(W_s-W_q=1/\mu\). Use them on every answer.
  • Time in the system is exponential with rate \(\mu-\lambda\); a fraction \(1-\rho\) of customers never wait at all. Report percentiles, not just means.
  • Congestion scales as \(\dfrac{1}{1-\rho}\) and therefore explodes near full utilisation. High utilisation and short queues are mutually exclusive goals.
  • A modest improvement in service rate delivers a disproportionately large reduction in waiting — the most actionable finding in the whole unit.

Next lesson: L25 — Model I applications: costing, design decisions and extensive practice.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → M/M/1 Explorer: drag \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), watch \(P_n\), \(L_s\) and \(W_s\) update live, and see the \(1/(1-\rho)\) blow-up on the congestion curve.

docs.title: Lesson 26: Model II: (M/M/1):(N/FCFS), the Finite-Capacity Queue
26.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive \(P_n\) for a queue with a finite system capacity \(N\), including the case \(\rho=1\).
  2. Compute the blocking probability \(P_N\) and the effective arrival rate \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\).
  3. Apply Little's law correctly in a system where customers are turned away.
  4. Explain why a finite queue is stable even when \(\lambda>\mu\).
  5. Choose the capacity \(N\) by marginal analysis of revenue against space cost.

docs.title: 26.2 The Model
docs.text:
Real systems have limits: a car park has bays, a telephone exchange has lines, a doctor's waiting room has chairs, a router has buffer memory. When the system holds \(N\) customers, further arrivals are turned away and lost forever.

Kendall notation. \((M/M/1):(N/\text{FCFS})\) — Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server, system capacity \(N\) (including the one in service, so there are \(N-1\) waiting places).

The birth–death rates are

\[\lambda_n=\begin{cases}\lambda & 0\le n\le N-1\\ 0 & n\ge N\end{cases} \qquad\qquad \mu_n=\mu \ \ (1\le n\le N).\]

Setting \(\lambda_n=0\) for \(n\ge N\) is the whole of the modelling: an arrival that finds the system full simply does not join.

docs.title: 26.3 Deriving the State Distribution
docs.text:
The cut equations are unchanged for \(n<N\), so \(P_n=\rho^nP_0\) for \(0\le n\le N\) where \(\rho=\lambda/\mu\) as usual. The only difference is that the normalising sum is now finite:

\[P_0\sum_{n=0}^{N}\rho^n = 1.\]

docs.title: Case ρ≠1
docs.text:
The finite geometric sum is \(\dfrac{1-\rho^{N+1}}{1-\rho}\), so

Result 1. $\(\boxed{\ P_0=\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho^{\,N+1}},\qquad P_n=\frac{(1-\rho)\rho^{\,n}}{1-\rho^{\,N+1}},\ \ 0\le n\le N\ }\tag{2.1}\)$

docs.title: Case ρ=1
docs.text:
The sum becomes \(\sum_{n=0}^{N}1 = N+1\), so

Result 2. $\(\boxed{\ P_n=\frac{1}{N+1}\ \text{ for all } n,\qquad L_s=\frac{N}{2}\ }\tag{2.2}\)$ a uniform distribution over the \(N+1\) states.

This case is not a curiosity. In the infinite model \(\rho=1\) was catastrophic — the queue grew without bound. Here it is perfectly well behaved. Truncation always restores stability.

docs.title: Stability requires nothing
docs.text: There is no stability condition. The sum \(\sum_{n=0}^{N}\rho^n\) is finite for every \(\rho\), including \(\rho>1\). Formula (2.1) is valid for an overloaded system; the excess demand simply appears as blocked customers rather than as an exploding queue.

docs.title: Expected number in the system
docs.text:
Differentiating the finite geometric sum gives, for \(\rho\ne1\),

\[\boxed{\ L_s=\frac{\rho\left[1-(N+1)\rho^{\,N}+N\rho^{\,N+1}\right]}{(1-\rho)\left(1-\rho^{\,N+1}\right)}\ }\tag{3.1}\]

and \(L_s=N/2\) when \(\rho=1\).

docs.title: The two arrival rates — the heart of this model
docs.text:
Blocking probability. \(P_N\) is the probability the system is full. An arrival at such a moment is lost.

\[\text{customers lost per unit time}=\lambda P_N,\qquad \boxed{\ \lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_N)\ }\tag{3.2}\]

\(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) is the rate at which customers actually enter the system, and it is the throughput. There are three equivalent expressions for it, and checking that they agree is the best possible verification of an answer:

\[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_N)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\lambda P_n=\mu(1-P_0). \tag{3.3}\]

The last form says: what goes in must come out. Output is \(\mu\) whenever the server is busy, which is a fraction \(1-P_0\) of the time.

docs.title: Queue length and the waiting times
docs.text:
\[L_q=L_s-(1-P_0) \tag{3.4}\]

because \(1-P_0\) is the expected number in service.

The one error everyone makes. Little's law must be applied with the effective rate: $\(\boxed{\ W_s=\frac{L_s}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}},\qquad W_q=\frac{L_q}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}\ }\tag{3.5}\)$ Using the nominal \(\lambda\) here divides by too large a number and understates the waiting time. Customers who were turned away never waited, so they must not appear in the denominator.

docs.title: Problem 1 — The complete finite-capacity calculation
docs.text:
A single-chair barber's shop has room for \(5\) people in total (one in the chair, four waiting). Customers arrive at \(\lambda = 6\) per hour and haircuts take an exponential mean of \(7.5\) minutes (\(\mu = 8\) per hour). Find the state distribution, all four performance measures, the proportion of customers turned away, and compare with the infinite-capacity model.

Solution. \(\rho=6/8=0.75\), \(N=5\).

Step 1 — \(P_0\). \(\rho^{N+1}=0.75^{6}=0.177979\).

\[P_0=\frac{1-0.75}{1-0.177979}=\frac{0.25}{0.822021}=\mathbf{0.30413}\]

Step 2 — the distribution. \(P_n=P_0(0.75)^n\):

\(n\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 \(P_n\) 0.30413 0.22810 0.17107 0.12830 0.09623 0.07217

(Sum \(=1.00000\) ✓)

Step 3 — blocking and throughput.

\[P_5=\mathbf{0.07217}\ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{7.22 % of customers are turned away}\] \[\text{lost} = 6(0.07217)=\mathbf{0.433\text{ customers per hour}}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=6(1-0.07217)=\mathbf{5.567\text{ per hour}}\]

Check: \(\mu(1-P_0)=8(1-0.30413)=8(0.69587)=5.567\) ✓

Step 4 — the measures. From (3.1) with \(\rho=0.75\), \(N=5\):

\[L_s=\frac{0.75\left[1-6(0.75)^5+5(0.75)^6\right]}{(0.25)(0.822021)}=\mathbf{1.7009\text{ customers}}\] \[L_q=L_s-(1-P_0)=1.7009-0.69587=\mathbf{1.0051\text{ customers}}\] \[W_s=\frac{1.7009}{5.567}=0.30554\text{ h}=\mathbf{18.33\text{ minutes}}\] \[W_q=\frac{1.0051}{5.567}=0.18054\text{ h}=\mathbf{10.83\text{ minutes}}\]

Check: \(W_s-W_q=0.075\) h \(=7.5\) min \(=1/\mu\) ✓

Step 5 — comparison with \(N=\infty\).

\(N=5\) \(N=\infty\) \(P_0\) 0.3041 0.2500 \(L_s\) 1.701 3.000 \(L_q\) 1.005 2.250 \(W_s\) 18.33 min 30.00 min Throughput 5.567/h 6.000/h Customers lost 7.22 % 0 %

Interpretation. The finite room looks better on every congestion measure — shorter queue, shorter wait, more idle time. It is not better; it is hiding the demand it turned away. The four chairs are, in effect, rationing service. Any comparison of two systems with different capacities must put throughput and lost customers alongside the queue statistics, or it will reward the system that serves fewest people.

docs.title: Problem 2 — The case ρ = 1
docs.text:
A single-server system has \(\lambda=\mu=8\) per hour and capacity \(N=4\). Find the distribution, \(L_s\), throughput and \(W_s\).

Solution. Since \(\rho=1\), use (2.2):

\[P_n=\frac{1}{N+1}=\frac{1}{5}=\mathbf{0.2}\quad\text{for } n=0,1,2,3,4\]

Every state is equally likely — a striking result: the system is as often empty as it is full.

\[L_s=\frac{N}{2}=\mathbf{2\text{ customers}},\qquad L_q=L_s-(1-P_0)=2-0.8=\mathbf{1.2}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_4)=8(0.8)=\mathbf{6.4\text{ per hour}}\] \[W_s=\frac{2}{6.4}=0.3125\text{ h}=\mathbf{18.75\text{ min}},\qquad W_q=\frac{1.2}{6.4}=\mathbf{11.25\text{ min}}\]

Interpretation. With unlimited waiting room, \(\rho=1\) would make \(L_s\to\infty\). Here the answer is a comfortable \(2\) customers — but \(20\,\%\) of demand is destroyed to achieve it. Truncation buys stability with lost business, and the price is exactly \(\lambda P_N\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — An overloaded system (ρ > 1)
docs.text:
A petrol pump with one nozzle has space for \(3\) vehicles. Cars arrive at \(10\) per hour; service takes an exponential mean of \(10\) minutes (\(\mu = 6\) per hour). Analyse the system.

Solution. \(\rho = 10/6 = 1.6667 > 1\) — an infinite queue would be unstable. The finite model applies without difficulty.

\[\rho^{N+1}=(1.6667)^4=7.7160,\qquad P_0=\frac{1-1.6667}{1-7.7160}=\frac{-0.6667}{-6.7160}=\mathbf{0.09926}\] \(n\) 0 1 2 3 \(P_n\) 0.09926 0.16544 0.27574 0.45956 \[P_3=\mathbf{0.45956}\ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{46 % of arriving cars are turned away!}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=10(1-0.45956)=\mathbf{5.404\text{ per hour}}\qquad \text{(check: } \mu(1-P_0)=6(0.90074)=5.404\ \checkmark)\] \[L_s=2.0956,\quad L_q=L_s-(1-P_0)=2.0956-0.90074=1.1949\] \[W_s=\frac{2.0956}{5.404}=0.38776\text{ h}=\mathbf{23.27\text{ min}},\qquad W_q=\mathbf{13.27\text{ min}}\]

Interpretation. The pump is busy \(90\,\%\) of the time and the average queue is barely two cars — figures a manager might call satisfactory. They are not. Nearly half of all customers drive away, costing \(4.6\) sales per hour. In an overloaded finite system the queue statistics look good precisely because the system is failing. The number that matters is \(\lambda P_N\), and it should be the first quantity reported.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Choosing the capacity to meet a blocking target
docs.text:
For the barber's shop of Problem 1 (\(\lambda=6\), \(\mu=8\)), management wants no more than \(5\,\%\) of customers turned away. What is the smallest capacity \(N\)?

Solution. Compute \(P_N=\dfrac{(1-\rho)\rho^N}{1-\rho^{N+1}}\) for successive \(N\):

\(N\) \(P_N\) Lost per hour \(L_s\) \(W_s\) 3 0.15429 0.926 1.149 13.58 min 4 0.10371 0.622 1.444 16.11 min 5 0.07217 0.433 1.701 18.33 min 6 0.05135 0.308 1.922 20.26 min 7 0.03708 0.223 2.110 21.91 min

\(N=6\) still blocks \(5.14\,\%\); \(N=7\) blocks \(3.71\,\%\).

\[\boxed{N=7\ \text{(one chair in use plus 6 waiting places)}}\]

Interpretation. Note the trade-off in the last two columns: every chair added reduces blocking but lengthens the wait for those already inside. Going from \(N=3\) to \(N=7\) cuts blocking from \(15.4\,\%\) to \(3.7\,\%\) but raises the average visit from \(13.6\) to \(21.9\) minutes. There is no capacity that is best on both counts; the choice depends on whether a lost customer or an annoyed one costs more. Note too the diminishing returns: the first extra chair saves \(0.30\) customers per hour, the fourth saves only \(0.09\).

docs.title: Problem 5 — The economically optimal capacity
docs.text:
Each customer actually served yields a contribution of \(₹40\). Each waiting place costs \(₹8\) per hour in rent and furniture. With \(\lambda=6\), \(\mu=8\) as before, find the profit-maximising \(N\).

Solution. Net profit per hour \(=40\lambda_{\text{eff}}-8(N-1)\), since a capacity of \(N\) requires \(N-1\) waiting places.

\(N\) \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) Revenue \(40\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) Space cost \(8(N-1)\) Net 2 4.5405 ₹181.62 ₹8 ₹173.62 3 5.0743 ₹202.97 ₹16 ₹186.97 4 5.3777 ₹215.11 ₹24 ₹191.11 5 5.5670 ₹222.68 ₹32 ₹190.68 6 5.6919 ₹227.68 ₹40 ₹187.68 7 5.7775 ₹231.10 ₹48 ₹183.10 \[\boxed{N^{*}=4:\ \text{one chair in use and 3 waiting places, net }₹191.11\text{ per hour}}\]

Marginal analysis — the professional way to present this.

Extra place Marginal revenue Marginal cost Add it? 2 → 3 ₹21.35 ₹8 yes 3 → 4 ₹12.14 ₹8 yes 4 → 5 ₹7.57 ₹8 no — stop here 5 → 6 ₹5.00 ₹8 no

Marginal revenue falls monotonically (each extra chair rescues fewer customers than the one before) while marginal cost is constant. Expand while MR > MC and stop the moment it is not. The answer is robust: the net-profit column is nearly flat between \(N=4\) and \(N=5\), so a manager who picks either loses less than fifty paise an hour.

docs.title: 26.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda=4\)/h, \(\mu=6\)/h, \(N=3\). Find \(P_0\), \(P_3\), \(L_s\) and \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\). (Answer: \(0.41538\), \(0.12308\), \(1.01538\), \(3.5077\)/h)
  2. Show algebraically that (2.1) tends to \((1-\rho)\rho^n\) as \(N\to\infty\) when \(\rho<1\), and explain why the limit fails for \(\rho>1\).
  3. A car park holds \(4\) cars; arrivals \(8\)/h, mean parking time \(30\) min. What fraction of drivers find it full? (Answer: \(\rho=4\), \(P_4=0.75073\) — three drivers in four)
  4. For Problem 3's pump, how large must \(N\) be to bring blocking below \(20\,\%\)? Compute \(P_N\) for \(N=4,6,8,10\) first. (Answer: impossible: \(P_N\to1-1/\rho=0.40\) as \(N\to\infty\), so blocking can never fall below \(40\,\%\). Throughput is capped at \(\mu=6\)/h against demand of \(10\)/h; no amount of waiting space serves customers a single server has no time for. When \(\rho>1\) you must add CAPACITY, not SPACE.)
  5. Verify the three expressions for \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) in (3.3) numerically for Problem 1.

docs.title: 26.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Finite capacity means \(\lambda_n=0\) for \(n\ge N\); everything else is unchanged.
  • \(P_n=\dfrac{(1-\rho)\rho^n}{1-\rho^{N+1}}\) for \(\rho\ne1\), and \(P_n=\dfrac{1}{N+1}\) for \(\rho=1\).
  • No stability condition is needed. The model is valid for any \(\rho\), including \(\rho>1\).
  • \(P_N\) is the blocking probability; \(\lambda P_N\) customers are lost per unit time; the throughput is \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_N)=\mu(1-P_0)\).
  • Always use \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\) in Little's law. This is the single most common error in the topic.
  • Truncation makes congestion statistics look good by discarding demand. Report lost customers alongside \(L_q\) and \(W_q\), always.
  • Capacity should be set by marginal analysis: add a place while its marginal revenue exceeds its marginal cost. Marginal revenue falls fast, so the optimum is usually small.

Next lesson: L27 — Model III, \((M/M/c):(\infty/\text{FCFS})\), the multi-server queue and the Erlang-C formula.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Finite Capacity Lab: set \(N\) with a slider and watch \(P_N\), throughput and \(W_s\) trade off against one another.

docs.title: Lesson 27: Model III: (M/M/c):(∞/FCFS), the Multi-Server Queue
27.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Set up the birth–death rates for \(c\) parallel servers and derive \(P_0\).
  2. State and use the Erlang-C formula for the probability of waiting.
  3. Compute \(L_q, L_s, W_q, W_s\) for an \(M/M/c\) system and verify them.
  4. Distinguish the offered load \(r\) from the utilisation \(\rho\).
  5. Explain quantitatively why \(c\) servers of rate \(\mu\) differ from one server of rate \(c\mu\).

docs.title: 27.2 The Model
docs.text:
\(c\) identical servers work in parallel, fed by a single queue. A customer who finds a free server goes straight into service; otherwise all \(c\) are busy and the customer joins the common line.

Kendall notation. \((M/M/c):(\infty/\text{FCFS})\) — Poisson arrivals rate \(\lambda\), exponential service rate \(\mu\) per server, \(c\) servers, infinite capacity, one shared queue.

                        +--> (server 1)
   arrivals --> [ Q ] --+--> (server 2)
      lam                +--> ...
                        +--> (server c)     each at rate mu

docs.title: The birth–death rates
docs.text:
Arrivals are unaffected by the state: \(\lambda_n=\lambda\) for all \(n\).

Service is state-dependent. With \(n\) customers present, the number of busy servers is \(\min(n,c)\), and each contributes \(\mu\) to the departure rate:

\[\mu_n=\begin{cases} n\mu & 1\le n < c \quad\text{(some servers idle)}\\[2pt] c\mu & n\ge c \quad\text{(all servers busy)}\end{cases}\]

docs.title: Two different ratios — do not confuse them
docs.text:
Offered load. \(\quad r=\dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}\quad\) — the expected number of busy servers, measured in erlangs. It may exceed 1.

Utilisation. \(\quad \rho=\dfrac{\lambda}{c\mu}=\dfrac{r}{c}\quad\) — the fraction of total capacity in use. Stability requires \(\rho<1\), i.e. \(\lambda<c\mu\).

Confusing \(r\) with \(\rho\) is the commonest source of wrong answers in this model. In Problem 1 below, \(r = 2.5\) (two and a half servers are busy on average) while \(\rho = 0.833\).

docs.title: 27.3 Deriving the Distribution
docs.text:
Apply the general birth–death result \(P_n=P_0\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\lambda_k/\mu_{k+1}\).

For \(n\le c\) the denominators are \(\mu,2\mu,\dots,n\mu\):

\[P_n=P_0\frac{\lambda^n}{n!\,\mu^n}=\frac{r^{\,n}}{n!}P_0, \qquad 0\le n\le c. \tag{2.1}\]

For \(n>c\) the first \(c\) factors are as above and the rest each contribute \(\lambda/(c\mu)\):

\[P_n=P_0\frac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\left(\frac{r}{c}\right)^{n-c}=\frac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\rho^{\,n-c}P_0, \qquad n\ge c. \tag{2.2}\]

Normalising. The tail is geometric with ratio \(\rho\), converging iff \(\rho<1\):

\[\sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\frac{r^n}{n!}P_0+\frac{r^c}{c!}P_0\sum_{n\ge c}\rho^{\,n-c} =P_0\left[\sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\frac{r^n}{n!}+\frac{r^c}{c!}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\rho}\right]=1\]

Result 1. $\(\boxed{\ P_0=\left[\ \sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\frac{r^{\,n}}{n!}\ +\ \frac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\rho}\ \right]^{-1}}, \qquad r=\frac\lambda\mu,\ \ \rho=\frac{r}{c}<1 \tag{2.3}\)$

docs.title: The probability that a customer must wait
docs.text:
An arrival waits precisely when all \(c\) servers are busy, i.e. \(n\ge c\):

Result 2 (Erlang-C formula). $\(\boxed{\ C(c,r)=\Pr[\text{wait}]=\sum_{n\ge c}P_n=\frac{r^{\,c}}{c!\,(1-\rho)}P_0\ }\tag{3.1}\)$

This is the single most used formula in call-centre and telephony design. (Its cousin Erlang-B applies to loss systems with no queue and is the \(M/M/c/c\) model.)

docs.title: Expected queue length
docs.text:
Only customers beyond the \(c\) in service are waiting:

\[L_q=\sum_{n=c}^{\infty}(n-c)P_n=\frac{r^c}{c!}P_0\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k\rho^{k} =\frac{r^c}{c!}P_0\cdot\frac{\rho}{(1-\rho)^2}\]

Result 3. $\(\boxed{\ L_q=\frac{r^{\,c}\rho}{c!\,(1-\rho)^2}P_0 \;=\; C(c,r)\cdot\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\ }\tag{3.2}\)$

The second form is memorable: the mean queue is the probability of waiting times the \(M/M/1\)-style congestion factor.

docs.title: The rest, by two identities
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\ L_s=L_q+r,\qquad W_q=\frac{L_q}{\lambda},\qquad W_s=W_q+\frac1\mu=\frac{L_s}{\lambda}\ }\tag{3.3}\]

The identity \(L_s-L_q=r\) generalises \(L_s-L_q=\rho\) from \(M/M/1\): the expected number in service equals the offered load. Since \(r\) is also \(c\rho\), it is the expected number of busy servers. Use this as the standard check.

docs.title: The complete recipe
docs.text:
1. Compute \(r=\lambda/\mu\) and \(\rho=r/c\); verify \(\rho<1\).
  2. Compute \(P_0\) from (2.3) — this is the only laborious step.
  3. Compute \(C(c,r)\) from (3.1) and \(L_q\) from (3.2).
  4. Get \(L_s=L_q+r\), then \(W_q=L_q/\lambda\) and \(W_s=W_q+1/\mu\).
  5. Check \(L_s-L_q=r\) and \(W_s-W_q=1/\mu\).

docs.title: Problem 1 — A three-server help desk
docs.text:
A help desk has \(c=3\) agents. Calls arrive at \(\lambda=10\) per hour and each agent handles calls at \(\mu=4\) per hour. Find \(P_0\), the probability of waiting, \(L_q\), \(L_s\), \(W_q\) and \(W_s\).

Solution.

Step 1 — the two ratios.

\[r=\frac{10}{4}=2.5\ \text{erlangs},\qquad \rho=\frac{2.5}{3}=0.8333<1\ \checkmark\]

On average 2.5 of the 3 agents are busy.

Step 2 — \(P_0\).

\[\sum_{n=0}^{2}\frac{r^n}{n!}=1+2.5+\frac{6.25}{2}=1+2.5+3.125=6.625\] \[\frac{r^3}{3!}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\rho}=\frac{15.625}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{0.16667}=2.604167\times6=15.625\] \[P_0=\frac{1}{6.625+15.625}=\frac{1}{22.25}=\mathbf{0.044944}\]

Step 3 — Erlang-C.

\[C(3,2.5)=\frac{r^3}{3!(1-\rho)}P_0=15.625\times0.044944=\mathbf{0.70225}\]

Seven callers in ten must wait.

Step 4 — the measures.

\[L_q=C(c,r)\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}=0.70225\times\frac{0.83333}{0.16667}=0.70225\times5=\mathbf{3.5112\text{ callers}}\] \[L_s=L_q+r=3.5112+2.5=\mathbf{6.0112\text{ callers}}\] \[W_q=\frac{L_q}{\lambda}=\frac{3.5112}{10}=0.35112\text{ h}=\mathbf{21.07\text{ minutes}}\] \[W_s=W_q+\frac1\mu=0.35112+0.25=0.60112\text{ h}=\mathbf{36.07\text{ minutes}}\]

Checks. \(L_s-L_q=2.5=r\) ✓. \(\lambda W_s=10(0.60112)=6.011=L_s\) ✓.

Interpretation. Each agent is busy \(83\,\%\) of the time — high but not extreme — yet a caller waits \(21\) minutes for a \(15\)-minute call. The \(1/(1-\rho)\) blow-up of Lesson 24 is at work here too.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Is a fourth agent worth it?
docs.text:
Continue Problem 1. Evaluate adding a fourth agent.

Solution. Now \(c=4\), \(r=2.5\) unchanged, \(\rho=2.5/4=0.625\).

\[\sum_{n=0}^{3}\frac{r^n}{n!}=1+2.5+3.125+\frac{15.625}{6}=1+2.5+3.125+2.604167=9.229167\] \[\frac{r^4}{4!}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\rho}=\frac{39.0625}{24}\cdot\frac{1}{0.375}=1.627604\times2.66667=4.340278\] \[P_0=\frac{1}{13.569445}=\mathbf{0.073695}\] \[C(4,2.5)=\frac{r^4}{4!(1-\rho)}P_0=4.340278\times0.073695=\mathbf{0.31986}\] \[L_q=0.31986\times\frac{0.625}{0.375}=0.31986\times1.66667=\mathbf{0.5331}\] \[L_s=0.5331+2.5=3.0331,\quad W_q=0.05331\text{ h}=\mathbf{3.20\text{ min}},\quad W_s=\mathbf{18.20\text{ min}}\] \(c=3\) \(c=4\) change Utilisation \(\rho\) 0.833 0.625 \(-25\,\%\) \(\Pr[\text{wait}]\) 0.7022 0.3199 \(-54\,\%\) \(L_q\) 3.511 0.533 \(\mathbf{-85\,\%}\) \(W_q\) 21.07 min 3.20 min \(\mathbf{-85\,\%}\)

Interpretation. A 33 % increase in staff cuts waiting by 85 %. Near-saturated systems respond dramatically to a small capacity addition, which is why the marginal fourth agent is very often worth hiring even at full salary. Lesson 29 turns this into a formal cost comparison.

docs.title: Problem 3 — M/M/2 against M/M/1 of the same total capacity
docs.text:
A depot handles \(\lambda=18\) jobs per hour. Compare two counters at \(\mu=12\)/h each (\(M/M/2\)) with a single counter at \(\mu=24\)/h (\(M/M/1\)). Both have total capacity \(24\)/h.

Solution.

\(M/M/2\): \(r=18/12=1.5\), \(\rho=0.75\).

\[\sum_{n=0}^{1}\frac{r^n}{n!}=1+1.5=2.5,\qquad \frac{r^2}{2!}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\rho}=\frac{2.25}{2}\times4=4.5\] \[P_0=\frac{1}{7}=\mathbf{0.142857},\qquad C(2,1.5)=4.5\times0.142857=\mathbf{0.642857}\] \[L_q=0.642857\times\frac{0.75}{0.25}=0.642857\times3=\mathbf{1.9286}\] \[L_s=1.9286+1.5=3.4286,\qquad W_s=\frac{3.4286}{18}=0.19048\text{ h}=\mathbf{11.43\text{ min}}\]

\(M/M/1\) with \(\mu=24\): \(\rho=0.75\).

\[L_s=\frac{0.75}{0.25}=3,\qquad W_s=\frac{1}{24-18}=\frac16\text{ h}=\mathbf{10\text{ min}}\] \(M/M/2\), \(\mu=12\) \(M/M/1\), \(\mu=24\) \(\rho\) 0.750 0.750 \(P_0\) 0.1429 0.2500 \(L_s\) 3.4286 3.0000 \(W_s\) 11.43 min 10.00 min

Interpretation. The single fast server wins, by \(14\,\%\) on waiting time. The reason is structural: in \(M/M/2\) a job can be stuck behind a long job at one counter while the other counter is free but already committed. Two half-speed servers can never match one full-speed one.

But — and this matters — the \(M/M/2\) system is more robust. If the single server fails, the system stops entirely; if one of two servers fails, capacity halves but service continues. Choosing between them is a trade-off between efficiency and resilience, not a pure optimisation.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Designing to a service-level target
docs.text:
A clinic has \(\lambda=6\) patients per hour and each doctor serves at \(\mu=4\) per hour. Management requires that no more than 25 % of patients wait at all. How many doctors are needed?

Solution. \(r = 6/4 = 1.5\). Stability alone needs \(c\ge2\). Compute Erlang-C for successive \(c\):

\(c\) \(\rho=r/c\) \(P_0\) \(C(c,r)=\Pr[\text{wait}]\) \(L_q\) \(W_q\) 2 0.7500 0.14286 0.64286 1.92857 19.29 min 3 0.5000 0.21053 0.23684 0.23684 2.37 min 4 0.3750 0.22099 0.07459 0.04475 0.45 min 5 0.3000 0.22277 0.02014 0.00863 0.09 min

With \(c=2\), \(64\,\%\) wait — far above target. With \(c=3\), only \(23.7\,\%\) wait.

\[\boxed{c=3 \text{ doctors}}\]

Interpretation. Look at how fast the numbers improve. Going from \(2\) to \(3\) doctors cuts waiting time by a factor of eight; going from \(3\) to \(4\) cuts it by a further factor of five but from an already small base. The first server past the point of saturation delivers almost all of the benefit — a rule of thumb worth carrying into any staffing discussion.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Reading a real system
docs.text:
A bank's three tellers each serve \(20\) customers per hour; arrivals average \(50\) per hour. The branch manager reports "utilisation is 83 %, and average queue length is under four people — we are running efficiently." Compute the figures and evaluate the claim.

Solution. \(r=50/20=2.5\), \(\rho=2.5/3=0.8333\). These are precisely Problem 1's numbers scaled in time, so \(P_0=0.044944\), \(C=0.70225\), \(L_q=3.511\).

\[W_q=\frac{3.511}{50}=0.070225\text{ h}=\mathbf{4.21\text{ minutes}},\qquad W_s=4.21+3=\mathbf{7.21\text{ minutes}}\]

Evaluating the claim. The manager's two facts are correct but the conclusion does not follow:

  • \(L_q=3.51\) is under four — but \(70\,\%\) of customers wait, and a queue of four people is what a customer sees on arrival, which shapes their impression of the branch.
  • Utilisation of \(83\,\%\) leaves the branch on the steep part of the \(1/(1-\rho)\) curve. A \(10\,\%\) rise in arrivals to \(55\)/h gives \(\rho=0.9167\), and \(L_q\) rises to \(\mathbf{9.31}\) — queue length nearly triples for a 10 % rise in demand.
  • All the same, \(W_q=4.2\) minutes is genuinely acceptable for a bank branch.

Verdict. The system is performing acceptably today but has almost no margin. The right recommendation is not "add a teller now" but "monitor arrivals; at \(55\)/h the fourth teller becomes necessary." Report the sensitivity, not just the level — that is what distinguishes an OR analysis from a status report.

docs.title: 27.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda=8\)/h, \(\mu=5\)/h, \(c=2\). Find \(r\), \(\rho\), \(P_0\), \(\Pr[\text{wait}]\), \(L_q\), \(W_q\). (Answer: \(1.6\), \(0.8\), \(0.11111\), \(0.71111\), \(2.84444\), \(21.33\) min)
  2. Show that (2.3) and (3.2) reduce to the \(M/M/1\) formulas when \(c=1\).
  3. A workshop has \(\lambda=12\)/h and \(\mu=5\)/h per bench. What is the minimum number of benches for stability, and what is \(W_q\) at that number? (Answer: \(c=3\); \(\rho=0.8\), \(W_q=12.94\) min)
  4. For Problem 1's help desk, what happens to \(W_q\) if arrivals rise from \(10\) to \(11\) per hour with \(c=3\)? (Answer: \(\rho=0.9167\), \(L_q=9.314\), \(W_q=50.8\) min — a \(10\,\%\) demand rise more than doubles the wait)
  5. Explain in two sentences why \(L_s - L_q = r\) rather than \(\rho\) in this model.

docs.title: 27.7 Summary
docs.text:
• \(M/M/c\): \(c\) parallel servers, one shared queue. Service rate is \(\min(n,c)\mu\).
  • Offered load \(r=\lambda/\mu\) (mean busy servers, may exceed 1) is not the same as utilisation \(\rho=r/c\) (must be \(<1\)).
  • \(P_0=\left[\sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\dfrac{r^n}{n!}+\dfrac{r^c}{c!(1-\rho)}\right]^{-1}\) — the one laborious step.
  • Erlang-C \(C(c,r)=\dfrac{r^c}{c!(1-\rho)}P_0\) is the probability of waiting; then \(L_q=C(c,r)\dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\).
  • \(L_s=L_q+r\) and \(W_s=W_q+1/\mu\) are the standard checks.
  • Adding one server to a near-saturated system produces an enormous improvement (85 % in Problem 2); further servers add little.
  • One server of rate \(c\mu\) beats \(c\) servers of rate \(\mu\) — but is far less resilient to failure.
  • Always report the sensitivity of the answer to \(\lambda\), because near \(\rho=1\) a small demand increase produces a large service collapse.

Next lesson: L28 — Models IV and V: \((M/M/c):(N/\text{FCFS})\) and finite-source (machine-repair) queues.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Multi-Server Lab: set \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) and \(c\), see the Erlang-C curve, and find the smallest \(c\) meeting a service-level target.

docs.title: Lesson 28: Models IV and V: (M/M/c):(N/FCFS) and Finite-Source Queues
28.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Combine multiple servers with finite capacity to analyse \((M/M/c):(N/\text{FCFS})\).
  2. Analyse the machine-repair (finite-source) model with one or several repairmen.
  3. Use the Erlang-B loss formula for systems with no waiting room.
  4. Recognise when the calling population must be treated as finite.
  5. Explain why service discipline (FCFS, LIFO, SIRO) does not change the mean measures.

docs.title: 28.2 Model IV — (M/M/c):(N/FCFS)
docs.text:
This model simply combines Lessons 26 and 27: \(c\) servers and a limit \(N\) on the number in the system (\(N\ge c\), leaving \(N-c\) waiting places).

\[\lambda_n=\begin{cases}\lambda & n<N\\ 0 & n\ge N\end{cases} \qquad \mu_n=\begin{cases}n\mu & n<c\\ c\mu & c\le n\le N\end{cases}\]

The birth–death machinery gives, with \(r=\lambda/\mu\) and \(\rho=r/c\):

Result 1. $\(P_n=\begin{cases}\dfrac{r^{\,n}}{n!}P_0 & 0\le n\le c\\[8pt] \dfrac{r^{\,n}}{c!\,c^{\,n-c}}P_0=\dfrac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\rho^{\,n-c}P_0 & c\le n\le N\end{cases}\tag{1.1}\)$ $\(P_0=\left[\sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\frac{r^{\,n}}{n!}+\frac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\sum_{n=c}^{N}\rho^{\,n-c}\right]^{-1} =\left[\sum_{n=0}^{c-1}\frac{r^{\,n}}{n!}+\frac{r^{\,c}}{c!}\cdot\frac{1-\rho^{\,N-c+1}}{1-\rho}\right]^{-1}\tag{1.2}\)$ (the last factor becomes \(N-c+1\) when \(\rho=1\)).

No stability condition is required — the sum is finite, so \(\rho>1\) is permitted, exactly as in Lesson 26. The measures are

\[L_q=\sum_{n=c}^{N}(n-c)P_n,\qquad L_s=\sum_{n=0}^{N}nP_n,\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_N),\qquad W_q=\frac{L_q}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}},\qquad W_s=W_q+\frac1\mu.\]

Careful. In the finite-capacity case the identity \(L_s = L_q + r\) fails, because the mean number busy is not \(r\) but \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}/\mu\). Use $\(L_s = L_q + \frac{\lambda_{\text{eff}}}{\mu}\)$ or simply compute \(L_s=\sum nP_n\) directly. This is the trap in Model IV.

docs.title: Why the calling population matters
docs.text:
Every model so far assumed an infinite calling population, so that \(\lambda\) did not depend on how many customers were already in the system. That fails whenever the population is small.

The machine-interference problem. \(M\) machines are each liable to break down. A broken machine cannot break down again, so the more machines are already waiting for repair, the lower the rate at which new breakdowns occur.

\[\boxed{\ \lambda_n=(M-n)\lambda\ \text{ for } 0\le n<M,\qquad \lambda_M = 0\ }\]

where \(\lambda\) is the failure rate of one running machine. With \(c\) repairmen, \(\mu_n = \min(n,c)\mu\).

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
Result 2. With \(c\) repairmen and \(M\) machines, $\(P_n = \begin{cases}\dbinom{M}{n}\left(\dfrac\lambda\mu\right)^{n}P_0 & 0\le n\le c\\[10pt] \dfrac{M!}{(M-n)!\,c!\,c^{\,n-c}}\left(\dfrac\lambda\mu\right)^{n}P_0 & c\le n\le M\end{cases}\tag{2.1}\)$ with \(P_0\) from normalisation. There is never a stability condition: the population regulates itself.

The key quantities:

\[L_s=\sum_{n=0}^{M}nP_n \quad\text{(machines DOWN)},\qquad \textbf{machines running}=M-L_s,\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda\,(M-L_s), \qquad W_s=\frac{L_s}{\lambda_{\text{eff}}} \quad\text{(mean downtime per breakdown)}.\]

Two derived measures that managers actually ask for:

  • Machine availability \(=\dfrac{M-L_s}{M}\) — the fraction of the fleet productive at any moment.
  • Repairman utilisation \(=\dfrac{\text{mean number busy}}{c}=\dfrac{1}{c}\sum_n\min(n,c)P_n\).

docs.title: 28.4 Erlang-B: Loss Systems with No Queue
docs.text:
When \(N=c\) there is no waiting room at all: an arrival finding every server busy is lost. This is the classic telephone-trunk model.

Erlang-B (loss) formula. $\(B(c,r)=P_c=\frac{r^{\,c}/c!}{\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{c}r^{\,n}/n!} \tag{3.1}\)$

A recursion that is trivial to evaluate by hand, and numerically stable:

\[\boxed{\ B(0,r)=1,\qquad B(c,r)=\frac{r\,B(c-1,r)}{c+r\,B(c-1,r)}\ }\tag{3.2}\]

Remarkable fact (insensitivity). Erlang-B depends on the service-time distribution only through its mean. Whether calls are exponential, constant or wildly variable, the blocking probability is the same. This is why (3.1) has been trusted in telecommunications for a century.

docs.title: 28.5 On Service Discipline
docs.text:
\(M/M/c\) has been analysed under FCFS throughout. What if service is LIFO, or SIRO (service in random order), or by priority?

Theorem. For any work-conserving, non-anticipating discipline that does not use service-time information, the distribution of the number in the system — and hence \(L_s\), \(L_q\), \(W_s\), \(W_q\) — is unchanged.

The reason is that the number present changes only when someone arrives or someone departs, and neither rate depends on which customer is chosen for service.

What does change is the variance of the waiting time. FCFS is the fairest: everyone waits about the same. LIFO and SIRO have the same mean wait but a much longer tail — some unlucky customer waits a very long time. Priority disciplines lower the mean wait for urgent classes at the direct expense of the rest, which is exactly what a hospital triage system is designed to do.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Two servers with limited waiting room
docs.text:
A clinic has \(c=2\) doctors and room for \(N=5\) patients in total. Patients arrive at \(\lambda=6\) per hour; each doctor serves at \(\mu=4\) per hour. Analyse the system.

Solution. \(r=6/4=1.5\), \(\rho=1.5/2=0.75\), \(c=2\), \(N=5\).

Step 1 — the coefficients \(C_n=P_n/P_0\).

\(n\) formula \(C_n\) 0 \(1\) 1.00000 1 \(r\) 1.50000 2 \(r^2/2!\) 1.12500 3 \(C_2\rho\) 0.84375 4 \(C_3\rho\) 0.63281 5 \(C_4\rho\) 0.47461 \(\sum C_n\) 5.57617 \[P_0=\frac{1}{5.57617}=\mathbf{0.17933}\] \(n\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 \(P_n\) 0.17933 0.26900 0.20175 0.15131 0.11349 0.08511

Step 2 — blocking and throughput.

\[P_5=\mathbf{0.08511}\Rightarrow 8.51\,\%\text{ turned away}=6(0.08511)=\mathbf{0.511\text{ patients/h}}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=6(1-0.08511)=\mathbf{5.4893\text{ per hour}}\]

Step 3 — the measures.

\[L_q=\sum_{n=3}^{5}(n-2)P_n=1(0.15131)+2(0.11349)+3(0.08511)=\mathbf{0.63363}\] \[L_s=\sum nP_n=\mathbf{2.00595}\] \[W_q=\frac{0.63363}{5.4893}=0.11543\text{ h}=\mathbf{6.93\text{ min}},\qquad W_s=6.93+15=\mathbf{21.93\text{ min}}\]

Check. \(L_s-L_q=1.3723\), and \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}/\mu=5.4893/4=1.3723\) ✓ — note this is not \(r=1.5\), exactly as warned in §1.

Interpretation. Only \(6.93\) minutes of waiting looks excellent, but \(8.5\,\%\) of patients are sent away. In a clinic those patients do not vanish — they return later, sicker. A loss model must always be paired with a statement of where the lost demand goes.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Machine repair with one repairman
docs.text:
A factory has \(M=6\) machines. Each running machine fails at \(\lambda=0.1\) per hour; one repairman repairs at \(\mu=0.4\) per hour. Find the distribution of broken machines, the average number running, the repairman's utilisation and the average downtime.

Solution. \(\lambda/\mu=0.25\), \(c=1\), so \(C_n=\dfrac{M!}{(M-n)!}(0.25)^n\).

\(n\) \(C_n\) \(P_n\) 0 1.00000 0.11716 1 \(6(0.25)=1.5\) 0.17574 2 \(6\cdot5(0.0625)=1.875\) 0.21968 3 \(6\cdot5\cdot4(0.015625)=1.875\) 0.21968 4 \(360(0.00390625)=1.40625\) 0.16476 5 \(720(0.0009766)=0.703125\) 0.08238 6 \(720(0.000244)=0.17578\) 0.02059 \(\sum=8.53516\) 1.00000 \[L_s=\sum nP_n=\mathbf{2.4687\text{ machines down}},\qquad \text{running}=6-2.4687=\mathbf{3.5314}\] \[\text{Availability}=\frac{3.5314}{6}=\mathbf{58.9\,\%}\] \[\lambda_{\text{eff}}=0.1(3.5314)=\mathbf{0.35314\text{ failures per hour}}\] \[W_s=\frac{2.4687}{0.35314}=\mathbf{6.991\text{ hours downtime per failure}}\] \[\text{Repairman utilisation}=1-P_0=\mathbf{88.3\,\%}\]

Interpretation. Repair itself takes only \(2.5\) hours; the other \(4.49\) hours are waiting for the repairman. The fleet is producing at only \(59\,\%\) of capacity while the repairman is busy \(88\,\%\) of the time — a system in visible distress, and precisely the situation the finite-source model was invented to expose.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Would a second repairman pay?
docs.text:
Continue Problem 2. A repairman costs \(₹150\) per hour; each machine down costs \(₹500\) per hour in lost output. Evaluate hiring a second repairman.

Solution. With \(c=2\), \(C_n=\dfrac{M!}{(M-n)!\,2!\,2^{\,n-2}}(0.25)^n\) for \(n\ge2\):

\(n\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 \(P_n\) 0.24204 0.36307 0.22692 0.11346 0.04255 0.01064 0.00133 \[L_s=\mathbf{1.3886\text{ down}},\qquad \text{running}=6-1.3886=\mathbf{4.6114}\] \[\text{Availability}=\mathbf{76.9\,\%},\qquad W_s=\frac{1.3886}{0.1(4.6114)}=\mathbf{3.011\text{ h}}\] \[\text{Utilisation per repairman}=\mathbf{57.6\,\%}\]

The economics.

\(c=1\) \(c=2\) Machines down \(L_s\) 2.4687 1.3886 Availability 58.9 % 76.9 % Downtime cost \(500L_s\) ₹1234.32 ₹694.31 Labour cost \(150c\) ₹150.00 ₹300.00 Total per hour ₹1384.32 ₹994.31

Hire the second repairman: it saves \(₹390\) per hour, about \(₹31\) lakh a year on a single shift.

Interpretation. Note the second repairman is idle \(42\,\%\) of the time and is still worth hiring. Judging staffing by "are they busy enough?" is exactly backwards when the cost of the thing waiting dwarfs the cost of the server. The right question is never "is the server busy?" but "what does the queue cost?"

docs.title: Problem 4 — A loss system: how many trunk lines?
docs.text:
A small exchange offers \(r=3\) erlangs of traffic. Calls finding all lines busy are lost (no queue). How many lines are needed to keep blocking below \(5\,\%\)?

Solution. Use the recursion \(B(c,r)=\dfrac{rB(c-1,r)}{c+rB(c-1,r)}\) with \(B(0,3)=1\):

\(c\) working \(B(c,3)\) 1 \(3(1)/(1+3)\) 0.75000 2 \(3(0.75)/(2+2.25)\) 0.52941 3 \(3(0.52941)/(3+1.58824)\) 0.34615 4 \(3(0.34615)/(4+1.03846)\) 0.20611 5 \(3(0.20611)/(5+0.61832)\) 0.11005 6 \(3(0.11005)/(6+0.33016)\) 0.05216 7 \(3(0.05216)/(7+0.15647)\) 0.02186

\(c=6\) gives \(5.22\,\%\) — just above target; \(c=7\) gives \(2.19\,\%\).

\[\boxed{c=7\text{ lines}}\]

Interpretation. Seven lines to carry three erlangs — an "efficiency" of only \(43\,\%\). That over-provisioning is unavoidable: blocking falls roughly geometrically in \(c\), so each extra line buys less than the last. This is also why trunking works: a single exchange carrying \(30\) erlangs needs about \(37\) lines (\(123\,\%\) of load) whereas ten separate exchanges of \(3\) erlangs need \(70\). Consolidation of demand is the whole business case for shared infrastructure.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Choosing between models
docs.text:
For each situation, state which model applies and why.

Situation Model Reason (a) 5 machines, 2 mechanics, plant floor Finite source, \(c=2\) The population is small and a broken machine cannot break again (b) Call centre, 40 agents, callers hang up if all busy Erlang-B, \(M/M/c/c\) No waiting facility; blocked calls are lost (c) Call centre, 40 agents, callers hold in a queue \(M/M/c\), Erlang-C Unlimited holding, infinite caller population (d) Clinic, 3 doctors, waiting room seats 8 \((M/M/c):(N)\) with \(c=3, N=11\) Both multiple servers and finite capacity (e) Petrol pump, 2 nozzles, forecourt holds 6 cars \((M/M/c):(N)\) with \(c=2, N=6\) As above; the forecourt is the capacity (f) Website, thousands of users, 20 threads \(M/M/c\) Population effectively infinite relative to servers

The decision rule. Use a finite-source model whenever the population is less than about \(10\) times the number of servers; otherwise the infinite-source approximation is safe. Use a finite capacity model whenever customers are physically turned away rather than allowed to wait.

Why it matters. Applying \(M/M/1\) to situation (a) with \(\lambda = 5(0.1) = 0.5\) and \(\mu = 0.4\) gives \(\rho = 1.25 > 1\) — the model reports an unstable system that in reality runs perfectly well. Choosing the wrong model does not give a slightly wrong answer; it gives a meaningless one.

docs.title: 28.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \((M/M/2):(4)\) with \(\lambda=4\)/h, \(\mu=3\)/h. Find \(P_0\), \(P_4\) and \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}\). (Answer: \(0.23754\), \(0.09384\), \(3.6246\)/h)
  2. Four machines, \(\lambda=0.2\)/h each, one repairman at \(\mu=1\)/h. Find the availability. (Answer: \(L_s=0.99171\), availability \(75.2\,\%\))
  3. Use the Erlang-B recursion to find \(B(5, 2)\). (Answer: \(0.03670\))
  4. Repeat Problem 3 with the downtime cost reduced to \(₹200\) per machine-hour. Is the second repairman still justified? (Answer: \(c=1\) costs \(₹643.74\), \(c=2\) costs \(₹577.72\) — yes, but only just; the break-even downtime cost is \(₹138.9\) per hour)
  5. Explain in three sentences why LIFO and FCFS give the same \(L_q\) but very different waiting-time variances.

docs.title: 28.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Model IV \((M/M/c):(N)\) combines multiple servers with finite capacity. No stability condition; \(\lambda_{\text{eff}}=\lambda(1-P_N)\); and \(L_s = L_q + \lambda_{\text{eff}}/\mu\), not \(L_q+r\).
  • Model V (finite source) has \(\lambda_n=(M-n)\lambda\): the population regulates itself, so the system is always stable. Report availability \((M-L_s)/M\), not just \(L_s\).
  • Downtime in a repair system is dominated by waiting for the repairman, not by repair itself.
  • Erlang-B \(B(c,r)\) handles loss systems with no queue and is computed by the recursion \(B(c,r)=rB(c-1,r)/[c+rB(c-1,r)]\). It is insensitive to the service distribution beyond its mean.
  • Loss systems need heavy over-provisioning at low load, but pooling demand makes them far more efficient — the argument for shared infrastructure.
  • Service discipline does not change the mean measures — only the variance of the waiting time and the fairness of the outcome.
  • Choosing the wrong model class (finite vs infinite source) is not a small error: it can report an unstable system that in fact works perfectly.

Next lesson: L29 — Applications and the economic analysis of queues.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Model Selector: describe a system in words and the lab identifies the right model, then solves it.

docs.title: Lesson 19: Network Scheduling: The Critical Path Method (CPM)
19.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define the basic terms of project networks and draw an AON diagram.
  2. Perform the forward pass (ES, EF) and the backward pass (LS, LF).
  3. Compute total float and free float, and identify the critical path.
  4. Interpret float for resource and risk management.
  5. Perform crashing to shorten a project at minimum cost.

docs.title: 19.2 Project Networks
docs.text: Definition. A project is a set of interrelated activities, each with a duration and precedence requirements, that together achieve a defined objective.

docs.title: Basic terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Activity a task consuming time and resources Event / node a point in time marking a start or finish Predecessor an activity that must finish before another can start Successor an activity that cannot start until another finishes Dummy activity zero-duration arrow showing a precedence relation only (AOA networks) Path any chain of activities from project start to finish Critical path the longest path — it determines the project duration Float / slack how much an activity can be delayed without harming the project

docs.title: Two network conventions
docs.text: AON (Activity on Node) AOA (Activity on Arrow) Activities are nodes arrows Arrows show precedence activities Dummy activities never needed often needed Modern usage standard (MS Project, Primavera) older textbooks \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{This course uses AON — it is simpler and needs no dummies.}\ } \]

docs.title: CPM versus PERT
docs.text:
CPM PERT (L20) Durations deterministic (single estimate) probabilistic (three estimates) Origin DuPont, 1957 (plant maintenance) US Navy Polaris, 1958 Emphasis cost–time trade-off (crashing) uncertainty and risk Best for repetitive projects with known times novel projects (R&D, construction)

In practice the two have merged; most software offers both.

docs.title: 19.3 The Forward Pass — Earliest Times
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{ES}_j \ =\ \max_{i \in \text{predecessors}(j)} \ \text{EF}_i, \qquad \text{EF}_j \ =\ \text{ES}_j + d_j\ } \]

Start with \(\text{ES} = 0\) for activities with no predecessors, and work left to right.

The \(\max\) is essential: an activity cannot start until every predecessor has finished, so the latest of them governs.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Project duration } T \ =\ \max_j \text{EF}_j\ } \]

docs.title: 19.4 The Backward Pass — Latest Times
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{LF}_i \ =\ \min_{j\in\text{successors}(i)}\ \text{LS}_j, \qquad \text{LS}_i \ =\ \text{LF}_i - d_i\ } \]

Start with \(\text{LF} = T\) for activities with no successors, and work right to left.

The \(\min\) is essential: an activity must finish before the earliest of its successors must start.

docs.title: Total float
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{TF}_i \ =\ \text{LS}_i - \text{ES}_i \ =\ \text{LF}_i - \text{EF}_i\ } \]

How long activity \(i\) can be delayed without delaying the PROJECT.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical activity} \iff \text{TF} = 0\ } \]

The critical path is the chain of zero-float activities from start to finish. Every project has at least one, and it is the longest path through the network.

docs.title: Free float
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{FF}_i \ =\ \min_{j\in\text{successors}(i)}\text{ES}_j \ -\ \text{EF}_i\ } \]

How long activity \(i\) can be delayed without delaying ANY SUCCESSOR's earliest start.

Always \(0 \le \text{FF} \le \text{TF}\).

Total float Free float Delaying by this much affects nothing (project safe) nothing at all Delaying beyond it delays the project delays a successor, but perhaps not the project Shared between activities? yes — using it consumes other activities' float no — belongs to that activity alone \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Free float is "safe" float. Total float is shared and must be managed centrally.}\ } \]

docs.title: Independent float
docs.text:
\[ \text{IF}_i = \max\Big(0,\ \min_j \text{ES}_j - \max_k\text{LF}_k - d_i\Big) \]

Float available even if all predecessors finish as late as possible and all successors start as early as possible. Rarely used in practice.

docs.title: Forward pass
docs.text:
Activity Predecessors ES \(= \max(\text{EF of preds})\) EF \(=\) ES \(+ d\) A — 0 4 B — 0 6 C A \(\max(4) = 4\) 7 D A \(\max(4) = 4\) 9 E B, C \(\max(6,\ 7) = \mathbf{7}\) 9 F D \(\max(9) = 9\) 16 G E, F \(\max(9,\ 16) = \mathbf{16}\) 20 \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Project duration } T = 20 \ \text{weeks}\ } \]

Note how the \(\max\) operates: E waits for C (finishing at 7), not B (finishing at 6); G waits for F (16), not E (9).

docs.title: Backward pass
docs.text:
Start with \(\text{LF}_G = T = 20\).

Activity Successors LF \(=\min(\text{LS of succs})\) LS \(=\) LF \(- d\) G — 20 16 F G \(\min(16) = 16\) 9 E G \(\min(16) = 16\) 14 D F \(\min(9) = 9\) 4 C E \(\min(14) = 14\) 11 B E \(\min(14) = 14\) 8 A C, D \(\min(11,\ 4) = \mathbf{4}\) 0

Note the \(\min\) for A: it must finish by 4 to let D start on time, even though C could wait until 11.

docs.title: Float and the critical path
docs.text:
Activity \(d\) ES EF LS LF TF FF Critical? A 4 0 4 0 4 0 0 ✓ B 6 0 6 8 14 8 1 C 3 4 7 11 14 7 0 D 5 4 9 4 9 0 0 ✓ E 2 7 9 14 16 7 7 F 7 9 16 9 16 0 0 ✓ G 4 16 20 16 20 0 0 ✓ \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical path: } A \to D \to F \to G, \qquad \text{length } 4+5+7+4 = 20\ \checkmark\ } \]

Verify by checking all paths.

Path Length \(A\to C\to E\to G\) \(4+3+2+4 = 13\) \(A\to D\to F\to G\) \(4+5+7+4 = \mathbf{20}\) ← longest \(B\to E\to G\) \(6+2+4 = 12\)

The critical path is the longest path ✓ — and its length equals the project duration.

docs.title: Reading the float
docs.text:
Activity B: TF = 8 but FF = 1.

  • B can be delayed up to 8 weeks without delaying the project.
  • But delaying B by more than 1 week pushes E's earliest start (from 7 to beyond 7).
  • The remaining 7 weeks of B's total float are shared with C and E — if C uses its float, B's shrinks.

Activity E: TF = FF = 7. E's float is entirely its own — delaying E by up to 7 weeks affects nothing at all, because G cannot start before 16 anyway (waiting for F).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Manage total float centrally; free float can be devolved to activity owners.}\ } \]

docs.title: 19.7 Crashing — the Cost–Time Trade-Off
docs.text:
Definition. Crashing shortens an activity by adding resources, at extra cost.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Crash cost slope} \ =\ \frac{\text{crash cost} - \text{normal cost}} {\text{normal time} - \text{crash time}} \qquad (\text{₹ per unit time saved})\ } \]

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Compute the critical path at NORMAL times
2. Among CRITICAL activities that can still be crashed,
       choose the one with the LOWEST cost slope
3. Crash it by 1 unit (or until it hits its crash limit, or another path becomes critical)
4. RECOMPUTE the critical path -- it may have CHANGED
5. If multiple paths are now critical, crash an activity COMMON to all of them,
       or one on EACH, whichever is cheaper
6. Repeat until the target duration is met, or no further crashing is possible

Step 4 is the one most often forgotten. Crashing one path can make another path critical, and crashing further on the original path then achieves nothing.

docs.title: The total-cost trade-off
docs.text:
\[ \text{Total cost} = \underbrace{\text{direct costs}}_{\text{rise when crashing}} + \underbrace{\text{indirect costs}}_{\text{fall with duration}} \]

Indirect costs (supervision, site overheads, equipment hire, penalty clauses) accrue per unit time. The optimum duration minimises the sum, and it is generally shorter than the normal duration but longer than the fully crashed one.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Full CPM analysis
docs.text:
Analyse the project below.

Activity Duration (days) Predecessors A 3 — B 4 — C 2 A D 5 A, B E 3 C F 4 D, E

Solution.

Forward pass.

Act ES EF A 0 3 B 0 4 C \(\max(3) = 3\) 5 D \(\max(3, 4) = \mathbf{4}\) 9 E \(\max(5) = 5\) 8 F \(\max(9, 8) = \mathbf{9}\) 13 \[ T = \mathbf{13\ \text{days}} \]

Backward pass (\(\text{LF}_F = 13\)).

Act Successors LF LS F — 13 9 E F 9 6 D F 9 4 C E 6 4 B D 4 0 A C, D \(\min(4, 4) = 4\) 1

Float table.

Act \(d\) ES EF LS LF TF FF Critical? A 3 0 3 1 4 1 0 B 4 0 4 0 4 0 0 ✓ C 2 3 5 4 6 1 0 D 5 4 9 4 9 0 0 ✓ E 3 5 8 6 9 1 1 F 4 9 13 9 13 0 0 ✓ \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical path: } B \to D \to F, \qquad 4+5+4 = 13\ \checkmark\ } \]

All paths.

Path Length \(A\to C\to E\to F\) \(3+2+3+4 = 12\) \(A\to D\to F\) \(3+5+4 = 12\) \(B\to D\to F\) \(4+5+4 = \mathbf{13}\) ✓

Note the near-critical paths. Two paths have length 12, only 1 day shorter than critical.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{This project is FRAGILE: a 1-day slip on A, C or E makes a second path critical.}\ } \]

Management implication. Do not focus attention solely on B, D and F. Activities A, C and E have only 1 day of float and must be monitored almost as closely. A project with many near-critical paths carries far more schedule risk than its single critical path suggests.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Total float versus free float
docs.text:
In the §5 example, activity B has TF = 8 and FF = 1. Explain the difference concretely and state the management consequence.

Solution.

The scenario. B has ES = 0, EF = 6, LS = 8, LF = 14. Its only successor is E, with ES = 7.

Free float = 1.

\[ \text{FF}_B = \text{ES}_E - \text{EF}_B = 7 - 6 = \mathbf{1} \]

If B is delayed by 1 day, it finishes at 7 — exactly when E is scheduled to start. Nothing else moves.

Delaying B by 5 days (still within TF = 8): B finishes at 11. E cannot start until 11, so E runs 11 → 13, and G still starts at 16 (waiting for F).

\[ \textbf{The project is NOT delayed} \ \checkmark \]

But E's earliest start has been pushed from 7 to 11, so E's free float has been consumed: E's remaining float is now \(16 - 13 = 3\), down from 7.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{B's total float was SHARED with C and E. Using it took float away from them.}\ } \]

Delaying B by 9 days (beyond TF = 8): B finishes at 15, E runs 15 → 17, and G cannot start until 17 instead of 16.

\[ \textbf{Project duration becomes 21 — DELAYED by 1 day.} \]

The management consequence.

Float type Who may spend it Governance Free float (1 day for B) B's owner, unilaterally devolve — no coordination needed Total float (8 days for B) only with project-level approval centralise — it is shared \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Publishing total float to activity owners invites double-spending. Publish FREE float; hold TF centrally.}\ } \]

A common project-management failure. Each activity owner sees "8 days of float" on the Gantt chart and each uses it, believing they are safe. Collectively they overspend the shared buffer and the project slips — a phenomenon Goldratt called "student syndrome" and addressed with critical chain buffering.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Crashing to a deadline
docs.text:
The §5 project (duration 20 weeks) must finish in 17 weeks. Crash data:

Activity Normal time Crash time Normal cost Crash cost A 4 3 20 26 B 6 4 30 40 C 3 2 15 22 D 5 3 25 35 E 2 2 10 10 F 7 5 40 52 G 4 3 20 28

Solution.

Step 1 — cost slopes.

Activity Max crash Cost increase Slope (₹/week) Critical? A 1 6 6 ✓ B 2 10 5 ✗ C 1 7 7 ✗ D 2 10 5 ✓ E 0 — — ✗ F 2 12 6 ✓ G 1 8 8 ✓

Step 2 — crash 1 (target 19). Critical path is \(A\to D\to F\to G\). Cheapest critical slope is D at ₹5/week.

Crash D by 1 (5 → 4 weeks). New durations: \(A=4, D=4, F=7, G=4\).

\[ \text{Path } A{-}D{-}F{-}G = 4+4+7+4 = \mathbf{19} \] \[ \text{Path } A{-}C{-}E{-}G = 4+3+2+4 = 13, \qquad \text{Path } B{-}E{-}G = 6+2+4 = 12 \]

Still the only critical path. Cost so far: ₹5.

Step 3 — crash 2 (target 18). D can be crashed one more week (limit 3).

Crash D by 1 more (4 → 3). \(A{-}D{-}F{-}G = 4+3+7+4 = \mathbf{18}\).

Other paths: 13 and 12. Still critical alone. Cost so far: ₹10.

Step 4 — crash 3 (target 17). D is now at its crash limit. Remaining critical candidates: A (₹6), F (₹6), G (₹8).

Choose A or F, both at ₹6. Take F (it has 2 weeks of crash room, giving future flexibility).

Crash F by 1 (7 → 6). \(A{-}D{-}F{-}G = 4+3+6+4 = \mathbf{17}\) ✓

Other paths: 13, 12. Target met.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Crash D by 2 weeks and F by 1 week. Project duration 17 weeks.}\ } \]

Total crashing cost.

\[ 2\times₹5 + 1\times₹6 = 10 + 6 = \mathbf{₹16} \]

Total project cost.

\[ \text{Normal direct} = 20+30+15+25+10+40+20 = ₹160 \] \[ \text{Crashed direct} = 160 + 16 = \mathbf{₹176} \]

Step 5 — is crashing worthwhile? Suppose indirect costs are ₹8 per week.

Duration Direct Indirect Total 20 160 \(20\times8 = 160\) 320 19 165 152 317 18 170 144 314 17 176 136 312 ← 16 \(176+6 = 182\) 128 310 ← lower still! 15 \(182+6 = 188\) 120 308 ← 14 \(188+8 = 196\) 112 308

(Beyond 17: crash A by 1 (₹6) → 16; crash F by 1 more (₹6) → 15; then only G (₹8) remains → 14.)

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The minimum-total-cost duration is 15 weeks at ₹308 — SHORTER than the 17-week deadline.}\ } \]

Advice. "Meeting the 17-week deadline costs ₹16 in crashing but saves ₹32 in indirect costs — a net gain of ₹16. Moreover, crashing further to 15 weeks saves another ₹4. Recommend targeting 15 weeks."

A caveat. Crashing compresses the schedule and removes float, increasing risk. At 15 weeks the near-critical paths may also become critical, making the project fragile. Recommend 16 weeks as a balance — near the cost optimum with slightly more buffer.

docs.title: Problem 4 — When crashing stops helping
docs.text:
Continuing Problem 3, suppose we crash aggressively and reach a duration where a second path becomes critical. Explain what changes and compute the correct next step.

Solution.

When does path \(A\to C\to E\to G\) (length 13) become critical? Only when the main path is crashed down to 13 — which would require crashing \(A{-}D{-}F{-}G\) from 20 to 13, i.e. by 7 weeks. Maximum available crashing on that path is \(1(A)+2(D)+2(F)+1(G) = 6\) weeks, reaching 14.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The absolute minimum duration is 14 weeks.}\ } \]

But note that A and G are on BOTH paths. Crashing A shortens \(A{-}D{-}F{-}G\) and \(A{-}C{-}E{-}G\) simultaneously.

The general rule when multiple paths are critical.

IF an activity lies on ALL critical paths:
      crash it -- one crash shortens every path (cheap per week of project time)
ELSE:
      must crash one activity on EACH critical path simultaneously
      -> cost per week = SUM of those slopes

Worked illustration. Suppose after crashing we reach a state where two paths are critical:

\[ P_1: A\to D\to F\to G \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_2: A\to C\to E\to G \]

Option 1 — crash A (₹6). A is on both, so both paths shorten by 1 ⟹ project shortens by 1 week for ₹6.

Option 2 — crash D (₹5) and C (₹7). D shortens \(P_1\); C shortens \(P_2\). Project shortens by 1 week for ₹5 + ₹7 = ₹12.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Crashing A costs ₹6; crashing D and C costs ₹12. Choose the common activity.}\ } \]

The general principle.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Activities on MULTIPLE critical paths are the most valuable to crash — one payment, several savings.}\ } \]

Why this must be checked every iteration. If you continue crashing D after \(P_2\) has become critical, the project duration does not change at all — you pay ₹5 and gain nothing, because \(P_2\) still takes the same time. Recomputing the critical path after every crash is not optional.

docs.title: Problem 5 — A complete project-management study
docs.text:
A software firm must deliver a system. Analyse, identify risks and advise.

Activity Description Duration (weeks) Predecessors A Requirements 3 — B System design 4 A C Database design 3 A D UI development 5 B E Backend development 6 B, C F Integration 3 D, E G Testing 4 F H Documentation 5 B I Deployment 2 G, H

Solution.

Forward pass.

Act ES EF A 0 3 B 3 7 C 3 6 D 7 12 E \(\max(7,6) = 7\) 13 H 7 12 F \(\max(12,13) = \mathbf{13}\) 16 G 16 20 I \(\max(20, 12) = \mathbf{20}\) 22 \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Project duration} = 22\ \text{weeks}\ } \]

Backward pass (\(\text{LF}_I = 22\)).

Act LF LS I 22 20 G 20 16 H 20 15 F 16 13 D 13 8 E 13 7 C \(\min(\text{LS}_E) = 7\) 4 B \(\min(8, 7, 15) = \mathbf{7}\) 3 A \(\min(3, 4) = 3\) 0

Float table.

Act \(d\) ES EF LS LF TF FF Critical A 3 0 3 0 3 0 0 ✓ B 4 3 7 3 7 0 0 ✓ C 3 3 6 4 7 1 1 D 5 7 12 8 13 1 1 E 6 7 13 7 13 0 0 ✓ F 3 13 16 13 16 0 0 ✓ G 4 16 20 16 20 0 0 ✓ H 5 7 12 15 20 8 8 I 2 20 22 20 22 0 0 ✓ \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical path: } A\to B\to E\to F\to G\to I, \quad 3+4+6+3+4+2 = 22\ \checkmark\ } \]

Advice to the firm.

1. Focus management attention on the critical path. A, B, E, F, G, I have zero float. Any slip on any of them delays delivery day for day. Assign the strongest staff and the tightest monitoring to E (backend, 6 weeks) — the longest critical activity and therefore the largest single risk.

2. Documentation (H) has 8 weeks of float — and it is FREE float. H's owner can start any time between weeks 7 and 15 without coordinating with anyone.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Redeploy documentation staff to the critical path during weeks 7–13, then write documentation in weeks 13–18.}\ } \]

This is the single most actionable finding: 8 person-weeks of effort can be moved to where it matters, at no schedule cost.

3. Near-critical activities need watching. C and D have only 1 week of float. A 2-week slip on either creates a second critical path.

Path Length Slack \(A\to B\to E\to F\to G\to I\) 22 0 \(A\to C\to E\to F\to G\to I\) 21 1 \(A\to B\to D\to F\to G\to I\) 21 1 \(A\to B\to H\to I\) 14 8

Three of four paths are within 1 week of critical ⟹ the schedule is tight and fragile.

4. Quantify the risk. With 6 activities on the critical path, even modest per-activity variability compounds. If each critical activity has a standard deviation of 0.5 weeks, the path standard deviation is

\[ \sigma_{\text{path}} = \sqrt{6\times0.5^2} = \sqrt{1.5} = 1.22 \ \text{weeks} \]

so a 22-week commitment has roughly a 50 % chance of being met, and a 95 % confident promise would be \(22 + 1.645(1.22) \approx \mathbf{24\ \text{weeks}}\). This is exactly what PERT (L20) formalises.

5. The recommendation.

"Commit to 24 weeks externally while managing to 22 internally. Move documentation staff onto the backend during weeks 7–13. Monitor C and D weekly — they have only 1 week of float. If the deadline is firm at 22 weeks, crash the backend (E) first, as it is the longest critical activity."

6. What CPM does NOT tell you. It assumes durations are known. They are not, especially in software. Use PERT (L20) for the probabilistic view, and re-run the network weekly as actuals come in — a schedule computed once and filed is worthless.

docs.title: 19.9 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Activities: A(2,—), B(3,A), C(4,A), D(2,B,C). Find \(T\) and the critical path. [Ans: \(T=8\), \(A\to C\to D\)]
  2. If ES = 5, EF = 9, LS = 7, LF = 11, what is TF? [Ans: 2]
  3. An activity has TF = 5 and FF = 0. Interpret.
  4. Compute the crash slope: normal (8 days, ₹40), crash (5 days, ₹58). [Ans: ₹6/day]
  5. Why must the critical path be recomputed after each crash?
  6. Which is safer to devolve to activity owners, TF or FF? Why?
  7. A project has 5 paths of lengths 20, 19, 19, 12, 10. Comment on its risk.

docs.title: 19.10 Summary
docs.text:
• CPM uses deterministic durations; AON networks need no dummy activities.
  • Forward pass: \(\text{ES}_j = \max_i \text{EF}_i\), \(\text{EF}_j = \text{ES}_j + d_j\); project duration \(T = \max \text{EF}\).
  • Backward pass: \(\text{LF}_i = \min_j \text{LS}_j\), \(\text{LS}_i = \text{LF}_i - d_i\), starting from \(\text{LF} = T\).
  • Total float \(= \text{LS}-\text{ES}\) — delay tolerable without delaying the project; free float \(= \min\text{ES}_{\text{succ}} - \text{EF}\) — delay tolerable without affecting any successor.
  • Critical path = the chain of zero-float activities = the longest path, and its length is the project duration.
  • Total float is SHARED; free float is not. Publish free float to activity owners and hold total float centrally, or it will be double-spent.
  • Crashing: rank critical activities by cost slope \(\frac{\Delta\text{cost}}{\Delta\text{time}}\), crash the cheapest, and recompute the critical path every iteration. Activities on several critical paths are the most valuable to crash.
  • The minimum-total-cost duration balances rising direct costs against falling indirect costs, and is often shorter than the deadline.
  • Many near-critical paths mean high schedule risk — a fact the single critical path conceals.

Next lesson: L20 — PERT and probabilistic project scheduling.

Practise now: unit2-games-networks-lab.html → CPM/PERT Lab: enter activities, see the network drawn automatically, with the critical path highlighted and a float table computed live.

docs.text: Field Detail Course Code DSC301 Course Title Optimization Methods L–T–P 3 – 0 – 1 Total Credits 4 Lecture Credits 3 Tutorial Credits 0 Practical / Practice Credits 1 Eligibility Criteria Graduation Pre-requisite NIL Semester III (M.Sc. Computer Science) Course Type Discipline Specific Core (DSC) Total Lecture Hours 45 (10 + 10 + 15 + 10) Total Practical Hours 30

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text: The course aims to impart comprehensive knowledge about operations research and optimization techniques. Its objectives are to help students understand the fundamental concepts of operations research, to discuss and analyze the need for various optimization techniques, to design and develop appropriate mathematical models, and to formulate and optimize real-world problems using these models.

docs.title: Course Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
On completing this course, the student will be able to:

  1. Understand the operations research concepts.
  2. Analyse the need of optimisation techniques.
  3. Able to design and develop mathematical models for real applications.
  4. Inculcate modeling skills necessary to describe and formulate optimization problems.

docs.title: Unit I  (10 Hours)
docs.text: Introduction to the modelling approach of operation research, introduction to linear programming, formulating and solving linear programming models, graphical method, simplex methods. Transportation problems: mathematical formulation, balanced transportation problem, unbalanced transportation problem. Assignment problem — mathematical formulation, Hungarian assignment method, travelling salesman problem.
