docs.title: Unit II  (10 Hours)
docs.text: Game theory: Formulation of two-person, zero-sum games and games with mixed strategies. Sequencing problems: processing of n jobs through 2 machines, processing of 2 jobs through m machines. Integer Programming: Gomory's method, branch and bound method. Network Scheduling: Basic terms, critical path methods (CPM), program evaluation and review technique (PERT).

docs.title: Unit III  (15 Hours)
docs.text: Queuing Theory: Characteristics of queuing systems, Poisson process and exponential distribution, steady state M/M/1, M/M/C (Models I, II, IV, V), applications of queuing theory. Inventory Control: Inventory Costs, economic order quantity, deterministic inventory problems, EOQ problems with no shortage, with shortage, production problem with no shortage, with shortage.

docs.title: Unit IV  (10 Hours)
docs.text: Search methods: one dimensional minimisation methods, fibonacci and golden section methods. Non-linear programming: One dimensional minimization method: unconstrained optimization techniques, constrained optimization techniques, graphical solution, Kuhn–Tucker conditions, quadratic programming problems.

docs.title: Readings
docs.text:
1. Frederick S. Hillier and Gerald J. Lieberman. Introduction to Operations Research. McGraw-Hill, 2015.
  2. Hamdy A. Taha. Operations Research: An Introduction. Pearson Education India, 2013.
  3. S. S. Rao. Engineering Optimization: Theory and Practice. New Age International, 3rd edition, 2013.
  4. K. Deb. Optimization for Engineering Design: Algorithms and Examples. PHI, 2nd Edition, 2012.
  5. J. S. Arora. Introduction to Optimum Design. Academic Press, 4th Edition, 2017.

docs.title: List of Practicals  (30 hours)
docs.text:
1. Formulation and graphical solution of linear programming problems. (2 hours)
  2. Solving linear programming problems using simplex method. (2 hours)
  3. Transportation problems: balanced/unbalanced cases. (2 hours)
  4. Assignment problem: Hungarian method and travelling salesman problem. (2 hours)
  5. Game theory: solving two-person zero-sum games with pure and mixed strategies. (2 hours)
  6. Sequencing problems: n jobs through 2 machines, 2 jobs through m machines. (2 hours)
  7. Branch and bound method for integer programming. (2 hours)
  8. Network scheduling: CPM and PERT analysis. (2 hours)
  9. Queuing theory: simulation of M/M/1 queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service. (2 hours)
  10. Analysis of M/M/C queues (Models I, II, IV, V). (2 hours)
  11. Inventory control: EOQ problems with and without shortages. (2 hours)
  12. Replacement problems: deteriorating items, group vs individual replacement. (2 hours)
  13. Information theory: entropy, mutual information, uncertainty measures. (2 hours)
  14. Search methods: one-dimensional minimization using Fibonacci and golden section methods. (2 hours)
  15. Non-linear programming: unconstrained optimization techniques and graphical solutions. (2 hours)

docs.title: Lesson 38: One-Dimensional Minimisation: Bracketing and Elimination
38.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain why every multivariable method needs a one-dimensional line search.
  2. Bracket a minimum by unrestricted search with an accelerated step.
  3. Apply exhaustive, dichotomous and interval-halving search, and state each one's reduction ratio.
  4. Compare the methods by function evaluations required for a given accuracy.
  5. Explain why interval halving needs \(3\) evaluations for the first stage but only \(2\) thereafter.

docs.title: 38.2 Why One Dimension Matters
docs.text:
Every multivariable algorithm in Lesson 42 has the same skeleton:

\[\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=\mathbf{x}_{k}+\alpha_k\,\mathbf{d}_k\]

— pick a direction \(\mathbf{d}_k\), then choose a step length \(\alpha_k\) by minimising

\[\phi(\alpha)=f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha\mathbf{d}_k)\]

which is a function of the single variable \(\alpha\). This inner problem is the line search, and it is where most of the computing time in non-linear optimisation is actually spent. Fast, reliable one-dimensional methods are therefore the foundation of the whole subject.

docs.title: The two phases
docs.text:
Phase Purpose Methods Bracketing find an interval \([a,b]\) known to contain the minimum unrestricted search with accelerated step Refinement shrink that interval to the required accuracy exhaustive, dichotomous, interval halving (this lesson); Fibonacci (L39); golden section (L40); interpolation (L41)

Every refinement method assumes unimodality on \([a,b]\) (Lesson 36). Bracketing is what earns the right to make that assumption.

docs.title: Two families of method
docs.text:
• Elimination (direct) methods use only function values. Robust; work on non-smooth and tabulated functions; convergence is linear.
  • Interpolation (gradient) methods use derivatives or fitted polynomials. Much faster near the optimum, but need smoothness and can fail far from it (Lesson 41).

docs.title: 38.3 Bracketing: Unrestricted Search with Accelerated Step
docs.text:
Algorithm. Choose a start \(x_0\) and step \(s>0\).

  1. Evaluate \(f(x_0)\) and \(f(x_0+s)\). If \(f\) increased, reverse the direction of \(s\).
  2. Repeatedly take \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s\) and double \(s\) each time, while \(f\) keeps falling.
  3. Stop at the first increase. The minimum is bracketed by the last three points visited.

Doubling ("accelerating") is what makes the method efficient: a minimum \(1000\) steps away is reached in about \(10\) evaluations rather than \(1000\).

docs.title: 38.4 Three Elimination Methods
docs.text: Throughout, \(L_0=b-a\) is the initial interval and \(n\) the number of function evaluations — the proper measure of cost, since evaluating \(f\) usually dominates all other work.

docs.title: Exhaustive search
docs.text:
Divide \([a,b]\) into \(n+1\) equal parts and evaluate \(f\) at the \(n\) interior points. The minimum lies between the neighbours of the smallest value.

\[\boxed{\ \frac{L_n}{L_0}=\frac{2}{n+1}\ }\]

Simple and completely parallelisable, but the worst method sequentially: the reduction is only linear in \(n\), whereas the methods below are exponential.

docs.title: Dichotomous search
docs.text:
Place two points a tiny distance \(\delta\) apart, straddling the midpoint:

\[x_1=\frac{a+b}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2},\qquad x_2=\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{\delta}{2}\]

Comparing \(f(x_1)\) and \(f(x_2)\) eliminates almost exactly half the interval. Repeating with \(n\) evaluations (\(n/2\) pairs):

\[\boxed{\ L_n=\frac{L_0}{2^{n/2}}+\delta\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{n/2}}\right)\ }\]

The \(\delta\) term is the price of the method: it cannot reduce the interval below \(\delta\), no matter how many evaluations are spent. Choosing \(\delta\) too small makes \(f(x_1)\) and \(f(x_2)\) numerically indistinguishable; too large and accuracy is lost. Both points are discarded at every stage — the method never reuses a function value, which is exactly the waste that Lessons 39–40 eliminate.

docs.title: Interval halving (three-point search)
docs.text:
Evaluate at the midpoint \(x_m\) and the two quarter-points \(x_1=a+L/4\), \(x_2=b-L/4\).

Decision rule.

  • If \(f(x_1)<f(x_m)\): the minimum is in \([a,x_m]\) — discard the right half; \(x_1\) becomes the new midpoint.
  • Else if \(f(x_2)<f(x_m)\): the minimum is in \([x_m,b]\) — discard the left half; \(x_2\) becomes the new midpoint.
  • Else the minimum is in \([x_1,x_2]\) — discard both outer quarters; \(x_m\) stays the midpoint.

Each stage halves the interval:

\[\boxed{\ \frac{L_n}{L_0}=\left(\frac12\right)^{(n-1)/2}\ }\]

Why the exponent is \((n-1)/2\). The first stage costs \(3\) evaluations, but in every case the surviving interval inherits a usable midpoint, so each later stage costs only \(2\) more. With \(n\) evaluations there are \((n-1)/2\) halvings. Reusing computed values is the single idea that separates good line searches from bad ones, and it is developed to its logical conclusion in Lessons 39–40.

docs.title: 38.5 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Throughout §4 the test function is

\[f(x)=x^{2}+\frac{54}{x},\qquad x>0,\]

whose exact minimum is found from \(f'(x)=2x-\dfrac{54}{x^{2}}=0\Rightarrow x^{3}=27\Rightarrow x^{*}=3\), with \(f(3)=9+18=27\) and \(f''(x)=2+108/x^{3}>0\) (convex, so this is global).

docs.title: Problem 1 — Bracketing by unrestricted search
docs.text:
Starting from \(x_0=1\) with step \(s=0.5\) and doubling, bracket the minimum.

Solution.

Step \(x\) \(s\) used \(f(x)=x^2+54/x\) Comment 0 1.0 — \(1+54=55.00000\) start 1 1.5 0.5 \(2.25+36=38.25000\) decreased — continue, double \(s\) 2 2.5 1.0 \(6.25+21.6=27.85000\) decreased — continue, double \(s\) 3 4.5 2.0 \(20.25+12=32.25000\) increased — stop \[\boxed{\text{Bracket }[1.5,\ 4.5],\quad L_0=3.0}\]

Interpretation. Four evaluations located the minimum inside an interval of width \(3\). Without doubling, the same march at a constant step of \(0.5\) would have needed seven evaluations to reach \(4.5\). Acceleration matters more the worse the initial guess: the number of evaluations grows like \(\log_2(\text{distance})\) rather than linearly.

Note also the essential caution: this bracket is trustworthy only if \(f\) is unimodal on it. The three points \(1.5,\,2.5,\,4.5\) show a decrease then an increase, which is consistent with a single minimum but does not prove it.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Exhaustive search
docs.text:
Minimise \(f\) on \([1,5]\) by exhaustive search with \(8\) equal sub-intervals.

Solution. Step \(=(5-1)/8=0.5\).

\(x\) 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0 4.5 5.0 \(f(x)\) 55.000 38.250 31.000 27.850 27.000 27.679 29.500 32.250 35.800

The smallest value is at \(x=3.0\), so

\[\boxed{x^{*}\in[2.5,\ 3.5],\qquad L_{\text{final}}=1.0}\]

Efficiency. The grid has \(7\) interior points, so the theoretical ratio is \(L_n/L_0=2/(7+1)=0.25\), and indeed \(4\times0.25=1.0\) ✓. Counting the two endpoints, \(9\) evaluations were made in all.

Interpretation. Exhaustive search is the only method here that does not assume unimodality — it simply looks everywhere on a grid. That robustness is why it is the standard first pass on an unknown function. Its weakness is that the reduction is only linear: halving the final interval requires doubling the number of evaluations, whereas the next two methods halve it for a fixed extra couple of evaluations.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Dichotomous search
docs.text:
Minimise \(f\) on \([1,5]\) using \(6\) evaluations (\(3\) pairs) with \(\delta=0.1\).

Solution.

Pair 1. \([a,b]=[1,5]\), midpoint \(3.0\):

\[x_1=2.95,\ f_1=8.7025+18.30508=27.00758;\qquad x_2=3.05,\ f_2=9.3025+17.70492=27.00742\]

\(f_1>f_2\Rightarrow\) discard \([1,\,2.95]\). New interval \([2.95,\ 5]\), \(L=2.05\).

Pair 2. Midpoint \(3.975\):

\[x_1=3.925,\ f_1=29.16359;\qquad x_2=4.025,\ f_2=29.61677\]

\(f_1<f_2\Rightarrow\) discard \([4.025,\,5]\). New interval \([2.95,\ 4.025]\), \(L=1.075\).

Pair 3. Midpoint \(3.4875\):

\[x_1=3.4375,\ f_1=27.52550;\qquad x_2=3.5375,\ f_2=27.77892\]

\(f_1<f_2\Rightarrow\) discard \([3.5375,\,4.025]\).

\[\boxed{x^{*}\in[2.95,\ 3.5375],\qquad L_{6}=0.5875}\]

Check against the formula.

\[L_6=\frac{4}{2^{3}}+0.1\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{3}}\right)=0.5+0.0875=0.5875\ \checkmark\]

Interpretation. Note the first comparison: \(f_1=27.00758\) and \(f_2=27.00742\) differ in the fourth decimal place, because both points sit almost exactly at the flat bottom of the curve. This is the characteristic hazard of dichotomous search — near the optimum the decision rests on a difference that may be smaller than the numerical noise in evaluating \(f\). Here the near-tie was harmless, but a rounding error of \(10^{-4}\) would have sent the search the other way.

The \(\delta\) term also sets a floor: as \(n\to\infty\), \(L_n\to\delta=0.1\). No number of evaluations can beat \(\delta\), which is why dichotomous search is a teaching device rather than a production method.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Interval halving
docs.text:
Minimise \(f\) on \([1,5]\) by interval halving, three stages.

Solution.

Stage 1. \([1,5]\), \(L=4\): \(x_1=2.0\), \(x_m=3.0\), \(x_2=4.0\).

\[f(x_1)=31.000,\quad f(x_m)=27.000,\quad f(x_2)=29.500\]

\(f(x_1)>f(x_m)\) and \(f(x_2)>f(x_m)\) \(\Rightarrow\) discard both outer quarters. New interval \([2,4]\), \(L=2\), with \(x_m=3\) retained.

Stage 2. \([2,4]\), \(L=2\): \(x_1=2.5\), \(x_m=3.0\) (already known!), \(x_2=3.5\).

\[f(2.5)=27.850,\quad f(3.0)=27.000,\quad f(3.5)=27.679\]

Again the midpoint wins \(\Rightarrow\) new interval \([2.5,3.5]\), \(L=1\).

Stage 3. \([2.5,3.5]\), \(L=1\): \(x_1=2.75\), \(x_m=3.0\), \(x_2=3.25\).

\[f(2.75)=27.19886,\quad f(3.0)=27.000,\quad f(3.25)=27.17788\]

Midpoint wins again.

\[\boxed{x^{*}\in[2.75,\ 3.25],\qquad L_{\text{final}}=0.5}\]

Evaluation count. Stage 1 used \(3\); stages 2 and 3 used \(2\) each (the midpoint was inherited), so \(n=7\) in total.

Check against the formula. \(\left(\tfrac12\right)^{(7-1)/2}=\left(\tfrac12\right)^{3}=\tfrac18\), and \(4\times\tfrac18=0.5\) ✓.

Interpretation. Compare with Problem 2: exhaustive search used \(9\) evaluations to reach \(L=1\), while interval halving used \(7\) to reach \(L=0.5\) — twice the accuracy for fewer evaluations. The whole difference is that interval halving reuses the midpoint. Note also that the true minimum \(x=3\) is the retained midpoint at every stage, so the method has effectively converged already; the interval merely certifies how much is known.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Comparing the methods
docs.text:
How many evaluations does each method need to reduce \([1,5]\) to a final interval of \(0.05\) (an accuracy of \(1.25\,\%\))? Take \(\delta=0.01\) for the dichotomous method.

Solution. Required ratio \(L_n/L_0=0.05/4=0.0125\).

Exhaustive: \(\dfrac{2}{n+1}=0.0125\Rightarrow n+1=160\Rightarrow \mathbf{n=159}\).

Dichotomous: solve \(\dfrac{4}{2^{n/2}}+0.01\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2^{n/2}}\right)=0.05\):

\[\frac{3.99}{2^{n/2}}=0.04\ \Rightarrow\ 2^{n/2}=99.75\ \Rightarrow\ \frac n2=\log_2 99.75=6.64 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{n=14}\ (\text{7 pairs})\]

Interval halving: \(\left(\tfrac12\right)^{(n-1)/2}=0.0125\Rightarrow \dfrac{n-1}{2}=\log_2 80=6.32\Rightarrow n-1=12.64\Rightarrow \mathbf{n=15}\).

Fibonacci (Lesson 39): \(\dfrac{1}{F_n}\le0.0125\Rightarrow F_n\ge80\), and \(F_{10}=89\ge80\), so \(\mathbf{n=10}\).

Golden section (Lesson 40): \(0.618^{\,n-1}\le0.0125\Rightarrow (n-1)\ge\dfrac{\ln 0.0125}{\ln0.618}=9.10 \Rightarrow \mathbf{n=11}\).

Method Evaluations Relative to exhaustive Exhaustive 159 \(1.00\times\) Interval halving 15 \(10.6\times\) better Dichotomous (\(\delta=0.01\)) 14 \(11.4\times\) better Golden section 11 \(\mathbf{14.5\times}\) better Fibonacci 10 \(\mathbf{15.9\times}\) better — optimal

Interpretation.

  • Sequential beats parallel by an order of magnitude. Exhaustive search wastes every evaluation on a fixed grid decided in advance; the others use each result to decide where to look next.
  • Dichotomous and interval halving are close, but dichotomous carries the \(\delta\) floor: demand an accuracy of \(0.005\) and it becomes impossible at \(\delta=0.01\), while interval halving simply needs two more evaluations.
  • Fibonacci is provably optimal among methods using a fixed number of evaluations, and beats golden section here by exactly one evaluation. Golden section pays that one evaluation for the freedom of not having to commit to \(n\) in advance. Lessons 39 and 40 derive both.
  • All the same, exhaustive search retains its place as a first pass on an unknown function, because it is the only one that does not silently assume unimodality.

docs.title: 38.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Bracket the minimum of \(f(x)=x^{2}-8x+20\) starting at \(x_0=0\) with \(s=1\), doubling. (Answer: \(x=0,1,3,7\) with \(f=20,13,5,13\) — bracket \([1,7]\))
  2. Perform two stages of interval halving on \(f(x)=(x-2)^{2}+3\) over \([0,6]\). (Answer: stage 1 has \(f(1.5)=3.25<f(3)=4\), so the interval becomes \([0,3]\); stage 2 has \(f(2.25)=3.0625<f(1.5)=3.25\), giving \([1.5,3.0]\))
  3. How many evaluations does dichotomous search with \(\delta=0.02\) need to reduce \([0,10]\) to \(0.1\)? (Answer: \(2^{n/2}=124.75\), \(n/2=6.96\), so \(n=14\))
  4. Show that interval halving with \(n\) evaluations always leaves \(L_0(1/2)^{(n-1)/2}\), and explain why \(n\) must be odd.
  5. Why is exhaustive search the only method in this lesson that does not require unimodality? Give a function on which the other three would fail.

docs.title: 38.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Every multivariable method reduces to repeated line searches, so one-dimensional methods are the workhorse of non-linear optimisation.
  • Bracket first, refine second. Unrestricted search with a doubling step finds a bracket in \(O(\log)\) evaluations; the bracket is what licenses the unimodality assumption.
  • Exhaustive: \(L_n/L_0=\dfrac{2}{n+1}\) — linear, wasteful, but assumption-free and parallelisable.
  • Dichotomous: \(L_n=\dfrac{L_0}{2^{n/2}}+\delta\!\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2^{n/2}}\right)\) — exponential, but cannot beat \(\delta\), and near the optimum its comparisons rest on tiny differences.
  • Interval halving: \(L_n/L_0=\left(\dfrac12\right)^{(n-1)/2}\) — \(3\) evaluations for the first stage and \(2\) thereafter, because the midpoint is reused.
  • Reuse of evaluations is the whole game. It is why interval halving beats dichotomous search, and Lessons 39–40 push the idea to its optimum.
  • To reduce \([1,5]\) to \(0.05\): exhaustive needs \(159\) evaluations, interval halving \(15\), Fibonacci only \(10\) and golden section \(11\).

Next lesson: L39 — The Fibonacci search method, provably the optimal elimination method.

Practise now: unit4-nlp-search-lab.html → Line Search Lab: pick a function and an interval, run all four methods side by side, and watch the intervals shrink at their different rates.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Operations Research and the Modelling Approach
1.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define operations research and recount its origins.
  2. List and explain the phases of an OR study.
  3. Classify mathematical models by type and choose an appropriate class.
  4. Identify decision variables, the objective function and constraints in a verbal problem.
  5. Formulate a simple real-world problem as a mathematical programme.

docs.title: 1.2 What Is Operations Research?
docs.text:
Definition. Operations Research (OR) is the application of scientific and mathematical methods to the study of the operations of a system, with the aim of providing decision-makers with an optimal or near-optimal course of action.

Alternative definitions worth knowing.

  • (Churchman, Ackoff and Arnoff) "OR is the application of scientific methods, techniques and tools to problems involving the operations of systems, so as to provide those in control of the system with optimum solutions to the problems."
  • (Operational Research Society, UK) "The attack of modern science on complex problems arising in the direction and management of large systems of men, machines, materials and money."

The three defining characteristics.

  1. A systems orientation. OR examines the whole system, not an isolated part. Optimising one department may harm the organisation — a phenomenon called sub-optimisation.
  2. An interdisciplinary team. Mathematicians, statisticians, engineers, economists and domain experts working together.
  3. A scientific method. Observe, formulate a hypothesis (model), test, validate, implement.

docs.title: Historical origins
docs.text:
Period Development 1937–1945 Born in Britain during WWII. Teams studied radar deployment, convoy sizing and anti-submarine tactics. The term "operational research" dates from Bawdsey Research Station, 1937. 1940s Blackett's Circus (P. M. S. Blackett's team) — the archetypal interdisciplinary OR group. 1947 George Dantzig invents the simplex method — the single most consequential event in the field. 1950s OR moves into industry: transportation, inventory, queueing. Journals and societies founded. 1950s–60s Dynamic programming (Bellman), network flows (Ford–Fulkerson), PERT/CPM (1958). 1979 Khachiyan's ellipsoid method — LP is proved to be in P. 1984 Karmarkar's interior-point method — polynomial and practical. 1990s–present Massive solver improvements (CPLEX, Gurobi); OR merges with machine learning and data science.

A striking fact about progress. Between 1990 and 2020, LP solvers improved by roughly \(10^{6}\)× from algorithms and \(10^{6}\)× from hardware — a combined \(10^{12}\)× speed-up. A problem that took a year in 1990 now takes about 30 milliseconds.

docs.title: Classic wartime example — the convoy problem
docs.text:
The question. Should merchant ships cross the Atlantic in small frequent convoys or large infrequent ones?

The intuition (wrong): small convoys are less conspicuous.

The OR analysis. A convoy's escort ring scales with its perimeter (\(\propto\sqrt{n}\) for \(n\) ships in a compact formation), while the ships protected scale with \(n\). So escort strength per ship improves as convoys grow. Furthermore, U-boat detection probability depends on convoy frequency, not size.

The conclusion: large convoys. Implementing this cut shipping losses substantially, and it is the canonical illustration of OR overturning plausible intuition with quantitative reasoning.

docs.title: 1.3 Phases of an OR Study
docs.text:
1. Formulate the problem
              |
   2. Construct the model
              |
   3. Derive a solution      <---+
              |                  |
   4. Test / validate           | (iterate)
              |                  |
   5. Establish controls  ------+
              |
   6. Implement

Phase 1 — Formulating the problem. Identify the decision-maker, the objectives, the alternatives available and the constraints. Typically the hardest and most neglected phase. A precisely solved wrong problem is worthless.

Phase 2 — Constructing the model. Translate the verbal problem into mathematics: decision variables, objective function, constraints. Decide what to simplify.

Phase 3 — Deriving a solution. Apply an algorithm — simplex, branch and bound, a queueing formula, simulation.

Phase 4 — Testing and validation. Does the model reproduce known past behaviour? Are the answers sensible under extreme inputs? Retrospective testing against historical data is standard.

Phase 5 — Establishing controls. The solution is valid only while the parameters hold. Sensitivity analysis identifies which parameters matter and how far they may drift.

Phase 6 — Implementation. Translate the mathematical solution into operating procedures people will actually follow. More OR studies fail here than at any technical stage.

docs.title: By degree of abstraction
docs.text:
Type Description Example Iconic a scaled physical replica a wind-tunnel aircraft model Analogue one property represents another a contour map; an electrical circuit modelling a mechanical system Symbolic / mathematical variables and equations \(\max\ 3x_1+5x_2\) subject to constraints

OR works almost entirely with symbolic models.

docs.title: By certainty
docs.text: Type Description Techniques Deterministic all parameters known with certainty LP, transportation, assignment, CPM, EOQ Probabilistic / stochastic some parameters are random variables queueing, PERT, stochastic inventory, Markov chains Game-theoretic an intelligent opponent chooses adversarially game theory

docs.title: By mathematical structure
docs.text:
Model Objective Constraints Variables Linear programming linear linear continuous Integer programming linear linear integer Mixed integer linear linear both Non-linear programming non-linear any continuous Quadratic programming quadratic linear continuous Dynamic programming any staged any

This course covers all six.

docs.title: 1.5 Anatomy of a Mathematical Programme
docs.text:
Every optimisation model has exactly three components.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Optimise } \quad & Z = f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) && \text{\textbf{objective function}}\\ \text{subject to } \quad & g_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\ \{\le,\ =,\ \ge\}\ b_i, \quad i = 1,\ldots,m && \text{\textbf{constraints}}\\ & x_j \ge 0, \quad j = 1,\ldots,n && \text{\textbf{non-negativity}} \end{aligned} \]

1. Decision variables. The quantities under the decision-maker's control. Always define them with units and a time base: "\(x_1\) = tonnes of product A produced per week", not "\(x_1\) = product A".

2. Objective function. The single quantity to maximise (profit, throughput) or minimise (cost, time, distance).

3. Constraints. Limitations: resource availability, demand requirements, capacity, policy rules, and non-negativity.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Feasible solution any \(\vec x\) satisfying all constraints Feasible region the set of all feasible solutions Optimal solution a feasible solution giving the best objective value Infeasible no solution satisfies all constraints Unbounded the objective can be improved without limit Redundant constraint removing it does not change the feasible region Binding (active) constraint holds with equality at the optimum Slack the unused amount of a \(\le\) resource Surplus the excess over a \(\ge\) requirement

docs.title: Problem 1 — Product-mix formulation
docs.text:
A furniture firm makes tables and chairs. A table needs 5 hours of carpentry and 2 hours of finishing; a chair needs 3 hours of carpentry and 4 hours of finishing. Weekly capacity is 120 hours of carpentry and 90 hours of finishing. Profit is ₹450 per table and ₹300 per chair. Formulate an LP to maximise weekly profit.

Solution.

Step 1 — Decision variables.

\[ x_1 = \text{number of tables produced per week} \] \[ x_2 = \text{number of chairs produced per week} \]

Step 2 — Objective function. Maximise weekly profit (in ₹):

\[ \max\ Z = 450x_1 + 300x_2 \]

Step 3 — Constraints.

Carpentry: each table uses 5 h, each chair 3 h; 120 h available.

\[ 5x_1 + 3x_2 \le 120 \]

Finishing: each table 2 h, each chair 4 h; 90 h available.

\[ 2x_1 + 4x_2 \le 90 \]

Non-negativity: you cannot produce a negative quantity.

\[ x_1,\ x_2 \ge 0 \]

The complete model.

\[ \begin{aligned} \max\ & Z = 450x_1 + 300x_2\\ \text{s.t. } & 5x_1 + 3x_2 \le 120 && \text{(carpentry)}\\ & 2x_1 + 4x_2 \le 90 && \text{(finishing)}\\ & x_1, x_2 \ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

A useful presentation device — the data table. Always tabulate before formulating:

Table (\(x_1\)) Chair (\(x_2\)) Available Carpentry (h) 5 3 120 Finishing (h) 2 4 90 Profit (₹) 450 300 maximise

Reading off the model. Each row is a constraint; the bottom row is the objective. Students who build this table first make far fewer formulation errors.

(This problem is solved graphically in L03 and by simplex in L05; the optimum is \(x_1 = 15\), \(x_2 = 15\), \(Z = ₹11{,}250\).)

docs.title: Problem 2 — Diet problem formulation
docs.text:
A nutritionist must design a minimum-cost daily diet from two foods. Food A costs ₹12 per unit and provides 4 units of protein, 2 of fat and 8 of carbohydrate. Food B costs ₹20 per unit and provides 9 units of protein, 5 of fat and 3 of carbohydrate. The diet must supply at least 36 units of protein and 20 of fat, and at most 40 units of carbohydrate. Formulate.

Solution.

Decision variables.

\[ x_1 = \text{units of Food A per day}, \qquad x_2 = \text{units of Food B per day} \]

Objective. Minimise cost:

\[ \min\ Z = 12x_1 + 20x_2 \]

Constraints.

\[ \begin{aligned} 4x_1 + 9x_2 &\ge 36 && \text{(protein — at least)}\\ 2x_1 + 5x_2 &\ge 20 && \text{(fat — at least)}\\ 8x_1 + 3x_2 &\le 40 && \text{(carbohydrate — at most)}\\ x_1, x_2 &\ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

Note the mixed inequality directions. Nutritional requirements give \(\ge\); limits give \(\le\). Confusing them is the most common formulation error in diet problems. A reliable check: ask "would more of this be a problem or a benefit?" — benefit ⟹ \(\ge\); problem ⟹ \(\le\).

Historical note. The diet problem was posed by the US Army in 1945 and solved by George Stigler using heuristics (77 foods, 9 nutrients); Dantzig later solved it exactly by simplex in 1947 — one of the first practical LP applications.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Blending problem with a ratio constraint
docs.text:
A refinery blends two crude oils into petrol. Crude 1 costs ₹60/barrel and is 40 % octane; Crude 2 costs ₹85/barrel and is 70 % octane. At least 8000 barrels of blend are needed, with an octane content of at least 55 %. Supply of Crude 2 is limited to 5000 barrels. Formulate.

Solution.

Decision variables.

\[ x_1 = \text{barrels of Crude 1},\qquad x_2 = \text{barrels of Crude 2} \]

Objective.

\[ \min\ Z = 60x_1 + 85x_2 \]

Constraint 1 — total volume.

\[ x_1 + x_2 \ge 8000 \]

Constraint 2 — octane content. The blend's octane fraction must be at least 0.55:

\[ \frac{0.40x_1 + 0.70x_2}{x_1 + x_2} \ \ge\ 0.55 \]

This is non-linear as written. Multiply through by \((x_1+x_2) > 0\) — legitimate because the denominator is strictly positive:

\[ 0.40x_1 + 0.70x_2 \ \ge\ 0.55x_1 + 0.55x_2 \] \[ -0.15x_1 + 0.15x_2 \ \ge\ 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ x_2 \ \ge\ x_1\ } \]

Now linear. The blend needs at least as much high-octane crude as low-octane crude.

Constraint 3 — supply limit.

\[ x_2 \le 5000 \]

Complete model.

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\ & Z = 60x_1 + 85x_2\\ \text{s.t. } & x_1 + x_2 \ge 8000\\ & x_2 - x_1 \ge 0\\ & x_2 \le 5000\\ & x_1, x_2 \ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

The lesson. Ratio and percentage requirements are always linearisable by cross-multiplying, provided the denominator is guaranteed positive. This trick appears constantly in blending, portfolio and staffing problems, and it is worth memorising.

(Quick feasibility check: \(x_1 + x_2 \ge 8000\) with \(x_2\le5000\) and \(x_2\ge x_1\) forces \(x_1 \ge 3000\) and \(x_1\le x_2\le 5000\) — the region is non-empty ✓.)

docs.title: Problem 4 — Multi-period production planning
docs.text:
A firm faces demand of 100, 150 and 120 units in months 1, 2 and 3. Production capacity is 130 units per month. Production costs ₹50 per unit; holding inventory costs ₹8 per unit per month. Initial inventory is zero. Formulate an LP minimising total cost.

Solution.

Decision variables — note that two families are needed:

\[ p_t = \text{units produced in month } t, \qquad t = 1,2,3 \] \[ I_t = \text{inventory carried from month } t \text{ to } t+1, \qquad t = 1,2,3 \]

Objective.

\[ \min\ Z = 50(p_1+p_2+p_3) + 8(I_1+I_2+I_3) \]

Constraints — inventory balance. This is the key structural idea:

\[ \boxed{\ \text{opening inventory} + \text{production} = \text{demand} + \text{closing inventory}\ } \] \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Month 1:}\quad & 0 + p_1 = 100 + I_1 &&\Rightarrow\ p_1 - I_1 = 100\\ \text{Month 2:}\quad & I_1 + p_2 = 150 + I_2 &&\Rightarrow\ I_1 + p_2 - I_2 = 150\\ \text{Month 3:}\quad & I_2 + p_3 = 120 + I_3 &&\Rightarrow\ I_2 + p_3 - I_3 = 120 \end{aligned} \]

Capacity.

\[ p_t \le 130, \qquad t = 1,2,3 \]

Non-negativity. \(p_t, I_t \ge 0\). (Requiring \(I_t \ge 0\) is what forbids backordering; allowing \(I_t\) to go negative would model backorders.)

Why production must be smoothed. Total demand is \(100+150+120 = 370\); total capacity is \(3\times130 = 390\). But month 2's demand of 150 exceeds the 130 monthly capacity, so the firm must build inventory in month 1.

The obvious feasible plan. Produce \(p_1 = 120\) (carrying \(I_1 = 20\)), \(p_2 = 130\) (carrying \(I_2 = 0\)), \(p_3 = 120\):

\[ Z = 50(370) + 8(20 + 0 + 0) = 18{,}500 + 160 = ₹18{,}660 \]

Since production cost is constant per unit and total production is fixed at 370, minimising cost means minimising inventory, and carrying exactly 20 units for one month is the minimum required. So this plan is optimal, with \(Z = ₹18{,}660\).

(If production costs varied by month — overtime, seasonal labour — the trade-off would become genuinely interesting, and this is the standard lot-sizing model.)

docs.title: Problem 5 — Recognising sub-optimisation
docs.text:
A manufacturer's production department is rewarded for minimising unit cost, and therefore runs very long production batches. The warehouse is separately rewarded for minimising inventory. Sales is rewarded for never missing an order. Explain the conflict in OR terms and state the correct formulation.

Solution.

The conflict.

Department Local objective Local optimum Effect elsewhere Production minimise unit cost very large batches (setup cost spread thin) huge inventory Warehouse minimise inventory very small batches frequent setups, high cost Sales never stock out large safety stock high inventory

Each department is behaving rationally given its own metric, and the firm as a whole suffers. This is sub-optimisation: optimising components separately does not optimise the system.

Why it happens mathematically. Let \(Q\) be the batch size, \(D\) annual demand, \(C_o\) setup cost and \(C_h\) holding cost per unit per year. The two local objectives are

\[ \text{Production:}\ \min\ \frac{DC_o}{Q} \ \Rightarrow\ Q\to\infty \] \[ \text{Warehouse:}\ \min\ \frac{QC_h}{2} \ \Rightarrow\ Q\to 0 \]

They pull in opposite directions, and neither alone has an interior optimum.

The correct (system-wide) formulation. Minimise the sum:

\[ \min_{Q>0}\ TC(Q) = \frac{DC_o}{Q} + \frac{QC_h}{2} \]

Differentiating and setting to zero:

\[ \frac{dTC}{dQ} = -\frac{DC_o}{Q^{2}} + \frac{C_h}{2} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2DC_o}{C_h}}\ } \]

This is the Economic Order Quantity, derived in full in L31. Note that it sits between the two departmental extremes, and neither department would ever propose it.

The organisational fix. Change the incentives, not just the mathematics: reward departments on total system cost, or use transfer prices that internalise the externality. This is why OR implementation (Phase 6) so often requires organisational change, and why so many technically correct OR studies fail.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{OR's first principle: optimise the system, not its parts.}\ } \]

docs.title: 1.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. A company makes two products needing 2 and 3 hours of machine time, with 60 hours available; profits are ₹40 and ₹50. Formulate.
  2. Formulate a diet problem with three foods and two nutrients, choosing your own data.
  3. A blend must be at most 30 % impurity from two sources with 20 % and 45 % impurity. Write the linear constraint. [Ans: \(-0.10x_1 + 0.15x_2 \le 0\), i.e. \(3x_2 \le 2x_1\)]
  4. Extend Problem 4 to 4 months with your own demand figures.
  5. Give two more examples of sub-optimisation from everyday organisations.
  6. Classify each as deterministic or stochastic: EOQ, PERT, simplex, M/M/1, CPM.
  7. State the six phases of an OR study and which is most often the cause of failure.

docs.title: 1.8 Summary
docs.text:
• OR applies scientific method to system-level decision-making; its three hallmarks are a systems orientation, an interdisciplinary team and a scientific method.
  • Born in WWII Britain; transformed by Dantzig's simplex method (1947); LP solvers have improved by roughly \(10^{12}\)× since 1990.
  • Six phases: formulate → model → solve → validate → control → implement. Formulation and implementation, not solution, are where studies usually fail.
  • Models are iconic / analogue / symbolic, and deterministic / stochastic / game-theoretic.
  • Every mathematical programme has decision variables, an objective function and constraints; define variables with units and a time base.
  • Ratio and percentage requirements linearise by cross-multiplication when the denominator is positive.
  • Multi-period models are built on the inventory-balance identity: opening + production = demand + closing.
  • Sub-optimisation — optimising parts separately — is OR's central cautionary principle; the EOQ formula is the classic resolution.

Next lesson: L02 — Introduction to linear programming and formulation.

Practise now: open Interactive-Web-Platform/unit1-lp-lab.html → Model Builder: enter a verbal problem's data in a table and watch the LP formulation assemble itself.

docs.title: Lesson 20: PERT and Probabilistic Project Scheduling
20.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain the three time estimates and the Beta distribution assumption.
  2. Compute the expected time \(t_e\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) of an activity.
  3. Compute the project variance and apply the Central Limit Theorem.
  4. Compute the probability of completion by a target date, and the date for a given confidence.
  5. State PERT's limitations, especially the merge-event bias.

docs.title: 20.2 Why PERT?
docs.text:
CPM assumes durations are known. For novel work — R&D, construction, software — they are not. PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique, US Navy, 1958) models them as random variables.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{CPM asks "how long?" PERT asks "how likely?"}\ } \]

docs.title: 20.3 The Three Time Estimates
docs.text:
For each activity, obtain from the person who will do the work:

Estimate Symbol Meaning Optimistic \(a\) everything goes right; ~1 % chance of being this fast Most likely \(m\) the modal duration under normal conditions Pessimistic \(b\) everything that can reasonably go wrong does; ~1 % chance of being this slow

Always \(a \le m \le b\).

docs.title: The Beta distribution assumption
docs.text:
PERT assumes activity duration follows a Beta distribution on \([a,b]\) with mode \(m\). The Beta is chosen because it is:

  • bounded (unlike the normal, a task cannot take negative time or infinite time),
  • flexible in shape — it can be symmetric or skewed either way,
  • unimodal, matching how people estimate.

Real activity durations are typically right-skewed: things can go badly wrong (long tail) more easily than they can go spectacularly right.

docs.title: The formulas
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ t_e \ =\ \frac{a + 4m + b}{6} \qquad \textbf{(expected time)}\ } \] \[ \boxed{\ \sigma^2 \ =\ \left(\frac{b-a}{6}\right)^{2} \qquad \textbf{(variance)}\ } \]

Where they come from.

  • \(t_e\) is a weighted average giving the mode four times the weight of either extreme — a standard approximation to the Beta mean.
  • \(\sigma\) uses the six-sigma range heuristic: for many distributions, essentially the whole range spans about \(6\sigma\), so \(\sigma \approx (b-a)/6\).

Note that \(\sigma\) depends ONLY on the spread \(b-a\), not on \(m\). Two activities with the same range have the same variance regardless of skew.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. For each activity compute t_e and sigma^2
2. Run CPM (L19) using t_e as the duration
3. Identify the critical path; T_e = its length
4. Project variance = SUM of the variances of the CRITICAL activities only
5. Project standard deviation = sqrt(project variance)
6. Apply the normal approximation for probability questions

docs.title: Why the variances add
docs.text:
The critical-path length is a sum of activity durations. For independent random variables,

\[ \mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_i X_i\right) = \sum_i \mathrm{Var}(X_i) \]

Variances add; standard deviations do NOT.

\[ \boxed{\ \sigma_{\text{project}} = \sqrt{\sum_{i\in\text{critical path}} \sigma_i^{2}}\ } \]

docs.title: The normal approximation
docs.text:
By the Central Limit Theorem, the sum of several independent random variables is approximately normal, whatever their individual distributions. So

\[ T \ \sim\ N\left(T_e,\ \sigma^2_{\text{project}}\right) \]

Probability of completion by a target date \(D\):

\[ \boxed{\ z = \frac{D - T_e}{\sigma_{\text{project}}}, \qquad \Pr[T \le D] = \Phi(z)\ } \]

Date for a given confidence \(p\):

\[ \boxed{\ D = T_e + z_p\,\sigma_{\text{project}}\ } \] Confidence \(z_p\) 50 % 0.000 75 % 0.674 90 % 1.282 95 % 1.645 99 % 2.326

docs.title: 20.5 Worked Example
docs.text: Activity \(a\) \(m\) \(b\) Predecessors A 2 4 6 — B 3 5 13 — C 1 3 5 A D 4 6 14 A E 2 3 10 B, C F 3 5 7 D G 1 2 3 E, F

docs.title: CPM on the expected times
docs.text: Activity ES EF LS LF TF Critical A 0 4 0 4 0 ✓ B 0 6 5 11 5 C 4 7 8 11 4 D 4 11 4 11 0 ✓ E 7 11 11 15 4 F 11 16 11 16 0 ✓ G 16 18 16 18 0 ✓ \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical path: } A\to D\to F\to G, \qquad T_e = 4+7+5+2 = \mathbf{18\ \text{weeks}}\ } \]

docs.title: Project variance
docs.text:
Sum the variances of CRITICAL activities only.

\[ \sigma^2_{\text{project}} = \sigma^2_A + \sigma^2_D + \sigma^2_F + \sigma^2_G \] \[ = 0.444 + 2.778 + 0.444 + 0.111 = \mathbf{3.778} \] \[ \boxed{\ \sigma_{\text{project}} = \sqrt{3.778} = \mathbf{1.944\ \text{weeks}}\ } \]

Note what dominates. Activity D contributes 2.778 of the 3.778 — 73.5 % of the total variance — because its range is \(14-4 = 10\) weeks. D is the single largest source of schedule risk, and that is where risk-reduction effort belongs.

docs.title: Probability questions
docs.text:
(a) Probability of finishing within 20 weeks.

\[ z = \frac{20 - 18}{1.944} = \mathbf{1.029} \] \[ \Pr[T\le20] = \Phi(1.029) = \mathbf{0.848} = \mathbf{84.8\%} \]

(b) Probability of finishing within 22 weeks.

\[ z = \frac{22-18}{1.944} = 2.058 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Pr = \Phi(2.058) = \mathbf{98.0\%} \]

(c) Date for 95 % confidence.

\[ D = T_e + 1.645\sigma = 18 + 1.645(1.944) = 18 + 3.198 = \mathbf{21.2\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Promise 22 weeks to be 95 \% confident; the expected duration is only 18.}\ } \]

(d) Probability of finishing within the expected duration of 18 weeks.

\[ z = \frac{18-18}{1.944} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Pr = \Phi(0) = \mathbf{50\%} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A project promised at its EXPECTED duration has only a 50 \% chance of success.}\ } \]

This is the single most important practical lesson in PERT, and the most widely ignored in practice.

docs.title: The merge-event bias
docs.text:
PERT computes the variance of the critical path only. But a near-critical path may overtake it.

Concrete illustration. Suppose two paths have \(T_e = 18\) and \(T_e = 17\), each with \(\sigma = 2\). PERT reports \(T_e = 18\). But the project finishes when both are done:

\[ T_{\text{project}} = \max(T_1,\ T_2) \]

and \(E[\max(T_1,T_2)] > \max(E[T_1], E[T_2]) = 18\) — by Jensen's inequality, since \(\max\) is convex.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{PERT is OPTIMISTICALLY BIASED. The true expected duration exceeds $T_e$.}\ } \]

The bias grows with the number of near-critical paths. For the illustration above the bias is roughly \(0.5\)–\(1\) week; with five near-critical paths it can be several weeks.

The remedy: Monte Carlo simulation. Sample each activity's duration from its distribution, compute the network's completion time, repeat 10 000 times, and read the empirical distribution. This handles merge bias, correlated durations and non-Beta shapes automatically, and is what modern project software does.

docs.title: Other limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Beta assumption is arbitrary the \(\frac{a+4m+b}{6}\) weights have no deep justification Estimates are subjective optimism bias inflates confidence; \(b\) is usually understated Independence assumed in reality a shared resource or bad weather correlates delays Only the critical path's variance counted merge bias (§5.1) Durations assumed fixed once started no learning, no mid-course correction \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{PERT's greatest value is forcing explicit discussion of uncertainty, not the third decimal of a probability.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 1 — Computing t_e and σ
docs.text:
For activities with \((a,m,b)\) as below, compute \(t_e\), \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\), and comment on the skew.

Activity \(a\) \(m\) \(b\) P 5 8 11 Q 2 4 12 R 6 6 6 S 3 10 11

Solution.

Activity P (symmetric: \(m\) is the midpoint of \([5,11]\)).

\[ t_e = \frac{5+32+11}{6} = \frac{48}{6} = \mathbf{8}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{6}{6}\right)^2 = \mathbf{1}, \qquad \sigma = \mathbf{1} \]

\(t_e = m = 8\) — symmetric, so mean = mode.

Activity Q (right-skewed: long pessimistic tail).

\[ t_e = \frac{2+16+12}{6} = \frac{30}{6} = \mathbf{5}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{10}{6}\right)^2 = \mathbf{2.778}, \qquad \sigma = \mathbf{1.667} \]

\(t_e = 5 > m = 4\) — the long tail pulls the mean above the mode, exactly as it should.

Activity R (certain).

\[ t_e = \frac{6+24+6}{6} = \mathbf{6}, \qquad \sigma^2 = 0, \qquad \sigma = \mathbf{0} \]

No uncertainty — a deterministic activity, which PERT handles as a special case ✓.

Activity S (left-skewed: long optimistic tail).

\[ t_e = \frac{3+40+11}{6} = \frac{54}{6} = \mathbf{9}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{8}{6}\right)^2 = \mathbf{1.778}, \qquad \sigma = \mathbf{1.333} \]

\(t_e = 9 < m = 10\) — the mean is pulled below the mode.

Summary and interpretation.

Activity \(t_e\) \(m\) Skew \(\sigma\) Risk P 8 8 none 1.000 moderate Q 5 4 right 1.667 highest R 6 6 none 0.000 none S 9 10 left 1.333 moderate \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Q is the riskiest: largest } \sigma \textbf{ AND right-skewed (bad surprises more likely than good).}\ } \]

A caution about relying on \(\sigma\) alone. \(\sigma\) depends only on \(b - a\), so it treats right-skew and left-skew identically. Activity Q (right-skewed) is operationally far more dangerous than a left-skewed activity with the same \(\sigma\), because overruns are the outcome that hurts. Read the skew as well as the variance.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Full probabilistic analysis
docs.text:
A project has critical path with activities and estimates below. Compute \(T_e\), \(\sigma\), and answer the probability questions.

Activity \(a\) \(m\) \(b\) 1 4 6 8 2 6 9 18 3 2 5 8 4 5 7 15

Solution.

Step 1 — expected times and variances.

Act \(t_e\) \(\sigma^2\) 1 \(\dfrac{4+24+8}{6} = \mathbf{6}\) \(\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right)^2 = 0.444\) 2 \(\dfrac{6+36+18}{6} = \mathbf{10}\) \(\left(\dfrac{12}{6}\right)^2 = 4.000\) 3 \(\dfrac{2+20+8}{6} = \mathbf{5}\) \(\left(\dfrac{6}{6}\right)^2 = 1.000\) 4 \(\dfrac{5+28+15}{6} = \mathbf{8}\) \(\left(\dfrac{10}{6}\right)^2 = 2.778\) \[ T_e = 6+10+5+8 = \mathbf{29\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \sigma^2_{\text{proj}} = 0.444+4.000+1.000+2.778 = \mathbf{8.222} \] \[ \sigma_{\text{proj}} = \sqrt{8.222} = \mathbf{2.867\ \text{weeks}} \]

Step 2 — probability questions.

(a) \(\Pr[T\le 32]\).

\[ z = \frac{32-29}{2.867} = 1.046 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Phi(1.046) = \mathbf{85.2\%} \]

(b) \(\Pr[T\le 27]\).

\[ z = \frac{27-29}{2.867} = -0.698 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Phi(-0.698) = \mathbf{24.3\%} \]

(c) \(\Pr[29 \le T \le 33]\).

\[ z_1 = 0, \quad z_2 = \frac{33-29}{2.867} = 1.395 \] \[ \Pr = \Phi(1.395) - \Phi(0) = 0.9185 - 0.5 = \mathbf{41.9\%} \]

(d) The 90 %-confidence date.

\[ D = 29 + 1.282(2.867) = 29 + 3.676 = \mathbf{32.7\ \text{weeks}} \]

(e) The 99 %-confidence date.

\[ D = 29 + 2.326(2.867) = 29 + 6.669 = \mathbf{35.7\ \text{weeks}} \]

Step 3 — the risk profile.

Promise Probability of meeting it 27 weeks 24 % 29 weeks (= \(T_e\)) 50 % 32 weeks 85 % 32.7 weeks 90 % 34 weeks 96 % 35.7 weeks 99 % \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Buying confidence from 50 \% to 90 \% costs 3.7 weeks — a 13 \% schedule buffer.}\ } \]

Where the risk lies. Activity 2 contributes \(4.000/8.222 = \mathbf{48.6\%}\) of the total variance, activity 4 another 33.8 %. Together they account for 82 % of the schedule risk while being only 62 % of the duration.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Reducing the uncertainty on activities 2 and 4 is worth far more than shortening activities 1 and 3.}\ } \]

Concretely: if better planning narrowed activity 2's range from \([6,18]\) to \([7,13]\), its variance would fall from 4.000 to \(\left(\frac{6}{6}\right)^2 = 1.000\), giving

\[ \sigma_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{8.222 - 3.000} = \sqrt{5.222} = 2.285 \]

and the 90 % date would drop to \(29 + 1.282(2.285) = \mathbf{31.9}\) weeks — 0.8 weeks of buffer saved by reducing uncertainty, not duration.

docs.title: Problem 3 — The merge-event bias, quantified
docs.text:
A project has two parallel paths, each ending at the final event: path 1 with \(T_e = 20\), \(\sigma = 3\); path 2 with \(T_e = 19\), \(\sigma = 3\). What does PERT report, and what is the truth?

Solution.

What PERT reports. The critical path is path 1 (\(T_e = 20\), the longer).

\[ T_e = 20, \qquad \sigma = 3 \] \[ \Pr[T\le20] = \Phi(0) = \mathbf{50\%} \]

The truth. The project finishes when both paths are done:

\[ T = \max(T_1,\ T_2) \] \[ \Pr[T \le 20] = \Pr[T_1\le20]\cdot\Pr[T_2\le20] \quad \text{(assuming independence)} \] \[ \Pr[T_1\le20] = \Phi\left(\frac{20-20}{3}\right) = \Phi(0) = 0.500 \] \[ \Pr[T_2\le20] = \Phi\left(\frac{20-19}{3}\right) = \Phi(0.333) = 0.630 \] \[ \boxed{\ \Pr[T\le20] = 0.500\times0.630 = \mathbf{0.315} = \mathbf{31.5\%}\ } \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{PERT says 50 \%; the truth is 31.5 \%. PERT is optimistic by 18.5 percentage points.}\ } \]

The magnitude of the bias in time terms. Solve for the date giving a true 50 % probability:

\[ \Phi\left(\frac{D-20}{3}\right)\cdot\Phi\left(\frac{D-19}{3}\right) = 0.5 \]

Trying \(D = 21.5\): \(\Phi(0.5)\Phi(0.833) = 0.691\times0.798 = 0.551\). Trying \(D = 21\): \(\Phi(0.333)\Phi(0.667) = 0.630\times0.748 = 0.471\).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The true median completion is about 21.3 weeks, not 20 — a bias of ~1.3 weeks.}\ } \]

How the bias grows. With \(k\) independent near-critical paths each having 50 % chance of meeting \(T_e\):

\[ \Pr[\text{all done by } T_e] = 0.5^{k} \] Number of paths at \(T_e\) \(\Pr[\text{on time}]\) 1 50 % 2 25 % 3 12.5 % 5 3.1 % 10 0.1 % \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A project with 5 equally critical paths has a 3 \% chance of meeting its PERT date.}\ } \]

The practical remedies.

  1. Monte Carlo simulation — the correct answer, and standard in project software.
  2. Add an explicit buffer — Goldratt's critical chain method removes safety from individual activities and pools it into a single project buffer, sized at roughly \(\frac12\sqrt{\sum\sigma^2}\) across all paths.
  3. Count near-critical paths as a risk indicator. Report "this project has 4 paths within 2 weeks of critical" alongside the PERT date.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Never quote a PERT probability without checking how many paths are near-critical.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 4 — Setting a defensible deadline
docs.text:
Using the §4 example (\(T_e = 18\), \(\sigma = 1.944\)), a client demands a fixed delivery date with a penalty of ₹5 lakh per week late. Internal cost of finishing early is ₹1 lakh per week of idle resources. What date should be promised?

Solution.

The trade-off. Promising date \(D\):

\[ E[\text{cost}] = 5\,E[\max(T-D,\ 0)] + 1\cdot E[\max(D-T,\ 0)] \]

This is the newsvendor structure (which reappears in inventory theory, L32). The optimal \(D\) satisfies

\[ \Pr[T \le D] = \frac{c_u}{c_u+c_o} \]

where \(c_u = 5\) (underage: penalty per week late) and \(c_o = 1\) (overage: idle cost per week early).

\[ \boxed{\ \Pr[T\le D^{*}] = \frac{5}{5+1} = \frac56 = 0.8333\ } \]

Find \(D^{*}\). From the normal table, \(\Phi(z) = 0.8333\) gives \(z = 0.967\).

\[ D^{*} = T_e + 0.967\sigma = 18 + 0.967(1.944) = 18 + 1.880 = \mathbf{19.88 \approx 20\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Promise 20 weeks.}\ } \]

Verify the economics at \(D = 20\).

\[ \Pr[\text{late}] = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{20-18}{1.944}\right) = 1 - \Phi(1.029) = 1-0.848 = \mathbf{15.2\%} \]

Expected weeks late (for a normal, \(E[\max(T-D,0)] = \sigma\left[\phi(z) - z(1-\Phi(z))\right]\)):

\[ \phi(1.029) = 0.2349, \qquad E[\text{late}] = 1.944\left[0.2349 - 1.029(0.152)\right] \] \[ = 1.944(0.2349 - 0.1564) = 1.944(0.0785) = \mathbf{0.153\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \text{Expected penalty} = 5\times0.153 = ₹0.76\ \text{lakh} \]

Compare with alternative promises.

Promise \(D\) \(\Pr[\text{late}]\) \(E[\text{penalty}]\) \(E[\text{idle cost}]\) Total 18 50.0 % ₹3.88 L ₹0.78 L ₹4.65 L 19 30.3 % ₹1.88 L ₹1.38 L ₹3.26 L 20 15.2 % ₹0.77 L ₹2.15 L ₹2.92 L ← 21 6.1 % ₹0.26 L ₹3.05 L ₹3.31 L 22 2.0 % ₹0.07 L ₹4.01 L ₹4.08 L \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{20 weeks minimises expected total cost at ₹2.92 lakh.}\ } \]

Advice to the negotiator.

"Promise 20 weeks. Our expected duration is 18, so this gives a 2-week buffer and an 85 % chance of delivering on time. The expected penalty exposure is ₹0.77 lakh. Promising 18 weeks would look attractive but carries a 50 % chance of penalty and an expected cost 63 % higher."

A crucial caveat. This uses PERT's \(\sigma = 1.944\), which ignores merge bias (§5.1). If the project has near-critical paths, the true \(\sigma\) is larger and the true \(T_e\) higher.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Recommend running a Monte Carlo simulation before signing a penalty clause.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 5 — A complete PERT study with risk management
docs.text:
A pharmaceutical firm is planning a clinical trial. Analyse and produce a risk-management plan.

Activity Description \(a\) \(m\) \(b\) Predecessors A Protocol design 4 6 14 — B Ethics approval 8 12 28 A C Site selection 3 5 7 A D Patient recruitment 12 20 40 B, C E Treatment phase 24 26 34 D F Data analysis 4 6 8 E G Report writing 3 4 11 F

Solution.

Step 1 — expected times and variances.

Act \(a\) \(m\) \(b\) \(t_e\) \(\sigma^2\) \(\sigma\) A 4 6 14 \(\dfrac{4+24+14}{6} = \mathbf{7}\) \(\left(\dfrac{10}{6}\right)^2 = 2.778\) 1.667 B 8 12 28 \(\dfrac{8+48+28}{6} = \mathbf{14}\) \(\left(\dfrac{20}{6}\right)^2 = 11.111\) 3.333 C 3 5 7 \(\dfrac{3+20+7}{6} = \mathbf{5}\) \(\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right)^2 = 0.444\) 0.667 D 12 20 40 \(\dfrac{12+80+40}{6} = \mathbf{22}\) \(\left(\dfrac{28}{6}\right)^2 = 21.778\) 4.667 E 24 26 34 \(\dfrac{24+104+34}{6} = \mathbf{27}\) \(\left(\dfrac{10}{6}\right)^2 = 2.778\) 1.667 F 4 6 8 \(\dfrac{4+24+8}{6} = \mathbf{6}\) \(\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right)^2 = 0.444\) 0.667 G 3 4 11 \(\dfrac{3+16+11}{6} = \mathbf{5}\) \(\left(\dfrac{8}{6}\right)^2 = 1.778\) 1.333

Step 2 — CPM on expected times.

\[ \text{ES}_A = 0,\ \text{EF}_A = 7 \] \[ \text{ES}_B = 7,\ \text{EF}_B = 21; \qquad \text{ES}_C = 7,\ \text{EF}_C = 12 \] \[ \text{ES}_D = \max(21, 12) = \mathbf{21},\ \text{EF}_D = 43 \] \[ \text{ES}_E = 43,\ \text{EF}_E = 70; \qquad \text{ES}_F = 70,\ \text{EF}_F = 76 \] \[ \text{ES}_G = 76,\ \text{EF}_G = \mathbf{81} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Critical path: } A\to B\to D\to E\to F\to G, \quad T_e = 81\ \text{weeks}\ } \]

(C has float: \(\text{LF}_C = 21\), \(\text{LS}_C = 16\), so \(\text{TF}_C = 16-7 = \mathbf{9}\) weeks.)

Step 3 — project variance.

\[ \sigma^2 = 2.778 + 11.111 + 21.778 + 2.778 + 0.444 + 1.778 = \mathbf{40.667} \] \[ \sigma = \sqrt{40.667} = \mathbf{6.377\ \text{weeks}} \]

Step 4 — the risk decomposition — the key analytical output.

Activity \(\sigma^2\) % of total risk \(t_e\) % of duration A 2.778 6.8 % 7 8.6 % B 11.111 27.3 % 14 17.3 % D 21.778 53.6 % 22 27.2 % E 2.778 6.8 % 27 33.3 % F 0.444 1.1 % 6 7.4 % G 1.778 4.4 % 5 6.2 % \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{D (recruitment) and B (ethics) contribute 81 \% of the risk but only 44 \% of the duration.}\ } \]

Note that E (treatment) is the longest activity at 27 weeks but contributes only 6.8 % of risk — because its duration is protocol-fixed and predictable.

Step 5 — completion probabilities.

Target \(z\) \(\Pr\) 81 weeks 0.00 50.0 % 85 weeks 0.627 73.5 % 90 weeks 1.412 92.1 % 91.5 weeks 1.645 95.0 % 96 weeks 2.353 99.1 %

Step 6 — the risk-management plan.

Priority 1 — patient recruitment (D): 53.6 % of all risk.

  • Range \([12, 40]\) weeks — the pessimistic case is more than three times the optimistic.
  • Actions: open more sites than strictly needed; pre-screen patient databases before D begins; build recruitment incentives into site contracts; establish weekly enrolment tracking with a trigger to add sites if behind plan.
  • Target: narrow the range to \([15, 30]\), reducing \(\sigma^2\) from 21.778 to \(\left(\frac{15}{6}\right)^2 = 6.25\).

Priority 2 — ethics approval (B): 27.3 % of risk.

  • Range \([8, 28]\) weeks; delays are usually caused by protocol queries.
  • Actions: pre-submission consultation with the ethics committee; engage an experienced regulatory writer for the protocol (activity A); prepare responses to common queries in advance.
  • Target: narrow to \([10, 20]\), reducing \(\sigma^2\) from 11.111 to \(\left(\frac{10}{6}\right)^2 = 2.778\).

Impact of both improvements.

\[ \sigma^2_{\text{new}} = 2.778 + 2.778 + 6.25 + 2.778 + 0.444 + 1.778 = \mathbf{16.806} \] \[ \sigma_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{4.100\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \text{95 \% date: } 81 + 1.645(4.100) = 81 + 6.75 = \mathbf{87.7\ \text{weeks}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Risk mitigation cuts the 95 \% date from 91.5 to 87.7 weeks — a 3.8-week saving with NO reduction in expected duration.}\ } \]

Priority 3 — exploit C's float. Site selection has 9 weeks of float. Start it early and in parallel with ethics approval, so that recruitment (D) can begin the moment ethics clears.

Step 7 — the recommendation to the board.

"Expected completion is 81 weeks, but we recommend committing externally to 92 weeks (95 % confidence). Patient recruitment and ethics approval carry 81 % of the schedule risk despite being under half the duration. With the mitigation plan above, the 95 % date falls to 88 weeks. We also recommend a Monte Carlo simulation before any regulatory filing commitment, since PERT systematically understates duration when parallel paths exist."

docs.title: 20.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Compute \(t_e\) and \(\sigma\) for \((a,m,b) = (3, 7, 11)\). [Ans: \(t_e=7\), \(\sigma=1.333\)]
  2. A critical path has variances 1, 4, 2, 2. Find \(\sigma_{\text{project}}\). [Ans: 3]
  3. \(T_e = 40\), \(\sigma = 4\). Find \(\Pr[T\le45]\). [Ans: \(z=1.25\), 89.4 %]
  4. \(T_e = 30\), \(\sigma = 5\). What date gives 90 % confidence? [Ans: 36.4]
  5. Why do variances add but standard deviations not?
  6. Explain the merge-event bias in three sentences.
  7. A project has 4 near-critical paths. What is the approximate probability of meeting \(T_e\)? [Ans: \(\approx 0.5^4 = 6\%\)]

docs.title: 20.9 Summary
docs.text:
• PERT replaces CPM's single duration with three estimates \(a, m, b\), assuming a Beta distribution: \(t_e = \frac{a+4m+b}{6}\) and \(\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{b-a}{6}\right)^2\). Note \(\sigma\) depends only on the range, not the skew.
  • Run CPM on the \(t_e\) values; the project variance is the sum of the CRITICAL activities' variances — variances add, standard deviations do not.
  • By the Central Limit Theorem, \(T\sim N(T_e, \sigma^2)\), so \(\Pr[T\le D] = \Phi\!\left(\frac{D-T_e}{\sigma}\right)\) and the \(p\)-confidence date is \(T_e + z_p\sigma\).
  • A project promised at its expected duration has only a 50 % chance of success — the most important and most ignored fact in project management.
  • Risk decomposition is PERT's most valuable output: identify which activities contribute most variance, not most duration, and target mitigation there. Reducing uncertainty saves buffer without shortening any activity.
  • Merge-event bias: PERT counts only the critical path's variance, so it is optimistically biased whenever parallel near-critical paths exist. With \(k\) equally critical paths, \(\Pr[\text{on time}]\approx0.5^{k}\).
  • The remedy is Monte Carlo simulation; PERT's enduring value is forcing an explicit conversation about uncertainty.

Unit II is now complete. You can solve games, sequence jobs, formulate and solve integer programmes, and schedule projects deterministically and probabilistically.

Next lesson: L21 — Characteristics of queuing systems (Unit III begins).

Practise now: unit2-games-networks-lab.html → CPM/PERT Lab: switch to PERT mode, enter three estimates per activity, and see the probability curve, risk decomposition and Monte Carlo comparison.

docs.title: Lesson 45: Quadratic Programming and Course Capstone
45.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the standard form of a quadratic programme and recognise where QPs arise.
  2. Write the KKT system of a QP and see that it is linear except for complementary slackness.
  3. Apply Wolfe's method — modified simplex with a restricted-entry rule.
  4. Outline Beale's method and say when it is preferred.
  5. Assemble the whole course into one decision framework.

docs.title: 45.2 The Quadratic Programme
docs.text:
Standard form. $\(\begin{aligned} \text{maximise}\quad & f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{x}+\tfrac12\mathbf{x}^{T}Q\mathbf{x}\\ \text{subject to}\quad & A\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b},\qquad \mathbf{x}\ge\mathbf{0} \end{aligned}\)$ with \(Q\) symmetric. The objective is quadratic; all constraints are linear.

If \(Q\) is negative semi-definite the maximisation is concave (equivalently, minimising a convex function), the feasible region is a polyhedron, and by Lesson 44 any KKT point is the global optimum. Indefinite \(Q\) makes the problem NP-hard, so this lesson assumes the definite case.

docs.title: Why QP matters
docs.text:
Application Quadratic term Portfolio selection (Markowitz, Nobel 1990) risk \(=\mathbf{x}^{T}\Sigma\mathbf{x}\) Least squares with constraints \(\lVert A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}\rVert^{2}\) Support vector machines the margin objective Model-predictive control tracking error plus control effort Production with price effects revenue \(=p(x)x\)

QP is also the inner problem of sequential quadratic programming (SQP), the leading general non-linear method: at each iteration a general NLP is approximated by a QP and solved.

docs.title: 45.3 The KKT System of a QP
docs.text:
Apply Lesson 44 to the standard form (with \(\mathbf{y}\) for the \(A\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}\) multipliers and \(\mathbf{s}\) for \(\mathbf{x}\ge0\)):

\[\mathbf{c}+Q\mathbf{x}-A^{T}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{0} \tag{2.1a}\] \[A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b} \tag{2.1b}\] \[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{s},\mathbf{v}\ge\mathbf{0} \tag{2.1c}\] \[\boxed{\ s_jx_j=0\ \text{ and }\ y_iv_i=0\ \text{ for all }i,j\ }\tag{2.1d}\]

The crucial observation. Equations (2.1a)–(2.1c) are linear. Only the complementary slackness conditions (2.1d) are non-linear — and even they are combinatorial rather than truly non-linear: each says "at most one of this pair is positive."

This is why a QP can be solved by a modified simplex method: run the simplex algorithm on the linear system, and simply forbid any pivot that would make a complementary pair both positive.

docs.title: 45.4 Wolfe's Method
docs.text:
Algorithm (Wolfe, 1959).

  1. Write the problem in standard form; check \(Q\) is negative semi-definite (for a maximisation).
  2. Form the KKT system (2.1a)–(2.1c), adding slacks \(\mathbf{v}\) and surpluses \(\mathbf{s}\).
  3. Add artificial variables to (2.1a) and set up a Phase I problem: minimise the sum of the artificials.
  4. Run the simplex method with one extra rule — the restricted-entry rule: $\(\textbf{never let } x_j \textbf{ and } s_j \textbf{ (or } y_i \textbf{ and } v_i) \textbf{ be basic at the same time.}\)$
  5. When all artificials reach zero, the current basic solution satisfies every KKT condition and is therefore optimal.

Properties. Finite termination when \(Q\) is definite; each iteration costs the same as an ordinary simplex pivot; and the method is genuinely simple to implement given a simplex code. Its drawback is that Phase I roughly doubles the tableau.

docs.title: 45.5 Beale's Method
docs.text:
Beale's method works directly on the objective rather than on the KKT system.

Outline. 1. Split the variables into basic and non-basic using the constraints. 2. Express the objective in terms of the non-basic variables only by substitution. 3. Compute \(\partial f/\partial(\text{non-basic})\) at the current point. If all partials indicate no improvement, stop. 4. Otherwise choose an entering variable and increase it until either a basic variable hits zero (an ordinary simplex ratio test) or the relevant partial derivative reaches zero (an unconstrained minimum along that edge) — whichever happens first. 5. In the second case introduce a free variable to record the interior point reached; repeat.

Wolfe Beale Works on the KKT system the objective directly Extra variables artificials (Phase I) free variables Tableau size roughly doubles grows slowly Interior optima reached via KKT reached naturally by step 4 Best when constraints dominate the optimum is interior or near it

Both are exact for definite \(Q\); the choice is a matter of convenience.

docs.title: Problem 1 — A QP with one active constraint
docs.text:
\[\text{maximise } f=4x_1+6x_2-2x_1^{2}-2x_1x_2-2x_2^{2} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_1+2x_2\le2,\ x_1,x_2\ge0.\]

Solution.

Step 0 — check concavity.

\[Q=\nabla^{2}f=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_1=-4<0,\quad \det=16-4=12>0\]

Signs alternate from negative \(\Rightarrow\) negative definite \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\) is strictly concave, so any KKT point is the global maximum.

Step 1 — try the unconstrained optimum.

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}=4-4x_1-2x_2=0,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}=6-2x_1-4x_2=0\]

Solving: \(x_1=\tfrac13\), \(x_2=\tfrac43\). Then \(x_1+2x_2=\tfrac13+\tfrac83=3>2\): infeasible.

Step 2 — assume the constraint active. With multiplier \(u\) on \(x_1+2x_2-2\le0\):

\[4-4x_1-2x_2-u=0 \tag{i}\] \[6-2x_1-4x_2-2u=0 \tag{ii}\] \[x_1+2x_2=2 \tag{iii}\]

From (iii), \(x_1=2-2x_2\). Substituting into (i): \(4-4(2-2x_2)-2x_2-u=0\), i.e. \(-4+6x_2-u=0\), so \(u=6x_2-4\). Substituting into (ii): \(6-2(2-2x_2)-4x_2-2u=0\), i.e. \(2-2u=0\), giving

\[u=1\ \Rightarrow\ 6x_2-4=1\ \Rightarrow\ x_2=\frac56,\qquad x_1=2-\frac53=\frac13\] \[\boxed{x_1^{*}=\tfrac13,\quad x_2^{*}=\tfrac56,\quad u=1,\quad f^{*}=\tfrac{25}{6}=4.1\overline{6}}\]

Step 3 — verify all KKT conditions.

Condition Check Stationarity (i) \(4-\tfrac43-\tfrac53-1=4-3-1=0\) ✓ Stationarity (ii) \(6-\tfrac23-\tfrac{10}{3}-2=6-4-2=0\) ✓ Primal feasibility \(\tfrac13+\tfrac53=2\le2\) ✓; \(x_1,x_2>0\) ✓ Dual feasibility \(u=1\ge0\) ✓ Complementary slackness \(u(x_1+2x_2-2)=1(0)=0\) ✓; \(x_1,x_2>0\) so their multipliers are \(0\) ✓

Objective check.

\[f=4\left(\tfrac13\right)+6\left(\tfrac56\right)-2\left(\tfrac19\right)-2\left(\tfrac13\right)\left(\tfrac56\right)-2\left(\tfrac{25}{36}\right) =\tfrac43+5-\tfrac29-\tfrac59-\tfrac{25}{18}=\tfrac{25}{6}\ \checkmark\]

Interpretation. The unconstrained maximum was \(f=\tfrac{14}{3}=4.667\) at \((\tfrac13,\tfrac43)\), so the constraint costs \(4.667-4.167=0.500\). The multiplier \(u=1\) predicts that relaxing the constraint to \(x_1+2x_2\le3\) would gain about \(1\). But \(3\) is exactly where the unconstrained optimum becomes feasible (\(\tfrac13+\tfrac83=3\)), so beyond that the constraint stops binding and the true gain is only \(0.500\). Once again the shadow price is a tangent and over-predicts across a change of active set (compare Lesson 44, Problem 1).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Wolfe's method, set up in full
docs.text:
Set up Problem 1 for Wolfe's method and state the tableau.

Solution.

The KKT system. With slack \(v\) on the constraint and surpluses \(s_1,s_2\) on \(x_1,x_2\ge0\):

\[4-4x_1-2x_2-u+s_1=0\ \Longrightarrow\ 4x_1+2x_2+u-s_1=4\] \[6-2x_1-4x_2-2u+s_2=0\ \Longrightarrow\ 2x_1+4x_2+2u-s_2=6\] \[x_1+2x_2+v=2\]

Phase I. Add artificials \(A_1,A_2\) to the first two rows and minimise \(A_1+A_2\):

Basis \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(u\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) \(v\) \(A_1\) \(A_2\) RHS \(A_1\) 4 2 1 \(-1\) 0 0 1 0 4 \(A_2\) 2 4 2 0 \(-1\) 0 0 1 6 \(v\) 1 2 0 0 0 1 0 0 2 \(-w\) 6 6 3 \(-1\) \(-1\) 0 0 0 10

The restricted-entry rule. At every pivot, \(x_1\) may not enter while \(s_1\) is basic, \(x_2\) may not enter while \(s_2\) is basic, and \(u\) may not enter while \(v\) is basic (and vice versa in each pair). Subject to that restriction, pivot as usual.

The outcome. Phase I terminates with \(A_1=A_2=0\) and the basis \(\{x_1,\ x_2,\ u\}\) — note that \(s_1,s_2,v\) are all non-basic, so every complementary pair is respected. Reading the values gives \(x_1=\tfrac13\), \(x_2=\tfrac56\), \(u=1\), matching Problem 1.

Interpretation. Wolfe's method is ordinary simplex plus one prohibition. No new machinery is needed — which is precisely its appeal, and why quadratic programming was practicable long before modern interior-point codes. The prohibition is what enforces the only non-linear part of the KKT system.

Note also what the method does not need: no line search, no gradient iteration, no convergence tolerance. Like the simplex method, it terminates exactly in finitely many pivots.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Portfolio selection
docs.text:
An investor allocates fractions \(x_1,x_2\) of a portfolio to two assets with expected returns \(12\,\%\) and \(8\,\%\), variances \(0.04\) and \(0.01\), and covariance \(0.005\). Minimise risk subject to a required return of at least \(10\,\%\) and \(x_1+x_2=1\), \(x_i\ge0\).

Solution.

Formulate.

\[\text{minimise } \sigma^{2}=0.04x_1^{2}+0.01x_2^{2}+2(0.005)x_1x_2\] \[\text{s.t. } 0.12x_1+0.08x_2\ge0.10,\qquad x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_i\ge0\]

Simplify. Substituting \(x_2=1-x_1\) into the return constraint:

\[0.12x_1+0.08-0.08x_1\ge0.10\ \Rightarrow\ 0.04x_1\ge0.02\ \Rightarrow\ x_1\ge0.5\]

The risk becomes a function of \(x_1\) alone:

\[\sigma^{2}(x_1)=0.04x_1^{2}+0.01(1-x_1)^{2}+0.01x_1(1-x_1) =0.04x_1^{2}+0.01-0.02x_1+0.01x_1^{2}+0.01x_1-0.01x_1^{2}\] \[=0.04x_1^{2}-0.01x_1+0.01\]

Unconstrained minimum. \(\dfrac{d\sigma^{2}}{dx_1}=0.08x_1-0.01=0\) gives \(x_1=0.125\), which violates \(x_1\ge0.5\). Since \(\sigma^{2}\) is convex and increasing for \(x_1>0.125\), the constrained minimum is at the boundary:

\[\boxed{x_1^{*}=0.5,\quad x_2^{*}=0.5,\quad \sigma^{2}=0.04(0.25)-0.005+0.01=0.015}\] \[\sigma=\sqrt{0.015}=12.25\,\%,\qquad \text{return}=0.5(12)+0.5(8)=10\,\%\]

Interpretation.

  • The minimum-variance portfolio would hold only \(12.5\,\%\) of the risky asset, with \(\sigma^{2}=0.01-0.000625=0.009375\), i.e. \(\sigma=9.68\,\%\) — but it returns only \(0.125(12)+0.875(8)=8.5\,\%\).
  • Demanding \(10\,\%\) instead of \(8.5\,\%\) raises risk from \(9.68\,\%\) to \(12.25\,\%\). That is the efficient frontier: every extra unit of return is bought with risk, and the QP traces the trade-off exactly.
  • Markowitz's insight, and the reason this is a QP rather than an LP, is that risk is quadratic because assets covary. Note that the two-asset portfolio at \((0.5,0.5)\) has variance \(0.015\), less than the \(0.025\) average of the individual variances — diversification is precisely the cross-term \(2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2x_1x_2\) doing its work.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Recognising the right method
docs.text:
Classify each problem and name the method from this course.

Problem Class Method Lesson Maximise \(3x_1+5x_2\) s.t. linear constraints LP Simplex 5 As above, \(x_j\) integer ILP Gomory / branch and bound 16, 18 Ship from 3 plants to 4 depots at least cost Transportation VAM + MODI 8, 9 Assign 5 workers to 5 jobs Assignment Hungarian 10 Two firms choose prices simultaneously Game Saddle point / LP 11, 13 Schedule 6 jobs on 2 machines Sequencing Johnson's rule 14 Project of 20 activities, uncertain durations Network PERT 20 Staff a call centre Queueing \(M/M/c\) + cost model 27, 29 Order quantity with price breaks Inventory Discount algorithm 35 Minimise \(x^{2}+54/x\) on \([1,5]\), no derivatives 1-D NLP Golden section 40 Fit 50 parameters, gradients available Unconstrained NLP Conjugate gradient / BFGS 42 Minimise cost s.t. a fixed volume Equality-constrained Lagrange multipliers 43 Minimise risk s.t. return \(\ge r\) and \(\sum x_i=1\) QP Wolfe / Beale 45

The three questions that select a method.

  1. Is the objective linear? If yes and the constraints are linear, use LP (and check whether integrality is required). If no, go to 2.
  2. Are there constraints? If none, use Lessons 38–42. If they are equalities only, use Lagrange (L43). If inequalities, use KKT (L44).
  3. Is the objective quadratic and the constraints linear? Then it is a QP and Wolfe's method applies directly (L45).

docs.title: Problem 5 — The capstone: one framework for the whole course
docs.text:
State the common structure of every model in DSC301.

Solution. Every technique in this course is an instance of

\[\text{optimise } f(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf{x}\in S,\]

and differs only in the form of \(f\) and \(S\), which in turn dictates the algorithm.

Unit \(f\) \(S\) Structural insight I — LP linear polyhedron Optimum at a vertex; duality gives shadow prices II — IP, games, networks linear + integrality / combinatorial discrete Relax, then branch or cut to restore integrality III — queues, inventory convex non-linear usually a box Balance a falling cost against a rising one IV — NLP general defined by \(g,h\) Convexity decides whether local means global

Five ideas that recur in every unit.

  1. Trade-offs are the subject. Ordering against holding (L31), waiting against service (L29), utilisation against responsiveness (L24), risk against return (§5 Problem 3). Optimisation is the arithmetic of a trade-off, never the elimination of one.
  2. Shadow prices are the most useful output. LP duals (L7), MODI's \(u_i+v_j\) (L9), queueing marginal analysis (L29), Lagrange \(\lambda\) (L43), KKT \(\mu\) (L44) are the same object: the rate of change of the optimum with a constraint. Managers act on shadow prices more often than on the optimal solution itself.
  3. Convexity is the dividing line. It converts local into global, guarantees that the simplex method and KKT terminate at the answer, and is what makes EOQ and \(M/M/c\) formulas trustworthy.
  4. Systems behave badly near their limits. Queues explode as \(\rho\to1\) (L24); batch sizes explode as \(P\to D\) (L33); steepest descent crawls as \(\kappa\to\infty\) (L42). Never design a system to run at its capacity.
  5. Optima are flat, so answers are robust. The EOQ costs \(2\,\%\) extra for a \(20\,\%\) error (L31); the staffing optimum was within \(1\,\%\) over two values of \(c\) (L29). This is what makes these models usable with imperfect data — and it means that a model's value lies in the structure it reveals, not in the last decimal of its answer.

A final caution. Every result in this course is conditional on a model, and every model is wrong in some respect: demand is not really constant, service times are not really exponential, and costs are not really known. The professional skill is not solving the model — a computer does that — but choosing the model, stating its assumptions, and knowing which of its conclusions survive when the assumptions do not. That judgement is what the forty-five hours have been for.

docs.title: 45.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Maximise \(f=2x_1+3x_2-x_1^{2}-x_2^{2}\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2\le1\), \(x_i\ge0\). (Answer: unconstrained \((1,1.5)\) infeasible; constraint active gives \(u=1.5\), \(\mathbf{x}^{*}=(0.25,\ 0.75)\), \(f^{*}=2.125\))
  2. Show that \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix}\) is negative definite, and state what would change if \(Q\) were indefinite.
  3. Write the KKT system for \(\min\ x_1^{2}+x_2^{2}\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2\ge2\), \(x_i\ge0\), and solve it. (Answer: \(\mathbf{x}^{*}=(1,1)\), \(\mu=2\), \(f^{*}=2\))
  4. In Problem 3 of §5, recompute the optimal portfolio for a required return of \(11\,\%\). (Answer: \(x_1\ge0.75\) binds; \(\mathbf{x}^{*}=(0.75,\ 0.25)\), \(\sigma^{2}=0.025\), \(\sigma=15.81\,\%\))
  5. Name the method you would use for: (a) blending fuel at least cost; (b) choosing which of \(20\) projects to fund with a fixed budget; (c) deciding how many ambulances to station. (Answers: LP; \(0\)–\(1\) integer programming via branch and bound; \(M/M/c\) with a cost model)

docs.title: 45.8 Summary
docs.text:
• A quadratic programme has a quadratic objective and linear constraints. Negative semi-definite \(Q\) (for a maximisation) makes it convex, so any KKT point is global.
  • Its KKT system is linear except for complementary slackness, which is combinatorial rather than genuinely non-linear.
  • Wolfe's method = simplex on the KKT system, with artificials for Phase I and the restricted-entry rule forbidding a complementary pair from being basic together. It terminates exactly, in finitely many pivots.
  • Beale's method works on the objective directly using free variables, and handles interior optima more naturally.
  • QP is the model behind portfolio selection, constrained least squares, SVMs and MPC, and is the inner problem of SQP, the leading general NLP method.
  • The course in one sentence: optimisation is the arithmetic of trade-offs; shadow prices are its most useful output; convexity decides whether a local answer is a global one; systems misbehave near capacity; and optima are flat enough that the structure a model reveals matters more than its last decimal.

Course complete. The forty-five hours have run from formulating a linear programme to certifying a constrained non-linear optimum. Every technique met here is implemented in standard software; what this course provides is the ability to choose the model, defend the assumptions and interpret the multiplier — the parts no solver performs.

Practise now: unit4-nlp-search-lab.html → QP Solver: enter \(Q\), \(\mathbf{c}\) and the constraints, watch Wolfe's restricted-entry pivots, and see the optimum on a contour plot with the active constraints highlighted.

docs.title: Lesson 35: Quantity Discounts and Consolidation of Unit III
35.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain why a price break makes the total-cost curve discontinuous and the EOQ inapplicable.
  2. Apply the all-units discount algorithm correctly, including the feasibility test.
  3. Handle the case \(C_h=iC\), where the holding cost itself changes with the price.
  4. Solve a constrained multi-item inventory problem by Lagrange multipliers.
  5. Consolidate the whole of Unit III — queuing and inventory — into a single decision framework.

docs.title: 35.2 Why Discounts Break the EOQ
docs.text:
In Lessons 31–34 the unit price \(C\) was constant, so the purchase cost \(DC\) was a constant and could be dropped. With a quantity discount, \(C\) depends on \(Q\), so the purchase term must be kept:

\[TC(Q)=DC(Q)+\frac{C_oD}{Q}+\frac{C_hQ}{2}. \tag{1.1}\]

Two structural consequences:

  1. \(TC\) is discontinuous. At each price break it drops vertically, because the whole order suddenly becomes cheaper. Calculus cannot find the minimum of a discontinuous function.
  2. \(C_h\) usually changes too. With \(C_h=iC\), a lower price means a lower holding cost, so the EOQ for each price band is different: \(Q^{*}_{j}=\sqrt{2C_oD/(iC_j)}\).
  TC
    |\                             all-units discount
    | \    \                       (3 price bands)
    |  \    \       \
    |   \____\__     \____
    |         \  \___     \______
    |__________|________|__________ Q
              q1       q2

Each curve is valid only on its own interval; the answer is the lowest point of the visible envelope.

docs.title: 35.3 The All-Units Discount Algorithm
docs.text:
All-units discount. If \(Q\ge q_j\), then every unit costs \(C_j\). (Contrast the incremental discount, where only the units beyond \(q_j\) are cheaper — a different and less common scheme.)

The algorithm.

  1. Start with the cheapest price (the largest \(q_j\)) and work upwards in price.
  2. For price band \(j\), compute \(Q^{*}_{j}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{iC_j}}\).
  3. Feasibility test: is \(Q^{*}_{j}\ge q_j\) (within the band)?
    • Yes → this is a feasible EOQ. Compute \(TC\) at \(Q^{*}_{j}\). Stop testing cheaper bands; no lower price is attainable, so evaluate only this band and the bands above it at their break points.
    • No → the unconstrained optimum lies below the band's lower limit. Since \(TC\) is decreasing on the left of the EOQ, the best point within the band is its lower boundary \(q_j\). Evaluate \(TC(q_j)\).
