Let \(T\) be the time until the next arrival. Then

\[ \Pr[T > t] = \Pr[\text{no arrivals in } (0,t]] = P_0(t) = e^{-\lambda t} \]

So the cumulative distribution function is

\[ \boxed{\ F(t) = \Pr[T\le t] = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad t \ge 0\ } \]

and differentiating gives the density

\[ \boxed{\ f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad t\ge0\ } \]

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
\[ E[T] = \frac{1}{\lambda}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[T] = \frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}, \qquad \sigma_T = \frac{1}{\lambda} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{MEAN} = \textbf{STANDARD DEVIATION} \ \text{— so the coefficient of variation is exactly 1.}\ } \]

This is a high-variability distribution. A "10-minute average" service time that is exponential has a standard deviation of 10 minutes: some customers take 30 seconds, others 40 minutes.

The median is \(\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 0.693/\lambda\) — well below the mean, so the distribution is strongly right-skewed. Most service times are shorter than average; a few are far longer.

docs.title: 22.5 The Memoryless Property
docs.text:
Theorem. The exponential is the only continuous distribution with

\[ \boxed{\ \Pr[T > s+t \mid T > s] \ =\ \Pr[T > t] \qquad \text{for all } s,t \ge 0\ } \]

Proof.

\[ \Pr[T>s+t \mid T>s] = \frac{\Pr[T>s+t \ \cap\ T>s]}{\Pr[T>s]} = \frac{\Pr[T>s+t]}{\Pr[T>s]} = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = \Pr[T>t] \]

\(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: What it means
docs.text:
The process has no memory of elapsed time. If a customer has already been in service for 10 minutes, the distribution of the remaining service time is exactly the same as at the start.

Concretely:

  • "This bulb has burned 1000 hours" tells you nothing about its remaining life.
  • "The last bus left 20 minutes ago" tells you nothing about when the next will come.
  • "The machine has run 5 hours since the last breakdown" gives no information about the next one.

docs.title: Why it is both essential and questionable
docs.text:
Why it is essential. Memorylessness is what makes queuing models Markovian — the future depends only on the current number in the system, not on how long anyone has been waiting. Without it, we would need to track every customer's elapsed time, and the state space would be infinite and continuous.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Memorylessness is what makes the mathematics tractable.}\ } \]

Why it is questionable. Real service times often are not memoryless:

  • A haircut takes 20 ± 3 minutes — nearly deterministic.
  • A machine that has run 5 hours is more likely to fail soon (wear-out).
  • A customer already served 10 minutes is often nearly finished.

When the exponential assumption is reasonable.

Reasonable Questionable Arrivals from a large independent population Scheduled arrivals (appointments) Telephone call arrivals Batch arrivals (a tour bus) Radioactive decay, equipment failures in the useful-life phase Wear-out failures Highly variable service (hospital A&E, IT helpdesk) Standardised service (car wash, assembly) \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The exponential assumption is usually far better for ARRIVALS than for SERVICE times.}\ } \]

docs.title: The practical consequence of getting it wrong
docs.text:
For \(M/G/1\) (general service), the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula gives

\[ L_q = \frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma_s^{2} + \rho^{2}}{2(1-\rho)} \]

where \(\sigma_s^2\) is the variance of service time. Compare:

Service distribution \(\sigma_s^2\) \(L_q\) at \(\rho = 0.8\), \(\mu = 1\) Deterministic (D) 0 \(\dfrac{0+0.64}{0.4} = \mathbf{1.60}\) Exponential (M) \(1/\mu^2 = 1\) \(\dfrac{0.64+0.64}{0.4} = \mathbf{3.20}\) High variability \(4/\mu^2\) \(\dfrac{2.56+0.64}{0.4} = \mathbf{8.00}\) \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Exponential service gives EXACTLY TWICE the queue of deterministic service.}\ } \]

So \(M/M/1\) results are a conservative (pessimistic) estimate when real service is more regular — which is usually the case. This is a useful thing to tell a client.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Poisson probability calculations
docs.text:
Customers arrive at a bank at a Poisson rate of 12 per hour. Find the probability that in a 15-minute period there are (a) exactly 2 arrivals, (b) no arrivals, (c) at least 3 arrivals, (d) at most 1 arrival.

Solution.

Set up. \(\lambda = 12\)/hour and \(t = 15\) minutes \(= 0.25\) hours, so

\[ \lambda t = 12\times0.25 = \mathbf{3} \]

(a) Exactly 2.

\[ P_2 = \frac{3^{2}e^{-3}}{2!} = \frac{9(0.049787)}{2} = \frac{0.448084}{2} = \mathbf{0.2240} \]

(b) No arrivals.

\[ P_0 = \frac{3^{0}e^{-3}}{0!} = e^{-3} = \mathbf{0.0498} \]

(c) At least 3.

\[ \Pr[N\ge3] = 1 - P_0 - P_1 - P_2 \] \[ P_1 = \frac{3^{1}e^{-3}}{1!} = 3(0.049787) = 0.1494 \] \[ \Pr[N\ge3] = 1 - 0.0498 - 0.1494 - 0.2240 = \mathbf{0.5768} \]

(d) At most 1.

\[ \Pr[N\le1] = P_0 + P_1 = 0.0498 + 0.1494 = \mathbf{0.1992} \]

Summary table.

\(n\) \(P_n\) Cumulative 0 0.0498 0.0498 1 0.1494 0.1992 2 0.2240 0.4232 3 0.2240 0.6472 4 0.1680 0.8153 5 0.1008 0.9161

Two observations.

  1. \(P_2 = P_3 = 0.2240\). For a Poisson with integer mean \(\lambda t = 3\), the distribution has two modes, at \(n = \lambda t - 1\) and \(n = \lambda t\). (In general the mode is \(\lfloor \lambda t\rfloor\).)

  2. Check the mean and variance.

    \[ E[N] = \lambda t = 3, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[N] = 3, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt3 = 1.732 \]

    So arrivals in a 15-minute window are \(3 \pm 1.73\) — substantial relative variability. With probability 0.58 there are 3 or more; with probability 0.05 there are none at all.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A "12 per hour" bank is empty for 5 \% of its quarter-hours. Averages conceal a great deal.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — Exponential calculations and the memoryless property
docs.text:
Service times at a counter are exponential with mean 6 minutes. Find (a) \(\Pr[T \le 4]\); (b) \(\Pr[T > 10]\); (c) \(\Pr[T > 16 \mid T > 6]\); (d) the median service time.

Solution.

Set up. Mean \(= 1/\mu = 6\) minutes, so \(\mu = \tfrac16\) per minute.

(a) \(\Pr[T\le4]\).

\[ F(4) = 1 - e^{-4/6} = 1 - e^{-0.6667} = 1 - 0.5134 = \mathbf{0.4866} \]

(b) \(\Pr[T>10]\).

\[ 1 - F(10) = e^{-10/6} = e^{-1.6667} = \mathbf{0.1889} \]

(c) \(\Pr[T>16\mid T>6]\) — the memoryless test.

\[ \Pr[T>16\mid T>6] = \frac{\Pr[T>16]}{\Pr[T>6]} = \frac{e^{-16/6}}{e^{-6/6}} = \frac{e^{-2.6667}}{e^{-1}} = e^{-1.6667} = \mathbf{0.1889} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{IDENTICAL to (b).}\ } \]

The interpretation. A customer who has already been served for 6 minutes has exactly the same probability of needing 10 more minutes as a customer just beginning.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The 6 minutes already spent count for NOTHING. That is memorylessness.}\ } \]

(d) The median.

\[ 1 - e^{-m/6} = 0.5 \ \Longrightarrow\ e^{-m/6} = 0.5 \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{m}{6} = \ln2 \] \[ m = 6\ln2 = 6(0.6931) = \mathbf{4.16\ \text{minutes}} \]

The mean is 6 minutes but the median is only 4.16.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{More than HALF of all customers are served in under 4.2 minutes, yet the average is 6.}\ } \]

Why. The distribution is strongly right-skewed: a small number of very long services pull the mean up. Specifically,

\[ \Pr[T > 3\times\text{mean}] = \Pr[T>18] = e^{-3} = 0.0498 \]

One customer in twenty takes more than three times the average. Reporting only the mean badly misrepresents customer experience — a lesson that applies to any right-skewed service metric.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Testing whether data are Poisson
docs.text:
A shop records the number of customers arriving in each of 100 five-minute intervals:

Arrivals \(n\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 ≥6 Frequency 12 27 28 19 9 4 1

Test whether the arrivals are consistent with a Poisson process.

Solution.

Step 1 — estimate the mean.

\[ \bar n = \frac{0(12)+1(27)+2(28)+3(19)+4(9)+5(4)+6(1)}{100} \] \[ = \frac{0+27+56+57+36+20+6}{100} = \frac{202}{100} = \mathbf{2.02} \]

Step 2 — compute the sample variance.

\[ \overline{n^2} = \frac{0+27+112+171+144+100+36}{100} = \frac{590}{100} = 5.90 \] \[ s^2 = \overline{n^2} - \bar n^2 = 5.90 - (2.02)^2 = 5.90 - 4.0804 = \mathbf{1.82} \]

Step 3 — the mean/variance test.

\[ \frac{s^2}{\bar n} = \frac{1.82}{2.02} = \mathbf{0.90} \]

For a Poisson process this ratio should be close to 1 ✓ — 0.90 is well within sampling variation for \(n = 100\).

Step 4 — a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Expected frequencies with \(\lambda t = 2.02\):

\(n\) Observed \(O_i\) \(P_n\) Expected \(E_i = 100P_n\) \(\dfrac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}\) 0 12 0.1327 13.27 0.122 1 27 0.2680 26.80 0.001 2 28 0.2707 27.07 0.032 3 19 0.1823 18.23 0.033 4 9 0.0920 9.20 0.004 ≥5 5 0.0543 5.43 0.034 100 100.00 \(\chi^2 = 0.229\)

(Categories 5 and ≥6 are pooled so that every expected frequency exceeds 5, as the test requires.)

Step 5 — the decision.

Degrees of freedom \(= (\text{6 categories}) - 1 - (\text{1 estimated parameter}) = \mathbf{4}\).

Critical value at 5 %: \(\chi^2_{0.05,4} = 9.488\).

\[ 0.229 \ \ll\ 9.488 \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Do NOT reject. The data are entirely consistent with a Poisson process with } \lambda t = 2.02.\ } \]

Practical conclusion. With 5-minute intervals and \(\lambda t = 2.02\):

\[ \lambda = \frac{2.02}{5\ \text{min}} = 0.404\ \text{per minute} = \mathbf{24.2\ \text{per hour}} \]

The queuing models of L24–L28 may be applied with \(\lambda = 24.2\)/hour.

What a failure would have looked like.

  • If \(s^2/\bar n \approx 2\), the arrivals are overdispersed — likely clustered (groups arriving together) or a time-varying rate (busier at some times). Remedy: split the data by time period and fit separately, or use a compound Poisson model.
  • If \(s^2/\bar n \approx 0.3\), arrivals are too regular for Poisson — suggesting appointments or scheduling. Remedy: use a \(D/M/1\) or \(E_k/M/1\) model.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Always test the Poisson assumption before applying the formulas. It takes ten minutes and can save a wrong recommendation.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 4 — Superposition and thinning in practice
docs.text:
A call centre receives calls from three regions at Poisson rates 8, 12 and 5 per hour. (a) What is the combined process? (b) 30 % of calls require a specialist — what is the specialist arrival process? (c) If the specialist can handle 6 calls/hour, is one specialist enough?

Solution.

(a) Superposition. The sum of independent Poisson processes is Poisson with the summed rate:

\[ \lambda_{\text{total}} = 8 + 12 + 5 = \mathbf{25\ \text{calls/hour}}, \qquad \text{still Poisson} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Merging Poisson streams gives a Poisson stream — the rates simply add.}\ } \]

(b) Thinning. Each call independently requires a specialist with probability \(p = 0.3\):

\[ \lambda_{\text{specialist}} = 25\times0.3 = \mathbf{7.5\ \text{calls/hour}}, \qquad \text{still Poisson} \]

And the complementary stream (general calls) is Poisson at \(25\times0.7 = 17.5\)/hour — and, remarkably, the two thinned streams are independent of each other.

(c) Is one specialist enough?

\[ \rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} = \frac{7.5}{6} = \mathbf{1.25} \ >\ 1 \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{NO — the system is UNSTABLE. The specialist queue would grow without bound.}\ } \]

How many specialists are needed?

\[ \rho = \frac{7.5}{6c} < 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ c > 1.25 \ \Longrightarrow\ \boxed{c \ge 2} \]

With 2 specialists (\(M/M/2\), \(r = \lambda/\mu = 1.25\), \(\rho = 0.625\)):

\[ P_0 = \left[1 + 1.25 + \frac{1.25^2}{2(1-0.625)}\right]^{-1} = \left[1+1.25+2.0833\right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{4.3333} = 0.2308 \] \[ L_q = \frac{P_0\,r^{c}\rho}{c!\,(1-\rho)^2} = \frac{0.2308(1.5625)(0.625)}{2(0.140625)} = \frac{0.2254}{0.28125} = \mathbf{0.801} \] \[ W_q = \frac{L_q}{\lambda} = \frac{0.801}{7.5} = 0.1068\ \text{hours} = \mathbf{6.4\ \text{minutes}} \]

Recommendation. "Employ 2 specialists. With 1, the queue is mathematically unbounded — callers would wait indefinitely and the system would collapse. With 2, utilisation is 62.5 % and the average specialist wait is 6.4 minutes."

The value of superposition and thinning. They let us decompose a complex system into tractable pieces: we analysed the specialist sub-system in isolation, and were entitled to, because thinning preserves the Poisson property and independence. Without these theorems the decomposition would be invalid.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Testing the exponential assumption, and what it costs to be wrong
docs.text:
A workshop records 20 service times (minutes): 2, 15, 4, 9, 1, 22, 6, 3, 11, 5, 8, 30, 2, 7, 14, 3, 19, 5, 10, 4. (a) Test whether these are consistent with an exponential distribution. (b) If arrivals are Poisson at 5/hour, compute \(L_q\) under both the exponential assumption and the actual variability, and compare.

Solution.

(a) Testing exponentiality.

Step 1 — the sample mean.

\[ \sum x_i = 2+15+4+9+1+22+6+3+11+5+8+30+2+7+14+3+19+5+10+4 = 180 \] \[ \bar x = \frac{180}{20} = \mathbf{9.0\ \text{minutes}} \]

Step 2 — the sample standard deviation.

\[ \sum x_i^{2} = 4+225+16+81+1+484+36+9+121+25+64+900+4+49+196+9+361+25+100+16 = 2726 \] \[ s^{2} = \frac{2726}{20} - 9^{2} = 136.3 - 81 = 55.3 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad s = \mathbf{7.44} \]

Step 3 — the coefficient of variation.

\[ \boxed{\ CV = \frac{s}{\bar x} = \frac{7.44}{9.0} = \mathbf{0.827}\ } \]

For an exponential distribution, \(CV = 1\) exactly. Our sample gives 0.827.

Is 0.827 close enough? For \(n = 20\) the sampling standard error of \(CV\) is roughly \(1/\sqrt{2n} = 1/\sqrt{40} = 0.158\). So

\[ z = \frac{0.827 - 1}{0.158} = -1.09 \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Not significant at 5 \% — the data are CONSISTENT with exponential service.}\ } \]

A supporting check — the median. Sorting the data, the 10th and 11th values are 6 and 7, so the sample median is 6.5. For an exponential with mean 9, the median should be \(9\ln2 = 6.24\). Observed 6.5 versus expected 6.24 ✓ — an excellent match, and the right kind of right-skew (median well below the mean of 9).

(b) The cost of the assumption.

\[ \lambda = 5/\text{hour}, \qquad \bar x = 9 \ \text{min} \Rightarrow \mu = \frac{60}{9} = 6.667/\text{hour} \] \[ \rho = \frac{5}{6.667} = \mathbf{0.75} \]

Under the exponential assumption (\(M/M/1\)):

\[ L_q = \frac{\rho^2}{1-\rho} = \frac{0.5625}{0.25} = \mathbf{2.25\ \text{jobs}} \] \[ W_q = \frac{2.25}{5} = 0.45\ \text{hours} = \mathbf{27\ \text{minutes}} \]

Using the ACTUAL variability (\(M/G/1\), Pollaczek–Khinchine). In hours, \(\sigma_s = 7.44/60 = 0.124\) h, so \(\sigma_s^2 = 0.01538\):

\[ L_q = \frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma_s^{2}+\rho^{2}}{2(1-\rho)} = \frac{25(0.01538) + 0.5625}{2(0.25)} = \frac{0.3845+0.5625}{0.5} = \frac{0.947}{0.5} = \mathbf{1.894} \] \[ W_q = \frac{1.894}{5} = 0.379\ \text{h} = \mathbf{22.7\ \text{minutes}} \]

Comparison.

Model \(L_q\) \(W_q\) Error vs actual \(M/M/1\) (assumed exponential) 2.25 27.0 min +19 % \(M/G/1\) (actual \(\sigma\)) 1.89 22.7 min — \(M/D/1\) (if service were constant) 1.125 13.5 min −41 % \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The exponential assumption OVERSTATES the queue by 19 \% here — it is CONSERVATIVE.}\ } \]

Why this direction matters. Because \(CV < 1\) (service is slightly more regular than exponential), \(M/M/1\) predicts a worse queue than reality. Being conservative is the safe direction for a capacity recommendation — you will not under-provision.

The general rule.

\[ \boxed{\ CV < 1 \Rightarrow M/M/1 \text{ is pessimistic (safe)}; \qquad CV > 1 \Rightarrow M/M/1 \text{ is OPTIMISTIC (dangerous)}.\ } \]

When \(CV > 1\) — the real danger. Service times with occasional very long jobs (IT support, medical diagnosis, machine repair) often have \(CV\) of 1.5–3. At \(CV = 2\) and \(\rho = 0.75\):

\[ L_q = \frac{25(4\times0.01538)+0.5625}{0.5} = \frac{1.538+0.5625}{0.5} = \mathbf{4.20} \]

— 87 % worse than the \(M/M/1\) prediction. A capacity plan built on \(M/M/1\) would badly under-provision.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Always compute the sample } CV \textbf{ before trusting an } M/M/1 \textbf{ recommendation.}\ } \]

docs.title: 22.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\lambda = 6\)/hour. Find \(\Pr[\text{exactly 3 in 30 minutes}]\). [Ans: \(\lambda t=3\), \(P_3 = 0.2240\)]
  2. Exponential with mean 5 minutes. Find \(\Pr[T>8]\). [Ans: \(e^{-1.6}=0.2019\)]
  3. Verify the memoryless property numerically for \(\mu = 0.2\), \(s=3\), \(t=5\).
  4. A sample has mean 10 and variance 25. Is it consistent with Poisson? [Ans: no — overdispersed, ratio 2.5]
  5. Three Poisson streams at 4, 7, 9/hour merge. What is the combined process? [Ans: Poisson, 20/hour]
  6. 20 % of a Poisson stream at 50/hour is diverted. What is the diverted process? [Ans: Poisson, 10/hour]
  7. Service data have \(CV = 1.8\). Is \(M/M/1\) optimistic or pessimistic? [Ans: optimistic — dangerous]

docs.title: 22.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Poisson counts and exponential times are two views of the same process. The three axioms are independence, stationarity and orderliness.
  • \(P_n(t) = \dfrac{(\lambda t)^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}\), with \(E[N] = \mathrm{Var}[N] = \lambda t\). Mean = variance is the Poisson signature, and the ratio \(s^2/\bar n\) is the standard diagnostic.
  • Superposition (rates add) and thinning (rate \(\times p\)) both preserve the Poisson property — these theorems justify decomposing complex systems.
  • Inter-arrival times are exponential: \(f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\), with \(E[T] = \sigma_T = 1/\lambda\), so \(CV = 1\) exactly. The median \(= 0.693/\lambda\) is well below the mean — strongly right-skewed.
  • Memorylessness \(\Pr[T>s+t\mid T>s] = \Pr[T>t]\) characterises the exponential uniquely. It is what makes queuing models Markovian and tractable — and it is often unrealistic for service times, though usually fine for arrivals.
  • The Pollaczek–Khinchine formula shows exponential service gives exactly twice the queue of deterministic service. So \(M/M/1\) is conservative when \(CV<1\) and dangerously optimistic when \(CV>1\).
  • Test both assumptions before using the formulas: \(s^2/\bar n \approx 1\) for Poisson arrivals, \(CV\approx1\) for exponential service.

Next lesson: L23 — Birth–death processes and steady-state balance equations.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → Distribution Explorer: generate Poisson and exponential samples, see the histograms, and test your own data against both.

docs.title: Lesson 33: The Production (Finite Replenishment) Model without Shortages
33.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain how finite replenishment changes the inventory profile from sawtooth to trapezoid.
  2. Derive the maximum inventory \(I_{\max}=Q(1-D/P)\) from the geometry.
  3. Derive the Economic Production Quantity \(Q^{*}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_h(1-D/P)}}\).
  4. Interpret the inflation factor \(1/\sqrt{1-D/P}\) and the limits \(P\to\infty\) and \(P\to D\).
  5. Apply the model to batch-sizing and machine-loading decisions.

docs.title: 33.2 Why the EOQ Profile Is Wrong for a Factory
docs.text:
Classical EOQ assumes the whole order \(Q\) arrives at once. That is right for purchasing but wrong for manufacturing: a machine producing at \(P\) units per day delivers the batch gradually, and meanwhile the item is also being consumed at \(D\) units per day.

Economic Production Quantity (EPQ), also called the Economic Batch Quantity or the Economic Manufacturing Quantity. Same trade-off, different geometry.

Assumptions — those of Lesson 31, with assumption 4 replaced:

  • Production occurs at a finite, constant rate \(P\) units per unit time, with \(P > D\).
  • Consumption continues during production at rate \(D\).
  • No shortages permitted; all other assumptions unchanged.

The condition \(P>D\) is essential: if \(P\le D\), production can never get ahead of demand, no inventory ever accumulates and the machine must simply run continuously.

docs.title: 33.3 The Inventory Profile
docs.text:
stock
      |      /\              /\
 Imax |    /   \           /   \
      |   /      \        /      \
      |  /         \     /         \       slope +(P-D) rising
      | /            \  /            \     slope  -D    falling
    0 |/_______________\/_______________\____ time
      |<-tp->|<- td ->|
      |<------- t ------>|
Phase Duration Net rate of change of stock Production (produce and consume) \(t_p=Q/P\) \(+(P-D)\) Depletion (consume only) \(t_d = t-t_p\) \(-D\) Full cycle \(t=Q/D\) —

The profile is a trapezoid, not a sawtooth, and the peak is lower than \(Q\): some of the batch has already been consumed by the time the last unit is made.

docs.title: Maximum inventory
docs.text:
Stock builds at rate \((P-D)\) for time \(t_p=Q/P\):

\[I_{\max}=(P-D)\frac{Q}{P}\]

Result 1. $\(\boxed{\ I_{\max}=Q\left(1-\frac{D}{P}\right)=Qf,\qquad f\equiv1-\frac{D}{P}\ }\tag{2.1}\)$ and the average inventory is \(\dfrac{I_{\max}}{2}=\dfrac{Qf}{2}\), not \(\dfrac{Q}{2}\).

The factor \(f=1-D/P\) is the fraction of the batch that is still on hand when production stops. It is the only structural difference from Lesson 31.

Check: \(P\to\infty\) gives \(f\to1\) and \(I_{\max}\to Q\) — the instantaneous-delivery sawtooth.

docs.title: 33.4 Deriving the Optimum
docs.text:
\[TRC(Q)=\underbrace{\frac{C_oD}{Q}}_{\text{setup}}+\underbrace{\frac{C_hQf}{2}}_{\text{holding}}\]

This is exactly the EOQ cost function with \(C_h\) replaced by \(C_hf\). So by the same calculus:

Result 2 (EPQ formulas). $\(\boxed{\ Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_oD}{C_h\left(1-D/P\right)}}=\frac{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}{\sqrt{f}}\ }\tag{3.1}\)$ $\(\boxed{\ TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2C_oDC_h\left(1-\frac DP\right)}=TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\sqrt{f}\ }\tag{3.2}\)$ $\(I_{\max}=Q^{*}f,\qquad t=\frac{Q^{*}}{D},\qquad t_p=\frac{Q^{*}}{P},\qquad n=\frac{D}{Q^{*}}\)$

And, as always, at the optimum setup cost equals holding cost.

docs.title: Reading the inflation factor
docs.text:
Everything is governed by \(1/\sqrt f = \left(1-D/P\right)^{-1/2}\):

\(D/P\) (machine utilisation) \(f\) \(Q^{*}/Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\) \(TRC^{*}/TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\) 0 (instant supply) 1.00 1.000 1.000 0.25 0.75 1.155 0.866 0.50 0.50 1.414 0.707 0.75 0.25 2.000 0.500 0.90 0.10 3.162 0.316 0.99 0.01 10.000 0.100

The EPQ is always larger and always cheaper than the EOQ for the same data. Larger, because gradual delivery means a big batch never all sits in the store at once; cheaper, for the same reason — average stock is lower.

The limits are worth stating explicitly:

  • \(P\to\infty\): \(f\to1\), and (3.1)–(3.2) become the EOQ formulas exactly.
  • \(P\to D\): \(f\to0\), so \(Q^{*}\to\infty\) and \(TRC^{*}\to0\). Interpretation: a machine that can barely keep up must run continuously, so there are no setups and no accumulated stock. The formula's advice ("produce infinitely large batches") really means "never stop".

docs.title: Problem 1 — The standard EPQ calculation
docs.text:
A firm needs \(10{,}000\) units a year of a part it makes itself. The machine produces \(25{,}000\) units a year. Setup costs \(₹150\); holding costs \(₹8\) per unit per year. Find \(Q^*\), \(I_{\max}\), \(TRC^*\), the cycle time, the production time per cycle and the number of runs per year.

Solution.

\[f=1-\frac{D}{P}=1-\frac{10000}{25000}=1-0.4=0.6\] \[Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2(150)(10000)}{8(0.6)}}=\sqrt{\frac{3{,}000{,}000}{4.8}}=\sqrt{625000}=\mathbf{790.57\text{ units}}\] \[I_{\max}=790.57(0.6)=\mathbf{474.34\text{ units}}\] \[TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2(150)(10000)(8)(0.6)}=\sqrt{14{,}400{,}000}=\mathbf{₹3794.73\text{ per year}}\]

Check: setup \(=\dfrac{150(10000)}{790.57}=₹1897.37\); holding \(=\dfrac{8(474.34)}{2}=₹1897.37\) ✓ equal.

\[t=\frac{790.57}{10000}=0.0791\text{ yr}=\mathbf{28.9\text{ days}},\qquad t_p=\frac{790.57}{25000}=0.0316\text{ yr}=\mathbf{11.5\text{ days}}\] \[n=\frac{10000}{790.57}=\mathbf{12.65\text{ runs per year}}\]

Comparison with EOQ (Lesson 31, same data): \(Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=612.37\), \(TRC^{*}=₹4898.98\).

EOQ (bought in) EPQ (made in-house) Batch size 612.37 790.57 (\(\times1.291\)) Peak stock 612.37 474.34 Average stock 306.19 237.17 Relevant cost ₹4898.98 ₹3794.73 (\(\times0.775\))

Interpretation. The batch is \(29\,\%\) larger and yet the peak stock is \(23\,\%\) smaller, so the cost falls by \(23\,\%\). Both effects come from the same fact: \(40\,\%\) of each batch is consumed before the run finishes. The machine runs \(11.5\) days and stands idle (for this part) for \(17.4\) days in every \(28.9\)-day cycle — which is the capacity available for other products.

docs.title: Problem 2 — A high-utilisation machine
docs.text:
A plant needs \(9000\) units a year; the machine can make \(12{,}000\) a year. Setup costs \(₹400\), holding \(₹6\) per unit per year. Find the policy, and compare it with the EOQ answer.

Solution.

\[f=1-\frac{9000}{12000}=1-0.75=0.25\] \[Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2(400)(9000)}{6(0.25)}}=\sqrt{\frac{7{,}200{,}000}{1.5}}=\sqrt{4{,}800{,}000}=\mathbf{2190.89\text{ units}}\] \[I_{\max}=2190.89(0.25)=\mathbf{547.72\text{ units}}\] \[TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2(400)(9000)(6)(0.25)}=\sqrt{10{,}800{,}000}=\mathbf{₹3286.34\text{ per year}}\] \[t=\frac{2190.89}{9000}=0.2434\text{ yr}=\mathbf{88.9\text{ days}},\qquad t_p=\frac{2190.89}{12000}=0.1826\text{ yr}=\mathbf{66.6\text{ days}}\] \[n=\mathbf{4.11\text{ runs per year}}\]

Against EOQ: \(Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=\sqrt{2(400)(9000)/6}=1095.45\) and \(TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}=₹6572.67\).

\[\frac{Q^{*}_{\text{EPQ}}}{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.25}}=2.000,\qquad \frac{TRC^{*}_{\text{EPQ}}}{TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}=\sqrt{0.25}=0.500\]

Interpretation. At \(75\,\%\) machine utilisation the batch doubles and the cost halves relative to the purchased case. Note also that the machine is producing this part for \(66.6\) of every \(88.9\) days — it is nearly dedicated to this product. Using the EOQ formula here would have recommended batches of \(1095\), less than half the right size, and overstated the cost by a factor of two. Ignoring finite replenishment is a large error, not a small one.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Sensitivity to the production rate
docs.text:
For Problem 1's data (\(D=10{,}000\), \(C_o=₹150\), \(C_h=₹8\)), tabulate the policy as \(P\) varies.

Solution.

\(P\) \(D/P\) \(f\) \(Q^{*}\) \(I_{\max}\) \(TRC^{*}\) \(\infty\) 0.000 1.000 612.37 612.37 ₹4898.98 100 000 0.100 0.900 645.50 580.95 ₹4647.58 40 000 0.250 0.750 707.11 530.33 ₹4242.64 25 000 0.400 0.600 790.57 474.34 ₹3794.73 20 000 0.500 0.500 866.03 433.01 ₹3464.10 12 500 0.800 0.200 1369.31 273.86 ₹2190.89 10 500 0.952 0.0476 2806.24 133.63 ₹1069.04

Interpretation.

  • \(Q^{*}\) rises steeply and \(I_{\max}\) falls as \(P\) approaches \(D\). Batch size and peak stock move in opposite directions — a genuinely counter-intuitive result that follows directly from \(I_{\max}=Q f\) with \(Q\propto f^{-1/2}\), so \(I_{\max}\propto \sqrt f\).
  • The last row is a warning: the formula recommends a batch of \(2806\) — nearly a third of annual demand — because the machine has almost no spare capacity. That is mathematically right and practically fragile: any breakdown becomes a stock-out, and the model has no concept of risk. At \(D/P>0.8\), treat the recommendation as an indication and add a capacity or risk constraint.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Choosing between making and buying
docs.text:
A firm can buy an item for \(₹52\) per unit (\(C_o=₹150\) for a purchase order) or make it at a variable cost of \(₹48\) per unit on a machine running at \(25{,}000\) units a year with a setup cost of \(₹450\). Demand is \(10{,}000\) a year and \(C_h=₹8\) per unit per year in both cases. Which is cheaper?

Solution. Here the purchase/production cost is decision-relevant, because it differs between the options — unlike in Lessons 31–32.

Option A — buy. \(Q^{*}=612.37\), \(TRC^{*}=₹4898.98\) (Lesson 31).

\[TC_A = 10000(52)+4898.98 = 520000+4898.98=\mathbf{₹524{,}898.98}\]

Option B — make. \(f=0.6\), \(C_o=450\):

\[Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2(450)(10000)}{8(0.6)}}=\sqrt{1{,}875{,}000}=1369.31\text{ units}\] \[TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2(450)(10000)(8)(0.6)}=\sqrt{43{,}200{,}000}=₹6572.67\] \[TC_B = 10000(48)+6572.67=480000+6572.67=\mathbf{₹486{,}572.67}\] \[\boxed{\text{MAKE — saving }₹38{,}326.31\text{ per year}}\]

Interpretation. The decision is driven almost entirely by the \(₹4\) per unit difference in variable cost (\(₹40{,}000\) a year); the inventory costs differ by only \(₹1674\) and move the other way. When comparing options with different unit costs, the purchase term dominates and must be included — but notice that the higher setup cost of making did make the optimal batch more than twice as large, which is exactly the kind of operational consequence a purely accounting comparison would miss.

A complete analysis would also weigh the capacity consumed (\(t_p/t = D/P = 40\,\%\) of the machine's time), which is unavailable to other products and has an opportunity cost this model does not capture.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Multi-product machine loading
docs.text:
A machine makes three products. Using the EPQ for each, check whether the machine has enough capacity.

Product \(D\) (units/yr) \(P\) (units/yr) \(C_o\) (₹) \(C_h\) (₹/unit/yr) X 10 000 25 000 150 8 Y 6 000 30 000 200 5 Z 4 000 20 000 100 6

Solution.

Product \(f\) \(Q^{*}\) \(n=D/Q^{*}\) \(t_p\) per run (yr) Run time per year \(=D/P\) X 0.60 790.57 12.65 0.03162 0.4000 Y 0.80 774.60 7.75 0.02582 0.2000 Z 0.80 408.25 9.80 0.02041 0.2000 30.19 setups/yr 0.8000

Capacity check. Total production time is \(\sum D/P = 0.40+0.20+0.20=\mathbf{0.80}\), i.e. \(80\,\%\) of the year. That leaves \(20\,\%\) — about \(50\) working days — for setups, maintenance and slack.

If each setup takes \(4\) hours on a \(2000\)-hour year, \(30.19\) setups consume \(30.19\times4/2000=0.0604\), i.e. a further \(6.0\,\%\). Total load \(=86.0\,\%\).

\[\boxed{\text{Feasible, at }86.0\,\%\text{ utilisation — but with little margin}}\]

Interpretation. Two points that the single-product model cannot see.

  1. The EPQs were computed independently, yet the machine can make only one product at a time. Nothing guarantees the three cycles can be scheduled without collision. A proper treatment uses a common cycle time for all products, which is the subject of the multi-item extension.
  2. At \(86\,\%\) utilisation, Lesson 24's lesson applies: this machine is on the steep part of the congestion curve. A breakdown or a demand increase will cause queueing of jobs and missed schedules. A capacity check is not optional after an EPQ calculation — the formula happily recommends batch sizes for a machine that does not have the hours.

docs.title: 33.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(D=4800\)/yr, \(P=8000\)/yr, \(C_o=₹250\), \(C_h=₹12\). Find \(Q^*\), \(I_{\max}\), \(TRC^*\), \(t\) and \(t_p\). (Answer: \(707.11\), \(282.84\), \(₹3394.11\), \(0.1473\) yr, \(0.0884\) yr)
  2. Show that \(I_{\max}\propto\sqrt f\), and hence that peak stock falls as the machine gets busier.
  3. A firm computes EOQ instead of EPQ for a part with \(D/P=0.6\). By what percentage is its batch size wrong, and by how much does its cost exceed the true optimum? (Answer: batch \(36.75\,\%\) too small; using the sensitivity formula of Lesson 31 with \(k=\sqrt{0.4}=0.6325\) gives \(TRC/TRC^*=1.1068\), i.e. \(10.7\,\%\) too dear)
  4. At what value of \(D/P\) does the EPQ batch become exactly twice the EOQ batch? (Answer: \(f=0.25\), i.e. \(D/P=0.75\))
  5. In Problem 5, demand for X rises to \(15{,}000\)/yr. Recompute the capacity check and comment. (Answer: \(D/P\) for X becomes \(0.60\); total production load \(1.00\) — the machine is fully saturated with no time for setups. Infeasible.)

docs.title: 33.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Finite replenishment turns the sawtooth into a trapezoid: production and consumption overlap.
  • The whole model is EOQ with \(C_h\) replaced by \(C_hf\), where \(\boxed{f=1-D/P}\).
  • \(\boxed{I_{\max}=Qf}\) and average stock \(=Qf/2\) — not \(Q/2\).
  • \(\boxed{Q^{*}=\dfrac{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}}{\sqrt f}}\) and \(\boxed{TRC^{*}=TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\sqrt f}\). Bigger batches, lower cost, always.
  • \(I_{\max}\propto\sqrt f\), so batch size and peak stock move in opposite directions as \(P\) falls towards \(D\).
  • \(P\to\infty\) recovers EOQ exactly; \(P\to D\) says "never stop the machine".
  • Ignoring finite replenishment is a large error: at \(D/P=0.75\) it halves the batch and doubles the reported cost.
  • Always finish with a capacity check: \(\sum D_i/P_i\) plus setup time must be comfortably below 1.

Next lesson: L34 — The production model with shortages permitted, combining Lessons 32 and 33.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → EPQ Lab: drag \(P\) and watch the trapezoid flatten, \(Q^{*}\) grow and \(I_{\max}\) shrink at the same time.

docs.title: Lesson 34: The Production Model with Shortages Permitted
34.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Draw the four-phase inventory profile of the general production–backorder model.
  2. Derive \(Q^{*}\), \(I_{\max}\) and \(B^{*}\) for the combined model.
  3. Show that the general model reduces to each of Lessons 31–33 in the appropriate limit.
  4. Assemble the complete family of deterministic inventory models in one table.
  5. Select the right member of the family for a given situation.

docs.title: 34.2 The General Deterministic Model
docs.text:
This lesson combines the two extensions studied so far:

  • Finite replenishment (Lesson 33): production at rate \(P>D\), not instantaneous delivery.
  • Planned backorders (Lesson 32): shortages are permitted and cost \(C_s\) per unit per unit time.

The result is the most general deterministic EOQ-family model, with four parameters \((C_o, C_h, C_s, P)\) and two decision variables \((Q, I_{\max})\). Every earlier model is a special case.

docs.title: The four-phase profile
docs.text:
stock
       |        /\                    /\
  Imax |      /   \                 /   \
       |    /       \             /       \
     0 |---/----------\----------/----------\-------  time
       |  /            \        /            \
    -B | /              \______/              \____
       |<t1><--t2-->|<t3>|<-t4->|
       |<---------- t ----------->|
Phase What is happening Rate Duration \(t_1\) Production on; backlog \(B\) being cleared \(+(P-D)\) \(B/(P-D)\) \(t_2\) Production on; stock building to \(I_{\max}\) \(+(P-D)\) \(I_{\max}/(P-D)\) \(t_3\) Production off; stock depleting to zero \(-D\) \(I_{\max}/D\) \(t_4\) Production off; backlog building to \(B\) \(-D\) \(B/D\)

Production runs for \(t_1+t_2 = Q/P\) and the whole cycle is \(t=Q/D\).

docs.title: The average levels
docs.text:
As in Lesson 32, both averages are triangle areas divided by the full cycle. Writing \(f=1-D/P\) and noting that the peak-to-trough range is \(Qf\) (the same total build-up as in Lesson 33):

\[\text{average stock}=\frac{I_{\max}^{2}}{2Qf},\qquad \text{average shortage}=\frac{B^{2}}{2Qf},\qquad I_{\max}+B=Qf. \tag{1.1}\]

Setting \(f=1\) recovers Lesson 32; setting \(B=0\) recovers Lesson 33.

docs.title: 34.3 Deriving the Optimum
docs.text: \[TRC(Q,I_{\max})=\frac{C_oD}{Q}+\frac{C_hI_{\max}^{2}}{2Qf}+\frac{C_s(Qf-I_{\max})^{2}}{2Qf}\tag{2.1}\]

docs.title: Optimising over I_max
docs.text:
\[\frac{\partial TRC}{\partial I_{\max}}=\frac{C_hI_{\max}}{Qf}-\frac{C_s(Qf-I_{\max})}{Qf}=0\]

Result 1. $\(\boxed{\ I_{\max}^{*}=\frac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\,Qf,\qquad B^{*}=\frac{C_h}{C_h+C_s}\,Qf\ }\tag{2.2}\)$

The same critical ratio \(\dfrac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}\) as in Lesson 32, now applied to \(Qf\) instead of \(Q\).

docs.title: Optimising over Q
docs.text:
Substituting (2.2) into (2.1) reduces the holding-plus-shortage term to \(\dfrac{Qf}{2}\cdot\dfrac{C_hC_s}{C_h+C_s}\), giving an EOQ in disguise:

Result 2 (general production–backorder model). With $\(f=1-\frac{D}{P},\qquad k=\sqrt{\frac{C_h+C_s}{C_s}},\)$ $\(\boxed{\ Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_oD}{C_hf}}\cdot k=\frac{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\cdot k}{\sqrt f}\ }\tag{2.3}\)$ $\(\boxed{\ I^{*}_{\max}=\frac{Q^{*}f}{k^{2}}=\frac{Q^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\sqrt f}{k},\qquad B^{*}=Q^{*}f-I^{*}_{\max}\ }\tag{2.4}\)$ $\(\boxed{\ TRC^{*}=\frac{\sqrt{2C_oDC_h\,f}}{k}=\frac{TRC^{*}_{\text{EOQ}}\sqrt f}{k}\ }\tag{2.5}\)$

Both corrections multiply cleanly: \(\sqrt f\) from finite replenishment and \(1/k\) from backordering.

docs.title: 34.4 The Complete Family
docs.text:
Model \(P\) \(C_s\) \(Q^{*}\) \(TRC^{*}\) Lesson Classical EOQ \(\infty\) \(\infty\) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\) \(\sqrt{2C_oDC_h}\) 31 EOQ with backorders \(\infty\) finite \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\,k\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2C_oDC_h}}{k}\) 32 EPQ, no shortage finite \(\infty\) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_hf}}\) \(\sqrt{2C_oDC_h f}\) 33 General finite finite \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_hf}}\,k\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2C_oDC_hf}}{k}\) 34

with \(f=1-D/P\) and \(k=\sqrt{(C_h+C_s)/C_s}\).

One formula to remember. $\(Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\times\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt f}}_{\text{finite }P}\times\underbrace{k}_{\text{backorders}}, \qquad TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2C_oDC_h}\times\sqrt f\times\frac1k\)$ Both extensions increase \(Q\) and decrease \(TRC\), and they act independently.

docs.title: Problem 1 — The general model
docs.text:
\(D=10{,}000\) units/yr, \(P=25{,}000\) units/yr, \(C_o=₹150\), \(C_h=₹8\)/unit/yr, \(C_s=₹25\)/unit/yr. Find the complete policy and compare with all three earlier models.

Solution.

Step 1 — the two factors.

\[f=1-\frac{10000}{25000}=0.6,\qquad k=\sqrt{\frac{8+25}{25}}=\sqrt{1.32}=1.14891\]

Step 2 — the batch.

\[Q^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2(150)(10000)}{8(0.6)}}\times1.14891=790.57\times1.14891=\mathbf{908.30\text{ units}}\]

Step 3 — the levels. First \(Q^*f = 908.30(0.6)=544.98\) — the peak-to-trough range.

\[I^{*}_{\max}=\frac{25}{33}(544.98)=\mathbf{412.86\text{ units}}\] \[B^{*}=\frac{8}{33}(544.98)=\mathbf{132.12\text{ units}}\]

Step 4 — the cost.

\[TRC^{*}=\frac{\sqrt{2(150)(10000)(8)(0.6)}}{1.14891}=\frac{3794.73}{1.14891}=\mathbf{₹3302.89\text{ per year}}\]

Step 5 — verification by components.

\[\text{setup}=\frac{150(10000)}{908.30}=₹1651.45\] \[\text{holding}=\frac{8(412.86)^2}{2(908.30)(0.6)}=\frac{8(170{,}453)}{1089.96}=₹1251.10\] \[\text{shortage}=\frac{25(132.12)^2}{2(908.30)(0.6)}=\frac{25(17{,}455)}{1089.96}=₹400.35\] \[\text{TOTAL}=1651.45+1251.10+400.35=₹3302.90\ \checkmark\]

Again setup cost \(=\) holding \(+\) shortage.

Step 6 — the whole family, same data.

Model \(f\) \(k\) \(Q^{*}\) Peak stock \(TRC^{*}\) Saving vs EOQ EOQ (L31) 1.0 1.0000 612.37 612.37 ₹4898.98 — EOQ + backorders (L32) 1.0 1.1489 703.56 533.00 ₹4264.01 13.0 % EPQ (L33) 0.6 1.0000 790.57 474.34 ₹3794.73 22.5 % General (L34) 0.6 1.1489 908.30 412.86 ₹3302.89 32.6 %

Interpretation. Each relaxation makes the batch larger and the cost lower, and the two effects compose multiplicatively: \(0.775\times0.870=0.674\), and indeed \(3302.89/4898.98=0.674\) ✓. Peak stock falls monotonically down the table — from \(612\) to \(413\) units, a \(33\,\%\) reduction in the warehouse space required, achieved while increasing the batch size by \(48\,\%\).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Checking the limits
docs.text:
Verify that Result 2 reduces correctly in each of the three limiting cases, using Problem 1's data.

Solution.

(a) \(P\to\infty\) (instantaneous delivery). Then \(f\to1\):

\[Q^{*}\to 612.37(1.14891)=703.56,\quad TRC^{*}\to\frac{4898.98}{1.14891}=₹4264.01\]

— exactly Lesson 32's backorder model ✓.

(b) \(C_s\to\infty\) (no shortages tolerated). Then \(k\to1\) and \(I^*_{\max}\to Q^*f\), \(B^*\to0\):

\[Q^{*}\to790.57,\quad TRC^{*}\to₹3794.73\]

— exactly Lesson 33's EPQ ✓.

(c) Both. \(f\to1\) and \(k\to1\):

\[Q^{*}\to612.37,\quad TRC^{*}\to₹4898.98\]

— classical EOQ ✓.

Interpretation. Always test a general formula against its special cases. It costs two minutes, catches almost every algebraic slip, and is the technique by which the correctness of (2.3)–(2.5) can be confirmed without re-deriving them. A formula that fails a limit check is wrong, whatever the derivation looked like.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Reading the cycle structure
docs.text:
For Problem 1's policy, find the four phase durations and state how long the firm is out of stock.

Solution. \(Q^*=908.30\), \(I^*_{\max}=412.86\), \(B^*=132.12\), \(P-D=15{,}000\)/yr.

\[t=\frac{Q^{*}}{D}=\frac{908.30}{10000}=0.09083\text{ yr}=\mathbf{33.2\text{ days}}\ (365\text{-day year})\] Phase Formula Value (yr) Days \(t_1\) clearing backlog \(B/(P-D)=132.12/15000\) 0.00881 3.2 \(t_2\) building stock \(I_{\max}/(P-D)=412.86/15000\) 0.02752 10.0 \(t_3\) depleting stock \(I_{\max}/D=412.86/10000\) 0.04129 15.1 \(t_4\) building backlog \(B/D=132.12/10000\) 0.01321 4.8 Total 0.09083 33.2

Checks. Production time \(t_1+t_2=0.03632\) yr \(=Q^*/P=908.30/25000=0.03632\) ✓. Time in stock \(t_2+t_3 = 0.06881\); time short \(t_1+t_4=0.02202\).

\[\text{Fraction of time short}=\frac{0.02202}{0.09083}=\mathbf{24.24\,\%}\]

which equals \(\dfrac{C_h}{C_h+C_s}=\dfrac{8}{33}=0.2424\) ✓ — the critical ratio again, exactly as in Lesson 32.

Interpretation. The firm operates a \(33\)-day cycle in which the machine runs for \(13.2\) days and customers wait for \(8.1\) days. Both are deliberate. Notice that the fraction of time short depends only on \(C_h\) and \(C_s\) — not on \(D\), \(C_o\) or \(P\). That makes it the single most robust number in the whole model and the natural thing to negotiate with a customer: "we will be out of stock about a quarter of the time; is that acceptable, and if not, what is it worth to you?"

docs.title: Problem 4 — Selecting the right model
docs.text:
For each case, name the model and give the formula for \(Q^{*}\).

Case Situation Model \(Q^{*}\) (a) Buy screws from a supplier; delivery next day; no stock-outs allowed EOQ \(\sqrt{2C_oD/C_h}\) (b) Buy custom furniture; customers accept a 2-week wait EOQ + backorders \(\sqrt{2C_oD/C_h}\ k\) (c) Make brackets on a press at 400/day, use 150/day, no stock-outs EPQ \(\sqrt{2C_oD/(C_hf)}\) (d) Make machine tools at 8/week, demand 5/week, dealers accept backorders General \(\sqrt{2C_oD/(C_hf)}\ k\) (e) Make ice cream at 500 l/day, demand 300 l/day, cannot be stored over a week None of these —

Case (e) explained. Perishability imposes a maximum cycle length, which none of these models contains. If the unconstrained \(Q^{*}\) gives \(t=Q^{*}/D\) longer than the shelf life \(T_{\max}\), the answer is simply \(Q=DT_{\max}\) — the constraint binds and the optimisation is irrelevant. Because the cost curve is flat (Lesson 31), the penalty for this forced choice is usually small, which is a comforting result: a binding practical constraint rarely costs much in an EOQ-family model.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Sensitivity to C_s in the general model
docs.text:
For Problem 1's data, tabulate the general policy as \(C_s\) varies from \(₹2\) to \(\infty\).

Solution. \(f=0.6\) throughout, so \(Q^{*}_{\text{EPQ}}=790.57\) and \(TRC^{*}_{\text{EPQ}}=₹3794.73\) are the reference values.

\(C_s\) \(k\) \(Q^{*}\) \(Q^{*}f\) \(I^{*}_{\max}\) \(B^{*}\) % of cycle short \(TRC^{*}\) 2 2.2361 1767.77 1060.66 212.13 848.53 80.0 % ₹1697.06 8 1.4142 1118.03 670.82 335.41 335.41 50.0 % ₹2683.28 25 1.1489 908.30 544.98 412.86 132.12 24.2 % ₹3302.89 72 1.0541 833.33 500.00 450.00 50.00 10.0 % ₹3600.00 792 1.0050 794.55 476.73 471.96 4.77 1.0 % ₹3775.71 \(\infty\) 1.0000 790.57 474.34 474.34 0 0 % ₹3794.73

Interpretation.

  • \(I^{*}_{\max}\) rises and \(B^{*}\) falls as \(C_s\) increases, always summing to \(Q^{*}f\).
  • The percentage of the cycle spent short is exactly \(C_h/(C_h+C_s)\) — check the \(C_s=8\) row: with \(C_h=C_s=8\) the system is short exactly half the time, regardless of everything else.
  • As in Lesson 32, once \(C_s>10C_h\) (i.e. \(C_s>80\) here) the backorder refinement buys under \(5\,\%\) and is not worth the complexity. The general model earns its keep only when shortages are genuinely cheap.

docs.title: 34.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(D=6000\)/yr, \(P=15{,}000\)/yr, \(C_o=₹300\), \(C_h=₹10\), \(C_s=₹40\). Find \(Q^{*}\), \(I^{*}_{\max}\), \(B^{*}\) and \(TRC^{*}\). (Answer: \(f=0.6\), \(k=1.1180\); \(Q^{*}=866.03\), \(I^{*}_{\max}=415.69\), \(B^{*}=103.92\), \(TRC^{*}=₹4156.92\))
  2. Show that \(I^{*}_{\max}+B^{*}=Q^{*}f\) always, and explain what that quantity means physically.
  3. In Problem 1 of §4, what would \(C_s\) have to be for the firm to be out of stock only \(5\,\%\) of the time? (Answer: \(C_h/(C_h+C_s)=0.05\) gives \(C_s=₹152\))
  4. Prove that \(TRC^{*}\) for the general model is never greater than \(TRC^{*}\) for any of the three special cases with the same \(D\), \(C_o\) and \(C_h\).
  5. A firm using the general model finds \(Q^{*}=1000\), \(I^{*}_{\max}=480\) and \(B^{*}=120\). Deduce \(f\) and \(C_s/C_h\). (Answer: \(Q^*f = 600\) so \(f=0.6\), i.e. \(D/P=0.4\); \(B/(I_{\max}+B)=0.2=C_h/(C_h+C_s)\) so \(C_s=4C_h\))

docs.title: 34.7 Summary
docs.text:
• The general model has a four-phase cycle: clear backlog, build stock, deplete stock, build backlog.
  • The peak-to-trough range is \(Qf\), and both averages divide by the full cycle: average stock \(=I_{\max}^2/(2Qf)\), average shortage \(=B^2/(2Qf)\).
  • Critical ratio unchanged: \(I^{*}_{\max}=\dfrac{C_s}{C_h+C_s}Qf\), and the fraction of the cycle spent short is \(\dfrac{C_h}{C_h+C_s}\) — independent of \(D\), \(C_o\) and \(P\).
  • \(\boxed{Q^{*}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_oD}{C_h}}\cdot\dfrac{k}{\sqrt f}}\) and \(\boxed{TRC^{*}=\sqrt{2C_oDC_h}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt f}{k}}\) with \(f=1-D/P\), \(k=\sqrt{(C_h+C_s)/C_s}\).
  • The two corrections compose multiplicatively and each one raises \(Q\) while lowering \(TRC\).
  • Always check the limits \(P\to\infty\) and \(C_s\to\infty\): a general formula that does not collapse to its special cases is wrong.
  • The backorder refinement is worth having only when \(C_s\) is within about an order of magnitude of \(C_h\); beyond that, use the simpler model.
  • When a practical constraint (shelf life, storage space, minimum order) binds, take the constrained value — the flat cost curve makes the penalty small.

Next lesson: L35 — Quantity discounts and the consolidation of Unit III.

Practise now: unit3-queue-inventory-lab.html → General Model Lab: set \(P\) and \(C_s\) and watch the four-phase profile, with each phase duration labelled and the cost breakdown updating live.

docs.title: Lesson 4: The Simplex Method I: Theory
4.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define basic solution, basic feasible solution (BFS) and basis.
  2. State and use the theorem that BFS ⟺ extreme point.
  3. Count the maximum number of basic solutions and explain why enumeration is hopeless.
  4. Derive the optimality criterion (\(z_j - c_j\)) and the feasibility criterion (minimum ratio).
  5. State the simplex algorithm and explain why it terminates.

docs.title: 4.2 From Geometry to Algebra
docs.text:
L03 established that an optimum, if it exists, occurs at a corner. But in \(n\) dimensions you cannot draw the region. The simplex method's achievement is to characterise corners algebraically and to move between them systematically.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Corner point (geometry)} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \textbf{basic feasible solution (algebra)}\ } \]

docs.title: 4.3 Basic Solutions
docs.text:
Work in standard form: \(A\vec x = \vec b\) with \(\vec x \ge 0\), where \(A\) is \(m\times n\) with \(m < n\) and \(\mathrm{rank}(A) = m\).

The system is underdetermined — \(m\) equations, \(n\) unknowns — so it has infinitely many solutions. Simplex picks out a special finite subset.

Definition (Basic solution). Choose \(m\) of the \(n\) variables to be basic; set the remaining \(n - m\) non-basic variables to zero. If the resulting \(m\times m\) submatrix \(B\) (the basis matrix) is non-singular, solve

\[ B\vec x_B = \vec b \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec x_B = B^{-1}\vec b \]

The resulting \(\vec x\) is a basic solution.

Definition (Basic feasible solution, BFS). A basic solution with \(\vec x_B \ge \vec 0\).

Definition (Degenerate BFS). A BFS in which at least one basic variable equals zero.

docs.title: The counting
docs.text:
The number of ways to choose which \(m\) variables are basic is

\[ \binom{n}{m} = \frac{n!}{m!\,(n-m)!} \] \(m\) \(n\) \(\binom{n}{m}\) 2 4 6 3 6 20 5 10 252 10 20 184 756 20 40 \(1.4\times10^{11}\) 50 100 \(1.0\times10^{29}\)

Total enumeration is hopeless. At \(10^{9}\) solutions per second, the \(m=50\), \(n=100\) case would take \(3\times10^{12}\) years. Yet such problems are solved in milliseconds.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The simplex method's genius is visiting only a tiny fraction of the corners — typically } O(m) \textbf{ of them.}\ } \]

docs.title: 4.4 The Central Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. \(\vec x\) is a basic feasible solution of \(A\vec x = \vec b,\ \vec x\ge0\) if and only if \(\vec x\) is an extreme point of the feasible region.

Proof sketch (⟸). Let \(\vec x\) be an extreme point with positive components \(x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_k}\). If the corresponding columns \(\vec a_{j_1},\ldots,\vec a_{j_k}\) were linearly dependent, there would exist non-zero \(\vec d\) with \(A\vec d = 0\) supported on those indices; then \(\vec x \pm \epsilon\vec d\) would both be feasible for small \(\epsilon\), expressing \(\vec x\) as a midpoint — contradicting extremality. So the columns are independent, \(k \le m\), and they extend to a basis. \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary (the algorithm's licence). Since an optimum occurs at an extreme point (L03) and extreme points are exactly BFSs, it suffices to search over basic feasible solutions — a finite set.

docs.title: 4.5 The Simplex Tableau
docs.text:
Represent the system as a tableau. With \(c_B\) the objective coefficients of the basic variables:

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(\cdots\) \(x_n\) RHS \(x_{B_1}\) \(c_{B_1}\) \(a_{11}\) \(\cdots\) \(a_{1n}\) \(b_1\) \(\vdots\) \(x_{B_m}\) \(c_{B_m}\) \(a_{m1}\) \(\cdots\) \(a_{mn}\) \(b_m\) \(z_j - c_j\) \(Z\)

Definition (the \(z_j\) row).

\[ z_j = \sum_{i=1}^{m} c_{B_i}\,a_{ij} = \vec c_B^{T}B^{-1}\vec a_j \]

Definition (reduced cost / net evaluation).

\[ \Delta_j = z_j - c_j \]

docs.title: The economic meaning of z_j - c_j
docs.text:
Increasing a non-basic variable \(x_j\) by one unit:

  • Gains \(c_j\) directly from the objective.
  • Costs \(z_j\), because bringing in one unit of \(x_j\) forces the basic variables to adjust by \(-a_{ij}\) each, changing the objective by \(-\sum_i c_{B_i}a_{ij} = -z_j\).
\[ \boxed{\ \text{Net change in } Z \text{ per unit of } x_j \ =\ c_j - z_j \ =\ -\Delta_j\ } \]

So \(\Delta_j < 0\) means bringing \(x_j\) in improves \(Z\).

docs.title: Optimality criterion (for maximisation)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{The current BFS is optimal} \iff z_j - c_j \ \ge\ 0 \ \text{ for all } j\ } \]

If any \(\Delta_j < 0\), the solution can be improved.

Entering variable rule (Dantzig's rule). Choose

\[ j^{*} = \arg\min_j\ (z_j - c_j) \]

— the most negative \(\Delta_j\), giving the steepest per-unit improvement.

(For minimisation, either convert to maximisation, or reverse: optimal when all \(z_j - c_j \le 0\), and enter the most positive.)

docs.title: Feasibility criterion (the minimum-ratio test)
docs.text:
Once \(x_{j^*}\) is chosen to enter, how far can it increase? Basic variable \(x_{B_i}\) changes as

\[ x_{B_i} = b_i - a_{ij^*}\,x_{j^*} \]

which stays non-negative only while

\[ x_{j^*} \le \frac{b_i}{a_{ij^*}} \qquad \text{for every } i \text{ with } a_{ij^*} > 0 \] \[ \boxed{\ \theta = \min_{i\,:\,a_{ij^*}>0} \ \frac{b_i}{a_{ij^*}}\ } \]

The row \(r\) achieving the minimum determines the leaving variable \(x_{B_r}\), and \(a_{rj^*}\) is the pivot element.

Three rules that follow immediately.

  1. Ignore rows with \(a_{ij^*} \le 0\) — increasing \(x_{j^*}\) increases those basic variables, so they never become negative and impose no limit.
  2. If no \(a_{ij^*} > 0\) exists, the problem is UNBOUNDED — \(x_{j^*}\) can grow forever.
  3. A tie in the ratio test ⟹ degeneracy at the next iteration (some basic variable becomes 0).

docs.title: The pivot operation
docs.text:
Gauss–Jordan elimination on the pivot column:

1. Divide the pivot row by the pivot element  ->  pivot becomes 1
2. For every other row i:   row_i  <-  row_i  -  a[i][pivcol] * (new pivot row)
3. Replace x_{B_r} by x_{j*} in the basis list
4. Recompute the z_j - c_j row

docs.title: 4.7 The Algorithm and Its Termination
docs.text:
SIMPLEX (maximisation, standard form)

1. Find an initial BFS (slacks form the basis if all constraints are <=)
2. Compute z_j - c_j for all j
3. If all z_j - c_j >= 0  ->  STOP, optimal
4. Choose entering column j* = argmin (z_j - c_j)
5. If no a[i][j*] > 0  ->  STOP, unbounded
6. Choose leaving row r by the minimum-ratio test
7. Pivot on a[r][j*]
8. Go to 2

Why it terminates. Each iteration moves to an adjacent BFS with a strictly better objective value (provided no degeneracy). There are finitely many BFSs, and no value repeats, so the algorithm must stop.

The degeneracy caveat. With a degenerate BFS, the ratio test can give \(\theta = 0\), so the objective does not improve; in principle the algorithm can cycle. Two safeguards exist:

  • Bland's rule — among candidates, always choose the one with the smallest index. Guarantees termination, but is slow.
  • Lexicographic (perturbation) rule — perturb \(\vec b\) slightly to break all ties.

In practice cycling is vanishingly rare, and commercial solvers use Bland's rule only as a fallback after detecting stalling.

docs.title: Complexity — theory versus practice
docs.text:
Measure Result Worst case exponential — the Klee–Minty cube (1972) forces \(2^{n}-1\) iterations Average case \(O(m)\) to \(O(m\log n)\) pivots (Borgwardt, Smale; smoothed analysis by Spielman–Teng, 2004) Practical rule of thumb \(2m\) to \(3m\) iterations Guaranteed polynomial alternatives ellipsoid (Khachiyan 1979, impractical); interior point (Karmarkar 1984, practical)

A genuine paradox worth telling students. Simplex is exponential in the worst case yet is the algorithm of choice in practice, while the ellipsoid method is polynomial yet unusable. Worst-case complexity is not the same as practical performance.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Enumerating all basic solutions
docs.text:
For the system \(6x_1+4x_2+s_1 = 24\), \(x_1+2x_2+s_2 = 6\) (from L03), enumerate all basic solutions and identify which are feasible.

Solution.

\(m = 2\), \(n = 4\), so there are \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) basic solutions.

Basis \(\{s_1, s_2\}\). Set \(x_1 = x_2 = 0\):

\[ s_1 = 24,\ s_2 = 6 \ \Rightarrow\ (x_1,x_2) = (0,0) \ \textbf{FEASIBLE} \]

Basis \(\{x_1, s_2\}\). Set \(x_2 = s_1 = 0\): \(6x_1 = 24 \Rightarrow x_1 = 4\); \(4 + s_2 = 6 \Rightarrow s_2 = 2\):

\[ (x_1,x_2) = (4,0) \ \textbf{FEASIBLE} \]

Basis \(\{x_2, s_2\}\). Set \(x_1 = s_1 = 0\): \(4x_2 = 24 \Rightarrow x_2 = 6\); \(12+s_2 = 6\Rightarrow s_2 = -6\):

\[ (0,6) \ \textbf{INFEASIBLE} \ (s_2 < 0) \]

Basis \(\{x_1, s_1\}\). Set \(x_2 = s_2 = 0\): \(x_1 = 6\); \(36 + s_1 = 24 \Rightarrow s_1 = -12\):

\[ (6,0) \ \textbf{INFEASIBLE} \]

Basis \(\{x_2, s_1\}\). Set \(x_1 = s_2 = 0\): \(2x_2 = 6\Rightarrow x_2 = 3\); \(12 + s_1 = 24\Rightarrow s_1 = 12\):

\[ (0,3) \ \textbf{FEASIBLE} \]

Basis \(\{x_1, x_2\}\). Set \(s_1 = s_2 = 0\): solve \(6x_1+4x_2 = 24\), \(x_1+2x_2 = 6\):

\[ x_1 = 3,\ x_2 = 1.5 \ \textbf{FEASIBLE} \]

Summary.

Basis \((x_1,x_2)\) Feasible? \(Z = 5x_1+4x_2\) \(\{s_1,s_2\}\) \((0,0)\) ✓ 0 \(\{x_1,s_2\}\) \((4,0)\) ✓ 20 \(\{x_2,s_1\}\) \((0,3)\) ✓ 12 \(\{x_1,x_2\}\) \((3,1.5)\) ✓ 21 \(\{x_2,s_2\}\) \((0,6)\) ✗ — \(\{x_1,s_1\}\) \((6,0)\) ✗ —

Exactly the 4 feasible ones are the 4 corners found graphically in L03 ✓, confirming the BFS ⟺ extreme-point theorem. The 2 infeasible basic solutions correspond to intersections of constraint lines outside the feasible region.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Computing and interpreting z_j - c_j
docs.text:
For the tableau below with \(c = (5, 4, 0, 0)\), compute the \(z_j - c_j\) row and decide whether the solution is optimal.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_1\) 5 1 2/3 1/6 0 4 \(s_2\) 0 0 4/3 −1/6 1 2

Solution.

\[ z_j = \sum_i c_{B_i}a_{ij} = 5a_{1j} + 0\cdot a_{2j} = 5a_{1j} \] \(j\) \(a_{1j}\) \(z_j = 5a_{1j}\) \(c_j\) \(z_j - c_j\) \(x_1\) 1 5 5 \(0\) \(x_2\) 2/3 10/3 4 \(10/3 - 4 = \mathbf{-2/3}\) \(s_1\) 1/6 5/6 0 \(\mathbf{5/6}\) \(s_2\) 0 0 0 \(0\)

Current objective. \(Z = c_B^{T}\vec b = 5(4) + 0(2) = \mathbf{20}\).

Optimality check. \(z_2 - c_2 = -2/3 < 0\) ⟹ NOT optimal.

Interpretation of \(-2/3\). Bringing one unit of \(x_2\) into the solution changes \(Z\) by \(-(z_2-c_2) = +2/3\). Concretely: one unit of \(x_2\) earns \(c_2 = 4\) directly, but forces \(x_1\) down by \(2/3\) (its column entry), losing \(\frac23 \times 5 = \frac{10}{3}\). Net: \(4 - \frac{10}{3} = \frac{2}{3} > 0\) ✓ — an improvement.

Interpretation of \(z_{s_1} - c_{s_1} = 5/6\). This is the shadow price of resource 1: one extra unit of that resource is worth ₹5/6 of additional profit. Equivalently, forcing one unit of slack back in costs 5/6.

The minimum-ratio test. Entering \(x_2\) (column \(2/3\), \(4/3\)):

\[ \theta = \min\left\{\frac{4}{2/3},\ \frac{2}{4/3}\right\} = \min\{6,\ 1.5\} = \mathbf{1.5}, \ \text{ in row 2} \]

So \(s_2\) leaves, \(x_2\) enters, and \(x_2\) will take the value \(1.5\) — matching the graphical optimum \((3, 1.5)\) of L03 ✓.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Detecting unboundedness algebraically
docs.text:
A tableau has entering column \(x_2\) with entries \((-2, -3)\) and RHS \((5, 8)\). What happens?

Solution.

No entry in the pivot column is positive, so the minimum-ratio test has no candidates.

Why this means unbounded. The basic variables update as

\[ x_{B_1} = 5 - (-2)x_2 = 5 + 2x_2, \qquad x_{B_2} = 8 - (-3)x_2 = 8 + 3x_2 \]

Both increase as \(x_2\) grows, so feasibility is never violated:

\[ x_2 \to \infty \ \Longrightarrow\ x_{B_1}, x_{B_2} \to \infty, \ \text{ all still } \ge 0 . \]

And since \(z_2 - c_2 < 0\) (that is why \(x_2\) was chosen), \(Z\) increases without bound.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{UNBOUNDED: no positive entry in the pivot column.}\ } \]

The direction of unboundedness. The ray is

\[ \vec x(t) = \vec x^{(0)} + t\,\vec d, \qquad \vec d = (\ldots,\ \underbrace{1}_{x_2},\ldots,\ 2,\ 3,\ldots) \]

— i.e. increase \(x_2\) by 1 and the two basic variables by 2 and 3 respectively.

What to do in practice. Report the ray to the modeller. It shows exactly which activity can grow without limit, which almost always identifies the missing constraint. If the model says you can make infinite profit by producing more of product 2, you forgot product 2's capacity limit.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Degeneracy and its consequences
docs.text:
A minimum-ratio test gives ratios \(\{6, 4, 4\}\). Explain the consequence and the risk.

Solution.

A tie at \(\theta = 4\) between two rows. Either may be chosen to leave.

Consequence. Suppose row 2 leaves. Then row 3 had ratio \(4\) as well, so after pivoting:

\[ x_{B_3}^{\text{new}} = 4 - 4\times1 = \mathbf{0} \]

The new BFS has a basic variable equal to zero — it is degenerate.

Geometric meaning. Three or more constraints pass through the same corner (in 2-D, more lines meet at a point than the two needed). The same geometric corner corresponds to several different bases.

The risk — stalling and cycling. At a degenerate vertex the next minimum ratio may be \(\theta = 0\), so the pivot changes the basis but not the solution or the objective. If a sequence of such pivots returns to a previously visited basis, the algorithm cycles forever.

The classic example (Beale, 1955).

\[ \max\ \tfrac{3}{4}x_1 - 150x_2 + \tfrac{1}{50}x_3 - 6x_4 \] \[ \text{s.t. } \tfrac14x_1 - 60x_2 - \tfrac{1}{25}x_3 + 9x_4 \le 0, \quad \tfrac12x_1 - 90x_2 - \tfrac{1}{50}x_3 + 3x_4 \le 0, \quad x_3 \le 1 \]

With Dantzig's rule this cycles after 6 pivots, returning to the starting basis.

Two remedies.

Rule Statement Cost Bland's rule among eligible entering columns, take the smallest index; among tied leaving rows, take the variable with the smallest index provably terminates, but often many more pivots Lexicographic rule perturb \(b_i \to b_i + \epsilon^{i}\), making all ratios distinct provably terminates, more bookkeeping

Practical reality. Degeneracy is common (especially in transportation and assignment problems) but cycling is essentially never observed on real data — floating-point noise breaks the exact ties. Solvers monitor for stalling and switch to Bland's rule if the objective fails to improve for many iterations.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Why simplex beats enumeration
docs.text:
An LP has \(m = 30\) constraints and \(n = 80\) variables (after adding slacks). Compare complete enumeration of basic solutions with the expected simplex effort.

Solution.

Complete enumeration.

\[ \binom{80}{30} = \frac{80!}{30!\,50!} \approx 8.87\times10^{21} \]

Each candidate requires solving a \(30\times30\) system, roughly \(\frac{2}{3}(30)^3 \approx 18{,}000\) floating-point operations. Total:

\[ 8.87\times10^{21}\times1.8\times10^{4} = 1.6\times10^{26}\ \text{flops} \]

At \(10^{12}\) flops/second (a fast workstation):

\[ t = 1.6\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{5\ \text{million years}} \]

Simplex.

Empirically simplex needs about \(2m\) to \(3m\) pivots:

\[ \approx 2.5\times30 = \mathbf{75\ \text{iterations}} \]

Each pivot is a Gauss–Jordan elimination over the tableau: \(O(mn) = 30\times80 = 2400\) operations.

\[ \text{Total} = 75\times2400 = 1.8\times10^{5}\ \text{flops} \ \Longrightarrow\ t \approx \mathbf{0.18\ \mu s} \]

The comparison.

\[ \frac{5\times10^{6}\ \text{years}}{1.8\times10^{-7}\ \text{s}} \approx \mathbf{10^{21}\times\ \text{faster}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Simplex visits about 75 of } 8.9\times10^{21} \textbf{ corners — a fraction of } 10^{-20}.\ } \]

How can it possibly be right? Because of convexity. The optimality criterion \(z_j - c_j \ge 0\) is a local test — it examines only the corners adjacent to the current one. Convexity guarantees that a corner better than all its neighbours is better than every corner in the region. Simplex never needs to look further.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Convexity converts a global search into a local one. That is the whole trick.}\ } \]

(This is also why the same idea fails for integer programming (L16–L18) and non-convex non-linear programming (Unit IV): without convexity, local optimality does not imply global optimality, and the search really can require exponential effort.)

docs.title: 4.9 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. How many basic solutions for \(m=3\), \(n=7\)? [Ans: 35]
  2. Given \(c_B = (3,5)\) and column \(\vec a_j = (2,1)^T\) with \(c_j = 8\), compute \(z_j - c_j\). [Ans: \(11-8=3\)]
  3. Ratios are \(\{8, 3, 12\}\) — which row leaves, and what is \(\theta\)? [Ans: row 2, \(\theta=3\)]
  4. Pivot column \((-1, 0, -4)^T\): what do you conclude? [Ans: unbounded]
  5. State the optimality criterion for a minimisation problem in simplex form.
  6. Prove that increasing a non-basic variable changes \(Z\) at rate \(c_j - z_j\).
  7. Explain, in two sentences, why convexity lets a local test certify global optimality.

docs.title: 4.10 Summary
docs.text:
• Standard form has \(m\) equations and \(n > m\) variables. Choosing \(m\) basic variables and setting the rest to zero gives a basic solution; if it is non-negative it is a BFS.
  • BFS ⟺ extreme point — this theorem is what licenses an algebraic search for a geometric optimum.
  • There are up to \(\binom{n}{m}\) basic solutions — astronomically many, so enumeration is impossible.
  • \(z_j - c_j\) is the net rate at which \(Z\) worsens per unit of \(x_j\); the solution is optimal (for max) when all \(z_j - c_j \ge 0\). The entering variable is the most negative.
  • Minimum-ratio test \(\theta = \min_i \{b_i/a_{ij^*} : a_{ij^*}>0\}\) picks the leaving variable and preserves feasibility. No positive entry ⟹ unbounded; a tie ⟹ degeneracy.
  • Simplex terminates because each pivot strictly improves \(Z\) over a finite set of BFSs; degeneracy can cause stalling, cured by Bland's or the lexicographic rule.
  • Worst case is exponential (Klee–Minty) but practice is \(2m\)–\(3m\) pivots — around \(10^{21}\times\) faster than enumeration on a modest problem.
  • Convexity is why a local optimality test certifies a global optimum. Losing convexity (integer or non-convex problems) destroys this and is why those problems are hard.

Next lesson: L05 — The simplex tableau algorithm, worked in full.

Practise now: unit1-lp-lab.html → Basic Solutions Explorer: pick any two variables to be basic and see the resulting point plotted, with feasibility flagged.

docs.title: Lesson 5: The Simplex Method II: The Tableau Algorithm
5.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Set up the initial simplex tableau from an LP.
  2. Execute pivot operations accurately and efficiently.
  3. Read the optimal solution, slack values and shadow prices from the final tableau.
  4. Verify a solution independently.
  5. Recognise alternate optima from the final tableau.

docs.title: 5.2 Setting Up the Tableau
docs.text:
The recipe.

1. Convert to standard form (L02): all constraints '=', all b_i >= 0
2. Identify an initial basis -- the slack variables, if all constraints were <=
3. Build the table:  Basis | c_B | all variable columns | RHS
4. Compute the z_j - c_j row

Layout convention used throughout this course.

\(c_j \to\) \(c_1\) \(c_2\) \(\cdots\) \(c_n\) Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(\cdots\) \(x_n\) RHS \(x_{B_1}\) \(c_{B_1}\) \(a_{11}\) \(a_{12}\) \(a_{1n}\) \(b_1\) \(\vdots\) \(x_{B_m}\) \(c_{B_m}\) \(a_{m1}\) \(a_{m2}\) \(a_{mn}\) \(b_m\) \(z_j - c_j\) \(\Delta_1\) \(\Delta_2\) \(\Delta_n\) \(Z\)

docs.title: 5.3 The Pivot Operation, Step by Step
docs.text:
Given pivot element p = a[r][k]  (row r, column k):

1.  New pivot row  =  old pivot row / p
2.  For every other row i:
        new row i  =  old row i  -  a[i][k] x (new pivot row)
3.  Replace the basis label in row r by x_k, and c_B by c_k
4.  Recompute z_j - c_j

Three checks after every pivot — do these every time and errors become rare:

  1. The pivot column now reads \((0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T\) with the 1 in the pivot row.
  2. All RHS values are \(\ge 0\).
  3. \(Z\) has improved (or stayed the same, under degeneracy).

Work in fractions, not decimals. Simplex tableaus produce values like \(2/3\) and \(5/14\); decimal rounding accumulates and eventually corrupts the \(z_j-c_j\) signs, causing wrong termination.

docs.title: 5.4 Worked Example — Complete Trace
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \max\ & Z = 5x_1 + 4x_2\\ \text{s.t. } & 6x_1 + 4x_2 \le 24\\ & x_1 + 2x_2 \le 6\\ & x_1, x_2 \ge 0 \end{aligned} \]

(This is the problem solved graphically in L03; the optimum is \((3, 1.5)\) with \(Z = 21\).)

Standard form.

\[ 6x_1 + 4x_2 + s_1 = 24, \qquad x_1 + 2x_2 + s_2 = 6 \] \[ \max\ Z = 5x_1 + 4x_2 + 0s_1 + 0s_2 \]

docs.title: 5.5 Reading the Final Tableau
docs.text: The final tableau contains far more than the answer.

docs.title: The optimal solution
docs.text:
Basic variables take their RHS values; non-basic variables are zero:

\[ x_1 = 3, \quad x_2 = \tfrac32, \quad s_1 = 0, \quad s_2 = 0 \]

Both slacks are zero ⟹ both constraints are binding, so both resources are fully consumed.

docs.title: Shadow prices (dual values)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{Shadow price of constraint } i \ =\ (z_j - c_j) \text{ in the column of slack } s_i\ } \] \[ y_1 = \tfrac34 = 0.75, \qquad y_2 = \tfrac12 = 0.5 \]

Interpretation. One additional unit of resource 1 raises the optimum by ₹0.75; one additional unit of resource 2 raises it by ₹0.50.

Verification. Change \(b_1\) from 24 to 25 and re-solve: the new intersection of \(6x_1+4x_2 = 25\) and \(x_1+2x_2 = 6\) is \(x_1 = 13/4\), \(x_2 = 11/8\), giving

\[ Z = 5\left(\tfrac{13}{4}\right)+4\left(\tfrac{11}{8}\right) = \tfrac{65}{4}+\tfrac{11}{2} = 16.25 + 5.5 = 21.75 = 21 + 0.75 \ \checkmark \]

The shadow price is exact. This tells management the maximum they should pay for an extra unit of each resource — one of the most commercially valuable outputs of an LP.

docs.title: The dual solution
docs.text:
The shadow prices \((y_1, y_2) = (0.75, 0.5)\) are the optimal solution of the dual problem (L07). Note

\[ 24y_1 + 6y_2 = 24(0.75) + 6(0.5) = 18 + 3 = 21 = Z^{*} \ \checkmark \]

— strong duality, verified numerically.

docs.title: Detecting alternate optima
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A \emph{non-basic} variable with } z_j - c_j = 0 \textbf{ at optimality } \Longrightarrow \textbf{ alternate optima.}\ } \]

Here \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) have \(z_j-c_j = \frac34, \frac12 > 0\) — both strictly positive — so this optimum is unique, agreeing with L03's slope analysis.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Full simplex on the furniture problem
docs.text:
Solve \(\max\ Z = 450x_1+300x_2\) s.t. \(5x_1+3x_2\le120\), \(2x_1+4x_2\le90\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) by simplex, and extract the shadow prices.

Solution.

Standard form. \(5x_1+3x_2+s_1 = 120\), \(2x_1+4x_2+s_2 = 90\).

Iteration 0.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) (450) \(x_2\) (300) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS Ratio \(s_1\) 0 5 3 1 0 120 \(24\) ← \(s_2\) 0 2 4 0 1 90 \(45\) \(z_j-c_j\) −450 −300 0 0 0

Entering \(x_1\); ratios \(120/5 = 24\) and \(90/2 = 45\); leaving \(s_1\); pivot 5.

Iteration 1. Row 1 ÷ 5; row 2 ← row 2 − 2(new row 1).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS Ratio \(x_1\) 450 1 \(3/5\) \(1/5\) 0 24 \(40\) \(s_2\) 0 0 \(14/5\) \(-2/5\) 1 42 \(15\) ← \(z_j-c_j\) 0 −30 90 0 10 800

Check: \(z_2 = 450(\frac35) = 270\), so \(z_2-c_2 = 270-300 = -30\) ✓.

This is the corner \((24, 0)\) with \(Z = 10{,}800\) ✓ (matching L03's table).

Entering \(x_2\); ratios \(24 \div \frac35 = 40\) and \(42\div\frac{14}{5} = 15\); leaving \(s_2\); pivot \(14/5\).

Iteration 2. Row 2 ÷ \(\frac{14}{5}\) gives \((0,\ 1,\ -\frac17,\ \frac{5}{14},\ 15)\). Row 1 ← row 1 − \(\frac35\)(new row 2): \(s_1\): \(\frac15 - \frac35(-\frac17) = \frac15+\frac{3}{35} = \frac{10}{35} = \frac27\); \(s_2\): \(0 - \frac35\cdot\frac{5}{14} = -\frac{3}{14}\); RHS: \(24 - \frac35(15) = 15\).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_1\) 450 1 0 \(2/7\) \(-3/14\) 15 \(x_2\) 300 0 1 \(-1/7\) \(5/14\) 15 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 \(600/7\) \(75/7\) 11 250

All \(z_j-c_j \ge 0\) ⟹ OPTIMAL.

\[ \boxed{\ x_1^{*} = 15 \text{ tables},\ x_2^{*} = 15 \text{ chairs},\ Z^{*} = ₹11{,}250\ } \]

Shadow prices.

\[ y_1 = \frac{600}{7} = ₹85.71 \ \text{per carpentry hour}, \qquad y_2 = \frac{75}{7} = ₹10.71 \ \text{per finishing hour} \]

Management interpretation. Carpentry hours are worth 8× more than finishing hours at the margin. If overtime carpentry can be bought for less than ₹85.71/hour, buy it; if finishing overtime costs more than ₹10.71/hour, do not.

Duality check. \(120(600/7) + 90(75/7) = \frac{72000+6750}{7} = \frac{78750}{7} = 11{,}250 = Z^{*}\) ✓.

Iteration count. 2 pivots for a 2-constraint problem — consistent with the \(2m\)–\(3m\) rule of L04.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Recognising alternate optima in the tableau
docs.text:
A final tableau shows \(z_j - c_j = (0, 0, 0, 5/2, 0)\) where columns 1 and 2 are basic and columns 3, 4, 5 are non-basic. What do you conclude, and how do you find the second optimum?

Solution.

Diagnosis. Columns 3 and 5 are non-basic yet have \(z_j - c_j = 0\).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{ALTERNATE OPTIMA exist.}\ } \]

Why. Bringing \(x_3\) (or \(x_5\)) into the basis changes \(Z\) by \(-(z_j-c_j)\cdot\theta = 0\) — the objective is unchanged. So a different corner achieves the same optimal value.

Finding the second optimum. Perform one more pivot with \(x_3\) entering:

  1. Apply the minimum-ratio test to column 3 to find the leaving variable.
  2. Pivot as usual.
  3. The new tableau has the same \(Z\) but a different basic solution — the second optimal corner.

Describing all optima. With optimal corners \(\vec x^{(1)}\) and \(\vec x^{(2)}\), every point

\[ \vec x(\lambda) = \lambda\vec x^{(1)} + (1-\lambda)\vec x^{(2)}, \qquad \lambda\in[0,1] \]

is optimal, by the linearity argument of L03, Problem 3.

A caution. If the minimum-ratio test on column 3 gives no positive entries, then \(x_3\) can increase without limit at constant \(Z\) — the optimal set is an unbounded ray, not a bounded edge. The objective is still bounded; only the optimal set is infinite in extent.

Why report alternate optima. They give the decision-maker freedom to satisfy criteria the model omitted — supplier relationships, workforce stability, ease of implementation — at zero cost. A report that hides them gives away that freedom.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Degeneracy in action
docs.text:
Solve \(\max\ Z = 3x_1+9x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+4x_2\le8\), \(x_1+2x_2\le4\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), noting the degeneracy.

Solution.

Iteration 0.

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) (3) \(x_2\) (9) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS Ratio \(s_1\) 0 1 4 1 0 8 \(8/4 = 2\) ← \(s_2\) 0 1 2 0 1 4 \(4/2 = 2\) ← \(z_j-c_j\) −3 −9 0 0 0

A TIE in the minimum ratio (\(2 = 2\)) ⟹ degeneracy will occur.

Take row 1 (arbitrary choice); \(s_1\) leaves, pivot 4.

Iteration 1. Row 1 ÷ 4: \((\frac14,\ 1,\ \frac14,\ 0\ |\ 2)\). Row 2 ← row 2 − 2(new row 1): \((\frac12,\ 0,\ -\frac12,\ 1\ |\ 0)\).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_2\) 9 \(1/4\) 1 \(1/4\) 0 2 \(s_2\) 0 \(1/2\) 0 \(-1/2\) 1 0 ← degenerate \(z_j-c_j\) \(-3/4\) 0 \(9/4\) 0 18

\(s_2 = 0\) while basic ⟹ DEGENERATE BFS.

Not optimal (\(z_1-c_1 = -\frac34\)). Entering \(x_1\); ratios: row 1 \(2\div\frac14 = 8\); row 2 \(0\div\frac12 = \mathbf{0}\) ← minimum. Leaving \(s_2\), pivot \(\frac12\).

Iteration 2. Row 2 ÷ \(\frac12\): \((1,\ 0,\ -1,\ 2\ |\ 0)\). Row 1 ← row 1 − \(\frac14\)(new row 2): \((0,\ 1,\ \frac12,\ -\frac12\ |\ 2)\).

Basis \(c_B\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(s_1\) \(s_2\) RHS \(x_2\) 9 0 1 \(1/2\) \(-1/2\) 2 \(x_1\) 3 1 0 \(-1\) 2 0 \(z_j-c_j\) 0 0 \(3/2\) \(3/2\) 18

OPTIMAL. \(Z = 18\) — unchanged from iteration 1.

\[ \boxed{\ x_1^{*} = 0,\quad x_2^{*} = 2,\quad Z^{*} = 18\ } \]

What happened — a degenerate pivot. The ratio was \(\theta = 0\), so the entering variable came in at value zero. The basis changed, but the point did not move and \(Z\) did not improve. This is a stalling step.

Geometrically. Three lines pass through \((0,2)\): \(x_1+4x_2 = 8\), \(x_1+2x_2 = 4\) and \(x_1 = 0\). With three constraints meeting at a corner in 2-D, the corner is over-determined and corresponds to multiple bases — exactly what degeneracy means.

Why cycling is the theoretical risk. If a chain of such zero-improvement pivots returned to a previously seen basis, the algorithm would loop forever. Here it terminated after one degenerate pivot; Bland's rule (L04) guarantees this in general.

Practical note. Degeneracy is very common — every transportation problem with a degenerate basic solution (L09) exhibits it — but harmless. Recognise it, do not fear it.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Using shadow prices for a business decision
docs.text:
From the furniture problem's optimal tableau, \(y_1 = ₹85.71\) per carpentry hour and \(y_2 = ₹10.71\) per finishing hour. A supplier offers 10 extra carpentry hours for ₹700 total. Should the firm accept? What about 20 extra finishing hours for ₹150?

Solution.

Offer 1 — carpentry.

\[ \text{Value gained} = 10 \times ₹85.71 = ₹857.14 \] \[ \text{Cost} = ₹700 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \textbf{Net gain} = ₹157.14 \] \[ \boxed{\textbf{ACCEPT}} \]

But check the validity range. Shadow prices hold only while the basis stays optimal. From the final tableau, the \(s_1\) column is \((\frac27,\ -\frac17)^T\). Increasing \(b_1\) by \(\Delta\) changes the basic variables to

\[ x_1 = 15 + \tfrac27\Delta, \qquad x_2 = 15 - \tfrac17\Delta \]

Feasibility requires \(x_2 \ge 0\):

\[ 15 - \tfrac{\Delta}{7} \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \le 105 \]

\(\Delta = 10\) is well within range ✓, so the ₹85.71 rate applies fully.

Confirming: new plan \(x_1 = 15+\frac{20}{7} = 17.857\), \(x_2 = 15-\frac{10}{7} = 13.571\), giving

\[ Z = 450(17.857)+300(13.571) = 8035.7 + 4071.4 = ₹12{,}107.1 = 11{,}250 + 857.14 \ \checkmark \]

Offer 2 — finishing.

\[ \text{Value gained} = 20\times₹10.71 = ₹214.29 \] \[ \text{Cost} = ₹150 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \textbf{Net gain} = ₹64.29 \] \[ \boxed{\textbf{ACCEPT}} \]

Range check. The \(s_2\) column is \((-\frac{3}{14},\ \frac{5}{14})^T\). Increasing \(b_2\) by \(\Delta\):

\[ x_1 = 15 - \tfrac{3}{14}\Delta \ge 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \Delta \le 70 \]

\(\Delta = 20\) is within range ✓.

A crucial caveat if both offers are accepted together. Shadow prices are marginal rates valid for one-at-a-time changes. Simultaneous changes require the 100 % rule:

\[ \frac{10}{105} + \frac{20}{70} = 0.095 + 0.286 = 0.381 \ \le\ 1 \]

Since the fractions sum to less than 1, the basis remains optimal and both shadow prices remain valid, so the combined gain of ₹157.14 + ₹64.29 = ₹221.43 is correct.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Accept both. Combined net gain ₹221.43 — verified by the 100 \% rule.}\ } \]

This is the kind of concrete, defensible recommendation that makes LP valuable to management, and it comes entirely from the final tableau at no extra computational cost.

docs.title: 5.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Solve by simplex: \(\max\ 4x_1+3x_2\) s.t. \(2x_1+x_2\le10\), \(x_1+3x_2\le15\). [Ans: \(x_1=3,x_2=4\), \(Z=24\)]
  2. From the L05 example's final tableau, what is the shadow price of constraint 2? [Ans: 1/2]
  3. Perform one pivot on: pivot element 3 in row 2, column 1, with row 2 \(= (3, 6, 1, 0 \mid 9)\).
  4. A final tableau has \(z_j-c_j = (0,0,4,0)\) with column 4 non-basic. Interpret.
  5. Verify the duality check \(\vec b^{T}\vec y = Z^{*}\) for Problem 1 of §5.
  6. Solve \(\max\ 2x_1+3x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+x_2\le4\), \(x_1+3x_2\le6\) and identify any degeneracy.
  7. If a shadow price is 0, what does that tell you about the constraint?

docs.title: 5.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Build the tableau from standard form with the slacks as the initial basis; work in fractions.
  • Pivot: divide the pivot row by the pivot element, then eliminate the pivot column from every other row. Check the unit column, non-negative RHS and improved \(Z\) each time.
  • Read from the final tableau: optimal values (basic RHS), slacks (zero ⟹ binding), and shadow prices in the slack columns' \(z_j-c_j\) entries.
  • Shadow price = the marginal value of one extra unit of a resource; it is exactly the dual variable, and \(\vec b^T\vec y = Z^{*}\) (strong duality).
  • A non-basic variable with \(z_j-c_j = 0\) at optimality signals alternate optima — always report them.
  • Degeneracy (a basic variable equal to zero, arising from a tie in the ratio test) causes a \(\theta = 0\) pivot that changes the basis but not the solution. Common and harmless in practice.
  • Shadow prices are valid only within a range; simultaneous changes are checked by the 100 % rule (the fractions of the allowable ranges must sum to at most 1).

Next lesson: L06 — Big-M and two-phase methods, and the special cases.

Practise now: unit1-lp-lab.html → Simplex Stepper: enter any LP and step through the tableaus one pivot at a time, with the entering/leaving choices and ratios highlighted.

docs.title: Lesson 8: The Transportation Problem: Formulation and Initial Solutions
8.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Formulate a transportation problem and recognise its special structure.
  2. Balance an unbalanced problem using dummy rows or columns.
  3. Construct an initial BFS by the North-West Corner Method (NWCM).
  4. Construct an initial BFS by the Least Cost Method (LCM).
  5. Construct an initial BFS by Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM) and explain why it is superior.

docs.title: 8.2 The Transportation Problem
docs.text:
